凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Ode to the Land of Jin — A Reflection on the Beigu Terrace
By Xin Qiji

A thousand ages, this landscape remains—
yet heroes are gone; nowhere can one find
Sun Zhongmou. The terraces where music played,
where beauty reigned, all swept by wind and rain
into oblivion.

Slanting sun on grass and trees,
an ordinary lane—
so people say the warlord Liu Yu lived here once.
Imagine that time: bronze spears, armored steeds,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand miles, fierce as a tiger.

In the Yuanjia reign, a rash campaign—
to "seal the Wolf Mountain" like Huo Qubing of old—
won only a panicked retreat, glancing back in fear.

Forty-three years have passed;
gazing north, I still recall
the beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back?
At the shrine of the barbarian chief Foli,
crows peck at offerings, drums beat for the village god.

Who will ask—
like Lian Po, the old general—
"Though aged, can he still eat his fill of rice?"

[Translator's Note: This ci-poem was written in 1205 by Xin Qiji, a Song Dynasty patriot-general born in occupied northern China. Standing at the ancient fortress of Jingkou (modern Zhenjiang), he meditates on past heroes—Sun Quan of the Three Kingdoms, the warlord Liu Yu who reclaimed the north, and the disastrous Yuanjia campaign of 450 CE—drawing parallels to the Southern Song's own failure to recover the north from Jurchen invaders. The final allusion to Lian Po, an aged general who longed to serve his country, expresses the poet's own frustrated desire to lead the reconquest. "Foli" is the Chinese rendering of the Xianbei chieftain Tuoba Gui (Emperor Daowu of Northern Wei), whose captured shrine ironically stands on formerly Song territory.]"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。

元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

No hero to be found — where Sun Zhongmou dwelt.
Dance terraces and singing platforms,
Their elegance all washed away by wind and rain.
Slanting sun on grass and trees, an ordinary lane,
People say: here once lived the man called Jinu.
I think of those years — golden spears and iron-hoofed horses,
A spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia's hasty campaign, to seal the wolf at Junji,
Won only a hurried turning back in flight.
Forty-three years — gazing north, I still remember
The beacon fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can I bear to look back? Beneath the Fox Spirit Shrine,
A clump of temple crows and festival drums.
Who will ask: Is Lian Po too old?
Can he still eat his rice?"}

舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Through the ages, these rivers and mountains—
No hero to be found,
Not where Sun Zhongmou once stood.
Terraces for dance, platforms for song—
Their fame and grace,
Always wind- and rain-battered away.

Slanting sun, grass and trees,
Ordinary lanes and alleys—
Folk say Jinu once lived here.
Think of that year:
Golden spears, iron-hooved steeds,
A tiger’s breath swallowing ten thousand li.

Yuanjia’s rash campaign—
To be crowned at Langjuxu—
Only to glance north in panic.

Four-and-thirty years,
In this gaze I still remember:
Beacon fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can I bear to look back?
Under Bili’s shrine,
Crows of the shrine, drums of the village rite.

And who now asks—
Lian Po is old—
Can he still eat his fill?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

No hero can be found—where once was Sun Zhongmou.
Dance pavilions and singing terraces,
All their elegance is beaten down by wind and rain.
Slanting sun, grass and trees, an ordinary lane—
People say that Liu Yu once lived right here.
Think of those years: bronze spears, iron-clad horses,
A spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.
In Yuanjia they rushed to war,
Sought to seal Mount Langjuxu,
And won only a panicked glance back north.
Forty-three years,
Looking out, I still remember
The beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou.
How can I bear to look back?
Beneath the Foli Shrine,
A flock of crows and drums at the village festival.
Who will ask:
Is old Lian Po aged—
Can he still eat his fill?"}

Terraces where dancers swayed, stages where singers rang—
Their splendor all swept away by wind and rain.

The people say: here once lived Liu Yu, known as Ji Nu.
Recall those years of iron spears and armored steeds—
With might like a tiger devouring ten thousand miles.
Yuan Jia rushed to war, his aim to seal the Wolf mountain,
Yet won but panic, glancing north in flight.

I still recall the smoke and flames along the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back now?
Beneath the shrine of Foli, the spirit crows
Peck at offerings while drums of village rites resound.
Who will ask me, aging Lian Po—
Still capable of eating, I ask: can I still fight?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Through the ages, these rivers and mountains — no hero can be found
where Sun Zhongmou once stood.
Dance pavilions and song terraces:
all that elegance is swept away at last
by wind and rain.
Slanting sun on grass and trees,
in an ordinary lane —
people say that Ju Nu once lived here.
Think of those years:
bronze spears, iron steeds,
a spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia rushed matters,
wanted to seal the wolf on Mount Ju,
and came off with nothing but a panicked look back north.
Forty-three years on,
gazing out, I still remember
the beacon fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back —
under the shrine of the Fo-li,
a flock of temple crows and drums of the village feast.
Who will ask whether
Lian Po, old as he is,
can still eat his fill of rice?"}

Recalling those days: golden spears and iron horses, bold as a tiger devouring ten thousand miles.
Emperor Wen of Song, hasty and ill-prepared, sought to seal the wolf at Juxu, only to flee in panic northward.
Forty-three years have passed; from afar, I still recall the battlefield flames along the Yangzhou road.
How painful to look back—on the temple of Emperor Beili, crows fly, and drums sound for the village festival.
Who now dares ask: Old General Lianpo, is he still able to eat?"}

Dancing terraces, singing halls,
Their glamour swept away by wind and rain.
Slanting sun on grass and trees;

Think of that year —
Golden spears, iron steeds, a tiger's breath, ten thousand miles to swallow.
Yuanjia feigned might,
To seal Wolf Terrace, yet fled in panic northward.
Forty-three years,
In my gaze I still recall,
The beacon fires on the Yangzhou road.
How can I bear to look back —
Beneath the Fuli shrine,
Crows cry, drums of the festival sound.
Who will ask:
Lian Po is old,
Can he still eat?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。

元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

Sunset over grass and trees, in ordinary alleys, people say Li Tu once lived there.
Recall those days: golden spears and iron horses, a spirit devouring thousands of miles like a tiger.
Yuanjia’s hasty campaign, the dream of sealing Mount Xiongnu, ended in frantic retreat northward.
Forty-three years have passed, yet in sight I still remember the flames along the road to Yangzhou.
Hard to bear to look back—below the temple of Fu Li, crows flock and drums of sacrifice echo.
Who dares ask: Old General Lianpo, can he still eat?"}

But where can we find heroic spirits like Sun Zhongmou?
The pavilions and stages once filled with music and grace
Have all been swept away by wind and rain.
Sunset lights up the grass and trees,
In common alleys and lanes—
They say Liu Yu once lived here.
Recalling those days,
With golden weapons and iron horses,
His spirit swallowed a thousand miles like a tiger.
Yuanjia's campaign was hastily launched,
Seeking glory at Langjuxu,
Only to end in panic as he fled northward.
Forty-three years have passed;
Still vivid in my mind—
The fires of war along the road to Yangzhou.
How unbearable it is to look back:
At the temple of Foli, crows feast,
And drums beat for the gods.
Who would dare ask: Is General Lianpo old?
Can he still eat a full meal?"}

By Xin Qiji

Eternal rivers and mountains—
no trace of heroes remains,
not even of Sun Zhongmou.

Dance halls and singing terraces,
their elegance all swept away
by wind and rain.

Beneath the slanting sun, among grass and trees,
in ordinary lanes and byways,
they say the hut of Jinu once stood.

Think of those years—
spears of gold and armored horses,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.

Yuanjia's rash campaign,
seeking to seal the Wolf Altar,
won only a hasty retreat, glancing north in terror.

Forty-three years have passed—
in the distance I still recall
the beacon fires over Yangzhou's roads.

How can I bear to look back?
Beneath the Foli Shrine,
only crows and drums of the spring festival.

Who will ask:
Lian Po is old—
can he still eat his fill?"}

想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。

四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Timeless rivers and mountains, no trace of heroes, not where Sun Zhongmou once stood.
Dance pavilions and song stages, all that elegance now battered by wind and rain.
Sunset over grass and trees, in ordinary alleys, people say Liu Yu once lived here.
I think back to those days: golden spears and iron horses, roaring like a tiger devouring ten thousand miles.
Yuanjia's hasty campaign, seeking to seal victory at Longju, only brought frantic retreats northward.
Forty-three years on, still vividly remembered in sight—the flames along the road to Yangzhou.
Hard to bear to look back: at the temple of Fu Li, crows flocking, drums for the community gods.
Who dares ask—Lian Po, old as he is, can he still eat?"}

All elegance swept away at last by wind and rain's beating.

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Timeless rivers and mountains, heroes nowhere to be found—where once lay Sun Zhongmou.
Palaces of dance and halls of song, all grandeur now swept away by rain and wind.
Sunset among grass and trees, ordinary lanes and alleys—people say Li Tu once lived here.
Recall those days: golden spears and iron horses, roaring like a tiger devouring ten thousand miles.
Yuanjia’s hasty campaign, sealing the Wolf's Ridge, yet only frantic retreat northward ensued.
Forty-three years have passed; even in sight, I still remember the flames along the road to Yangzhou.
How unbearable it is to look back—Bolici Temple where crows clamor and drums of sacrifice echo.
Who dares ask: Old General Lianpo, can he still eat?"}

Ages of rivers and mountains—no hero to be found,
nowhere Sun Zhongmou stands.
The terraces of dance and song, their elegance all gone,
beaten by wind and rain away.

Slanting sun on grass and trees, the common lanes and streets,
where men say once the host of Jiwu dwelled.
Think of that year: golden lances, iron-clad steeds,
whose breath swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.

Yuan Jia’s careless haste, to ‘seal Mount Langju’—
only to win a panicked look back north.
Forty-three years since then, in my gaze I still remember,
the beacon-fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back? At the Shrine of the Fox Spirit,
crows squawk over drums for the village rites.
By whom will I be asked: ‘Is old Lian Po still fit enough
to eat his rice?’"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "To the Tune of Yong Yu Le: Recalling the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou

A thousand ages this river and hills have known,
But heroes like Sun Zhongmou are no longer to be found.
The dance-halls and singing-platforms, all their elegance,
Have been swept away by wind and rain.
Beneath the slanting sun, among grass and trees,
In those ordinary lanes and alleys,
People say the house of Jinu once stood.
I think of that year—
With spear of bronze and steed of iron,
His spirit swallowing ten thousand miles, fierce as a tiger.

Yet Yuanjao was rash,
Hoping to seal the wolf at Mount Ju,
Only to win a hurried flight, glancing back in dismay.
Forty-three years have passed—
Gazing north, I still remember
The beacon-fires over Yangzhou's roads.
How can I bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Foli,
Only crows and drums of the spring festival.

Who will ask:
Is old Lian Po still able,
Though aged, to eat his fill of rice?"}

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Yong Yu Le: Recalling the Past at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

Eternal rivers and mountains—
no trace of heroes to be found,
no sight of Sun Zhongmou.
Dance-halls and singing terraces,
all their elegance swept away
by wind and rain.
Slanting sun on grass and trees,
by an ordinary lane,
they say once dwelt Ji Nu.
Think of those years—
spears of bronze, steeds clad in iron,
spirits swallowing ten thousand li like tigers.
Yuan Jia's rash campaign,
seeking to seal the wolf on Mount Ju,
won only a panicked glance to the north.
Forty-three years gone,
gazing from here I still remember
the beacon fires on Yangzhou Road.
How can I bear to look back—
below the Fili Shrine,
a flock of crows and drums of the spring festival.
By whom will it be asked:
Lian Po is old—
can he still eat his fill?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Yong Yu Le — Thinking of the Past at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

A thousand ages, these rivers and mountains — no hero can be found
like Sun Zhongmou now.
Terraces of song and dance, all that elegance,
swept away by wind and rain.
Slanting sun on grass and trees, an ordinary lane —
people say that Liu Yu once lived here.
Think of those years: golden spears, iron cavalry,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li, like a tiger.

Yuanjade's careless campaign,
wolf-topped Xushu he sought to seal,
gained only a panicked glance to the north.
Forty-three years — in the distance I still remember
the beacon fires of Yangzhou Road.
How can one bear to look back?
Below the Fili Shrine,
a flock of crows and the drums of a village festival.
Who will ask —
like Lian Po, grown old,
can he still eat his rice?"}

The river and mountains endure through eternity,
But no hero can be found—where once was Sun Zhongmou.
Dancing terraces and singing platforms—
Their elegance is swept away at last,
Pelted by rain and blown by wind.
On slanting sun through grass and trees,
In common lanes and streets,
They say the dwelling of Jinu once stood.
Think of those years: golden spears and iron-hooved steeds,
A spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia’s rash campaign—
To confer the wolf on Mount Ju,
Won only a hurried glance back north in flight.
Forty-three years have passed,
Gazing out, I still remember
The beacon fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Foli,
A flock of crows and drums of the spring festival.
By whom shall it be asked—
Is Lian Po old indeed?
Can he still eat his fill of rice?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Yong Yu Le: Reflections at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

Eternal rivers and mountains — of heroes, none can be found,
Like Sun Zhongmou of old.
On terraces of dance and song,
The elegance of bygone years is beaten down by wind and rain,
Vanished forever.

Slanting sun on grass and trees,
In an ordinary lane,
They say the warlord Jilu once dwelt.
In those days —
With golden spears and iron cavalry,
His spirit devoured ten thousand li, fierce as a tiger.

Yuanjia acted rashly,
Seeking to seal the mountain like Huo Qubing at Langjuxu,
Only to win a panicked flight, glancing back in dread.

Forty-three years have passed —
Gazing north, I still remember
The beacon fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back?
Below the Fili Shrine,
A flock of crows and the drums of the spring festival.

Who will ask —
Like Lian Po, grown old,
Can he still eat his fill of rice?"}

舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Yong Yu Le: Reflections at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou

An age of rivers and mountains, yet no hero to be found —
Where once was Sun Zhongmou's glory.
The terraces of dance, the stages of song,
All their elegance swept away by wind and driving rain.
Beneath the slanting sun, among grass and trees,
In some ordinary lane, they say, once lived the man called Jinu.
Think of those days: golden spears and iron-hooved steeds,
A spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.

Yuan Jia, hasty and rash, sought to seal the wolf at Mount Ju,
Only to win a panicked glance back to the north.
Forty-three years have passed —
Gazing north, I still remember the beacon fires over Yangzhou Road.
How can I bear to look back?
At the foot of Foli Shrine, crows and festival drums fill the air.
Who will ask me now:
Like Lian Po, grown old —
Can he still eat his fill of rice?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Yong Yu Le: Reflections at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

By Xin Qiji

Ages of rivers and mountains — no place to find a hero like Sun Zhongmou.
Dancing terraces, singing platforms — their glory all washed away by wind and rain.
Slanting sun on grass and trees, in common lanes and streets, they say the house of Jinu once stood.
Think of those years: golden spears, iron steeds, a spirit swallowing ten thousand miles like a tiger.
Yuanjia's haste — to seal the wolf of Langjuxu — only earned a panicked glance to the north.
Forty-three years, gazing, I still remember the beacon fires on the road to Yangzhou.
How can I bear to look back — beneath Foli Shrine, a flock of crows and drums for the spring sacrifice.
Who will ask: is old Lian Po still able to eat his fill?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Yong Yu Le · Reflections at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

A thousand ages, these rivers and mountains —
no trace of heroes remains,
not even where Sun Zhongmou dwelt.
The terraces for dancing, the stages for song,
elegance and glory, all of it
beaten away by wind and driven off by rain.
Beneath the slanting sun, amid grass and trees,
on some ordinary lane and crossroad,
they say once lived the man called Ji Nu.
Think of those years —
with golden spears and iron-clad horses,
whose fury swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yet in Yuanjia, careless and hasty,
they sought to seal the wolf at Mount Ju,
only to win a frantic flight, glancing back northward.
Forty-three years have passed —
still from here I gaze and remember:
the beacon fires blazing along the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Foli,
nothing but crows circling the altar drums.
Who will ask, then —
"Can Lian Po, though old,
yet still eat his fill of rice?"}"}

舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。

元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

No trace of Sun Zhongmou can be found.
On dance terraces and song stages, grandeur is swept away
By rain and wind, as time has long since claimed them.
In the slanting sun, grass and trees stand by ordinary lanes,
Where people say Liu Yu once lived in humble days.
How vividly I recall, those years of golden armor and iron horses,
Burning through ten thousand miles like a tiger's fierce might.
Yuanjia’s campaign was hasty and ill-conceived;
He sought to seal the wolf’s den on Mount Juxu,
Yet fled in panic, glancing back northward in fear.
Forty-three years have passed, yet still I see in memory
The flames of war along the route to Yangzhou.
How painful it is to look back now
At the temple of Fuli, where crows scream and drums roll in divine frenzy.
Who dares ask: Old General Lianpo, am I still strong enough
To eat a full meal?"}

返景入深林，复照青苔上。"}, "translation": "Deer Enclosure

No one is seen on the empty mountain,

Returning sunlight enters the deep woods,

---
Notes on ambiguity:
1. "空山" (kōng shān) - translated as "empty mountain." It can imply both physical emptiness (deserted) and a sense of Buddhist "emptiness" or tranquility.
2. "但闻" (dàn wén) - translated as "Only...is heard." "但" here means "only/merely," emphasizing the contrast between unseen people and the sound of their voices.
3. "返景" (fǎn yǐng) - translated as "Returning sunlight." "景" (yǐng) is an archaic form of "影" (yǐng), here referring to sunlight (the reflected light of the sun). "返景" specifically denotes the slanting light of the setting sun that reflects back into the scene."}

- "疑" (yí): Means "to suspect" or "to wonder if", carrying a nuance of momentary uncertainty or dreamlike confusion, rendered here as "I take it for".
- "思故乡" (sī gùxiāng): "Think of / long for one's native place/home"."}

返景入深林，复照青苔上。"}, "translation": "Deer Enclosure

On the empty mountain, no one is seen,
Yet voices are heard echoing.
The returning light enters the deep woods
And shines again upon the green moss.

**Translation Notes:**

*   **空山不见人** -> "On the empty mountain, no one is seen": "空山" (empty mountain) is a key Chan Buddhist image of tranquility, rendered as "empty" to preserve its philosophical weight. "不见人" is a direct statement of visual absence.
*   **但闻人语响** -> "Yet voices are heard echoing": "但闻" (only hear) is translated as "Yet voices are heard" to highlight the contrast (sound vs. sight). "响" (resonate/echo) is explicitly rendered as "echoing" to emphasize the quality of the sound in the stillness.
*   **返景入深林** -> "The returning light enters the deep woods": "返景" (also written 返照) means the slanting rays of the setting sun. "Returning light" is a poetic and accurate translation. "入深林" is a simple, direct action.

劝君更尽一杯酒，西出阳关无故人。"}, "translation": "A Morning Rain in Wei Town

Morning rain in Wei Town dampens the light dust;
The inn is green, the willows fresh and new.
I urge you, friend, to drain another cup of wine—
West of Yang Pass, you'll find no old acquaintance there.

(Notes on ambiguity)
- "渭城" (Wei Town): the ancient city of Xianyang, a common departure point on the road west.
- "浥" (yi): to moisten, to dampen; here the rain settles the dust of the road.
- "更尽" (geng jin): to finish yet another; implies "one more for the road."
- "阳关" (Yang Pass): the frontier gate on the way to the Western Regions (Anxi).
- "故人" (gu ren): old friends, old acquaintances—those left behind."}

**Translator's Note on Ambiguity:**
The title contains a place name, **Guangling (广陵)**, which is an old name for **Yangzhou (扬州)**. The poem uses both names in succession. This is not an error, but a poetic technique: the title specifies the historical destination, while the body uses the more resonant, contemporary name for the city of pleasure and beauty. {"source": {"title": "黄鹤楼送孟浩然之广陵", "author": "李白", "text": "故人西辞黄鹤楼，烟花三月下扬州。

My old friend bids farewell to the west at Yellow Crane Tower,
And in the misty blossoms of March goes down to Yangzhou.
His lone sail, a distant shadow, vanishes into the blue,
Leaving only the Long River flowing to the edge of the sky.

---

**Notes:**
- "故人" (gùrén) → "old friend" — a standard poetic term for a close friend.
- "烟花三月" (yānhuā sānyuè) → "misty blossoms of March" — 烟花 evokes the hazy, blooming beauty of late spring.

{"source": {"title": "春望", "author": "杜甫", "text": "国破山河在，城春草木深。
感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。

白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。"}, "translation": "Spring Gazing

The state lies shattered, yet mountains and rivers remain;
In spring the city is thick with grass and trees.
Moved by the times, flowers shed tears;
Hating parting, birds startle the heart.
War's flames have burned for three long months—
A single letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.
White hairs grow thinner as I scratch my head,
So thin now they won't hold a hairpin."}

The state lies shattered, yet mountains and rivers remain,
In spring the city's deep with grass and trees.
Moved by the times, flowers weep in grief;
Hating parting, birds startle the heart with cries.

A letter from home is worth ten thousand pieces of gold.
My white hair grows thinner as I scratch my head,
So thin now it can hardly hold a hairpin."}

The nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain.
In the city, spring, the grass and trees grow thick.
Moved by the times, flowers draw my tears;
Hating separation, birds startle my heart.

A letter from home would be worth its weight in gold.
I scratch my white hair, ever thinner and more sparse—
Soon it will be too scant to hold a hairpin."}

The nation is broken; the hills and rivers remain.
In spring the city grass and trees grow thick.
Moved by the times, flowers draw tears;

A letter from home would be worth ten thousand in gold.
I scratch my white hair, it grows ever thinner—

- 城春草木深 → "In spring the city grass and trees grow thick."："deep"易歧，故用"grow thick"；依据："深"状草木之茂。
- 感时花溅泪 → "Moved by the times, flowers draw tears."：保留移情两解（花溅泪/人见花落泪）；不确定：主语歧义未定。
- 恨别鸟惊心 → "Hating parting, birds startle the heart."：与上句对仗；"恨别"指离乱之别，译作"parting"，未坐实对象。

   - (b) Flowers, moved by the times, splatter tears (the flowers themselves seem to weep). This gives the flowers a personified quality.
   - The translation follows reading (a), but reading (b) is a valid poetic interpretation.

2. "恨别鸟惊心" (hèn bié niǎo jīng xīn) can be read as:
   - (a) [The poet,] grieving at parting, [is startled by] birds [that] startle the heart (the sound of birds disturbs his mind, reminding him of separation).
   - (b) Birds, grieving at parting, startle the heart (the birds themselves seem distressed, mirroring his own feelings).
   - The translation follows reading (a), which pairs naturally with the previous line's structure.

3. "城春草木深" (chéng chūn cǎo mù shēn): The line describes the city in spring, where grass and trees grow thick. This may imply neglect and desolation (overgrown vegetation due to war) or simply the fullness of spring. The English keeps the ambiguity by stating the fact without explicit judgment."}

5. "Birds startle the heart" (鸟惊心): Similar ambiguity: "birds [make my] heart startle" or "birds themselves are startled in their hearts." The translation uses the former.

- 感时花溅泪 / 恨别鸟惊心 → parallel lines; "Moved by the times" / "Grieving at parting" — 感时 and 恨别 are personified emotional triggers; standard reading.
- 烽火连三月 → "Beacon fires have burned three months on end" — 烽火 = wartime beacon signals; 连三月 = continuous through spring.
- 家书抵万金 → "A letter from home would be worth ten thousand in gold" — 抵 = be worth; hyperbole well-established.
- 白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪 → "I scratch my white hair…too scant to hold a pin" — 短 = thin/short from worry; 不胜簪 = cannot support the hairpin (topknot collapsing). Idiomatic rendering kept close to image."}

Translator's Notes on Ambiguity:
1. Lines 3–4: The syntax "感时花溅泪" is famously ambiguous in its agency.
   (a) The speaker sees flowers and is moved to tears (objective scene, subjective emotion).
   (b) The flowers themselves seem to shed tears.
   The translation "flowers draw tears" leans toward (a) while retaining an echo of (b).
2. "恨别" (hating separation): "别" can refer to separation from one's family (a common reading) or the general parting/sorrow of the times. The translation uses "separation" to preserve this range.
3. "家书" (family letter): Literally "family book/writing." Contextually, a letter from home. The translation uses "letter from home."
4. "不胜簪" (cannot hold the hairpin): "不胜" means "cannot bear/cannot support." The translation renders it as "too scant to hold a hairpin.""}

感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。

白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。"}, "translation": "Spring View

The nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain.
The city in spring—grass and trees grow deep.
Moved by the times, flowers draw tears;
Hating parting, birds startle the heart.
Beacon fires stretch through three months;
A letter from home would be worth ten thousand in gold.
I scratch my white hair till it grows ever thinner—

Original: 国破山河在 — Translation: "The nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain" — Direct correspondence; 国 rendered as 'nation', 破 as 'broken', 在 as 'remain' (contrast of ruin and endurance).

Original: 城春草木深 — Translation: "The city in spring—grass and trees grow deep" — 深 implies overgrowth/neglect; rendered as 'grow deep' preserving ambiguity.

Original: 感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心 — Translation: "Moved by the times, flowers draw tears; Hating parting, birds startle the heart" — Ambiguity (does the poet weep, or do the flowers?) left open; 感时 as 'moved by the times', 恨别 as 'hating parting'.

Original: 烽火连三月 — Translation: "Beacon fires stretch through three months" — 烽火 literal 'beacon fires' = war; 连三月 as 'stretch through three months' (spring season of war).

Original: 家书抵万金 — Translation: "A letter from home would be worth ten thousand in gold" — 抵 as 'be worth'; 万金 idiom for immense value; 'would be' keeps subjunctive sense.

Original: 白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪 — Translation: "I scratch my white hair till it grows ever thinner— Soon it will be too scant to hold a pin" — 短 = thin/short (hair); 浑欲不胜簪 idiom: hair too sparse for the hairpin; 'scant' captures 浑欲 nuance."}

白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。"}, "translation": "Spring View

The state is shattered; mountains and rivers remain.
In spring the city is deep with grass and trees.
Moved by the times, flowers bring tears;
Hating parting, birds startle the heart.

A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.
I scratch my white hair, till it grows ever thinner—
scarcely able now to hold a hairpin."}

Moved by the times, flowers draw my tears;

A letter from home would be worth ten thousand in gold.
I scratch my white hair, it grows ever sparser,
Soon it will be too thin to hold a hairpin."}

感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。

白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。"}, "translation": "Spring View

The state is shattered; mountains and rivers remain.
The city in spring, grass and trees grow deep.
Moved by the times, flowers bring tears;
Hating parting, birds startle the heart.

A letter from home would be worth ten thousand in gold.
I scratch my white hair, growing ever thinner—
Soon it will be too scant to hold a hairpin."}

White hair, scratched more and more sparse,
So thin now it nearly cannot hold a hairpin."}

I scratch my white hair, it grows ever thinner,

感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。

Spring fills the city, grass and trees grow deep.
Flowers shed tears at the sight of ruined times,
Birds cry out in alarm at parting.

I scratch my white hair, now too thin and short,
To hold a hairpin any more."}

White-haired, I scratch my head—more and more sparse—

{"source": {"title": "山居秋暝", "author": "王维", "text": "空山新雨后，天气晚来秋。
明月松间照，清泉石上流。
竹喧归浣女，莲动下渔舟。
随意春芳歇，王孙自可留。"}, "translation": "**Autumn Evening in the Mountain Retreat**

Fresh rain has washed the empty sky,
As evening brings autumn's air.
The bright moon shines through the pine boughs,
Clear spring flows over the stones.

Bamboo rustles as the washerwomen return,
Lotus stirs as the fisherman's boat glides.
Let spring's blossoms fade at their will—
Here the noble one may well remain.

---
*Notes on ambiguity:* 
1. "王孙" (literally "prince's grandson") is a classical allusion (from the *Chu Ci*/*Songs of Chu*) that can mean: (a) a noble or reclusive person; (b) the poet himself; or (c) the reader/visitor. The translation uses "noble one" to keep this open.
2. "随意春芳歇" may carry a slight tone of defiance ("let spring do as it pleases") or simple acceptance ("let spring fade at its leisure")."}

After fresh rain on the empty mountains,
The air turns to autumn at dusk.
Bright moonlight shines among the pines;\nClear spring flows over the stones.
Bamboo rustles as washerwomen return;
Lotus leaves stir as a fishing boat glides down.
Let the spring blossoms fade at will—

Note on ambiguity:
- "王孙" (wáng sūn): literally "grandson of a king" or "noble scion," often used in classical poetry (cf. Chu Yuan's "Song of the Departed") to mean a reclusive gentleman or the poet himself. Here it may refer to Wang Wei's own choice to remain in the mountains, or to any cultivated person who appreciates such a dwelling.
- "随意春芳歇" (suíyì chūn fāng xiē): "Let the spring blossoms fade at will" — 随意 can mean "as one pleases" or "carelessly/heedlessly," and 歇 means "to cease" or "to wither." The line may express either a laissez-faire acceptance of nature's cycles or a deliberate turning away from the transient allure of spring in favor of autumn's clarity."}

On the clear isle, white sands, birds wheel and circle round.

Ceaseless, the rolling Yangtze surges on.

Ten thousand miles away, I grieve at autumn, forever a traveler far from home,
A hundred years of life, with many ailments, I climb the terrace all alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have thickened the frost on my temples,
Down and out, I've just now stopped my cup of cloudy wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "**Climbing High**
By Du Fu

The wind is swift, the sky is high, the gibbons cry in sorrow;
The isle is clear, the sand is white, the birds wheel in flight.
Boundless, the falling leaves descend rustling, rustling;
Endless, the Yangtze River rolls on, surging, surging.
Ten thousand miles away, I grieve at autumn, forever a stranger;\nA hundred years of life, full of sickness, I climb this terrace alone.
Hardship and bitter regret thicken the frost on my temples;
Worn out, I have just now set down my cup of turbid wine.

**Translator's Notes on Ambiguities:**
1. **渚 (zhǔ)**: Literally "a small islet in the water," translated here as "isle." Some read it as "the water's edge" or "a sandbar."
2. **鸟飞回**: "Birds wheel in flight" or "birds circle back." The character 回 suggests a returning or circular motion, possibly indicating birds caught in the wind or migrating.
3. **百年 (bǎi nián)**: Literally "a hundred years," a conventional expression for "a lifetime." It does not necessarily mean Du Fu was exactly one hundred years old.
4. **潦倒新停浊酒杯**: "Worn out, I have just now set down my cup of turbid wine." The phrase 新停 ("just now stopped") is often interpreted as Du Fu having ceased drinking due to illness (possibly a heart condition or gout). "Turbid wine" (浊酒) was the common, unfiltered wine of the era."}

Ten thousand miles from home, grieving at autumn, I am always a stranger;
All my life, sick so many times, I climb this terrace alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have thickened the frost on my temples;
Down and out, I have lately stopped my cup of turbid wine.

By Du Fu

The wind is sharp, the sky is high; the gibbons cry with grief,
The islet clear, the sand is white; birds circle in relief.

Boundless, the falling leaves come rustling down,\nEndless, the Yangtze rolls on toward the town.

Ten thousand miles: in autumn gloom, a guest who roams,
A hundred years: with many woes, I climb these lonely domes.

Hard times, bitter regret—my temples frosted o'er,
Down and out, I've lately stopped the turbid wine cup's pour.

- "百年" (bǎi nián): literally "a hundred years," metaphorically means "a lifetime" or "old age."
- "新停" (xīn tíng): "lately stopped"—whether he stopped drinking due to illness, poverty, or despair is left open."}

Endless, the Yangtze rolls its waves along.

Ten thousand miles away, I grieve at autumn, forever a stranger;

Worn out, I have lately stopped my cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "Swift wind, high sky—apes cry mournfully; Clear isles, white sands—birds wheel and return.
Boundless falling leaves rustle down; Endless Yangtze roars on and on.
A thousand miles of sorrow in autumn—always a stranger far away; A hundred years of illness—alone I climb the height.
Hardship and bitter regrets have whitened my hair with frost; In decline, I’ve just set down the cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is fierce, the sky vast, apes cry with sorrow, 
Islands clear, sands white—birds wheel and return. 
Endless falling leaves rustle down in sighs, 
Unending Yangtze surges forward in relentless flow. 
A thousand miles of grief in autumn, always a traveler, 
In my long life, ill and alone, I climb this height. 
The hardships of life, bitter regrets, have whitened my hair like frost, 
Now impoverished and broken, I've just set down my cup of cloudy wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is high, the sky is vast, the gibbons’ cries are mournful,
The islet bright, the sand white, birds circle back.
Boundless, the falling leaves come rustling down;
Endless, the Yangtze rolls on in its flood.
Ten thousand miles away, grieving at autumn, always a stranger,
A hundred years of illness, I climb the heights alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have hoar-frosted my temples;
In my ruin, I have lately ceased the cup of turbid wine."}

无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。

Boundless, the falling leaves rustle down,

A hundred years of sickness, I climb this terrace alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have thickened my frost-white temples,
In my destitution, I have just set down my cup of turbid wine."}

By Du Fu

The wind is sharp, the sky so high, gibbons cry with mournful sound,
The islet clear, the sand snow-white, birds wheel and fly around.

Boundless, the falling leaves come rustling down without an end,
Endless, the Yangtze surges on, its rolling waves descend.

Ten thousand miles from home, in autumn grief I dwell,
A sick old man, I climb alone this terrace high.

Hardship and sorrow, white my temples tell,
Down and in despair, I set my wine cup by."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is high, the sky profound;
The gibbons cry with mournful sound.
The islet clear, the sand is white,
Birds circle in their wheeling flight.

Without a bound, the falling leaves
Come rustling down from all the trees.
The endless river, rolling on,
Comes surging, never to be gone.

Ten thousand miles, in autumn grief,
A stranger, sick, beyond relief.
A hundred years, by illness tried,
I climb the terrace, lone, to hide.

Hardship and hate, my temples bear
The heavy frost of hoary hair.
In deep despair, I set aside
The turbid cup, my joy has died."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is sharp, the sky is high, the monkeys' cries are sad,
The islet clear, the sand white, birds wheel back.
Boundless, the falling leaves rustle down;
Endless, the Yangtze rolls on in its flood.
Ten thousand miles away, grieved by autumn, a wanderer long,
A hundred years of illness, I climb the heights alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have thickened my frosty temples;
In my ruin, I have lately stopped the cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is sharp, the sky is high, the apes cry mournfully,
The waters are clear, the sand is white, birds circle back.
Endless, falling leaves rustle and descend,
The endless Yangtze rolls and surges on.

All my life of sickness, I climb the terrace alone.
Hardships and bitter regrets have thickened the frost in my temples,
In my desolation, I have just stopped the cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is sharp, the sky is high, the apes cry mournfully,
The islet is clear, the sand is white, birds wheel and return.
Boundless fallen leaves rustle down,
The boundless Yangtze pours forth.
Ten thousand miles away, grieving at autumn, I am always a stranger;
A hundred years of sickness, I climb the terrace alone.
Hardships and bitter regrets have thickened the frost in my temples,
In my desolation, I have just stopped the cup of turbid wine."}

无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。

Hardship and bitter resentment have whitened my temples thick with frost; now, in poverty's decline, I've just stopped drinking my muddy wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is sharp, the sky is high, the monkeys’ cries are sad,
The islet clear, the sand white, birds wheel back.
Boundless, the falling leaves rustle down;
Endless, the Yangtze rolls on in its flood.
Ten thousand miles away, grieved by autumn, long have I wandered,
All my life sickly, I climb the heights alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have thickened my frosty temples;
In my ruin, I have lately stopped the cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is sharp, the sky is high, the apes wail their sorrow,
The islet is clear, the sand is white, birds circle about.
Endless, falling leaves rustle and descend,
The endless Yangtze rolls and surges on.
Ten thousand miles away, grieving at autumn, I am always a stranger;
A hundred years of sickness, I climb the terrace alone.
Hardships and bitter regrets have thickened the frost in my temples,
In my desolation, I have lately put down my cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。

The isle is clear, the sand is white, the birds wheel in their flight.
The boundless falling leaves come rustling down,
The endless Yangtze surges on its way.
Ten thousand miles of autumn gloom, a traveler always,
A hundred years of varied illness, alone I climb the terrace.
Hardship and bitter regret have thickened my frosty temples,
In my poverty, I have newly set down the cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is sharp, the sky is high, the apes cry mournfully,
The islet clear, the sand white, birds return in flight.
Boundless, the falling leaves rustle down;
Endless, the Yangtze rolls on in its flood.
Grieving through ten thousand autumns, a wanderer long,
A hundred years of illness, I climb the heights alone.
Hardship and bitter regret have frosted with grey my temples;
In my ruin, I have lately stopped the cup of wine of hardship."}

In my desolation, I have just stopped the cup of turbid wine."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is swift, the sky high, apes wail mournfully; 
Islands clear, sands white, birds wheel and return. 
Endless falling leaves rustle down in autumn's sigh, 
The endless Yangtze roars on, ceaselessly rolling by. 
A thousand miles of sorrow in autumn, I wander far, 
A hundred years of illness, alone I climb this lofty tower. 
Hardship and bitter resentment have whitened my temples thick with frost, 
Now, in poverty, I've just set down my cup of wine, no longer to drink."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa**

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted while my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no lutes or strings were there.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moon at parting.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to leave.
Seeking the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls she finally appeared,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the melody began, feeling already filled the air.
Each string, each note, was muted with deep thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
Brow lowered, casually she went on playing,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly strumming, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The big strings roared like rushing rain,
The small strings whispered like intimate talk.
Loud and soft, mixed and interlaced,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers,
Like a choked spring flowing under the ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings seemed to freeze,
Frozen and blocked, the sound paused for a while.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose—
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then a silver vase burst, water gushing forth,
Armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the pick across the center;
Four strings at once cracked like tearing silk.
All the boats east and west were hushed and still;
Only the autumn moon in mid-river shone white.
Meditatively she put the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her garments, rose and composed her face.
She said: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was below Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
After each song the best musicians praised me;
Each time I dressed up, the famous courtesans envied me.
Young nobles of Wuling competed to lavish me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
Ornaments and silver combs were broken keeping time;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Spring moons and autumn winds passed idly by.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Day and night went by, and my beauty faded.
Before my gate, carriages grew few, horses sparse;
Growing old, I became a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the bright moon and cold water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth;

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "A Farewell Song of the Pipa

BY BAI JUYI

At Xunyang River’s head, I saw a friend off at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
Down from my horse, I watched him board the boat;
We raised our cups, but no strings played.
Drunk without joy, we parted in gloom,
The vast river swallowed the moon as we said goodbye.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa—
The host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his farewells.
Following the sound, I asked softly who played,
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat closer and invited her on board,
Poured more wine, relit the lamps, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string whispered sorrow, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.\nBrows lowered, she played on without pause,
Pouring out all the endless matters of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly pinching, stroking and picking,
First the Rainbow Skirts, then the Six Yao.
The great strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings murmured like private talk.
Roars and murmurs tangled and intertwined,
Like pearls, big and small, dropped on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling beneath the flowers, smooth as silk,
Like a spring choked in ice beneath the stream.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and broke,
The broken sound ceased, and silence took its place.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—
Then, silence spoke louder than any sound.
Like a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Like armored riders charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ended with a stroke across the heart,
Four strings snapped as one, like tearing silk.
All around, in every boat, no one spoke—
Only the autumn moon, white on the river’s heart.
She sank in thought, tucked the plectrum in,
Adjusted her clothes, and composed her face.
“I am a woman from the capital,” she said,
“Whose home was by the Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name topped the first rank of the Music Bureau.
My playing once made the masters bow,
My beauty made the courtesans burn with envy.
The young men of the Five Tombs fought to reward me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
The jeweled comb beat time till it broke,
The blood-red skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
The spring moon and autumn wind passed in vain.
My brother went to war, my aunt died,
Day and night, my youth slipped away.
Before my door, horses grew rare,
I married a merchant in my old age.
The merchant values profit over parting,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I guard the empty boat at the river’s mouth,
The moonlight cold on the water around me.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth,
And wake to find my tears streaking my rouge.”

I sighed when I first heard her pipa,
And sighed again at her words.
“Both of us are wanderers at the world’s end—
Why must we have met before to understand?”
Last year I left the capital’s bright halls,
Exiled and ill in this city of Xunyang.
The land is remote, no music graces my ears,
Year-round, not a single string or flute.
I live by the Pan River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.
At dawn and dusk, what do I hear?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbon’s wail.
On spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moon,
I often drink alone by the river’s edge.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?\nTheir crude squawks grate on my ears.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s song,
It’s like celestial music, brightening my ears.
Please don’t refuse—stay and play one more,
For you, I’ll compose a song of the pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,
Then sat again, and the strings quickened.
The new tune, unlike the one before,
Made everyone in the room weep.
Who wept the most among the guests?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa**

One night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted as host; my guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or string.
Drunk yet not merry, we grieved at parting—
At parting, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to leave.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties she at last came out,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
Before a tune was formed, feeling already filled the air.
Each string, each note, was choked with longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, carelessly yet deftly she played on,
Pouring out the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, strumming and picking—
First the “Rainbow Garment,” then the “Six Minor.”
The great strings roared like pelting rain,
The small strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled and interwoven—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers,
Or a hidden spring trickling, frozen under ice.
The ice-cold spring congealed, the strings froze and snapped;
The sound, blocked and frozen, rested for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment rose—
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end she drew the pick across the center of the strings;
The four strings cried out as one, like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all was silent and hushed;
Only the autumn moon on the river’s heart, white and bright.
Muttering to herself, she tucked the pick among the strings;
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her countenance.
She spoke: “I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was beneath Toad Mound.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name headed the rolls of the Music Bureau.
After each song, even the finest musicians were impressed;
When made up, even the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young gallants of the Five Tombs competed to lavish gifts;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Ornamented combs and silver hairpins beat time till they broke;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy followed joy, year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by unheeded.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dusk came and dawn went, and my youth faded.
Before my gate, horses grew sparse, the visitors few;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and lightly parts from his wife—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I wait at the river’s mouth in an empty boat,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, my tears streaking my rouge.”

I had sighed already at the pipa’s song;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deep and long.
Both of us are wanderers at the world’s end—
Why must we have met before to know this bond?
Since last year I took leave of the imperial capital,
I have lived in exile, ill, in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year I have not heard lute or string.
My house is near the low, damp riverbank,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my gate.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbon’s mournful wail.
On flower-filled spring mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are raucous, jarring, hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa’s song,
Like hearing celestial music; my ears were cleared.
Do not refuse—sit and play once more,
And I will compose for you a ‘Song of the Pipa.’

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back and quickened the strings, faster and faster.
Desolate, unlike the sound before,
All who heard it anew wept into their sleeves.
Who wept the most among the company?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is swift, the sky vast, apes cry with sorrow; the islets clear, sands white, birds wheel and return.
Endless falling leaves rustle down in waves, the Yangtze River rolls without end.
A thousand miles of grief in autumn, I am ever a wanderer; in my years of illness, I climb alone to this platform.
Hardship and bitterness have silvered my temples, now that I’ve just stopped drinking my cloudy wine."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa**

At Xunyang River by the inn, I see a guest off into the night,
Where maple leaves and reeds in autumn rustle with the light.
The host dismounts, the guest embarks; they raise their cups to drink,
But there’s no music—no pipa, no lute—to make them think.
Drunk but not gay, they part in sorrow, just before they part,
The river swallows up the moon, so vast and bleak their heart.
Suddenly, from the water comes a pipa’s plaintive sound;
The host forgets to go, the guest’s boat doesn’t leave the ground.
They trace the sound and ask, “Who plays?” The music stops, then—slow
The player hesitates to speak. They move their boats close, you know,
Invite her out, add wine, relight the lamps, and feast anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally appears in view,
Still holding the pipa half across her face, shy and shy.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings a few, and though no tune is high,
Emotion fills the air before a single note is played.
Each string suppressed, each note a sigh, as if her life conveyed
Unfulfilled ambitions, all the sorrows she has known.
Brows low, she plays on, fingers moving, telling, one by one,
The countless things within her heart—no end to what she says.
She plucks and strums, sweeps and picks, with light and slow displays.
First “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Little Ones,” a classic pair.
The big strings roar like sudden rain, the small strings whisper there
Like secrets in the ear. The two, together, clash and blend,
Like pearls, big and small, upon a jade plate falling end.
Then notes as smooth as orioles singing under flowers’ bloom,
Then choked, like springs beneath the ice, a cold and stifled gloom.
The ice-bound springs, the strings grow stiff, and then the sound is gone;
The silence speaks of hidden griefs, where joys were never won.
Then—like a silver vase that breaks and water bursts apart,
Or armored horsemen charge with clash of sword and spear and dart.
At the song’s end, she sweeps the pick across the strings as one—
Four strings at once, like tearing silk, and then the music’s done.
From east to west, the boats are still; no one dares speak a word,
Only the autumn moon in river’s heart, white, is heard.
She tucks the pick among the strings, adjusts her robes with grace,
Her face composed, she stands and speaks, “I’m from the capital’s place,
My home was by the Toad Hill, where I learned to play at thirteen,
My name was listed first among the court’s musicians, keen.
After each song, the masters praised; each time I dressed with care,
The autumn beauties envied me, my beauty beyond compare.
The young lords of the Five Tombs competed to bestow
Their gifts on me; for just one song, red silk—no one could know
How many. Jeweled combs would break as we beat time with glee,
My blood-red silk skirts stained by wine, in revelry.
Year after year, I laughed and sang, through spring winds and autumn’s light,
Unmindful how the seasons passed, until the dark of night.
My brother went to war, my aunt died; one by one they went.
My beauty faded as the years, the days of youth were spent.
The horses at my door grew few, the guests no longer came,
And now, grown old, I married—yes—a merchant, for my shame.
The merchant cares for profit more than parting or for me,
Last month he left for tea in Fuliang, across the sea.
I wait alone beside the boat, the moon shines cold and bright,
The river chills around my craft, and through the lonely night.
I dreamed of youthful days, and woke, my tears on rouge-stained cheek,
My tears of dreams like lines of red, the sorrows that I seek.
I sighed when first I heard the pipa, and now, hearing your tale,
I sigh again, and sigh once more, my heart within me wail.
We both are wanderers in this world, cast off by fate’s own hand—
Why must we have met before, to understand and understand?
Since last year, I left the capital, and here in Xunyang lie,
Ill and banished, in this remote place, where music passes by.
No lute or flute is heard all year, no songs to soothe the soul,
Only the cuckoo’s bloody cry and gibbons’ mournful howl.
By reed-grown marsh and low, wet ground, with bitter bamboo around,
What sounds of day and night are there? The cuckoo and the gibbon’s sound.
On flower-lit spring days, or moonlit autumn nights, I pour
My wine and drink alone, and sigh, and ask, “What is the score?
Are there no village songs, no rustic flutes to fill the air?”
They’re harsh and crude and hard to bear, and no one seems to care.
But tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, it’s like celestial music bright—
My ears, at last, can hear again, and see again the light.
Don’t refuse, but sit and play one more song for me tonight,
I’ll compose a “Song of the Pipa” to fit your sound aright.
Moved by my words, she stands a while, then sits and tunes the strings
More tightly, faster, and the notes, like winter’s icy wings,
Are mournful, different from before; the whole room hears and weeps.
Who in this boat has shed the most? The Jiangzhou official, who keeps
His blue official’s robe in tears, and wets it with his grief."}

主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa**

At Xunyang River by the inn, I see a guest off into the night,
Where maple leaves and reeds in autumn rustle with the light.
The host dismounts, the guest embarks; they raise their cups to drink,
But there’s no music—no pipa, no lute—to make them think.
Drunk but not gay, they part in sorrow, just before they part,
The river swallows up the moon, so vast and bleak their heart.
Suddenly, from the water comes a pipa’s plaintive sound;
The host forgets to go, the guest’s boat doesn’t leave the ground.
They trace the sound and ask, “Who plays?” The music stops, then—slow
The player hesitates to speak. They move their boats close, you know,
Invite her out, add wine, relight the lamps, and feast anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally appears in view,
Still holding the pipa half across her face, shy and shy.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings a few, and though no tune is high,
Emotion fills the air before a single note is played.
Each string suppressed, each note a sigh, as if her life conveyed
Unfulfilled ambitions, all the sorrows she has known.
Brows low, she plays on, fingers moving, telling, one by one,
The countless things within her heart—no end to what she says.
She plucks and strums, sweeps and picks, with light and slow displays.
First “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Little Ones,” a classic pair.
The big strings roar like sudden rain, the small strings whisper there
Like secrets in the ear. The two, together, clash and blend,
Like pearls, big and small, upon a jade plate falling end.
Then notes as smooth as orioles singing under flowers’ bloom,
Then choked, like springs beneath the ice, a cold and stifled gloom.
The ice-bound springs, the strings grow stiff, and then the sound is gone;
The silence speaks of hidden griefs, where joys were never won.
Then—like a silver vase that breaks and water bursts apart,
Or armored horsemen charge with clash of sword and spear and dart.
At the song’s end, she sweeps the pick across the strings as one—
Four strings at once, like tearing silk, and then the music’s done.
From east to west, the boats are still; no one dares speak a word,
Only the autumn moon in river’s heart, white, is heard.
She tucks the pick among the strings, adjusts her robes with grace,
Her face composed, she stands and speaks, “I’m from the capital’s place,
My home was by the Toad Hill, where I learned to play at thirteen,
My name was listed first among the court’s musicians, keen.
After each song, the masters praised; each time I dressed with care,
The autumn beauties envied me, my beauty beyond compare.
The young lords of the Five Tombs competed to bestow
Their gifts on me; for just one song, red silk—no one could know
How many. Jeweled combs would break as we beat time with glee,
My blood-red silk skirts stained by wine, in revelry.
Year after year, I laughed and sang, through spring winds and autumn’s light,
Unmindful how the seasons passed, until the dark of night.
My brother went to war, my aunt died; one by one they went.
My beauty faded as the years, the days of youth were spent.
The horses at my door grew few, the guests no longer came,
And now, grown old, I married—yes—a merchant, for my shame.
The merchant cares for profit more than parting or for me,
Last month he left for tea in Fuliang, across the sea.
I wait alone beside the boat, the moon shines cold and bright,
The river chills around my craft, and through the lonely night.
I dreamed of youthful days, and woke, my tears on rouge-stained cheek,
My tears of dreams like lines of red, the sorrows that I seek.
I sighed when first I heard the pipa, and now, hearing your tale,
I sigh again, and sigh once more, my heart within me wail.
We both are wanderers in this world, cast off by fate’s own hand—
Why must we have met before, to understand and understand?
Since last year, I left the capital, and here in Xunyang lie,
Ill and banished, in this remote place, where music passes by.
No lute or flute is heard all year, no songs to soothe the soul,
Only the cuckoo’s bloody cry and gibbons’ mournful howl.
By reed-grown marsh and low, wet ground, with bitter bamboo around,
What sounds of day and night are there? The cuckoo and the gibbon’s sound.
On flower-lit spring days, or moonlit autumn nights, I pour
My wine and drink alone, and sigh, and ask, “What is the score?
Are there no village songs, no rustic flutes to fill the air?”
They’re harsh and crude and hard to bear, and no one seems to care.
But tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, it’s like celestial music bright—
My ears, at last, can hear again, and see again the light.
Don’t refuse, but sit and play one more song for me tonight,
I’ll compose a “Song of the Pipa” to fit your sound aright.
Moved by my words, she stands a while, then sits and tunes the strings
More tightly, faster, and the notes, like winter’s icy wings,
Are mournful, different from before; the whole room hears and weeps.
Who in this boat has shed the most? The Jiangzhou official, who keeps
His blue official’s robe in tears, and wets it with his grief."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。

At Xunyang River's head I saw a guest off one night,
Where maple leaves and reeds shiver in autumn's chill light.
The host dismounts, the guest boards the boat; we raise our wine, but no lute or string.
Drunk without joy, sad at parting, we face the vast river where the moon sinks.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Seeking the sound, we softly ask who plays;
The music stops, and she hesitates to speak.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to meet;
Add wine, relight the lamps, begin the feast anew.
After a thousand calls and ten entreaties she appears,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings—three, four notes;
Before the melody forms, feeling is already there.
Each string murmurs with hidden sorrow, each note heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow low, carelessly her fingers move on,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then plucking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Small Ones*.
The large strings rumble like sudden rain;
The small strings whisper like private speech.
Rumbling, whispering, mingled they play,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth among the flowers;
Like a choked spring flowing under ice.
Cold, sluggish, the strings seem to freeze and break;
The broken notes fall silent for a while.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment rises—
Then, silence speaks louder than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing;
Like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The song ends with a sweep across the center;
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, no word;
Only the river's heart, bright with autumn moon.
Thoughtfully she tucks the plectrum among the strings,
Adjusts her robes, rises with a solemn face.
She says: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was by Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the best players admired;
When I dressed up, even Qiuniang envied.
Young men of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
Ornaments and silver combs beat time till they broke;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
He values profit and lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
The moon shines bright around me, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, my makeup streaked with tears."

I had sighed at the pipa's song;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper.
Both of us are lost souls at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have met before to understand?
Since last year I left the capital,
An exiled official, ill, in Xunyang town.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year I hear no lute or string.
I live near the river, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my hut.
What do I hear morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower-filled spring mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
Often I take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are crude and harsh, impossible to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak,
It is like celestial music; my ears are blessed anew.
Do not refuse—sit and play once more;
For you, I will compose a *Song of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence;
Then sits again, tightens the strings, and the tempo quickens.
Sadder, sadder than before;
The whole company, hearing it again, weeps.
Who weeps the most among the guests?
The Master of Jiangzhou, his blue robe all wet."}

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a friend off one autumn night,
The maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the cold.
I dismounted; my guest stepped into his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to accompany us.
Drunk, yet without joy, we prepared to part in sorrow—
At the moment of farewell, the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go home; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly: "Who is playing?"
The music stopped; the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us.
We added wine, relit the lamps, and resumed our feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
Before the melody took shape, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and brooding, full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled dreams.
Brow lowered, she played on idly, carelessly,
Telling of the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
On the thick strings, a torrent like rushing rain;
On the thin strings, a whisper like private speech.
The loud and the soft, intertwined and crossed,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.\nLike orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers,
Or a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold; the strings seemed to freeze.
When the flow stopped, the sound paused for a moment.
A deeper sorrow, a hidden grief, then rose—
In that silence, more was said than by any sound.
Then, like a silver vase bursting, water flooding out,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging,
She ended the song with a sharp sweep across all four strings—
One crack, like silk being torn apart.
In the boats around us, all was silent and still;
Only the autumn moon in the river's heart shone white.
Thoughtfully, she tucked the pick into her strings,
Adjusted her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She spoke:
"I was once a girl from the capital,
Living near Haima Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
And my name was listed first in the Music Academy.
When I finished a song, even the finest masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, even the celebrated courtesans envied me.
The rich young men of Wuling competed to offer me gifts—
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
We beat time with jeweled combs until they broke,
And my blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and revelry,
The autumn moons and spring winds passed us by unnoticed.
Then my brother enlisted; my aunt died.
Days and nights wore on, and my beauty faded.
Fewer horses stopped at my door;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
But merchants value profit over parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in my empty boat,
Surrounded by the bright moon and the cold water.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my tears streaking my rouge."

I had sighed already at her pipa's song;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, deeper still.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to feel this bond?
Since last year, I left the capital's splendor
To live in exile, sick, here in Xunyang.
This place is remote; there is no music here—
All year, I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbons' mournful wails.
On spring river mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh, discordant, hard on the ear.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
It was like hearing celestial music—my ears came alive.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
And I will compose "A Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened her strings—they grew more urgent.
The sound was mournful, unlike the song before;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Who among us wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
