At Xunyang River's edge I bid my guest good-bye,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I dismount my horse, he boards the boat;
We lift our cups to drink, but there's no music.
Drunk without joy, we're sad, about to part,
Parting, the vast river is drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
I forget to go home, my guest delays his departure.
Seeking the sound, I softly ask who's playing;
The pipa stops, she hesitates to speak.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to meet;
Add wine, relight the lamp, reopen the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerges,
Still cradling the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings twice or thrice;
Before the tune is formed, emotion is there.
Each string, each note, suppressed with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled desires.
Brows low, she idly plays on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light touches, slow rubs, strokes and flicks,
First "Rainbow Skirts," then "Little Willows."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, mingled and mixed,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, smooth and swift,
Like a hidden spring choking under ice.
The icy spring freezes, the strings snap and cease;
The sound halts, broken off, and pauses.
An unseen sorrow, a hidden resentment, is born;
In this moment, silence is more than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she sweeps the拨 across the center;
The four strings cry out as if tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, no one speaks;
Only the autumn moon, white, in the heart of the river.
Thoughtfully, she puts the拨 between the strings,
Adjusts her robes, rises, and composes her face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Music Academy.
After her performance, even the finest players were humbled;
When adorned, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed for her favor;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins beat time and broke,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Spring breezes and autumn moons, spent without care.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, fewer horses and carriages;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit over parting;
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She comes and goes, guarding an empty boat at the river's mouth;
The moon shines around the boat, the river water is cold.
In the deep of night, she suddenly dreams of her youth;
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the end of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
I left the capital last year,
Banished and ailing in Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no music;
All year round, I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the low, damp banks of the Pen River,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On flower-filled spring days, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They're harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
Is like hearing the music of immortals, my ears briefly cleared.
Do not decline; sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose "A Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and plays faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the sound before,
The whole audience hears it again and weeps.
Who among us weeps the most?
The Xunyang official, his blue gown wet with tears."}

Telling all the endless things within her heart.

The sound halts, broken off, and pauses.

Living at the foot of Toad Hill.

Ranked first in the Music Academy.

When adorned, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed for her favor;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins beat time and broke,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Spring breezes and autumn moons, spent without care.

Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.

When I finished a song, even masters bowed;
When I dressed up, even beauties envied, and how!
The young blades of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts;
One song brought red silk beyond counting, in drifts.
Jeweled combs snapped keeping time, in fragments, in bits;
Blood-red skirts were stained by wine in its fits.
Year after year of laughter, of endless play;
Autumn moons, spring breeys, all wasted away.
My brother left for war, my aunt died;
Dawn came, dusk went, my youth slipped by.
Fewer horses stopped before my door;
I grew old, and married a merchant, poor.
The merchant values profit, not love, not staying;
Last month he sailed to Fuliang, his tea trade displaying.
I wait alone by the river mouth in my empty boat;
Around me, the moon shines bright, the water cold and remote.

I wake weeping, my tears cutting red rivers through my fears."

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "A Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night,
The maple leaves and reed blossoms rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no zither or string music.
Drunk, yet our hearts not merry, we parted sadly;
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties she at last came out,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the melody took shape, feeling was already there.
Every string, every note, was choked with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled aspirations.
Brow lowered, she played on idly, at ease,
Telling of all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
The roar and the whisper mingled together,
Like big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smoothly under the flowers,
Then, like a muffled spring flowing under ice.
The icy spring ran cold, the strings grew stiff and broke;
The broken strings fell silent, the sound paused for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, was born;
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing out;
Like an armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended with a sweep of the拨 across the center;
Four strings at once, like a bolt of silk being torn.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and still;
Only the autumn moon in the middle of the river, white and bright.
Thoughtfully she put the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, stood up, and composed her countenance.
She said she was originally a girl of the capital,
Her home was near Hama Ling.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Teaching Bureau.
When she finished a song, even the best musicians were impressed;
When she dressed up, even the most beautiful women were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to give her gifts;
For one song, she received countless red silks.
Ornaments and silver combs were smashed in time-keeping;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by unheeded.
Her brother went to join the army, her aunt died;
Day and night passed, and her beauty faded.
In front of her door, carriages and horses grew few;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone in the empty boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth;
In her dream she wept, her makeup washed by tears, red streaks on her face.
I had sighed at hearing her pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, and again.
We are both people lost at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
I have been living in illness in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no fine music;
All year round, I have not heard the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near Penjiang, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons mourning.
On spring river, flower-filled mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It is like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly enlightened.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song for me;
I will compose a "Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
The sound was mournful, unlike what she had played before;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept into their hands.
Who wept the most among the audience?
The Marshall of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**Ballad of the Pipa**
By Bai Juyi

I was seeing a guest off one night on the Xunyang River,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or string.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in sorrow,
When the vast river swallowed the moonlight at farewell.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the strings and plucked a few notes;
Before the melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and brooding, full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, carelessly, she played on and on,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
The large strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The small strings whispered like intimate secrets.
Rumbling and whispering, they intertwined and crossed,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then the oriole’s song over flowers, smooth and bright;
Then a choked spring, struggling under ice.
The icy spring ran cold, the strings froze and snapped;
Frozen, blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, arose;
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then a silver vase burst, water gushing forth;
Armored cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end, she swept her pick across the center;
All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all was silent and hushed;
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, was seen.
Muttering to herself, she tucked the pick among the strings;\nAdjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said, "I was once a girl from the capital,
My home was at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, Qiu Niang herself was jealous.
The young men of Wuling vied to shower me with gifts;
One song earned countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped as we beat time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed us by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Seasons passed, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
The moonlight around the boat is cold, the river water chill.
In the dead of night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my tears streaking my rouge."
I had sighed upon hearing her pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the sky;
Why must we have met before to understand each other?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and sick, I lie in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no lute or string.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbon’s mournful wail.
On spring river flower-viewing nights, autumn moonlit evenings,
Often, I take my wine and drink alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
They are harsh and grating, impossible to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s song,
Is like hearing immortal music; my ears are awakened.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
The mournful notes were unlike the sounds before;
The whole assembly, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Who in the room wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears.

---
**Translator's Notes on Ambiguities:**
1.  **霓裳 (Ní Cháng) & 六幺 (Liù Yāo):** These are names of famous Tang dynasty court music pieces. "Rainbow Skirts" and "Six Yao" are standard translations. "Six Yao" might also be rendered as "Liu Yao" or described as a quick-tempo piece.
2.  **善才 (Shàn Cái):** Literally "good talent," it refers to a master musician or music instructor. Translated here as "masters."
3.  **秋娘 (Qiū Niáng):** A famous courtesan or a generic term for a beautiful woman. Translated as "Qiu Niang," a name.
4.  **五陵年少 (Wǔ Líng Nián Shào):** Refers to the wealthy, fashionable young men from the aristocratic tombs district of Chang'an. Translated as "young men of Wuling."
5.  **江州司马 (Jiāng Zhōu Sī Mǎ):** The official title of the poet Bai Juyi at the time. "Sima" was a deputy prefect. Translated descriptively as "the Prefect of Jiangzhou" for poetic flow, though technically he was the Sima, a lower position.
6.  **青衫 (Qīng Shān):** "Blue robe," the uniform of a lower-ranking Tang official. It symbolizes his demoted status and sorrow."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "The wind is swift, the sky vast—the apes' cries mournful,
Islands clear, sands white—birds wheel and return.
Endless falling leaves rustle down,
The endless Yangtze rolls on without pause.
A thousand miles of sorrow in autumn, I wander afar,
A hundred years of illness, alone I climb this high terrace.
Hardship and hatred have whitened my temples with frost,
In poverty and decline, I've newly set aside my cloudy wine cup."}

At Xunyang River's edge I bid farewell to my guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn's crest.
The host dismounts, the guest boards ship;
He lifts his cup to drink, but no instruments stir.
Drunken yet without joy, we part in sorrow's shade,
As the vast river soaks the moon in its dark blade.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's cry—
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his fly.
We follow the sound, softly asking who plays,
The music stops; she hesitates, words delayed.
We move our boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight the lamp, and feast again right here.
After a thousand calls, she finally comes out,
Still clasping her pipa, half hiding her face about.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings—three, four notes clear,
Before the tune begins, emotion is already here.
Each string sobs with thought, each note a heavy sigh,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled desire.
Brow lowered, casually she plays on and on,
Telling all the boundless things she's held within so long.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping, then plucking bright,
First "Rainbow Skirt Dance," then "Six Yao" melody's light.
The big strings rumble like sudden rain's drum,
The small strings whisper as secrets, soft and numb.
The rumbling and whispering intertwine in flight,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on jade with light.
Like orioles singing sweetly beneath the flowers' spray,
Then choked like a spring flowing under ice's gray.
The icy spring stiffens, the strings freeze and cease,
Frozen and blocked, the sound pauses in its release.
A deeper sorrow and hidden hatred arise,
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sighs.
Then suddenly a silver vase breaks, water bursts out,
Armored cavalry charges, swords and spears clash about.
At the song's end, she sweeps the拨 across the strings' heart,
Four strings rip as one, like tearing silk apart.
On east and west boats, all sit in silent awe,
Only seeing the autumn moon, white on the river's maw.
Thoughtfully she puts the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises with solemn, composed things.
She says: "I was once a girl from the capital's grace,
Lived near Hama Mound in that place.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Ranked first in the Teaching坊's very heart.
After each song, even experts would admire,
When dressed, even beauties would envy my fire.
The young gallants of five tombs fought to shower me with gifts,
For one song, countless red silks they'd lift.
Silver hairpins shattered to keep the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine, oh so sweet.
Year after year of laughter, I spent my prime,
Autumn moons and spring winds—wasted, all the time.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died away,
Day after day, my youth and beauty decayed.
Before my door, carriages grew sparse and cold,
Old, I married a merchant, a story told.
He values profit over parting's sting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea's spring.
I wait alone at the river's mouth in my empty boat,
Around me, the bright moon and cold water float.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youthful past,
And wake crying, my tears staining my rouge, red and vast."

I sighed already at the pipa's first song,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, all night long.
Both of us are wanderers at the world's end,
Why must we have met before, to become friend?
Last year I left the capital's bright scene,
To live in illness in Xunyang, a place unclean.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music's grace,
All year I hear no strings or flutes in this place.
Near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my camp.
What do I hear here, morning and evening, dread?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes howling, unsaid.
On spring river flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and drink alone in my sights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes there?
They're harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech so clear,
Like celestial music, my ears suddenly hear.
Please don't refuse to sit and play another song,
For you, I'll compose this "Song of the Pipa" along.
Moved by my words, she stands long, then sits and tightens her strings,
The music turns urgent, sharp, and stings.\nSadder, sadder, unlike the sound before,
The whole audience weeps, hearing it once more.
Among the weepers, who shed the most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with fears."}

By Bai Juyi (772–846 CE)

I was seeing a guest off one autumn night by the Xunyang River,
Where maple leaves and reed blossoms rustled in the chill.
I dismounted; my guest stepped into his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
We grew drunk, yet found no joy—soon we must part,
And parting, saw only the vast river, drowned in moonlight.

Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa.
My guest forgot to leave; I forgot to go home.
We followed the sound, asking softly, “Who is playing?”
The music stopped, as if she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to meet us,
Poured more wine, relit the lamps, and feasted again.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerged,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She tuned the strings, plucked them two or three times—
Though no melody had formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string seemed choked with sorrow, each note with longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
She lowered her brow and played on, heedlessly,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
With light touches and slow twangs, she plucked and strummed—
First the “Rainbow Skirt,” then the “Six Minor.”

The low strings rumbled like a sudden downpour,
The high strings whispered like secret talk.
The rumble and the whisper intertwined and crossed—
Like pearls, large and small, dropping onto a jade plate.
Then the notes slid, swift as orioles singing under flowers,
Then grew choked, like a spring frozen beneath ice.
The ice-cold water congealed; the strings seemed about to snap,
And when they snapped, the sound ceased for a moment.
In that silence, a deeper sorrow, a hidden grief, arose—
At such a time, silence speaks more than sound.

Then—like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth,
Like an armored charge, swords and spears clashing—
The melody surged. At its end, she swept the plectrum across the strings,
And all four strings cried out at once, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, no one spoke—
We saw only the autumn moon, white upon the river’s heart.

Meditatively she tucked the plectrum into the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said: “I was once a girl of the capital,
Living near Hama Ling.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even master musicians were impressed;
When I dressed up, even the famous courtesans were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts—
For one song, I’d receive countless bolts of red silk.
We beat time with jeweled combs till they broke in pieces,
And wine-stained our blood-red silk skirts.
We laughed year after year,
And let the autumn moons and spring breezes pass us by.

Then my younger brother went off to war, my aunt died,
And day by day, my beauty faded.
Fewer horses waited at my door;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
But merchants care more for profit than for staying near—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone in our boat at the river’s mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face.”

I had sighed once already at her pipa;
Now, hearing her story, I sighed again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why need we have met before, to understand each other now?

I left the capital just last year,
And came, sick and demoted, to live in Xunyang.
This place is remote; there is no music here—
All year, I have not heard a single string or flute.
I live near the Pen River, on low, damp ground,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa Player**

At Xunyang River head, I bid my guest good-bye;
The maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn chill.
I dismounted, while my friend stayed on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no music filled the air.
Drunk yet not merry, we parted in gloom;
The river, vast and hazy, submerged the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa came;
I forgot to return, my guest delayed his leaving.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat closer, inviting her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the strings, plucked them a few times;
Before a melody formed, emotion already stirred.
String by string, note by note, suppressed and thoughtful;
As if telling the sorrows of a life unfulfilled.
With low brows and practiced hands, she played on,
Recounting endless tales from her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and flicking;
First the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Minor.
The thick strings roared like a sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private words.
Interlaced, the sounds tangled and clashed;
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing through flowers, smooth and swift;
Like a hidden stream choking under ice.
The cold, astringent current froze the strings;
The strings froze solid, and the sound paused.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose;
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water gushing;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the end, she swept the拨 across the strings;
All four strings cracked like tearing silk.
East boats, west boats, all fell silent;
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.
She pondered, tucked the拨 into the strings;\nStraightened her clothes, and composed her face.
She said: "I was once a girl from the capital,
Living near Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name was listed first in the Music Academy.
When I finished a song, even the masters admired;
When I dressed up, even the beauties envied.
The rich young men competed to shower me with gifts;

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa Player**

By the Xunyang River one autumn night I was seeing off a guest—
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the chill.
I dismounted, my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk yet not merry, we prepared to part in grief—
The parting light dissolved, the river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice—
I forgot to go home; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly: "Who is playing?"
The music stopped; she hesitated, about to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear;
We added wine, relit the lamp, and reopened the feast.

After a thousand calls she at last emerged,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings—
Before a tune took shape, feeling already filled them.
String after string, muted and brooding; note after note, full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled desire.
Eyes lowered, fingers tracing on, she played on and on,
Telling out all the countless things within her heart.

Light gathering, slow twisting, sweeping and picking—
First she played *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.
The bass strings roared like driving rain;
The treble strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, interlaced they sounded—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth among the blossoms;
Like a muffled stream, choked under ice.
The icy spring ran cold; the strings grew stiff and broke;
Broken, blocked, the sound for a moment ceased.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, was born—
In that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.

Like a silver vase suddenly shattered, water gushing;
Like armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she drew the pick across all four strings—
One split sound, like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all was silent, hushed;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, white.

She sank in thought, tucked the pick among the strings,
Straightened her robes, rose, and composed her countenance.
She spoke: "I was a girl of the capital,
My home stood by Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the master musicians admired me;
When I dressed up, the other girls envied me.
The young gallants of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts—
One song, and I knew not how many bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs struck in time till they broke;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
Autumn moons and spring winds I wasted without care.
Then my younger brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Dusk and dawn passed, and my beauty faded.
Horses and carriages before my door grew cold and few;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit, not parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I keep the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The bright moon circles the boat; the river water is cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my tears streaking my rouge." 

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, low and long.
We are both outcasts at the end of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?"

I left the capital only last year,
Banished and sick, I lie in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I have not heard strings or flutes.
I live near the Pan River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On flower-filled spring mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I往往 take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
It is like hearing celestial music—my ears are briefly made bright.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song for me,
And I will compose for you a *Song of the Pipa Player*.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster—
Melancholy, unlike the sounds before.
The whole assembly, hearing it again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among us wept the most?
The Xunzhou Sima—his blue gown was wet.""}

At Xunyang River's edge one autumn night I was seeing off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the chill of the fall.
Dismounted, I stood on the shore; my friend was already aboard.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to be heard.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieved that we must part;
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa came;
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show herself;
Wine was refilled, lamps relit, and the feast began anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Half-hiding her face behind the pipa she held.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before a tune was formed, feeling already spoke.
Each string, each note was choked with sighs and thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled desire.
Brow lowered, in no hurry, she played on and on,
Telling all the countless things that weighed upon her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
The low strings rumbled like a sudden rain;
The high strings whispered like a private conversation.
The rumbling and whispering were interwoven,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.
The trills were like orioles singing, smooth beneath the flowers;
The choked notes were like a spring, frozen beneath ice.
The icy spring grew cold and stiff; the strings seemed to snap;
Snapped and blocked, the sound paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, was born;
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water burst forth;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed.
At the end of the song, she swept the plectrum across the center;
All four strings cried out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and still;
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart, was seen.
Muttering to herself, she tucked the plectrum into the strings,
Adjusted her garments, and rose with a solemn mien.
She said, "I was a girl of the capital, born near Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, and my name topped the rolls of the Academy.
After one song, even the best musicians would bow;
When dressed, I was envied by the belles of the court.
The young gallants of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts;
For a single song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Ornaments and silver combs were smashed to keep the beat;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilt wine.
Year after year of laughter and gaiety;
The spring breezes and autumn moons were wasted in idle pleasure.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
As days and months passed, my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew rare and saddles few;
Growing old, I became the wife of a merchant.
The merchant values profit and cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I guard this empty boat alone;
Around it, the bright moon shines on the cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep, and my tears streak my rouge-stained face."
I had already sighed at the sound of her pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, and again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet like this?
Since last year I bade farewell to the imperial capital,
I have lived in illness and exile in Xunyang.
This place is remote and has no music;
All year long, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What do I hear from morning till night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbons' mournful howl.
On flower-filled spring mornings or moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing you speak in the language of your pipa,
Is like hearing celestial music; my ears are blessed.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
And I will compose a "Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
The sound was mournful, unlike the song before;
The whole room, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Among the guests, who wept the most?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**Song of the Pipa**

One autumn night at Xunyang by the river I was seeing off a guest;
The maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the chill.
I dismounted, my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
We drank but found no joy; soon the sad parting came;
At parting, the vast river was drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Tracing the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Adding wine, relighting the lamp, we reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs, plucked the strings a few times;
Before a melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was choked with sorrow;
As if telling of a lifetime of unfulfilled longing.
With lowered eyes, she played on carelessly,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, sweeping and plucking—
First "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Minor."
The thick strings roared like a sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled together,
Like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers;
Like a muffled stream struggling under ice.
The icy stream grew cold, the strings froze and snapped;
The sound, blocked, stopped for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, arose;
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she drew the pick across the center;
All four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and still;
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.
Thoughtfully she set the pick among the strings;
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.
She spoke: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music School.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, even the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
I beat time with a jeweled comb until it broke;
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
My brother went to war, my elder sister died;
Day by day, my beauty began to fade.
Before my door, horses grew sparse, visitors few;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
He values profit and lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I wait by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the bright moon, the cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep, my tears staining my rouge."

I had sighed already at her pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?!

Since last year, I left the capital;
I was banished, ill, to this city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I have not heard the sound of strings.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and dusk?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons mourning.
On flower-moon spring days and bright autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It is like hearing immortal music; my ears are briefly enlightened.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
For you, I will compose a "Song of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and they grew faster.
Sorrowful, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats wept again, covering their faces.
Who among us wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**Song of the Pipa**

On the Xunyang River, at night I was seeing off a guest;
maple leaves and reed blossoms, rustling in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse, my guest stepped into the boat;
we raised our cups to drink, yet there were no pipes or strings.
Drunk but not merry, sad we were about to part;
at parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
the pipa stopped, and the player hesitated before answering.
We moved the boat nearer, inviting her to show herself;
we added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties she at last came out,
half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
before the tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Every string, every note was suppressed and brooding, each sound a thought,
as if confessing a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered eyes and idle hand she went on playing,
telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
she began with the Rainbow Skirt and then the Six Small Ones.
The great strings roared like sudden rain,
the small strings whispered like secret talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled together they played,
like big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smoothly among the flowers,
like a muffled spring flowing under ice.
The icy spring turned cold and astringent, the strings congealed and broke;
congealed and broken, the sound stopped for a time.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment arose;
at that moment, silence was more expressive than sound.
Then a silver bottle suddenly burst, water gushing forth;
iron cavalry charged out, blades and spears clashing.
At the end of the song she swept the pick across the center of the strings;
all four strings at once, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all were silent and hushed;
only the autumn moon on the river's heart, white and bright.
Pondering, she tucked the pick back among the strings;
she straightened her garments and rose, composing her expression.
She said, "I was once a girl of the capital,
my home was by Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name was listed first in the Music Academy.
When my playing ended, even the masters were subdued;
when I made myself up, even the beauties of the season were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts;
for one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Jeweled combs and silver hairpins beat time till they shattered,
my blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed by unheeded.
My younger brother went off to the army, my aunt died;
night followed day, and my beauty faded.
Before my gate, carriages and horses grew sparse;
growing old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and thinks lightly of parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, and I guard an empty boat by the river,
the boat circled by bright moonlight and cold river water.
In the deep of night I suddenly dream of my youth;
in the dream I weep, my rouge-streaked tears staining my pillow.
"I had already sighed when I heard the pipa;
now hearing these words, I sighed again and again.
We both are people who have fallen to the ends of the earth;
why must we have known each other before to meet like this?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished and ill, I dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
all year round I hear no sound of strings and flutes.
I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thickly around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in sorrow.
On spring river days with flowers, on autumn moonlit nights,
often I fetch wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard on the ears.
Tonight I heard your pipa's voice;
it was like hearing immortal music, my ears for a moment made clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song;
for you I will turn this into a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
then she sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
Sorrowful, unlike the sound before;
all who heard it again wept, covering their faces.
Among the guests, whose tears fell the most?
The Jiangzhou司马, his blue robe soaked through."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "A Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a guest off on a night in autumn; maples and reeds rustled in the chill.
I dismounted while my guest boarded the boat; we raised our cups to drink, but there was neither zither nor string.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in gloom; at parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa; the host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing; the pipa ceased, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show herself; we added wine, relit the lantern, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged, still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times; before the tune was formed, feeling was already there.
String after string, suppressed and brooding, note after note, full of thought, as if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, at her ease, she played on and on, telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and then picking, first she played "Rainbow Skirt" and then "Six Yao."
The low strings roared like a sudden rain; the high strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, mixed together, like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers, or a hidden stream choking under ice.
The icy spring ran cold and the strings grew stiff and snapped; the snap blocked the flow, and the sound paused for a while.
A secret sorrow and a hidden resentment arose; at that moment, silence was better than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly bursting, water gushing forth, or armored cavalry charging out with swords and spears clanging.
At the song's end, she swept the pick across the center of the instrument; the four strings cried out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and hushed; only the autumn moon in mid-river shone white.
Musing, she tucked the pick among the strings, straightened her garments, rose, and composed her countenance.
She said: "I was once a girl of the capital, living at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa, and my name topped the roll of the First Division of the Teaching Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the master musicians were impressed; when I dressed up, I was envied by every famous courtesan.
The young blades of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts; for one song, I received countless red silks.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat; blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song, the autumn moons and spring breezes passed by in vain.
Then my younger brother went off to war, my aunt died, and day by day my youth and beauty faded.
Before my gate, carriages and horses grew few and cold; in my old age, I married a merchant.
But merchants value profit and think lightly of parting; last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone on the empty boat at the river's mouth; around me, the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth; in the dream I weep, and my tears streak my rouge."
I had already sighed on hearing the pipa; hearing her words, I sighed again and again.
We are both people fallen at the ends of the earth; why must we have known each other before to meet like this!
Since last year I took leave of the imperial capital, I have lain sick in exile in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music; all year I have not heard the sound of strings.
I live near the Pen River in low, damp ground; yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
From morning to dusk, what do I hear there? Only the cuckoo's bloody cries and the gibbon's mournful wails.
On spring river flower-mornings and autumn moon-nights, I often fetch wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? Their crude, jarring notes are hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, it was like hearing celestial music; my ears were briefly restored.
Do not refuse; sit and play another song, and I will compose "A Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence, then sat back and tightened the strings, which grew more urgent.
Sadder and sadder, unlike the sound before, everyone in the seats wept again as they listened.
Who wept the most among the audience? The Assistant Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "A Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang River's edge, on an autumn night, seeing off a guest—
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the chill.
I dismounted from my horse while my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no lute or strings were there.
Drunk, yet not cheered, we prepared to part in sorrow—
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Seeking the sound, I softly asked who played;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
Only after a thousand calls and entreaties did she come out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings—two or three notes;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already there.
String after string, muted and brooding, note after note full of longing,
As if telling of a lifetime of unfulfilled hopes.
With lowered brows, casually she went on playing,
Pouring out all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
The big strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like secrets told.
Roaring and whispering, tangled in play—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding slickly among the flowers,
Like a muffled stream struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings stiffened and snapped,
Snapped and blocked, the sound for a while ceased.
A separate sorrow, a hidden resentment was born—
At that moment, silence surpassed all sound.
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water gushing forth,
Armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the pick across the center of the strings;
The four strings at once, like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all were silent—
Only the autumn moon, white, was seen in the river's heart.
Pondering, she tucked the pick among the strings;
Adjusted her garments, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name headed the rolls of the First Division of the Academy.
When I finished a song, even the master musicians were impressed;
When I made myself up, the courtesans envied me.
The young blades of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received silks beyond counting.
Ornate combs of silver beat time till they broke;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy followed joy, year after year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed without notice.
Then my younger brother went to war, my aunt died;
Evenings went, mornings came, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
Merchants prize profit and lightly bear separation—
Last month he floated to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I guard the empty boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youthful days,
In the dream I weep, my makeup streaked with tears down my cheeks."
I had sighed upon hearing the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeply moved.
Both of us are people lost at the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I took leave of the imperial capital,
Banished and ailing, I lie in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, a low, damp place;\nYellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On flower-viewing spring days or moonlit autumn nights,
I often fetch wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
It is like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly cleared.
Please do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
For you, I shall compose "A Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
Sadder and more plaintive than the sound before,
The whole assembly, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Who wept the most among those present?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, whose blue gown was soaked."}"}

Hardship and bitter resentment crown my temples with frost,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a guest off one night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest boarded his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but no lute or string.
Drunk without joy, we grieved at our parting,
As the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound—
The host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his sail.
Following the sound, we asked softly: who plays?
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats near and invited her to appear,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings, three or two notes—
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string muffled with longing, each note steeped in thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled dreams.
Brow lowered, she played on casually,
Pouring out all the endless matters in her heart.
Gently gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and plucking,
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Yao.'
The large strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, strummed in tangled mix,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth among the flowers,
Or a spring choked under ice, hard to flow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings stiffened and snapped,
Frozen, impassable, the sound paused for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—
At that moment, silence was more than sound.
Then a silver vase burst, water gushing forth,
Iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she drew the pick across the center,
Four strings at once, like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all was silent and hushed—
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river.
Thoughtfully she put the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, rose, and composed her face.
She said: 'I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was below Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name headed the foremost troupe at court.
After each song, even masters were impressed;
When dressed, even beauties envied me.
The young gallants of Wuling vied to shower me with gifts,
For one song, countless scarves of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat,
Crimson skirts were stained and spoiled by spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed by at ease.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dusk turned to dawn, and my youthful looks faded.
Before my door, carriages grew cold, horses few;
Aging, I married a merchant.
He values profit, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone on the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth,
And woke weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face.'
I had sighed already hearing the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again and again.
Both of us are people lost at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to know this sorrow?
Since last year I bade farewell to the capital,
Demoted and ill, I lie in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no fine music—
All year I hear no lute or string.
I live near the river, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On spring river mornings, autumn moonlit nights,

At Xunyang River's edge, I saw a guest off one night,
Where maples and reeds shivered in autumn's pale light.
The host dismounted; the guest boarded his boat.
We raised our cups, but no lute or flute played a note.
Drunk without joy, we mourned our parting soon;
The river, vast and misty, bathed in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice did sound—
The host forgot to leave; the guest, his boat unbound.
We sought the song, softly asking, "Who plays there?"
The music stopped, as if hesitant to share.
We moved our boat near, invited her to appear,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted once more.
After much calling, she at last came into sight,
Holding her pipa, half hiding her face from the light.
She tuned her strings, plucking a few notes with care—
Before the melody, an emotion hung in the air.
Each string, suppressed, carried a sigh,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled high.
Brow low, she played at ease, her fingers flowing,
Telling of countless things her heart kept storing.
Light strokes and slow kneads, a pluck and then a toss,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Song of Six Degrees" across.
Low strings roared like sudden rain;
High strings whispered in soft strain.
A chaos of sounds, a tangle of tune,
Like pearls, big and small, on a jade plate strewn.
Oriole songs sliding smooth beneath the flowers;
A spring's choked flow trapped under icy bowers.
The ice-cold spring froze the strings to a halt,
The sound stuck, and silence took over the vault.
A hidden sorrow, a dark resentment grew—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound could do.
Then a silver vase burst, water gushing free;
An iron cavalry charged, clashing spear and quiver's plea.
The tune ended; a stroke down the center did fly,
Four strings snapped at once, like silk torn from the sky.
Boats east and west fell silent, no word to be said,
Only the autumn moon, white, in the river's bed.
She sank into thought, tucked her pick among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, rose, and composed her face's wings.
"I was once a girl from the capital's heart,
Lived by Hama Hill, where the river starts.
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Ranked first in the Music Bureau's part.
My finished songs made even masters bow,
My beauty made the jealous maidens vow.
Young men of Wuling fought to shower me with silk,
One song brought red gauze, a countless, rich bulk.
Hairpins and combs beat time till they broke;
Wine stained my crimson skirts, a passionate soak.
Year after year, laughter and light,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed without fight.
My brother left for war; my aunt passed away,
Dawn turned to dusk, and youth began to sway.
Before my gate, carriages grew sparse and cold,
I married, in my years, a merchant, old.
He valued profit over our embrace,
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang for tea's grace.
I guard this empty boat by the river's mouth,
Around it, the moon shines bright, the water's cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth's bright days,
Wake crying, my makeup streaked with tears' red haze.

I sighed at her pipa, and sighed again at her tale,
Both of us, drifters at the edge of the sky, pale.
Why must we have met, when we're both so lost?
We need no past acquaintance to count the cost.

I left the capital last year, exiled to this sickbed,
Washed up in Xunyang, where the river's spread.
Xunyang is remote, no music to hear,
All year, not a string or flute's note draws near.
I live by the river, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo around my camp.
What do I hear, dawn and dusk, but the cuckoo's cry,
And gibbons' mournful howl, as the days go by?
On spring days with flowers, autumn nights with moon,
I often take my wine, and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?\nThey're harsh and grating, not worth the roots.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's words so clear,
It's like celestial music, making my ears brighten.
Don't refuse—sit, and play one more song for me,
And I'll compose a "Song of the Pipa" for thee.

Moved by my words, she stood long in her place,
Then sat back, quickened her strings with haste.
The sound was mournful, unlike the tune before,
All present, hearing it again, wept to the core.
Who wept the most among us, sitting there?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with care."}

By the Xunyang River I bid my guest farewell that night,
The maples and reeds rustle in autumn's chilling light.
I dismounted; my friend stood aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but no music did we note.
Drunk without joy, we grieved at the parting's brink,
As the vast river swallowed the moon's reflection's brink.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's strain,
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot the plain.
We sought the sound, softly asked who played,
The music stopped; she hesitated, afraid.
We moved our boat near, invited her to show,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and the feast began to glow.
After a thousand calls, at last she came out,
Still hugging her pipa, half her face hid in doubt.
She tuned the strings, plucked two or three notes,
Before a melody formed, emotion already floats.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought,
As if telling of a life of battles fought.
Brow low, fingers skilled, she played on and on,
Recounting endless tales of what was gone.
She plucked and strummed, pressed and flicked with grace,
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Yao' to take its place.
The large strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like a private pain.
The loud and soft, a tangled weave,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on jade, you'd believe.
Like orioles singing smoothly in the flowers,
Then choking like a spring trapped under icy bowers.
Ice-cold, the strings grew stiff and still,
The sound congealed, a pause against our will.
A hidden sorrow, a secret pain arose,
In that silence, more than any music, it spoke of woes.
Then, like a silver vase breaking, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clash forth.
With a final sweep across the strings' heart,
A sound like tearing silk, the music tore apart.
In the east and west boats, all were silent, hushed,

She tucked her pick among the strings with a sigh,
Straightened her clothes, and with a solemn look, drew nigh.

My home was by Toad Hill, in the bustling town.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,

After my songs, even masters bowed in awe;
My beauty, once adorned, made the famous courtesans feel raw.
The dandies of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk my spirit lifts.
We beat time with jeweled combs till they broke in the fray,
Our blood-red skirts stained with the wine we spilled that day.
Joy followed joy, year after year,
The autumn moon and spring wind passed without a care.
My brother went to war; my aunt passed away,
As days and nights wore on, my youthful looks decay.
Before my door, the carriages grew few,
An old woman, I married a merchant, what could I do?
He values profit, holds light our separation's sting,
Last month, to Fuliang he went to buy tea's offering.
Alone at the river's mouth, I guard an empty boat,
Around it, the bright moon, the cold water afloat.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youthful days,
I wake weeping, my makeup streaked in crimson ways."

To hear your tale, my heart is doubly wrung.
Both of us, lost souls at the edge of the sky,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "A Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a guest off one night,
Where reeds and maple leaves rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no lute or harp played.
Drunk, yet not merry, we parted in sorrow,
As the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa—
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who played;
The pipa stopped, as if reluctant to speak.
We moved our boat near and invited her to appear;\nAdded wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and entreaties, she finally came,
Still half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the strings, plucked them a few times—
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, was stifled with longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled dreams.
Brow lowered, she played on with practiced ease,
Revealing the endless sorrows in her heart.
Lightly strumming, slowly picking, first "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao":
The large strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whispered like secret talk.
Loud and soft, fast and slow, they intertwined—
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smoothly beneath flowers,
Or a spring choked with ice, struggling to flow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze, then broke—
Held in that silence, a pause in the sound.
From that silent void, hidden sorrow and resentment rose—
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then, like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth,
Or an iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing!
At the song's end, she swept her pick across the strings—
All four strings snapped at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all sat in hushed silence,
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, white and bright.
She pondered, slid her pick into the strings,
Adjusted her robes, composed her features, and spoke:
"I was once a girl from the capital,
My home was near Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name topped the First Division of the Teaching Bureau.
My playing once made even the finest musicians bow,
My beauty often made other courtesans jealous.
The young nobles of Wuling vied to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless rolls of red silk.
Ornaments and silver combs shattered as we beat time,
My blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy followed joy, year after year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed without care.
Then my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
As days turned to nights, my youth began to fade.
Before my door, carriages grew rare, visitors few;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
But merchants value profit, not love; he seldom stays—
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my tears tracing red lines down my face."

I sighed when I heard her pipa;
Hearing her story, I sighed again.\
We are both wanderers at the world's edge—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished and ill, I live in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
Year-round, I hear no strings or pipes.
I live near the river, in low, damp ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What do I hear, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in sorrow.
On flower-filled spring days or moonlit autumn nights,
I often pour my wine and drink alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
They are harsh and grating, impossible to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It is like celestial music; my ears are refreshed.
Do not refuse—sit and play once more,
And I will compose "A Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, quickened the tempo—the strings grew urgent.
The mournful notes were not like the song before;
All present, hearing it again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among us wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

By Bai Juyi

---

Night at Xunyang River, seeing off a guest—
maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn rustling.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat.
He raises his cup to drink, but pipa and strings are wanting.
Drunk, not merry, they grieve at parting—
and as they part, the vast river fills with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa—
the host forgets to go home, the guest delays his departure.
Seeking the sound, he asks softly: "Who plays?"
The pipa falls silent; she hesitates to answer.
They move their boat nearer, invite her out;
more wine is brought, lamps relit, the banquet begins again.

After a thousand calls she finally appears,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She twists the pegs, plucks the strings a few times—
yet before the tune takes shape, feeling is already there.
String after string, muted and sighing, note after note full of longing,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.

Head bowed, unhurried, she plays on,
telling all the heart's unbounded sorrows.
Light pressing, slow rolling, sweeping, picking—
first a piece of Rainbow Skirts, then of Six Yao.
The great strings roar like driving rain,
the small strings whisper like private talk.
Roar and whisper, clashing and mingling—
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.

Then a warbler's song, smooth over the flowers,
then a choked spring, struggling under ice.
The ice-cold spring stifles; the strings grow stiff,
stiff, blocked—and for a moment, sound is gone.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, rises:
in that silence, more is said than by any sound.

Then—like a silver vase bursting, water spouting forth,
like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing—
the tune ends with a sweep across the center;
four strings at once, like tearing silk.

In boats east and west, all is silent and still;
one sees only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.
Pondering, she tucks the pick among the strings,
straightens her robes, rises, and composes her face.

"I was a girl of the capital," she says,
"my home was below Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name headed the rolls of the Academy.
When I finished a song, even the finest players admired me;
when I dressed up, even the famous beauties were jealous.
Young bloods of the Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts—
for one song, bolts of red silk beyond counting.

"Tinkling headpins and silver combs beat time till they broke;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Smiles and laughter, year after year,
autumn moons and spring winds, squandered easily.
Then my brother left for the army, my aunt died;
day by day my youth and beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew few, the horses sparse;
growing old, I married a merchant.

"The merchant cares for profit more than parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river's mouth in an empty boat;
around it, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Deep in the night I dream of my youth,
wake weeping, my rouge-streaked tears staining the railings."

---

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
Both of us are lost souls at the edge of the world—
why must we have met before to meet now?

Since last year I took leave of the imperial city,
exiled and ailing, I lie here in Xunyang.
This place is remote; there is no music here—
all year I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What sounds fill my days and nights?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.

On flower-filled spring mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are grating, shrill, impossible to listen to.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's voice,
it is like hearing immortal music—my ears come alive.

Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
and I will compose for you this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
then sits back, quickens the strings—and they grow urgent.
Sadder, sadder than any sound before;
the whole room hears it again, and weeps silently.
Who weeps the most among us all?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}
