At Xunyang River, on an autumn night, I was seeing off a guest—
maple leaves and reed flowers shivering in the cool.
My host had dismounted; the guest was aboard.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet not enjoying ourselves, gloomily we prepared to part—
and at parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
My host forgot to go home; the guest delayed his departure.
We sought the sound and softly asked: who is playing?
The pipa paused, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
we added wine, relit the lamps, and once more set the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand urgings she finally emerged,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes;
before a tune was formed, it was already full of feeling.
Every string, choked and muted, every note steeped in longing,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, idly, she went on playing,
saying all the countless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then picking—
first she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Minor Rounds."
The large strings murmured, rushing like sudden rain;
the small strings whispered, like intimate talk.
The rush and the whisper, tangled and interlarded,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers;
then, like a hidden stream choking under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and snapped—
snapped and blocked, the sound stopped for a while.
In that pause, secret sorrows and hidden griefs were born—
in that moment, silence spoke more than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
like armored cavalry charging out, blades and spears ringing—
At the end of the song she swept the拨 across the center of the strings;
four strings at once, like a bolt of silk being torn.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and hushed—
only the autumn moon, white at the center of the river.

Thoughtfully she put the拨 back among the strings,
adjusted her garments and rose with a composed expression.
She said: "I was once a girl of the capital,
living near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters would be impressed;
when I made myself up, the courtesans would be jealous.
The young gallants of Wuling would vie to lavish gifts—
for a single song, countless bolts of red silk.
Ornaments and silver combs snapped as we beat time;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
the autumn moons and spring breezes passed in idle ease.
Then my brother left for the army, my aunt died;
night gave way to morning, and my beauty faded.
Before my gate, carriages grew few, horses sparse;
grown old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I keep a empty boat at the river's mouth,
the bright moon all around the boat, the river water cold.
In the deep night I suddenly dream of my youth,
and wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face."

I had sighed already at the pipa's song;
hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth—
why must we have met before, to understand each other now?
Since last year I took leave of the capital,
and came, ill and demoted, to dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music—
all year I have not heard the sound of strings.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower-moon spring days or autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to bear.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
was like hearing celestial music—my ears were given light.
Do not refuse; sit, and play one more song,
and for you I will compose "A Song of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
then sat back, tightened the strings, and they grew faster.
Sorrowful, sorrowful, not like the earlier sound—
the whole company, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
And among us all, who wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears.

By Bai Juyi

One night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse, my guest took his place on the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to be heard.
Drunk yet not happy, we grieved at our impending parting;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped; she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties she finally emerged,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before a tune was formed, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and brooding, full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered eyes, at ease, she played on and on,
Telling all the boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and plucking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Little Branch."
The low strings roared like a sudden downpour;
The high strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, intertwined and mixed,
Like large and small pearls dropping on a jade plate.\nThen, like orioles gliding smoothly among flowers,
Or a spring choked with ice, its flow made slow.
The ice-cold spring, the strings grew numb and snapped;
The sound, blocked and broken, paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment welled up;
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Or iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The song ended; with a sweep of the拨 across the center,
All four strings burst as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and hushed;
Only the autumn moon, white, was seen in the middle of the river.
Pensively she tucked the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusted her garments, rose, and composed her countenance.
She said: "I was once a girl from the capital,
My home was by Hama Ling.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
When my makeup was done, the beauties envied me.
The young men of Wuling competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
Ornamental combs and silver hairpins were smashed to keep time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained and spoiled by spilled wine.
Year after year of joy and laughter,
The spring moons and autumn winds passed by in vain.
My younger brother left for the army, my aunt died;
As days and months went by, my youth faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse and cold;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and lightly bore separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I guard the empty boat by the river mouth;
Around the boat, the bright moon, the river water cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youthful days;
In my dream, I weep, my tears streaking my rouge."

"Hearing your pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing your words, I sighed again and again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have met before for this encounter?"

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
I have been exiled and ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year round, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons howling mournfully.
On spring river flower-mornings, autumn moon-nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
It is like hearing immortal music; my ears are suddenly enlightened.
Do not refuse; sit and play once more,
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
The sorrowful notes were unlike the earlier sound;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept into their hands.
Among the seated, whose tears fell the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."}

By Bai Juyi

One night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieved at our parting;
As we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show herself;
We refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and set the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Every string was muted, every note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
With lowered eyes, carelessly she played on,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
The big strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like private talk.
The roaring and whispering were interwoven,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers,
Like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and stopped;
The frozen stream ran no more, and the sound paused for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose;
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water gushing out,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears ringing.
At the song's end she swept the拨 across the center of the strings;
The four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent and hushed;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart could be seen, white.
Thoughtfully she put the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusted her garments, rose, and composed her countenance.
She said: "I was once a girl from the capital,
My home was near Homa Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the skilled musicians admired me;
When I dressed up, even the famous courtesans envied me.
The young gallants of Wuling competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Ornate combs and silver hairpins were broken to keep time;
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Evenings went and mornings came, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit and cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, leaving me to guard an empty boat;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep, my tears staining my rouge in streaks."
I had sighed already at the pipa's music;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeply moved.
We are both wanderers at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have met before to understand each other?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
I have lived in exile, ill, in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I have not heard the sound of strings.
I live near the Pan River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons mourning.
On spring river days with flowers, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight I heard your pipa's song;
It was like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly enlightened.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
For you, I will compose a "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and they grew faster.
The mournful notes were not like the ones before;
The whole company, hearing it again, wept into their hands.
Among us all, who wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

I was seeing a guest off one night at the Xunyang River;
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse; the guest was on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to toast by.
Drunk, yet far from merry, we were about to part in gloom—
when we parted, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly came the sound of a pipa from the water;
the host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to leave.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped; she hesitated to answer.
We shifted the boat nearer and invited her to meet us,
added wine, relit the lanterns, and laid out the feast again.
Only after a thousand entreaties did she come out,
half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
before a melody formed, feeling was already there.
Every string was pressed down in sorrow, every note full of longing,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, idly she went on playing,
saying all the countless things her heart held.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and flicking,
first she played "Rainbow Skirt and Feather Coat," then "Six Small Ones."
On the thick strings, a roar like sudden rain;
on the thin strings, a whisper like private speech.
The roar and whisper tangled and crossed—
large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then notes slipped like orioles singing under flowers,
then choked like a spring frozen under ice.
The icy spring grew cold; the strings congealed and stilled,
and when they stilled, the sound broke off.
A secret sorrow, a hidden bitterness rose—
then, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the song's end she swept the pick across all four strings
—like the tearing of silk.
In boats east and west, all was silent;
only the autumn moon on the river's heart shone white.
Thoughtfully she put the pick back among the strings,
straightened her clothes, and rose with a solemn face.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital once,
living near Homa Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the finest players were humbled;
when I dressed up, even the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts—
one song, and I could not count the bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped in time, broken;
wine-stained my blood-red silk skirts.
Year after year of laughter and revelry,
the autumn moon and spring wind passed by unheeded.
My younger brother went off to war; my aunt died.
Seasons turned, and my beauty faded.
Fewer horses tied before my door;
grown old, I married a merchant.
But merchants value profit over parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I guard the empty boat at the river's mouth,
surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth,
and wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face."

I had sighed already at the pipa's song;
hearing her story, I sighed again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
why must we have known each other before to meet like this?
Since last year I left the capital,
banished and sick, I've lain in Xunyang.
This place is remote—no music here;
all year I've heard no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.

Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
and I will turn it into a "Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood a long while,
then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Nothing like her earlier music—
everyone in the room wept again.
Who wept the most among the listeners?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue gown was soaked."}"}

By Bai Juyi


By the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off on an autumn night,
The maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the chilly light.
The host dismounted, the guest was aboard his boat;
He raised his cup to drink—but no lute or pipe played a note.
Drunk without joy, in sorrow we prepared to part,
When the vast river drowned the moon and pierced the heart.
Then, from the water, came the sound of a pipa’s strings—
The host forgot to leave; the guest stayed for the music it brings.
We asked in whispers who played the sound;
The music stopped, and she hesitated, as if afraid to be found.
We moved our boat near hers and invited her to meet;
Poured more wine, relit the lamps, and held our feast anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally appeared,
Still hiding half her face behind the pipa she revered.


She tuned the pegs, plucked a note or two;
Before the melody formed, emotion already shone through.
Each string, muted and lingering, sang a sigh,
As if telling of a life where dreams were denied.
With lowered eyes, she played on, unhurried and free,
Telling of the endless things her heart held in fee.
Light touching, slow twisting, sweeping and plucking with care,
First “Rainbow Garment,” then “Six Minor” filled the air.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like secrets in pain.
The roar and whisper tangled in one song,
Like pearls, great and small, on a jade plate falling along.\nLike orioles gliding in flowers, smooth and bright,
Or a spring choked with ice, struggling in the night.
The cold spring froze, the strings could not vibrate;
The sound stopped, but silence spoke—what words could relate?
Then a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment, was born;
The silence at that moment spoke more than sound ever could adorn.
Suddenly, a silver vase shattered, water burst free,
Armored riders charged, swords and spears clashing in glee.
At the song’s end, she swept the plectrum across the strings’ heart,
Four strings rang as one—like silk being torn apart.
The boats around fell silent, no one made a sound;
Only the autumn moon on the river’s heart could be found.


She sank into thought, tucked the plectrum among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, stood up, and composed her countenance as she sings:
"I am a girl from the capital, it is true,
My home was at the foot of Hama Hill, where I grew.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art,
Ranked first in the Music Bureau, the finest part.
My songs could make even the best players bow,
And when I dressed up, Qiu Niang would envy, I vow.
The young men of Wuling fought to give me gifts,
One song earned me countless red silks, no limits.
Ornaments and silver combs broke as I beat time,
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with wine, no crime.
Year after year, laughter and joy were my share,
The autumn moon and spring wind passed without a care.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt died away,
Days turned to nights, and my youth began to decay.
Fewer horses stopped at my door, my fame grew thin;
Old, I married a merchant, my life turned to sin.
He values profit over love, and leaves me forlorn;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, gone.
I wait alone by the river in my empty boat,
The moon shines bright around me, the river is cold as I float.
In the deep night, I dream of my youthful days,
Wake crying, my tears staining my rouge in hazy ways."


I sighed when I heard her pipa, and sighed again at her tale;
We are both wanderers at the world’s end—why did we meet, what a strange trail!
I left the capital last year, demoted and ill,
Lodging in Xunyang, a place with no music to fill.
Xunyang is remote, with no lute or pipe to hear,
All year, I’ve never heard a stringed note, only fear.
I live near the river, low and damp, where I dwell;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my cell.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk, night and day?
Only the cuckoo’s cry and the ape’s mournful lay.
On flower-filled spring days and moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone in the heights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to hear?\nTheir crude sounds are harsh, and give me only despair.
Tonight, I heard your pipa’s song, so clear and bright,
Like listening to celestial music, my ears took flight.
Please do not refuse; sit and play one more tune,
I will write a song for you, “Song of the Pipa,” a boon.
Moved by my words, she stood still for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played with a smile.
The melody was sadder than all that came before;
The whole audience wept, their tears falling to the floor.
Who wept the most among all the people there?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with care."}

By the Xunyang River I saw a guest off on an autumn night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted from my horse while the guest boarded his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow—
At parting, the river was vast, drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
We followed the sound and asked softly who was playing;
When the pipa stopped, she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us;
We refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and feasted again.
Only after a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties did she emerge,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings—two or three sounds;
Before the tune was formed, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, suppressed and brooding, full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, carelessly she played on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, strumming, then picking—
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like intimate talk.
Loud and soft, clashing and mingling, played together—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers;
Like a choked spring flowing, trapped beneath ice.
The cold spring froze, the strings stiffened and snapped;
The sound jammed and stopped, silenced for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then suddenly a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth;\nArmored cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing.
At the end of the song, she swept the拨 (pick) across the center;
The four strings, as one, sounded like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were silent, without a word;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, white.
Pondering, she tucked the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her countenance.
She spoke: "I am from the capital, I lived beneath Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, my name was first in the Music Academy.
After a song, even the finest players were impressed;
When I dressed up, even the beauties were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
Ornaments and silver combs beat time until they broke;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained and spoiled by wine.
Joy and laughter were renewed year after year;
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed by in vain.
My younger brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dawn to dusk, dusk to dawn, my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew cold and sparse;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and lightly parts from his wife;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I guard the empty boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
I wake weeping, the tears on my makeup streaking my face."

Now, hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?"

Demoted and ailing, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year round, I hear no string or wind instruments.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.

On the Xunyang Riverbank at night I was seeing off a guest;

maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn haze.

I dismounted; my guest boarded his boat.

We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.

Drunk without pleasure, gloomily we were about to part—

The pipa stopped, and a voice hesitated to reply.

I moved my boat nearer, invited her to show herself;

more wine, lamps relit, the feast spread again.

After a thousand calls she at last came out,

still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.



She turned the pegs, plucked the strings—two or three sounds;

before a tune took shape, feeling was already there.

Each string, each note, was stifled, brooding, full of thought,

as if telling a life of thwarted ambition.

Brow lowered, carelessly her fingers went on playing,

telling all the endless things within her heart.

Light gathering, slow twisting, sweeping and picking,

first the Rainbow Skirt, then the Song of Six Beats.



The thick strings clattered like driving rain;

the thin strings whispered like private talk.

Clattering and whispering, tangled together,

like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.

Then orioles fluting smoothly under the flowers,

then a choked spring struggling under ice.

The icy spring grew cold, the strings stiffened and snapped;

snapped and blocked, the sound paused for a while.

A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—

in that moment, silence said more than sound.

Then a silver bottle broke and water burst forth;

iron cavalry charged, swords and spears ringing.

The song ended: a sweep of the拨 across the middle;

four strings at once, like tearing silk.

Boats east and west were silent, hushed;

only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.



Thoughtfully she tucked the拨 among the strings,

straightened her clothes, rose, composed her features.

She said she was a girl of the capital,

whose home lay under Hama Hill.

At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,

her name listed first in the Music Academy.

When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;

when she dressed up, the court beauties envied her.

Young bloods of the Five Tombs vied to shower her with gifts;

for one song she'd get countless bolts of red silk.

Silver combs broken time and again to keep the beat,

crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.



Year after year of laughter and song,

autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.

Then her brother went to war, her aunt died;

day followed night, and her beauty faded.

Before her door, carriages grew few, horses sparse;

growing old, she married a merchant.

The merchant prized profit, thought little of parting;

last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,

the moon bright around her, the river water cold.

Deep in the night she suddenly dreams of her youth;

Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth—

I live near the Pen River, low and damp,

By Bai Juyi

On the Xunyang River bank at night I saw a friend off,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse; my guest stepped in his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to be heard.
Drunk, yet without joy, in gloom we prepared to part—
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked, “Who plays?”
The pipa stopped; she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerged,
Still clasping her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings three or two times—
Before a tune was formed, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note was muted and brooding, full of thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled desires.
With lowered brows, carelessly she played on and on,
Pouring out all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Yao.”
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, all interwoven—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.\nLike orioles gliding smoothly over flowers,
Or a choked spring trickling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
The break blocked the sound, and for a while it ceased.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment welled up—
The silence at that moment was more eloquent than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly smashing, water bursting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clanging.
At the song’s end, she drew the pick across the center of the strings;
The four strings together cried out like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all sat in hushed silence,
Only the autumn moon in the river’s heart, white and bright.
Musing, she tucked the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her garments, and rose with solemn mien.
She spoke: “I was once a girl from the capital,
My home was near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name headed the rolls of the Teaching Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the finest players were humbled;
When I dressed up, Qiu Niang herself was jealous of my beauty.
The young men of Wuling vied to shower me with gifts—
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Ornamented combs and silver hairpins were smashed to pieces as we beat time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained and spoiled by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and gaiety,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by with ease.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Dusk came and dawn went, and my youthful looks faded.
Before my door, carriages grew cold and horses sparse;
Old at last, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and cares little for parting:
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
The bright moon circles the boat, the river water is cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youthful days;
In the dream I weep, and my rouge-streaked tears streak my face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed already;
Hearing these words, I sighed again and again.
We are both lost souls at the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet and feel this kinship?
Since last year I bade farewell to the capital,
Banished here, sick in bed, in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote and has no music—
All year I have not heard the sounds of strings and flutes.
I live near the Pen River, the land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What can one hear here, morning and night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower-filled spring days or moonlit autumn nights,
Often I take my wine and drink alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
Their harsh, grating notes are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s song,
It is like hearing celestial music—my ears are blessed.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
And I will compose a ‘Song of the Pipa’ for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings—the music turned urgent.
Sad and sharp, it was not like the sounds before;
The whole assembly, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Among the guests, whose tears fell most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou—his blue gown was wet with weeping."}

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted, my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or string.
Drunk yet not merry, we were saddened at the parting;
The parting hour, the vast river drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, we asked in whispers who was playing;
The music stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat near hers and invited her to meet;
More wine was brought, lamps relit, the feast renewed.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand pleas, she finally emerged,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, a few sounds;
Before the tune began, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, suppressed and longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, she played on, her fingers moving freely,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Light strumming, slow rubbing, sweeping and picking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Minor*.
The low strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The high strings whispered like private talk.
Mingling the roar and the whisper, she played them together,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
The notes flowed smoothly like orioles singing under the flowers,
Then choked like a spring trapped beneath the ice.
The cold, astringent ice-water froze the strings silent;
The frozen strings, the sound blocked, paused for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, rose in its place;
In that moment, silence was more powerful than sound.
Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end, she swept her pick across the center of the strings,
The four strings together cracked like a torn bolt of silk.
In the boats east and west, all were silent and hushed,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river.
Pondering, she tucked her pick into the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home by the Hama Tomb.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Academy.
After a song, even the master pipa players were in awe;
When her makeup was done, even the famous courtesans were envious.
The young blades of Wuling competed to offer her gifts;
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Jeweled combs, silver hairpins, struck in time till they broke;
Blood-red silk skirts stained and spoiled by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter and joy;
Autumn moons and spring winds, passed by without a thought.
My younger brother went off to join the army, my aunt died;
Dusk came, dawn came, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, carriages grew few, visitors scarce;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
The moon shines bright around the boat, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth;
Waking, she weeps, her tears staining the rouge on her cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, in shared lament.
Both of us, castaways at the ends of the earth—
Why must we have met before to understand each other?
I left the capital last year,
Banished to this sickbed in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I have not heard a lute or a flute.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What is there to hear, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons’ mournful wails.
On spring river flower-mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh, discordant, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It is like hearing the music of immortals, my ears cleared.
Do not refuse, sit and play one more song,
And I will compose this *Song of the Pipa* for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Mournful, unlike the sound before,
All who heard it wept, their sleeves wet with tears.
Who wept the most among the listeners?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing a guest off;
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the chill.
I dismounted, my friend took his place on the boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without joy, heavy-hearted at parting,
we watched the vast river swallow the moonlight.
Then, from the water, came the sound of a pipa —
my host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to set sail.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
the music stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show herself,
added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After many calls she finally stepped out,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and strummed a few notes —
before the tune took shape, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each pause, was steeped in thought,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled longing.
Brow lowered, carelessly she kept on playing,
saying all the endless things her heart held.
Light strokes, slow twists, plucks and flicks —
first the Nishang melody, then the Liuyao.
The low strings roared like driving rain,
the high strings whispered like secret talk.
Roar and whisper, mingled and crossed —
like great pearls and small pearls spilling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among blossoms,
like a muffled spring trapped under ice.
The icy spring turned cold, the strings froze and snapped;
snapped and blocked, the sound paused for a while.
A deeper sorrow, a hidden grief rose up —
then, silence was more speak than sound.
Suddenly a silver vase burst, water gushing out;
armored cavalry charged, sabers and lances clashing.
The song ended with a sweep across the strings;
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
All around, boats and cabins were hushed and still —
only the autumn moon on the river, white and bright.
Thoughtfully she put down her pick, tucked it among the strings,
smoothed her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
living near Hama Hill.
I learned the pipa at thirteen,
listed first among the court performers.
When I finished a song, even the master teachers were humbled;
dressed up, I was always envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five tombs competed to lavish gifts;
one song earned me countless bolts of red silk.
Ornamental combs snapped as we beat time;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
autumn moons and spring winds passed without a care.
Then my brother left for the army, my aunt died;
nights gave way to days, and my youth faded.
Horses grew scarce before my door;
old and alone, I married a merchant.
He valued profit more than staying close;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
around me, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth —
I wake weeping, my rouge-streaked face streaked with tears."

I had sighed already at the pipa's song;
hearing her story, I sighed again, deeper still.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world —
why must we have met before to understand each other?
Since last year I left the capital,
exiled and ill in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote and barren of music;
all year I have not heard strings or flutes.
My house is near the low, damp riverbank,
surrounded by reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling mournfully.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,

When dressed up, the beauties envied me.
The young men of Wuling competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
Ornamental combs beat time till they broke;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring wind passed by in vain.
My younger brother went to the army; my aunt died.
Dawn came and dusk went; my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew few, horses rare.
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit, not our parting.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone on the empty boat at the river’s mouth,

Hearing her words, I sigh again.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth—

Living sick and exiled in Xunyang.

All year I hear no strings or flutes.

Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;

We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear;

After a thousand calls she at last came out,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,

Every string, every note, was stifled and full of thought,

Brow lowered, she played on absently,

Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and plucking,

The great strings roared like driving rain,
the small strings whispered like secret talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled and mixed,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then the oriole's song gliding under flowers,
then a choked spring struggling under ice.
The ice-cold spring, the strings grew stiff and broke;

A hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,

Thoughtfully she put the拨 back among the strings,

She spoke: "I was once a girl of the capital,
my home was below Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
when I made myself up, even the belles were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to lavish gifts;
for one song, I knew not how many bolts of red silk.
Silver hairpins snapped in time to the beat,
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
autumn moon and spring breeze passed by in vain.
My younger brother went off to war, my aunt died;
night went, morning came, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew few, horses sparse;
growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I keep the empty boat here at the river's mouth,
surrounded by bright moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth,
waking in tears, my rouge-streaked face streaming."

hearing her words, I sighed again and again.
Both of us are people lost at the edge of the world—
why must we have known each other before we met?

exiled and ill, I live in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
all year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the river, where the ground is low and damp,
reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing.

They are harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech,
and it is like hearing immortal music—my ears at last come alive.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
and I will compose a Song of the Pipa for you.

Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river lay flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances ringing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.
She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the Music Bureau's leading players.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young nobles from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.

By Bai Juyi

I was seeing a guest off one night at the Xunyang River,
where maples rustle and reed-blossoms whisper in the autumn chill.
Dismounting, I led my horse ashore; my guest was already aboard.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to go with it.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grew sad at the thought of parting—
and as we parted, the river spread wide, flooded with moonlight.

Then, suddenly, from out on the water came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home; the guest forgot to set sail.
We followed the music softly and asked, "Who is playing?"
The pipa fell silent, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show her face;
we poured more wine, relit the lamps, and laid the feast again.
After countless calls and entreaties she at last emerged,
still hiding half her face behind the pipa she clutched to her breast.

She turned the pegs, plucked the strings a time or two—
before a melody had formed, feeling was already there.
Every string, every phrase, was weighted with melancholy;
she seemed to be telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
With lowered eyes and an easy hand she played on,
unraveling all the countless things that weighed upon her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, a stroke, then a flick—
first she played the “Rainbow Skirts,” then the “Six Beats.”
The heavy strings roared like driving rain,
the light strings whispered like secret talk.
Roar and whisper, crossing and mingling—
like great pearls and small pearls spilling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
or a choked stream trickling under ice.
The icy spring ran cold, the strings grew stiff and broke;
they broke, the sound could not pass on, and the music paused.
A deeper sorrow, a hidden grief rose in its place—
then, in that silence, more than music spoke.
Then, like a silver vase bursting, water gushing forth,
or armored cavalry charging out, sabers and spears clanging—
she swept the pick across the strings at the heart of the sound,
and all four strings cried out as one, like silk being torn.

In every boat around us, no one stirred, no one spoke;
only the autumn moon, white on the heart of the river, could be seen.
Thoughtfully she tucked the pick back among the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.

She told us: “I was once a girl of the capital,
and lived there by Hama Hill.
I learned to play the pipa when I was thirteen,
and my name stood first in the rolls of the court academy.
When I finished a song, even the finest players would applaud;
when I had dressed and painted, the other beauties envied me.
The dashing young men of the Five Tombs would vie to shower me with gifts—
for a single song, who could count the rolls of red silk they gave?
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat,
and wine stained my crimson skirts.
One year of laughter followed another;
autumn moons and spring breezes passed me by as if for nothing.
Then my younger brother went off to war, my aunt passed away;
night followed day, and with them, my youth.
Before my gate the carriages grew few, the stirrups cold;
and so, in my old age, I married a merchant.
But merchants care for profit more than for parting—
just last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I keep watch over an empty boat,
the moon bright around me, the river cold.
In the deep of night I often dream of those younger days,
and wake weeping, my rouge-streaked makeup running in red lines down my face.”

I had already sighed once at the sound of the pipa;
now, hearing her story, I sighed again and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
why must we have known each other before we could meet like this?

Last year I took my leave of the capital,
and came to live, sick and in disgrace, in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote; there is no music here—
the whole year round I never hear a single string.
My house stands near the river, low and damp,
surrounded by reeds and bitter bamboo.
From dawn to dusk, what sounds are there to hear?
Only the cuckoo crying blood and gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring mornings when flowers bloom, on autumn nights when the moon is bright,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating—too unlovely to bear.
But tonight, hearing your pipa, it was as if celestial music
had made my ears alive again.
Stay, please—sit and play one more song,
and I will compose this ‘Song of the Pipa’ in your honor.

Moved by my words, she stood long without speaking;
then she sat back, tightened her strings, and the tempo quickened.
The new melody, mournful, was nothing like the one before—
and everyone in the boat, hearing it again, covered their face and wept.
And who wept the most of all those gathered there?
The Master of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River's edge I was seeing off a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn light.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or flute to note.
Drunk without joy, we parted in sorrow's gloom;
The river, vast and misty, was steeped in moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest could not depart.
Seeking the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show her face;
We added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Half-hiding her face behind the pipa she held.
She tuned the strings, plucked them a few times;
Before a melody formed, emotion already chimes.
Each string, each note, was steeped in thought and sigh,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled desire.
Eyes down, she played on with effortless grace,
Telling of the endless things in her heart's place.
She plucked and strummed, pressed and swept the strings,
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Minor' she sings.
The thick strings roared like a sudden shower;
The thin strings whispered like a private hour.
Roar and whisper intertwined in the song,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade gong.
Like orioles gliding smoothly over flowers;\Like a muffled spring struggling under icy hours.
The icy spring froze, the strings grew numb;\The sound halted, and silence came.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment was born;
At this moment, silence spoke more than sound could adorn.
Then, like a silver vase bursting, water gushed;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed.
The song ended with a sweep across the strings;
All four strings snapped at once, like tearing silk's wings.
Boats east and west were quiet, no one spoke;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart was seen, white as smoke.
Pensive, she tucked the plectrum among the strings;
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her bearing with stings.
She said, 'I was a girl from the capital's grace,
My home was by Hama Ling, in that place.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
My name was first in the Music Bureau's part.
My songs made even the best musicians bow;
My beauty made the famous courtesans envy my vow.
The young men of Wuling competed to lavish gifts on me;
For one song, I received countless bolts of silk, you see.
Jeweled hairpins broke to the beat of my song;
My blood-red silk skirts were stained with wine before long.
Year after year, I lived in laughter and cheer;
The autumn moons and spring winds passed without a tear.
Then my brother went to war, my aunt passed away;
Day followed night, and my youth began to decay.
Fewer horses stopped at my door, it grew cold;
I married a merchant when I grew old.
The merchant values profit over parting's sting;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea's wing.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone by the river's mouth;
The moonlight circles the boat, the river water is cold, in truth.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youthful days;
I wake crying, my makeup ruined, in red tears' haze.'
I sighed upon hearing her pipa's tale;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, without fail.
Both of us are lost souls at the world's end;
Why must we have known each other before, my friend?
Since last year, I left the capital's bright scene;
Exiled and ill, I lie in Xunyang, between.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to hear;
All year long, no lute or flute reaches my ear.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my camp.
What do I hear morning and evening, day and night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the ape's mournful flight.
On flower-filled spring days and moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone in the heights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to cheer?
They are harsh and grating, impossible to hear.
Tonight, I heard your pipa's speech;
It was like hearing celestial music, my spirit's reach.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song;
For you, I will write 'A Song of the Pipa' to prolong.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played with a smile.
The mournful notes were unlike the sounds before;\The whole audience wept, hearing it once more.
Who among us shed the most tears that night?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet with the water's light."}

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
With maple leaves and reed flowers, the air was crisp and chill.
I dismounted from my horse, he boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no strings or pipes were there.
Drunk but not merry, in sorrow we were about to part—
At the moment of parting, the vast river merged with the moon.
Suddenly we heard pipa music from the water;
The host forgot to return, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated, about to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to appear;
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the banquet.
After a thousand calls and ten entreaties she finally emerged,
Half covering her face with the pipa she held.
She tuned the strings and plucked two or three notes—
Before the melody formed, emotion already arose.
Each string, each phrase, was subdued and deeply thoughtful,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brows lowered, she played on with easy skill,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Lightly plucking, slowly pinching, sweeping and picking—
First she played “Rainbow Skirts,” then “Six Little Ones.”
The big strings roared like sudden rain;
The small strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, intertwined they played—
Like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing beneath the flowers, smooth and swift;
Like a hidden stream flowing under ice, hard to pass.
The icy spring grew cold and the strings stiffened and broke;\nWhen they broke and could not pass, the sound paused for a while.
A separate sorrow and hidden resentment arose—
In that moment, silence surpassed all sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly smashed, water bursting forth;
Like armored cavalry charging out, blades and spears clashing.
At the song’s end she swept the拨 across the center;
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
Across boats and cabins, all were silent and still;
Only the autumn moon on the river’s heart, white and bright.
She pondered, put away the拨, tucked it into the strings;
Adjusted her clothes and stood with solemn grace.
She said: “I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Academy.
When my songs ended, even the finest musicians admired me;
When my makeup was done, the beauties envied me.
The young nobles of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
One song earned me countless bolts of red silk.\nI beat time with my ornate comb until it broke;
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The spring moons and autumn breezes passed in vain.
Then my brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Day and night passed, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew rare and cold;
In old age I married a merchant.
But merchants value profit and lightly part from their wives;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I guard the empty boat at the river’s mouth;
Around the boat, bright moon and cold water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, my tears staining my rouge.”
Hearing this pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again and again.
Both of us are lost souls at the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Ill and confined, I dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year I hear no strings or pipes.
My home is near the low, wet banks of the Pan River;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my dwelling.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons mourning.
On spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moon,
Often I take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears briefly awaken.
Do not refuse—sit and play another song;
For you, I will compose this “Song of the Pipa.”
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back and tightened the strings, the tempo quickened.
The melancholy was not like the sound before;
The whole assembly, hearing it again, wept with hands covering faces.
Among the guests, whose tears fell the most?
The River District Marshal, his blue robe soaked through."}

By Bai Juyi

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing a guest off,
Where maples and reeds rustled in the chill.
I dismounted, my friend boarded the boat;
We raised our cups, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet joyless, we prepared to part—
When the wide river drowned the moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s sound;
The host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his sail.
We followed the tune, softly asking who played;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face;
We refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls she finally emerged,
Still hiding half her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the strings, plucked a few notes—
Before the melody, feeling already spoke.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled dreams.
Brows lowered, fingers wandered on,
Telling all the heart’s endless tales.
Light gathering, slow twisting, brushing, plucking—
First the “Rainbow Skirt,” then the “Six Yao.”
The great strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like secret talk.
Roars and whispers interlaced,
Like pearls, big and small, falling on jade plates.
Then warbling like orioles gliding over flowers,
Then choked like a spring beneath ice.
The icy spring freezes, the strings snap tight—
Sound and sense both pause, a silence deep.
In that quiet, hidden sorrows rise—
Sometimes, silence speaks more than sound.\nThen a silver vase shatters, water bursts;
Armored riders charge, swords and spears clash.
The song ends with a sweep across all strings—
One tearing sound, like silk split apart.
All boats around fell silent;
Only the white autumn moon on the river remained.
She tucked the pick, adjusted her dress, composed her face:
“I was once a girl of the capital,
Living near Hama Hill.
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Court School.
My playing made the masters bow;
My beauty made the court ladies sigh.
The dandies of Wuling competed for my favors;
One song won me silks beyond counting.
Ornaments shattered as we beat time;
Red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
The spring breezes and autumn moons passed by.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt died;
Day by day, my youth faded.
Fewer horses tied before my door;
In age, I married a merchant.
He values profit, not our parting;
Last month he left for tea in Fuliang.
Alone I guard the empty boat;
The moon shines round me, the river chills.
Deep in the night I dream of my youth—
I wake in tears, my makeup streaked.”

Hearing her pipa, I had sighed in pity;
Now hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us, far from home, lost in this world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the imperial city;
Exiled and ill, I dwell in Xunyang.
This remote place has no music;
All year, no sound of strings or flutes.
I live by the river, low and damp,
Where reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.
What do I hear from dusk to dawn?
The cuckoo’s cry, the gibbon’s wail.
On flower-filled spring days or moonlit autumn nights,
I often drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds hurt the ear.
But tonight, hearing your pipa’s words,
Is like hearing celestial music—my ears revive.
Stay, please, and play one more song;
I’ll compose a “Pipa Song” for you.
Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,
Then sat again and tightened the strings.
The new tune, mournful, unlike before,
Made all who heard it weep.

On Xunyang River's bank I saw a guest off one autumn night,
The maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the cold light.
I dismounted; the guest boarded the boat. We raised our cups, but there was no music to toast.
Drunk, yet not merry, we parted in gloom, our farewell drowned in the vast river's moon.
Suddenly, from the water came a pipa's strain;
The host forgot to go, the guest forgot to leave the lane.
Seeking the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated, her words delaying.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to appear;
We added wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew, right here.
After a thousand calls and pleas, she finally came out,
Holding her pipa, half hiding her face, filled with doubt.
She tuned the strings, plucked them a few times, three or two;\nBefore the melody began, emotion already shone through.
Each string, each note, was muted, heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life's ambitions, sorrowfully bought.
Lowering her brows, she played on with practiced ease,
Voicing the endless sorrows that her heart would never cease.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then picking,
First "Song of the Skirt" she played, then "Six Yao" she was tricking.
The large strings roared like a sudden shower,
The small strings whispered like a secret hour.
The roars and whispers interlaced, a complex art,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade surface, a bright part.
Like orioles singing smoothly through the flowers below,
Or a muffled spring struggling under ice, a stifled flow.
The icy spring grew cold and slow, the strings froze tight,
Frozen, the sound halted, and then there was a sudden night.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, was born in the pause,
At this moment, the silence was worth more than applause.
Then, like a silver vase breaking, water gushing out,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears in a shout.
At the song's end, she swept her pick across all four strings as one,
A sound like tearing silk, a sharp and final done.
In the boats east and west, all was silent, no one spoke,
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, a lonely stroke.
Thoughtfully, she tucked her pick among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, her face composed, and stood on the scene.
She spoke: "I was once a girl from the capital's heart,
My home was near Hama Hill, where I'd play my part.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, my fame was high,
Listed first in the Music Bureau's company.
When I finished a song, even the great players would admire,
When I dressed up, the other beauties would burn with fire.
The young men of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts,
One song would bring me countless rolls of silk, in drifts.
Hairpins and silver combs broke as we beat the time,
My crimson silk skirt was stained with wine, a crime.
Year after year, the laughter and joy would flow,
The autumn moons and spring winds I let go.
But my brother went to war, my aunt died, you see,
As days and nights passed, my youth fled from me.
Before my door, the carriages grew few, the world grew cold,
In my old age, I married a merchant, a story told.
The merchant values profit over parting's pain,
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea, in the rain.
He comes and goes; I guard the empty boat alone,
Around me, the bright moon and the cold river moan.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youthful years,
And wake crying, my makeup ruined by tears."
"I sighed when I heard the pipa, and hearing your tale, I sighed again,
We are both wanderers at the world's end, lost in the rain.
Why must we have known each other before to share this plight?"
"Since I left the capital last year, I've been exiled, ill, in this night.
I live in Xunyang, a remote place with no music to hear,
For a whole year, I've not heard a single string or cheer.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp, you know,\nSurrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, a woeful row.
What do I hear from morning to night, you ask?
The cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbon's mournful task.
On a spring river's flower-blossom morning or an autumn moon's night,
Often, I take my wine and drink alone, in the fading light.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to play?\nThey are harsh and jarring, impossible to hear, I say.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's words, it's like hearing celestial music, a brief reprieve,
Please, do not refuse to sit and play one more song, before you leave.
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa' to grieve."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time, then sat and tuned her strings,
They grew more urgent, a sorrow that stings.
The sound was more mournful than before, a different plea,
The whole audience heard it again and wept, for all to see.
Who wept the most among the listeners there?
The Master of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet with his despair."}

Thoughtfully she tucked the pick among the strings,
Smoothed her robe, stood up with solemn grace.
"I was a girl of the capital, she said,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Music Academy.
My finished songs made even masters bow,
My dressed-up beauty made the courtesans envy.
The young blades of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts,
One song, and red silk past counting.
Jeweled combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
Spring breezes and autumn moons I let pass by.
My brother went to war, my aunt died;
Day followed night, my beauty faded.
Before my gate the carriages grew few;
Old, I married a merchant.
He values profit, not parting;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone in the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The bright moon all around, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face."

Hearing her pipa I had already sighed;
Hearing her words I sighed again and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Since last year I left the capital's jade towers,
I have lain sick and banished here in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
The whole year round I hear no lute or pipe.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.
Morning and evening, what do I hear there?
The cuckoo's bloody cries, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On flower-filled spring days, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But they are harsh and grating to the ear.
Tonight I heard your pipa speak,
Like celestial music, my ears came alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
And I will write for you a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words she stood a long while,
Then sat and tightened the strings, which grew urgent.
Sadder, sadder than the tune before;
All present, hearing it again, covered their faces and wept.
Who wept the most among them all?
The Master of Jiangzhou—his blue gown was wet.

By Bai Juyi



At Xunyang River's edge I saw a friend off by night,

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn light.

I dismounted while my guest stepped aboard his boat;

We raised our cups to drink, but no music played a note.

Drunk without joy, we grieved at parting as we must—

The vast river drowned in moonlight held us in its dust.

When suddenly from the water came a pipa's sound,

I forgot to go; my guest delayed leaving the ground.

We sought the tune and softly asked who played it there;

The music stopped, and slow as if to speak, she'd stare.

We moved our boat beside her, invited her to meet,

Relit the lamps, poured wine again, and set a new seat.

After a thousand calls and pleas, at last she came out,

Half-hiding her face behind the pipa, filled with doubt.

She tuned the strings and plucked three notes, yet cold and dry—

Before the melody was born, the feeling caught the eye.

Each string seemed choked with grief, each note with longing deep,

As if she told of all her life's unfulfilled sleep.

Brow low, at ease, her fingers moved in endless flow,

Spilling the countless things her heart had held below.

Light gathering, slow twisting, stroking, then the flick—

First "Rainbow Skirts", then "Willow Twigs" played neat and quick.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain that lashes down,

The thin strings whispered softly, like a secret's sound.

The roar and whisper tangled in a rich design,

Like pearls, both great and small, that spill and bounce and shine.

Like orioles singing smoothly where the flowers bloom,

Then choked, like icy springs that freeze in winter's gloom.

The icy spring runs thick; the strings congeal and bind,

The sound is locked, and for a moment all is blind.

Then hidden sorrow, secret hatred start to rise—

The silence speaks more eloquently than the cries.

A silver vase is smashed; the water bursts and flies;

Armored horsemen charge out; blades and spears clash in the skies.

The song ends with a sweep, a slash across each string—

Four strings at once like tearing silk, a sudden sting.

In boats to left and right, no one dared speak a word—

Only the autumn moon upon the river shone, unstirred.

Thoughtful, she tucked the pick back, set her garment straight,

Rose with a solemn face, her composure newly great.

"I come," she said, "from the capital, my birthplace known—

I lived beneath Toad Hill, where once my youth was thrown.

At thirteen, I'd mastered the pipa's artful grace,

And held the foremost place among the palace's troupe's embrace.

When I finished a song, the finest masters bowed;

When I dressed up, the court beauties would envy me and crowd.

Young men from noble towns would fight to send me gifts,

One song earned me so much red silk, the number simply drifts.

Jeweled combs would break to clapping time; my crimson skirt

Would stain with wine from revels, never once to hurt.

Year after year of laughter, month after month of ease,

Autumn moons and spring winds—how carelessly they flew, like bees.

Then my brother left for war; my aunt died, one by one;

Dusk came and dawn, and all my youthful beauty was undone.

Before my gate, the carriage tracks grew sparse and cold;

I wed, when old, a merchant, for my story had grown old.

The merchant cares for profit more than parting's pain;

Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy his tea again.

Alone I guard the empty boat by the river's side,

The moon shines round the boat; the water's cold and wide.

Deep in the night, I dreamed of all my youthful years—

I woke and wept, my ruined makeup streaked with tears."

I'd sighed already at her pipa's mournful art;

Hearing her words, I sighed again, with a heavier heart.

Both of us are wanderers at the world's far end—

Why must we have met before, for our souls to blend?

Since last year I resigned my post in the capital's bright scene,

I've lived in illness here in Xunyang, sick and keen.

Xunyang is remote; no music graces my ear;

All year I hear no strings, no flutes—just silence here.

I live near the river where the land is low and wet;

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my cot, and yet—

What do I hear from dawn to dusk, and dusk to dawn's return?

The cuckoo's bleeding cry; the gibbons' mournful yearn.

On flower-moon spring days, or autumn nights so clear,

I often take my cup and drink alone, right here.

Have I no mountain songs, no rustic flute to hear?

They're harsh and grating, and they pain the listening ear.

But tonight I heard your pipa's voice, so clear and bright,

Like listening to celestial music—my ears took sudden flight.

Please do not refuse; sit, play another tune for me,

And I will write a "Song of the Pipa" for all to see.

Moved by my words, she stood for long in deep thought's trance,

Then sat again and quickened the strings with urgent dance.

The new tune, sad and shrill, was nothing like before;

The whole crowd wept again, as if to break and pour.

Who wept the most among us, sitting there that night?

The Prefect of Jiangzhou—his blue robe, soaked with light."}
