By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River's head that night I saw a guest away,
With maple leaves and reed-flowers rustling in the autumn gray.
The host dismounted; the guest sat in his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or flute's soft note.
Drunk but not merry, we were sad at parting soon;
At parting, the vast river lay drowned in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed his departure.
Seeking the sound, we asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved the boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lantern, and renewed the feast.
After a thousand calls and entreaties she at last came out,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa she held about.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a time or two;
Before the tune was formed, feeling already shone through.
Every string, every note, was choked with sighs,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes and unavailing tries.
With lowered brows, carelessly, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless things in her heart that had lain undone.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then plucking again,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Ya's" refrain.
The low strings rumbled like a sudden heavy rain;
The high strings whispered soft as secrets in the lane.
The rumble and the whisper mingled, fast and slow,
Like a shower of big and small pearls falling on a jade tray below.
Like orioles warbling smoothly under flowers in the glade,
Or a stifled spring struggling under ice that will not fade.
The ice-cold spring froze; the strings’ sound stopped and died;
Stopped and dead, the silence spoke of a deeper tide.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, rose in the air;
The silence then spoke more than any sound could declare.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly smashed, water gushed and burst;\nOr armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears in a clash immersed.
At the song’s end, she swept the拨across the center of the strings;
The four strings rang as one, like tearing silk in its flightings.
In the boats east and west, all was silent, hushed, and still;
Only the autumn moon on the river’s heart was seen, white and chill.
Musing, she tucked the拨among the strings and sat;
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her face, solemn and flat.
She said, "I was a girl of the capital, it is true,
My home was at the foot of Hama Hill, where I grew.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa, my art was complete;
My name was listed first in the Teaching Bureau’s elite.
My finished songs made even the master musicians bow;
My adorned beauty made the famous courtesans envious, then, and now.
The young gallants of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silk ribbons and lifts.
Ornamented combs and silver hairpins broke as I beat time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained and spoiled by spilled wine.
Joy and laughter followed year after year,
While the autumn moon and spring breeze passed without a care.
My younger brother left for the army; my aunt died away;
Days turned to nights, and my youthful beauty began to decay.
Before my gate, carriages and horses grew few and cold;
Growing old, I married a merchant, a story often told.
The merchant values profit and lightly parts from his wife;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea for his life.
He comes and goes; I guard this empty boat alone,
Circled by the bright moon and the cold river’s moan.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youthful days;
In the dream, I weep, and my tears wash the rouge in crimson ways."
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed with regret;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, with a deeper debt.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the sky;
Why must we have met before to feel this bond, you and I?
Since last year, I bade the capital farewell,
Demoted and assigned elsewhere, I lie ill in Xunyang’s cell.
Xunyang is remote, with no fine music to hear;
All year, I have not heard the sound of strings or flute clear.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp, it is true,
With yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing all around my dwelling anew.
What do I hear here, morning and evening, all day long?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry and the gibbon’s mournful song.
On flower-filled spring mornings or moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone, in lonely heights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to hear?\nThey are grating, harsh, and discordant, painful to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s words, so clear and bright,
It is like hearing celestial music, my ears given light.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more tune for me,
And I will compose this "Song of the Pipa" in return for thee.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time, then sat back and played,
Tightening the strings; the music grew more urgent and more pressed.
The sad, sad notes were unlike the sounds before;
All the listeners wept, their tears falling as before.
Among us all, whose tears fell the most, I say?
The River Prefecture Marshal’s blue robe was wet that day."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Jiangtou, Xunyang, on a night I saw a guest off, 
Maples and reeds in autumn, rustling with chill. 
Host dismounted, guest remained aboard, 
Raised wine—no music to accompany. 

Drunk yet joyless, heartbroken at parting, 
As we parted, the river swallowed the moon in haze. 
Suddenly heard a pipa from the water's face, 
Host forgot to return, guest delayed departing. 

Followed the sound, whispered: “Who plays?” 
Pipa paused—hesitant, words unspoken. 
Moved boat near, invited her to appear, 
Refilled wine, relit lamps, renewed the feast. 

Repeated calls—she emerged at last, 
Still clutching pipa, half-face veiled. 
Tuned, plucked three or two brief strains, 
No full tune yet—emotion already spun. 

Each string suppressed, each note laden with thought, 
As if recounting lifelong frustration. 
Head lowered, fingers moved without pause, 
Spoke all inner sorrows, never spoken. 

Gently brushed, slowly twirled, swept then plucked, 
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*. 
Broad strings loud like sudden rain, 
Thin strings soft as private talk. 

Clusters of loud and soft interwoven, 
Large pearls, small pearls pattering on jade plate. 
Like oriole’s voice through blossoms—light and smooth, 
Like underground spring beneath ice—choked and strained. 

Cold, stagnant springs—strings freeze in silence, 
Stilled—sound paused, breath held. 
Elsewhere, hidden sorrow stirs anew, 
In this silence, more than sound remains. 

Silver bottle bursts—water gushes forth, 
Iron horse charges—swords and spears cry aloud. 
Final stroke drawn across the heart of the string, 
Four strings one burst—like tearing silk. 

East and west boats silent, still, 
Only the autumn moon, white upon the river’s core. 

After deep pause, she slid the pick into strings, 
Adjusted robes, rose, composed her face. 

She said: “I am born from the capital’s heart, 
My home lies beneath the Toad Hill.” 
At thirteen, my pipa mastery complete, 
Named first among the imperial music hall. 

After every piece, even *Shancai* bowed, 
My makeup admired—yet *Qiuniang* envied me. 
Young lords vied to toss headbands, 
One song earned endless scarlet silks. 

Silver hairpins struck beat till broken, 
Crimson skirts overturned, soaked in wine stains. 
Laughter year after year, again, again, 
Autumn moons, spring breezes—wasted, unmarked. 

Brother marched away; aunt passed on, 
Mornings pass, evenings fade—beauty withers. 
Doorside now empty, no steeds to be seen, 
Old, I married a merchant’s wife. 

Merchant values wealth, scorns parting, 
Last month gone to Fuliang to buy tea. 
Came back—now guarding an empty boat, 
Moon circles—cold river, cold light. 

Deep night, dreamt of youth’s old days, 
Dreaming wept—makeup tears red down cheeks. 

I heard the pipa—already sighed, 
Now hearing these words—more sighs arise. 
We both are lost souls, adrift afar, 
Why must we know each other first? 

Since last year, I left the Emperor’s court, 
Exiled, sick, dwelling in Xunyang town. 
Xunyang remote—no music ever heard, 
Whole year, no strings, no bamboo sounds. 

Near Pien River, land low, damp, 
Yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow around the house. 
What do I hear day and night there? 
Cuckoo bleeds—apes wail in mournful cries. 

Spring mornings, flower-lit days, autumn nights, 
Often I pour wine—alone, again. 
Are there no mountain songs, village flutes? 
But their noise is harsh—hard to endure. 

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech, 
Like heavenly music—ears briefly clear. 
Do not refuse—sit, play one more, 
I’ll compose for you this *Pipa Xing*. 

Moved by my words, stood long in silence, 
Returned, tightened strings—now faster. 
Sadness differs from before—deeper now, 
All who heard again wept, hands over faces. 

Who shed most tears in this crowd? 
The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe—soaked with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the capital of the Son of Heaven,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.

Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa,
Like listening to the music of immortals, my ears came alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
I will compose a *Pipa Song* for you.

Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the sounds before,
All who heard it covered their faces and wept.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the capital of the Son of Heaven,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa,
Like listening to the music of immortals, my ears came alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
I will compose a *Pipa Song* for you.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the sounds before,
All who heard it covered their faces and wept.
Who wept the most among the guests?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

One night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stayed in the boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow—
when the parting came, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked in low voices who was playing;
the music stopped, and she hesitated before answering.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her out;
adding wine, trimming the lamps, we set the feast again.
After a thousand calls and entreaties she finally came out,
half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the strings and plucked them twice or thrice—
before the melody took shape, feeling was already there.
Every string was muted and brooding, every note full of longing,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
With lowered brows she played on and on,
saying all the countless things within her heart.
Gently gathering, slowly rubbing, stroking and picking,
she began with Nishang and then came to Liuyao.
The thick strings roared like driving rain,
the thin strings whispered like secret talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled together,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling beneath the flowers, smooth and bright,
or a hidden stream choking under ice.
The icy spring grew cold and harsh, the strings congealed and broke off;
suspended, unpassing, the sound briefly ceased.
A deeper sorrow, a hidden resentment rose—
then silence spoke more than sound.
Then a silver bottle suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
or armored horsemen charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the end of the tune she swept the plectrum across the center;
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were hushed and silent;
only the autumn moon on the river shone white.
Pondering, she tucked the plectrum among the strings,
straightened her garments, rose, and composed her features.
She said: "I was a girl from the capital,
my home was at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name was listed first among the court performers.
After a performance even the finest musicians were impressed;
when dressed up I was envied by every beauty.
Young men of the five tombs competed to lavish gifts on me—
for one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Silver hairpins snapped as we beat time;
my crimson skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
those autumn moons and spring breezes passed without a thought.
My younger brother went off to war, my aunt died;
night followed day, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew few, horses scarce;
growing old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep night I suddenly dream of my youth,
and wake weeping, my rouge-streaked tears staining my face."

I had sighed already at the sound of the pipa,
and now hearing these words I sighed again.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth—
why must we have met before to meet like this?
Since last year I took my leave of the capital,
exiled and ill, I dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, and there is no music here;
the whole year through I never hear strings or pipes.
I live near the Peng River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my house.
What can one hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, gibbons howling mournfully.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
often I take up my wine and drink alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa, and it is like hearing celestial music—
my ears, for a moment, are clear again.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
and for you I will turn this into a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
then sat back and tightened the strings, growing faster.
Sadder, different from the tune before;
the whole company, hearing it again, wept into their hands.
Among us all, who wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
The host had dismounted; the guest was already in the boat;
We raised our cups, about to drink, but there was no zither or flute.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
East boats and west barges sat hushed, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.
She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant prizes profit and thinks lightly of parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.
I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I clicked my tongue in deeper sorrow.

Why must we have met before to understand?

Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.

By Bai Juyi (Tang Dynasty)

Night on the Xunyang River, seeing off a guest:
The maples and reeds tremble in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest stands in the boat.
They raise their cups to drink — no lute or strings to fill
The empty air. Drunk, yet no joy; a bleak farewell.
At parting, the vast river swallows the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa.
The host forgets to leave; the guest delays his sail.
Following the sound, they ask softly: "Who plays?"
The music stops; she hesitates to reply.
They move their boat nearer, invite her to appear.
More wine is poured, lamps rekindled, the feast renewed.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings — two, three tones.
Before a tune is formed, feeling already stirs.
Each string, each note, suppressed and brooding,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
Brows lowered, fingers tracing, she plays on,
Telling all the heart's unbounded matters.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and picking:
First "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao" she plays.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private speech.
Rumbling, whispering, intertwined they sound:
Like pearls, large and small, dropped on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
Or muffled springs, choked under ice.
The icy spring freezes; the strings seem to snap.
The sound ceases, blocked, and silence reigns.
A secret sorrow, a hidden grief, now rises:
This wordless moment speaks more than sound itself.
Then — a silver vase bursting, water gushing forth;
Armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
The song ends; her pick sweeps the center of the strings.
All four strings snap at once, like tearing silk.
Across the boats, all is silent; none speaks.
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.
Pondering, she tucks the pick among the strings.
Adjusts her robes, stands, and composes her face.
She speaks: "I was a girl of the capital,
My home was near Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first among the Music Bureau's players.
My finished songs made even masters bow;
My painted beauty made the court ladies envious.
The young gallants of Wuling competed to reward me:
One song, and silks beyond counting.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
The spring moons and autumn winds were spent in vain.
My brother left for the army; my aunt passed away.
Dusk came and went; my youthful looks faded.
Before my gate, carriages grew sparse and cold.
Growing old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit, not parting.
Last month he went to Fuliang for tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat.
Around the boat, the bright moon, the cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth.
In dreams, I weep; my tears streak my rouge in red lines."
"I sighed at hearing her pipa; hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the sky —
Why must we have known each other before to meet tonight?"
"Last year I left the capital's jade towers,
Demoted and ailing, I lie in Xunyang.
This remote place has no music;
All year, I hear no lute or strings.
I live near the low, damp Pen River,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
From dawn to dusk, what do I hear?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbons' mournful howl.
On flower mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
Often, I take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are discordant, harsh — impossible to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's voice,
It is like celestial music; my ears are blessed.
Do not refuse — sit, play once more.
For you, I will compose a 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stands a long while.
Then sits closer, tightens the strings — faster, more urgent.
Sadder, sadder than before — not like the earlier sounds.
The whole audience hears, and weeps into their sleeves.
Who wept the most among the listeners?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

By the Xunyang River, seeing off a guest on an autumn night,
The maples and reeds shiver in the cold.
I dismount from my horse, the guest is on the board.
We raise our cups, ready to drink, but there's no music to hear.
Drunk, yet without joy, we are about to part in sorrow,
At parting, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa,
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his departure.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly, "Who is playing?"
The pipa stops; she hesitates to answer.
We move our boat nearer, inviting her to meet;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally comes out,
Still hiding half her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings a few times,
Before a tune is formed, feeling already stirs.
Each string, each note, sounds melancholic, full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
She lowers her brows, casually plucks on and on,
Telling the endless tales of her heart.
With light pressing, slow twisting, stroking, and picking,
First she plays 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Yao.'
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like secrets shared.
The rumbling and whispering are intertwined,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing smoothly under the flowers,
Or a choked spring flowing under the ice.
The icy spring freezes, the strings seem to snap,
The sound stuck, and for a moment, it stops.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arise,
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water gushing out,
Or an armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she draws the拨 (pick) across the center,
All four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
The boats on all sides are silent,
Only seeing the autumn moon, white, in the middle of the river.
Pondering, she puts the pick back among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.
She says, "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home was at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
After playing, even the skilled masters were impressed,
When dressed up, I was often envied by the courtesans.
The young men of Wuling competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I'd receive countless red silks.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs were broken to keep time,
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed by without care.
My younger brother went to the army, my aunt died,
As days and months passed, my youth faded.
Fewer horses and carriages stopped at my door,
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit and light on parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I wait by the river mouth in an empty boat,
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
In the dream, I weep, my tears staining my rouge.
"Hearing the pipa, I already sighed,
Hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both wanderers at the end of the world,
Why must we have known each other before to meet?"
Last year, I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill, I stayed in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music,
All year round, I hear no string or wind instruments.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What can I hear here, day and night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbon's mournful howl.
On a spring river flower morning or autumn moon night,
I often take wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It's like hearing celestial music, my ears are suddenly enlightened.
Please, don't refuse, sit and play one more song,
For you, I'll compose a 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits back, tightens the strings, which turn urgent.
The mournful sound is unlike the previous one,
The whole audience, hearing it again, weeps.
Who among the audience weeps the most?
The Jiangzhou Sima, whose blue robe is soaked."}"}

I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.

The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.

My brother left for the army, my aunt died,

By the Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night—
maple leaves and reed-flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
My guest had dismounted; I stood by the boat, cup raised, about to drink—
but there was no music.
Drunk without joy, we grieved at parting;
the wide, misted river held the moon within its flood.

Suddenly—music on the water, a pipa!
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to leave.
We followed the sound and asked softly, "Who plays?"
The playing stopped; she seemed about to speak, but would not.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her out,
refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and set the feast again.
Only after a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties did she appear,
still hiding half her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, three or four notes—
and before any melody took shape, the feeling was already there.
Each string was choked with sorrow, each note brimming with thought,
as if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
Brow lowered, in no hurry, she played on and on,
telling out all that her heart held, without end.
Light trills and slow rolls, strokes and flicks—
first the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Song of Six Minor Tones."

The heavy strings roared like driving rain;
the light strings whispered like secret talk.
Roar and whisper, the two entwined—
like great pearls and small pearls spilling on a jade plate.
Then, like an oriole gliding over flowers, smooth and sweet;
then like a brook choked, a spring struggling under ice.
The cold, congealed strings would not turn;
stuck, blocked, the sound died away—
and out of that silence, a hidden sorrow, a secret grief bloomed—
then silence spoke louder than sound.

Then—
like a silver vase bursting, water gushing;
like armored horsemen charging, swords and spears ringing.
At the end she swept the pick across all four strings at once—
and the sound split the air like tearing silk.

In all the boats around us, no one spoke.
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She tucked the pick away, straightened her clothes, rose with a composed face.
"I was a girl of the capital," she said, "my home was by Hama Hill.
At thirteen my pipa was perfected,
and my name stood first among the court musicians.
When I finished a song, even the masters bowed;
dressed and painted, I shamed the fairest beauties.
The dandies of Wuling fought to shower me with gifts—
one song, and silk scarves piled past counting.
Hairpins and combs snapped to the beat, broken;
red skirts were stained and splashed with wine.
Year after year of laughter, of revelry—
autumn moons and spring winds, all squandered away.
Then my brother went to war, my mother died;
night followed day, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, fewer and fewer horses;
in my old age I married a merchant.

"But merchants care only for profit, not for parting—
last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
the moon shines round the boat, and the river water is cold.
Deep in the night I dream of my youth,
and wake weeping, my rouge-streaked face in tears."

I had sighed already at her music;
now, hearing her story, I sighed again.
We are both outcasts at the edge of the world—
why should we have needed to meet before?

Since last year I left the capital,
I have lain sick and demoted here in Xunyang.
This place is remote; there is no music—
all year I have not heard a single string.
I live low and damp, near the Pen River,
with yellow reeds and bitter bamboo crowding my gate.
What do I hear, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's wail.
On flower-filled spring days, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
How could there be no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their shrill, broken notes are hard to bear.

Tonight I heard your pipa—
like hearing the music of the immortals, and my ears were cleansed.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
and I will write it out for you, as a "Song of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood long where she was—
then sat again, and tightened the strings; they quickened.
The new music was not like the old—
in all the boats, the listeners wept.
And who wept most of all?
This official of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a guest off one night,
Where maple leaves and reed blooms rustled in autumn's chill light.
The host had dismounted, the guest stood aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no lute or pipe played a note.
Drunk yet not merry, we grieved at our parting soon;
The river, vast and hazy, drowned the parting moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated, words delaying.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to appear;
Poured more wine, relit the lamps, and feasted once more.
After a thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa she held about.
She tuned the strings, plucked them twice or thrice;
Before the melody began, emotion was already precise.
Each string muffled with sorrow, each note brimming with thought,
As if telling a life of ambitions thwarted and caught.
Brow lowered, idly her fingers moved on with grace,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart's space.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Minor" quickening.
The large strings roared like a sudden heavy rain,
The small strings whispered like secrets, soft and plain.
Clashing and purling, the strings intertwined,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate, well-defined.
Like orioles warbling smoothly beneath the flowers' bloom,
Or a mountain spring choked with ice in its icy gloom.
The icy spring froze, the strings grew stiff and still;
The silence deepened, a pause against their will.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment arose;
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound's prose.
Then like a silver vase bursting, water surging out,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears in a shout.
The tune ended with a sweep across the strings' center;\nAll four strings roared as one, like tearing silk, a splendor.
The boats east and west were silent, no voice dared to speak;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, pale and bleak.
Pondering, she tucked the plectrum among the strings tight;\nAdjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face to recite.
"I was once a girl from the capital's bright scene,
My home was by Hama Hill, where shadows lingered serene.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art with fame,
Ranked first in the Imperial Music School's roll of name.
After each performance, even masters bowed in awe;
When dressed, even the finest beauties felt a flaw.
The wealthy youths of Wuling competed to bestow gifts on me;
One song earned countless bolts of red silk, carefree.
We beat time with jeweled combs till they snapped in the fray,
Our blood-red silk skirts stained with wine in our play.
Year after year of laughter, of joy and cheer,
Autumn moons and spring breezes vanished, year by year.
Then my brother left for the army, my aunt passed away;
Days turned to nights, and my youthful looks began to decay.
Before my gate, carriages grew rare, the crowds grew thin;
Growing old, I married a merchant, my life's new kin.
The merchant values profit over love's sweet tie;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea, and I
Wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
Circled by the bright moon and the cold water's float.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth's bygone days;
I weep in my dream, and my makeup streaks in red haze."
"Hearing your pipa, I sighed with a heavy heart;
Hearing your tale, my sighs tear me apart.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world's stage;
Why must we have met before, to turn this page?
Since last year, I left the capital's bright scene,
Demoted and sick, I lie in Xunyang's shadows, keen.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to delight;
All year, I hear no lute or pipe's sweet sound, day or night.
My home is by the low, damp Pen River's side,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo around my dwelling hide.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk, year in, year out?
Only the cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbon's mournful shout.
On spring river flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take my wine and drink alone in the moon's lights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to hear?\nTheir crude, jarring sounds are too harsh for the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech, so clear and bright,
Is like hearing celestial music, my ears taking flight.
Do not refuse; sit and play another tune for me;
I will compose a 'Song of the Pipa' for thee."
Moved by my words, she stood still for a long while;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, quickening the style.
The mournful notes were unlike the earlier sound;\nAll present wept again, their tears falling around.
Who wept the most among us, sitting there?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with his despair."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River head I saw a friend off by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn light.
I dismounted; my guest stepped aboard the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was neither lute nor flute.
Drunken, but not merry, we prepared to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moonlight in the dark.
Suddenly from the water came a lute's sound,
I forgot to go back, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a whisper who was playing,
The lute stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambitions.
She lowered her brows and played on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly she strummed, slowly she plucked, swept and flicked,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao tune.
The high strings roared like sudden rain in the sky,
The low strings whispered like secret words.
Roaring and whispering, they mingled and crossed,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and snapped,
The sound was blocked, and for a while there was silence.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—
In that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the plectrum across the center,
All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all sat in hushed awe,
Only the white autumn moon in the river's heart was seen.
Musing, she put the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was a girl of the capital,
Her home lay in the pleasure quarter of Hama Ling.
At thirteen she had mastered the lute,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After her songs, even the best players admired her,
When dressed, she was envied by the courtesans.
Young gallants from the Five Tombs competed to send her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Jeweled hairpins snapped to the beat, their ornaments broken,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed,
The autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died,
Dawn and dusk went by, her youthful bloom faded.
Few carriages and horses stopped at her door,
In old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river's mouth in an empty boat,
The moon shines bright around her, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream she weeps, her rouge-streaked tears staining her face.
I had already sighed on hearing the lute,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, with deeper grief.
We are both fallen souls at the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met before to share this bond?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
I have been exiled and ill in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year long, no sound of strings or flutes.
My home is near the river, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear from morning till night?
Only the cuckoo's blood-curdling cry and the gibbon's mournful howl.
On spring river flower-days, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my cup and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant noise is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your lute speak,
Is like hearing immortal music, my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
For you, I will compose this Song of the Lute.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Mournful and desolate, unlike the sound before,
All who heard it wept, their tears falling.
Who among the guests wept the most?
The Assistant Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue gown soaked through."}

Drunk without joy, we were about to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moon before our eyes.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa—

Brow low, in no hurry, she played on and on,
Pouring out all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Crumbling and whispering, they mingled and crossed—
Like great pearls and small pearls spilling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
Or a muffled stream that struggles under ice.
The icy spring freezes; the strings seem to snap;

A hidden sorrow, a secret grievance, was born—
At such a moment, silence speaks louder than sound.

She tucked the pick among the strings in thought,

At thirteen I mastered the pipa,

The young gallants of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;

Year after year of laughter and revelry,

I live by the Pen River in low, damp ground;

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
The maple leaves and reed blossoms rustled in the chill.
I had dismounted, my guest was already in the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without delight, we were about to part in gloom,
And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa—
The host forgot to go home, and the guest forgot to set off.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show herself,
Adding wine and relighting the lamps, we feasted again.
After a thousand calls, she at last came out,
Still hiding half her face behind her pipa.
She tuned the strings and plucked them a few times,
Before the melody began, the feeling was already there.
Each string seemed to sigh, each note to brood,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled aspirations.
With lowered brows, she played on carelessly,
Pouring out all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly strumming, slowly twisting, plucking and flicking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Little Branch."
The high strings rumbled like a sudden downpour,
The low strings whispered like intimate conversation.
The rumbling and whispering intertwined,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding among flowers, the notes flowed smoothly;
Then, like a mountain spring choked under ice, they grew hard to hear.
The icy spring froze, the strings grew numb and still;
The stillness held, the sound suspended for a time.
Then a hidden sorrow and secret resentment rose—
At that moment, the silence was more eloquent than sound.
Suddenly a silver vase burst, water gushing forth;
Armored cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept the拨 across the strings' heart;
All four strings cried out at once, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent and hushed;
Only the autumn moon in mid-river, white and bright.
Thoughtfully she tucked the拨 among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, and rose with solemn dignity.
She said she had once been a girl from the capital,
Her home near Hama Ling.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the Imperial Dance Academy.
After each performance she would win the admiration of master musicians;
Her beauty was often the envy of the famous courtesans.
The dashing young men of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, she would receive countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat, broken;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and merriment,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed her by unheeded.
Then her younger brother went off to war, and her aunt died;
As days and evenings passed, her youth and beauty faded.
Fewer horses and carriages stopped before her door;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
The moon shining around her, the river cold.
In the deep night she suddenly dreams of her youth,
And weeps in her dreams, her tears streaking her rouge.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her story, I sighed again and again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet like this?
Since last year I took leave of the capital,
I have lived in illness, banished to Xunyang.
This place is remote, and there is no music;
All year round I have not heard the sound of string or flute.
I live near the low, marshy banks of the Pen River,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can one hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's blood-curdling cry, the gibbons' mournful howl.
On spring river days with flowers, or autumn moonlit nights,
Often I fetch wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, jarring sound is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's language,
Is like hearing celestial music—my ears are suddenly enlightened.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
And I will compose "A Song of the Pipa" for you.
Touched by my words, she stood there a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
The mournful notes were unlike the sounds before;
The whole assembly, hearing them again, wept into their sleeves.
Who wept the most among the audience?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue gown was soaked with tears."}

Adjusts her clothes, rises, her face composed in wings.
She speaks: "I was once a girl of the capital's fame,
My home was near Toad Hill, a well-known name.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Ranked first in the Music Bureau, set apart.
When I finished a song, even masters bowed,
When I dressed up, beauties envied, and how!
The young men of Wuling competed for my favor,
For one song, countless red silks they'd deliver.
Jeweled hairpins snapped to keep the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained with wine, a sweet defeat.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
The autumn moons and spring winds passed in flight.
My brother left for war, my aunt passed away,
Day after day, my youth began to decay.
Before my door, carriages grew few and sparse,
I married a merchant in my years' reverse.
The merchant values profit, not our parting's pain,
Last month he left for Fuliang to trade again.
Alone I guard the empty boat by the river's mouth,
Around the boat, the moon shines bright, the water cold, forsooth.
In deep night, I dream of my youthful days,
Wake crying, my makeup streaked with tearful ways.
I sighed already at the pipa's song,
Hearing her words, I sigh again, along.
We both are lost souls at the world's ends,
Meeting here, why must we be old friends?
Since last year I left the capital's bright scene,
Exiled and sick, in Xunyang I've been.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow, a swamp.

Like hearing immortal music, my ears brighten, dear.

Then sits and tunes the strings, which quicken strong.

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。

其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge, I bid a guest farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, and my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no lutes or flutes played.
Drunk, yet not merry, we sorrowfully prepared to part;
At parting, the vast river mirrored the moon.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa;
I forgot to go home, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
Added wine, relit the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took shape, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, was muffled with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she casually continued to play,
Telling all the infinite things within her heart.
She lightly gathered, slowly twisted, strummed and plucked;
First "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Minor" she played.
The thick strings roared like heavy rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, mixed in a chaotic play,
Like big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding on flowers in a gurgling flow;
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring froze, the strings congealed and ceased;\nWhen congealed and blocked, the sound paused for a while.
A different, hidden sorrow and silent resentment arose;
At this moment, silence was better than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water gushing out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept the拨 across the center;
The four strings together sounded like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were silent, no one spoke;
Only the autumn moon in the river's heart, white and bright.
She pondered, put the拨 away, and tucked it in her strings;
Adjusting her clothes, she stood up with a solemn expression.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living below Hama Ridge.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa;
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
Her finished songs once made skilled players admire;
Her made-up beauty often made Qiuniang jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to give gifts;
For one song, countless red silks were given.
Ornamental combs struck time till they broke;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy;
The autumn moons and spring winds passed idly by.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died;
Day and night passed, and her youthful looks faded.
Before her door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
In old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Coming and going, she guards an empty boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the bright moon and cold river water.
Late at night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth;
In the dream, she wept, her tears staining her rouge.
I sighed upon hearing the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeply moved.
Both of us are fallen souls at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital;
I was banished and fell ill, living in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year round, I hear no strings or flutes.
Living near the low, damp Pen River;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons mourning sadly.
On flower-filled spring mornings or moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, harsh sounds are hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's voice,
It is like hearing celestial music, my ears briefly enlightened.
Please do not refuse, sit and play again;
For you, I will compose this "Pipa Ballad."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then she sat back and tightened the strings, which grew faster.
The sorrowful tune was unlike the previous one;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept.
Who wept the most among the listeners?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with tears."}

At Xunyang River's edge, I saw a guest away,
Through rustling reeds and maple leaves, the autumn's chill.
I dismounted; he embarked. We raised our cups to stay,
Yet no lute or string softened our farewell's sharp ill.

Drunk, but not merry, we prepared to part in gloom,
When the vast river, moon-submerged, stretched wide and bare.
Then a pipa's sound arose across the water's room—
The host forgot to leave, the guest no longer there.

We traced the sound and softly asked, "Who plays so fair?"
The music stopped; a hesitant reply was sought.
We moved our boat, invited her to share our air,
Poured wine, relit the lamps, and our small feast was caught.

After a thousand calls, she finally appeared,
Her pipa in her arms, half-hiding her pale face.
She tuned the strings—three notes, and before the tune adhered,
A deep emotion already filled the space.

Each string a sigh, each note a thought of deep despair,
As if to tell a life of thwarted, unmet aims.
With lowered eyes, she idly played, beyond all care,
Unveiling all the heart's immeasurable flames.

Light plucks and slow rubs, presses and pulls she threw,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao" in her deft art.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain that bursts anew,
The thin strings whispered like a secret in the heart.

The roaring and the whispering, a tangled stream,
Like pearls, both large and small, on a jade plate that falls.\Then like an oriole's smooth song in a flower's gleam,
Then like a stifled spring beneath the ice that stalls.

The icy spring ran cold, the strings congealed and broke,
And in the blocked-up silence, a profound hush grew.
A hidden sorrow, a dark hatred, there awoke—
The silence at that moment spoke more than it knew.

Then suddenly, a silver vase shatters, water flies,
An armored charge with clashing swords and spears in flight.
She swept the拨 across the strings with piercing cries—
Four strings as one, like tearing silk in the night.

All boats around were silent, no word, no sound,
Only the autumn moon on the river, white and clear.
She tucked her拨 among the strings without a bound,
Adjusted her robes, composed her face, her manner near.

"I was a girl from the capital, you see,
My home beneath Toad Hill, where I would dwell and grow.
At thirteen, I had mastered the pipa's mastery,
My name ranked first among the Music School's bright show.

When I finished a song, even the masters bowed,
And when I dressed, the beauties envied my own grace.
The young gallants of Wuling all for me avowed,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk would they face.

Hairpins and silver combs would snap to my fast beat,
My blood-red silk skirts stained with wine in the wild fray.
Year after year of laughter, bittersweet,
The autumn moon and spring wind just flew away.

My brother left for war, my aunt in death was lost,
As days and nights passed by, my youthful looks did fade.
Before my gate, the horses thinned, all joy was crossed,
An aging woman, to a merchant's wife was made.

The merchant values profit over love's own part,
Last month to Fuliang he went to buy his tea.
I guard this empty boat alone, and it's my art,
With the bright moon and cold river surrounding me.

In the deep night, I dream of my young, carefree days,
And wake in tears, my ruined makeup staining my face." 

I sighed already at her pipa's first appeal,
And now her story made me sigh in deep accord.
"We both are lost souls, far from home, on a common wheel,
Why must we have been strangers when our paths accord?" 

Since last year I left the capital's bright scene,
I've lived in sickly exile here in Xunyang.
This place is far from music, coarse and bleak, I ween,
A whole year without strings to hear all day long.

I live near the riverbank, damp and low and deep,\nWith yellow reeds and bitter bamboo around my door.
What sounds from dawn to dusk do I hear while I sleep?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful roar.

On spring river flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone, forlorn.
"Are there no mountain songs or village flute's delights?
They're harsh and grating, not worth hearing, worn and torn." 

"But tonight, hearing your pipa's speech, so clear and bright,
Is like hearing fairy music, my ears made new.
Please stay and play one more song, with all your might,
And I will write a 'Song of the Pipa' for you." 

Moved by my words, she stood for long with sad-eyed gaze,
Then sat and plucked the strings with urgent, hurried pace.
The new tune, mournful, unlike her previous lays,
Made everyone who heard it weep and hide their face.

Among the weeping, whose tears fell the most, the most?
The江州司马's, until his blue robe was wet with brine."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the capital of the Son of Heaven,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa,
Like listening to the music of immortals, my ears came alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
I will compose a Pipa Song for you.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the sounds before,
All who heard it covered their faces and wept.
Who wept the most among the guests?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the capital of the Son of Heaven,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa,
Like listening to the music of immortals, my ears came alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
I will compose a Pipa Song for you.

Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.

On Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night,
Wind rustling through the reeds and maple leaves in autumn chill.
I dismounted, the guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk yet not merry, we grew sad at parting—
As we said farewell, the river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to leave.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
We refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and began the feast anew.
After much calling out, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
Before the melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted with sorrow,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled dreams.
With lowered eyes, she played on idly,
Telling of all the endless things within her heart.
She plucked and strummed, gently and slowly—
First the Ni Shang melody, then the Liu Yao tune.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, fast and slow, they mingled—
Like pearls, big and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the blossoms,
Or like a spring choked under ice, struggling to flow.
The ice-cold spring froze, the strings went still;
The silence held, and the sound paused.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief, arose—
The silence then said more than any sound.
Then—like a silver vase bursting, water gushing forth,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept her pick across the strings—
All four snapped at once like tearing silk.
In boats all around, no one spoke;
Only the autumn moon on the river, white and bright.
She sank into thought, tucked her pick among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, and rose with solemn grace.
She said she had once been a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Imperial Music Academy.
Her playing could humble even the finest masters;
Her beauty made even the great courtesans envious.
Young men from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts—
For one song, she'd receive countless bolts of red silk.
They beat time with jeweled combs until they broke,
And her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
The spring moons and autumn winds passed by, unheeded.
Then her younger brother went to war, her aunt passed away;
Days and nights wore on, and her beauty faded.
Fewer horses tied at her door, fewer callers came;
Grown old, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared only for profit, not for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone at the river's mouth, in an empty boat;
Around her, bright moonlight, cold river water.
In the deep night, she dreams of her youth—
Waking, she weeps, her tears streaking red across her face.
