Hearing her story, I sighed again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand each other now?

Banished and sick, I dwell in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote—no music here;
All year, I've not heard a single string or flute.
I live near the river, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes here?
They're harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa—
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears come alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
And I will compose this Song of the Pipa for you.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence;
Then sat back, tightened the strings—they quickened.
The new tune, so mournful, unlike before;
Everyone in the room wept in silence.
Who wept the most among them all?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue robe was wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn light.
I dismounted; my guest stepped aboard the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was neither lute nor flute.
Drunken, but not merry, we prepared to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moonlight in the dark.
Suddenly from the water came a lute’s sound,
I forgot to go back, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a whisper who was playing,
The lute stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambitions.
She lowered her brows and played on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly she strummed, slowly she plucked, swept and flicked,
First the “Rainbow Skirt,” then the “Liu Yao” tune.
The high strings roared like sudden rain in the sky,
The low strings whispered like secret words.
Roaring and whispering, they mingled and crossed,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and snapped,
The sound was blocked, and for a while there was silence.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—
In that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver jar cracks, water bursts forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end she swept the plectrum across the center,
All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all sat in hushed awe,
Only the white autumn moon in the river’s heart was seen.
Musing, she put the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was a girl of the capital,
Her home was beneath Xia Ma Ling.
At thirteen she had mastered the lute,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After her songs, even the best players admired her,
When dressed, she was envied by the courtesans.
Young gallants from the Five Tombs competed to send her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Jeweled hairpins snapped to the beat, their ornaments broken,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed,
The autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died,
Dawn and dusk went by, her beauty faded.
Few carriages and horses stopped at her door,
In old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river’s mouth in an empty boat,
The moon shines bright around her, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream she weeps, her rouge-streaked tears staining her face.
I had already sighed on hearing the lute,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, with deeper grief.
We are both fallen souls at the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met before to share this bond?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
I have been exiled and ill in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year long, no sound of strings or flutes.
My home is near the river, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear from morning till night?
Only the cuckoo’s blood-curdling cry and the gibbon’s mournful howl.

I often take my cup and drink alone.

Is like hearing immortal music, my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,

By Bai Juyi

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing a guest off,
The maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted while my guest stepped into his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to cheer us.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in gloom—
At parting, the vast river lay drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show herself;
Added wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand urgings, she finally came out,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
Before a single melody took shape, feeling was already there.
String after string, notes suppressed and hushed, each one full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled longing.
Brow lowered, carelessly her fingers moved on and on,
Speaking of the endless things that weighed upon her heart.
Gently gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and plucking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Little Branch."
The low strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The high strings whispered like a secret conversation.
Rumbling and whispering, the notes tangled and intertwined—
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
Or a spring choked with ice, struggling to flow.
The icy spring froze, the strings grew stiff and broke;
The sound jammed, and for a while it ceased.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment welled up—
In that silence, more was said than any sound could tell.
Then, like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears all ringing.
The song ended—she swept the拨 across the center of all four strings;
One single sound, like silk being torn apart.
Boats east and west fell silent—no one spoke;
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart, was seen.
Musing, she tucked the拨 among the strings, straightened her clothes,
Rose to her feet and composed her features.
She spoke:
"I was once a girl from the capital, living beneath Hama Ling.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa, and my name headed the roll of the foremost in the Music Bureau.
My finished performances once made even the finest musicians bow;
When I dressed up, even the most beautified court ladies envied me.
The dandies of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
After a single song, I could not count the bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat, broken;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained and spoiled by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and revelry,
Autumn moon and spring wind passed by as if they were nothing.
Then my younger brother left for the army, my elder sister died;
Evening went and morning came, and my beauty began to fade.
Before my gate, carriages grew rare, the horses fewer;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
But merchants prize profit and think lightly of parting—
Last month he floated away to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep of night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my rouge-streaked tears streaking my face."
I had sighed already at the pipa's song;
Hearing her story now, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the end of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet as we do?
Since last year I took leave of the imperial capital,
I have lived in illness, banished to Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year I have not heard a single string or flute.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
Morning and evening, what is there to hear?—
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons howling their sorrow.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Of course there are mountain songs and village flutes,
But they are crude and harsh, and hard to listen to.
Tonight I heard your pipa speak,
And it was like hearing celestial music—my ears came alive.
Do not refuse; sit a while and play another song,
And I will compose for you this "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood long without moving;
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
Sadder, sadder than anything she had played before—
The whole gathering wept again, everyone covering their face.
Who among us shed the most tears?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge I see a guest away;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's gray.
I dismount, the guest steps aboard; we raise the cup to drink,
But there is no pipe or string to make the moments brink.
Drunk brings no joy; a bitter parting soon shall be,
As the vast river soaks the moon in its cold sea.
Suddenly from the water comes a pipa's sound;
The host forgets to leave, the guest stays on the ground.
We seek the source and softly ask who plays the tune;
The music stops; she hesitates, and answers soon.
We move our boat near hers and ask her to appear,
Pour wine, relight the lamp, and hold the feast again.
After a thousand calls she comes, her face half hid,
Still clasping the pipa, modestly in the light.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary notes;
Before the melody forms, emotion already floats.
Each string's subdued, each note is full of thought and sigh,
As if she told of all her life's defeats and cry.
Brow lowered, at her ease she plays on without pause,
Telling the endless matters of her heart's sad cause.
She gathers, twists, and picks with slow and light array,
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Song of Six-Four-Part' at play.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain on roof and stone;
The thin strings whisper soft as secrets overthrown.
The loud and soft in wild confusion interweave,
Like pearls, both great and small, that tumble down and cleave.
Like orioles singing fast through flowers, smooth and quick,
Then like a frozen stream beneath the ice that's thick.
The icy stream grows cold; the strings congeal and break;
The sound is blocked, and then a moment's silence take.
A hidden sorrow, secret hatred, rises there;
The silence then is more expressive than the air.
Like a silver vase that bursts and water floods the ground,
Like armored horsemen charging out with clash and sound.
At the song's end she sweeps the拨 across the middle string;
Four strings at once like rending silk, a sudden ring.
Boats to the east and west are silent in their awe;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart we saw.
She ponders, puts the拨 amid the strings, and stays,
Adjusts her robes, her face composed in solemn ways.
She says: 'I was a girl of the capital's fame,
My home was at the foot of Toad Hill, known by name.
At thirteen I had mastered pipa; my skill
Stood first in the Music Bureau, without rival.
When I finished a song, even masters bowed to me;
When I dressed up, the beauteous girls were jealous, you see.
The young gallants of Wuling all fought to give me gifts;
One song brought countless bolts of red silk in large drifts.
Hairpins and silver combs would break as we beat time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with wine in festive clime.
Year after year of laughter and of light,
The autumn moons and spring winds passed in my sight.
My brother went to war, my aunt, alas, is dead;
Days passed, and morning came; my youthful beauty fled.
Before my gate, few horses stopped; the crowd was gone;
I married, old, a merchant, to live on.
The merchant cares for profit more than parting's pain;
Last month he went to Fuliang for tea again.
I wait alone by the river mouth in empty space,
Around the boat, the bright moon chills the water's face.
Deep in the night I dream of my young years' bright art,
And wake to find my tear-streaked makeup, torn apart.'
I sighed already at her music's sad refrain,
But hearing this, I sighed and sighed again in pain.
We both are men who've lost our way in this world's end;
Why must we have been strangers when we meet, my friend?
Last year I left the capital's towers and halls,
And here I lie in illness in Xunyang's walls.
This place is remote; there's no music to be found;
All year I hear no string or flute's familiar sound.
I live near Pen River, low and damp the ground,
With yellow reeds and bitter bamboo all around.
What sounds do I hear morning and evening, pray?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful lay.
On flower-bright spring days or autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my cup and drink alone in fights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to hear?
They are so crude and harsh, they hurt the listening ear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's speech, so clear and bright,
Like listening to immortal music, a sudden light.
Please do not refuse; sit down and play another song;
For you, I'll write a 'Song of the Pipa' to prolong.
Moved by my words, she stands for long without a sound,
Then sits and tightens strings; the music rushes round.
So sad and cold, unlike the song we heard before;
All present hear it once more, and weep, unable to store.
Among the crowd, who wept the most, you ask, and see?
The River-Prefecture's official, his blue robe wet with glee."}

Loud strings like a sudden, driving rain,
Soft strings like whispers in the lane.

间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River head I saw a guest off by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn light.
I dismounted, my guest stepped aboard the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was neither lute nor flute.
Drunken, yet not merry, we prepared to part in gloom,
The vast river swallowed the moonlight in the dark.
Suddenly from the water came a lute’s sound,
I forgot to return, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a whisper who was playing,
The lute stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambitions.
She lowered her brows and played on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly she strummed, slowly she plucked, swept and flicked,
First the “Rainbow Skirt,” then the “Six Yao” tune.
The high strings roared like sudden rain in the sky,
The low strings whispered like secret words.
Roaring and whispering, they mingled and crossed,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and snapped,
The sound was blocked, and for a while there was silence.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—
In that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end she swept the plectrum across the center,
All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all sat in hushed awe,
Only the white autumn moon in the river’s heart was seen.
Musing, she put the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was a girl of the capital,
Her home was beneath Toad Hill.
At thirteen she had mastered the lute,
Her name listed first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After her songs, even the best players admired her,
When dressed, she was envied by the courtesans.
Young nobles from the aristocratic Five Tombs district competed to send her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Jeweled hairpins snapped to the beat, their ornaments broken,
Her crimson silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed,
The autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died,
Dawn and dusk went by, her beauty faded.
Few carriages and horses stopped at her door,
In old age, she became the wife of a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river’s mouth in an empty boat,
The moon shines bright around her, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream she weeps, her rouge-streaked tears staining her face.
I had already sighed on hearing the lute,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, with deeper grief.
We are both fallen souls at the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met before to share this bond?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
I have been exiled and ill in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year long, no sound of strings or flutes.
My home is near the river, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear from morning till night?
Only the cuckoo’s blood-curdling cry and the gibbon’s mournful howl.
On spring river flower-days, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my cup and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant noise is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your lute speak,
Is like hearing immortal music, my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
For you, I will compose this “Song of the Lute.”
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Mournful and desolate, unlike the sound before,
All who heard it wept, their tears falling.
Who among the guests wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue gown soaked through."}

By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River’s head I saw a guest off one night—
Maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn in the chill.
I, the host, dismounted; the guest stayed on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no string or flute.
Drunk, yet not happy, we prepared to part in sorrow—
At parting, the vast river lay drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s sound—
The host forgot to return; the guest would not depart.
Following the sound, I asked softly, “Who plays?”
The pipa stopped; she seemed to hesitate before speaking.
I moved my boat nearer and asked her to come out,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and we feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
Turning the pegs, she plucked three or four strings—
Before the tune took form, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, casually she played on and on,
Telling of the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then flicking—
First “Rainbow Skirts,” then “Six Minor.”
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private words.
The roar and whisper tangled in play—
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing smoothly among the flowers,
Or a mountain spring, choked under ice.
The icy spring grew cold; the strings froze and broke—
Frozen, blocked, the sound paused for a while.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—
The silence then said more than sound could say.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end, she swept her pick across the strings—
Four strings, one crack, like tearing silk.
Across the boats, east and west, all was silent—
Only the river’s heart showed autumn moon, white.
Thoughtfully she set down her pick inside the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and stood with solemn face.
She spoke: “I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Teaching Bureau.
My playing once made the finest masters bow;
My beauty often made the courtesans jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts—
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs and silver pins shattered to keep time;
My blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed by as nothing.
My brother went to war; my elder sister died—
Morning came and went; my youth grew old.
Before my door, carriages grew rare;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
But merchants prize profit over parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Back and forth, I guard the empty boat at the river’s mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth—
Waking from the dream, my tears stain my rouge-streaked face.”

I had sighed when first I heard the pipa;
Hearing these words, I sighed again.
Both of us are lost souls at the world’s end—
Meeting here, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the capital’s bright scene,
Sick and bedridden, I live in exile in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music at all—
All year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pan River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbons’ mournful howl.
On spring river days with flowers, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s words,
It is like hearing celestial music—my ears come alive.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
And I will compose a “Song of the Pipa Player” for you.
Moved by my words, she stood a long while,
Then sat back and tightened the strings—they grew urgent.
Desolate, unlike the sound before—
The whole room, hearing it again, wept silently.
Who wept the most among the listeners?
The Xunzhou official—his blue gown grew wet."}

At Xunyang Riverhead, seeing off a guest that night,
The maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest boards the boat.
They raise their cups to drink, but there is no music.
Drunk but not merry, they part in sorrow;
At parting, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa floats over the water—
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, they ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, and she hesitates to speak.
They move their boat closer to invite her out,
Add wine, relight the lamp, and reopen the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges,
Half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times,
Before the tune begins, emotion is already there.
Each string is muffled, each note full of thought,
As if telling the frustrations of a lifetime.
Brow lowered, she plays on casually,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Songs.
The great strings rumble like a sudden rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
The rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like pearls, big and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling beneath the flowers, smooth;
Like a hidden spring flowing under ice, hard.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings congeal and break,
The break silences the sound for a moment.
A secret sorrow and hidden resentment arise—
At this moment, silence is more than sound.
Suddenly, a silver vase shatters, water gushing;
Iron cavalry charges out, blades and spears clanging.
The tune ends with a stroke across the center;
All four strings snap like tearing silk.
Across boats, east and west, all is silent;
Only the autumn moon is seen, white on the river.
Thoughtfully she puts the plectrum back, tucks it in,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says, "I was a girl from the capital,
Living near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Music Bureau.
My playing once made the masters admire;
My beauty once made the courtesans envy.
The young lords of Wuling competed to reward me;
One song earned me countless bolts of red silk.
Ornaments and combs were broken to the beat;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Spring moons and autumn winds passed in vain.
My younger brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dusk came and dawn went, my beauty faded.
Before my gate, saddles grew rare and cold;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit and lightly parts;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, leaving me to guard an empty boat;
Around the boat, the bright moon and cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
Crying in my dream, tears staining my rouge.

When I heard your words, I sighed again.
Both of us are wanderers at the end of the world—
Why must we have met before?"

Demoted and ill, I dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year I hear no string or flute.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

I often take my wine and drink alone.

Like hearing immortal music, my ears briefly brightened.

At parting, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Seeking the sound, we asked softly who was playing;

We moved our boat closer and invited her to show her face;

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings three or four times,

Every string, every note was suppressed and full of thought,

In that moment, the silence spoke louder than the sound.

When she dressed up, she was envied by all the great beauties.

For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.

Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.

Her brother left for the army, her aunt passed away,
As days turned to nights, her youthful beauty faded.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's head I see a guest off at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn.
Down from his horse, the host; the guest aboard his boat;
He raises his cup to drink, but there is no music.
Drunk without joy, in gloom they part;
At parting, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his departure.
Seeking the sound, he softly asks who plays;
The pipa stops; she hesitates to speak.
He moves his boat near, invites her to appear;
Adds wine, relights the lamp, and reopens the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she comes out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three notes;
Before the tune is formed, there is already feeling.
Every string sobs with thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, carefree, she plays on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light strokes, slow twirls, sweeps, and picks;
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six-One.
The big strings rumble like a rushing rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, tangled and mixed,
Like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then orioles warble, smooth among the flowers;
Then a choked spring struggles under ice.
The cold astringency freezes the strings tight;
The sound stops, blocked off, and briefly halts.
A separate sorrow, a hidden resentment rises;
At this moment, silence is more than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly broken, water bursting forth;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she draws the pick across the center;
The four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.
The boats east and west are silent, no one speaks;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart shines white.
Musing, she tucks the pick among the strings;
Adjusts her robes, rises, and composes her face.
She says: I was a girl of the capital,
My home was below Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, even beauties were jealous.
The young men of Five Tombs competed to send gifts;
For one song, uncounted bolts of red silk.
Silver hairpins beat time till they broke;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed another;
Autumn moons and spring winds passed idly by.
My brother went to war, my mother died;\Evenings went, mornings came, and my looks faded.
Before my door, carriages grew cold and few;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I guard this empty boat at the river's mouth;
Moonlight surrounds the boat, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face.
I sighed when I first heard the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sigh again.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have met before to meet tonight?
Last year I took leave of the capital;
Banished and ill, I lodged in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no strings or flutes.
Living near the river, the land is low and damp;\nYellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful call.
On flower-moon spring days and autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech;
Like hearing fairy music, my ears are briefly cleared.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song;
For you, I will turn this into a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time;
Then sits back, quickens the strings, and they grow急.
The sound is mournful, not like before;
The whole audience weeps, hearing it again.
Among the guests, who weeps the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River’s edge I bid my guest good-bye,
The maple leaves and reeds shiver in autumn sigh.
I dismounted, he boarded; we raised our cups to part,
But no lute or flute could stir the heart.
Drunk, yet joyless, we prepared to bid farewell,
The river drowned in moonlight, vast and chill.
When suddenly from the water a pipa’s note did rise,
I forgot to go, he forgot to leave, both surprised.
I asked in the dark, “Who plays so well?”
The music stopped; she hesitated to tell.
We moved our boats near, invited her to meet,
Relit the lamps, poured wine, renewed the feast.
After many calls she finally appeared,
Holding her pipa, half her face veered.
She tuned the pegs, plucked the strings, a few clear sounds,
Before the melody, emotion already resounds.
Each string a sigh, each note a longing deep,
As if telling of a life in sorrow steeped.
Brow low, carefree, she played on and on,
Telling all the things her heart had borne.
Light strokes, slow twangs, first “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Minor,”
Loud strings like sudden rain, soft like whispers divine.
Loud and soft entwined in a tangled flight,
Like pearls, big and small, falling on jade bright.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, smooth and clear,
Or a choked spring trapped beneath ice, hard to hear.
The ice-bound spring froze, the strings held their breath,
A pause of silence, deeper than death.
A hidden sorrow, a secret pain took birth,
This silence spoke louder than any sound on earth.
Then a silver vase shattered, water burst forth,
An iron horse charged, blades clashing north and south.
She swept the拨across the strings, a single crack,
Four strings in one, like tearing silk, sharp and black.
The boats around fell silent, none dared speak,
Only the autumn moon on the river, pale and meek.
She tucked the拨among the strings, adjusted her gown,
Rose with a solemn face, composed and profound.
She said, “I was a girl from the capital’s heart,
My home by Toad Hill, where the city’s charms start.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa’s art,
Top of the Music Bureau, the very first part.
When I finished a song, even masters bowed,
When I dressed up, even beauties were envious and proud.
Wuling’s young men fought to shower me with red,
For one song, countless silks were spread.
Jeweled combs snapped beating time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, bittersweet.
Year after year, laughter and spring breezes flew,
Till my brother left for war, my aunt died, and youth withdrew.
Fewer horses at my door, the world grew cold,
I married a merchant, old and past my prime’s hold.
He values profit, not love, away he went,
To buy tea in Fuliang, on his business bent.
I wait alone at the river’s mouth, in my empty boat,
The moon shines round, the cold water afloat.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth’s bright days,
Wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face’s maze.
I sighed at her pipa, and sighed again at her tale,
Both of us, castaways, under this sky’s veil.
Why must we have met before to share this pain?
We’re both adrift, lost in the world’s vast lane.
I left the capital last year, demoted and ill,
Lodged in Xunyang, a place remote and still.
No music here, no lute or flute all year round,
Only the sound of nature, mournful and profound.
Near the river, low and damp, reeds and bitter bamboo grow,
At dawn and dusk, only the cuckoo’s cry and the ape’s woe.
On spring mornings, autumn nights, I drink alone,
No village songs or flutes, only a harsh, grating tone.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, my ears were blessed with light,
Like hearing celestial music, pure and bright.
Stay, play one more song, and I’ll compose this “Pipa Song” for you,
A tribute to our meeting, in this melancholy view.
Moved by my words, she stood long, then sat and played,
The strings grew faster, the melody more afraid.
Sadder than before, it pierced the soul,
The whole audience wept, unable to control.
Who wept the most among the crowd that night?
The Jiangzhou司马, whose blue gown was wet with tears’ flight."}

浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Xiamaling Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Imperial Music Academy.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made even Lady Qiu jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for keeping her company—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the capital of the Son of Heaven,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.

Like listening to the music of immortals, my ears came alive.

Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang's river-bend, I bid a guest goodbye;
The autumn wind stirs reeds and maples with a sigh.
The host has left his horse; the guest awaits in his boat—
We lift our cups to drink, but no lute does remote.
Drunken, we cannot cheer; the parting weighs on the heart;
And when we part, the river is wide, the moonlight apart.
Suddenly on the water, a pipa's notes arise—
The host forgets to go; the guest delays his goodbyes.

We follow the sound and softly ask who is playing;
The pipa falls silent, as if words were delaying.
We move our boats together and invite her to appear;
We add more wine, rekindle the lamp, and the banquet reopens here.
After a thousand calls, at last she steps into the light,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa, shy and slight.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings—a few sharp, clear tones—
Before the melody forms, the feeling already owns.

Each string is muted with sorrow, each note brims with sighs,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled, where ambition dies.
Lowering her eyes, she plays on, her fingers tracing the way,
Unfolding the endless tales her heart has hidden away.
She plucks, she rolls, she sweeps, she strums—first a courtly tune,
Then a lighter one, "Rainbow Skirt," beneath the moon.

The big strings rumble like sudden rain on the roof,
The small strings whisper like secrets, soft and aloof.
Loud and soft, the notes weave together with grace,
Like great pearls and small pearls tumbling onto jade's face.
Swift as orioles singing beneath flowering trees,
Then choked like a stream trapped beneath icy seas.
The icy stream freezes; the strings' voice is bound,
The sound halts in silence—no further note is found.

A deeper sorrow, a hidden regret, now is born,
And in this silence, more is said than in any sound or horn.
Then—like a silver vase bursting, water flooding the ground,
Or an armored charge, swords and spears clashing around—
At the end, a stroke across the strings, a crack like a tear,
Four strings snap as one, like silk ripping through the air.
In the boats on either side, no one dares to speak—
Only the autumn moon on the river, pale and meek.

She tucks the plectrum among the strings, sits up with care,
Adjusts her robes, and composes her face, pale and bare.
"I am from the capital," she says, her voice low,
"Once lived at the foot of Toad Hill, where the willows grow.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, my name at the head
Of the first troupe of the court, where the bravest were bred.
After each song, the master musicians bowed to my art,
And when I dressed, the other beauties envied my part.
The young lords of the Five Tombs vied for my favor with gifts,
And for one song, I'd earn rolls of silk, beyond all shifts.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat, broken in the fray,
And my blood-red silk skirts were stained with wine's disarray.
Year after year, I laughed and sang, carefree and bright,
Till spring winds and autumn moons passed without a fight.

Then my brother went to war, my aunt passed away,
And day by day, my youth and beauty began to fade.
No more did horses crowd my door, the guests grew few—
An older woman now, I married a merchant, forlorn and blue.
The merchant cares for profit, not for love or a tear—
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea this year.
He comes and goes; I wait alone by the river's side,
The boat wrapped in moonlight, the water cold and wide.
Deep in the night, I dream of my younger days, and I weep,
My rouge-stained tears streaking my pillow, lost in sleep."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed in despair;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, with a heavier air.
We both are wanderers, lost at the edge of the sky—
Why must we have known each other before, to say goodbye?
Last year I left the capital, banished, ill, and low,
To this distant Xunyang, where no music notes flow.
Here, year-round, no strings or flutes are ever heard,
Only the cuckoo's blood-cry and the gibbon's mournful word.
Near the river, the land is damp, the reeds and bamboo grow wild,
Surrounding my house, where mornings and evenings are mild.
On spring mornings or autumn nights, I pour my wine alone,
And listen to village songs and crude flutes, harsh and unknown.
But tonight, hearing your pipa, my ears are cleansed and bright—
Stay a little longer, and play one more song tonight,
And I will turn your music into a "Pipa Song" for you."

Moved by my words, she stands still, then sits down anew,
Tightens her strings, and the music turns sharp and fast,
A sorrowful strain, unlike the one that had passed.
Everyone in the room, hearing it again, is moved to tears—
And who wept the most? The official from Jiangzhou, in his green years."}

Maple leaves and reed-flowers shiver in autumn chill.
I dismount, the guest boards the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but no lute or strings are near.
Drunk without joy, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is flooded with moon.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a lute;
I forget to go, the guest delays his sailing.

The lute stops, she hesitates to speak.

Still half-hiding her face behind the lute.

Before the tune is formed, feeling already flows.
Every string muffled with thought, every note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled desires.
Brow low, carelessly her fingers keep on playing,
Telling all the heart's unending cares.
Light pressing, slow twisting, stroking, then flicking,
First the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Yao.

Thin strings whisper like private talk.

Like a choked spring flowing under ice.

The break blocks the sound, and briefly it rests.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment arise;
At this moment, silence speaks more than sound.

Armored cavalry charge out, swords and spears clash.

Four strings at once, like rending silk.

Straightens her robes, rises, and composes her face.

My home was under Hailong Hill.

My name was listed first in the Music Academy.

When I dressed up, the beauties envied me.
Young men of the Five Tombs competed to lavish gifts;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Gilded combs beat time till they broke;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed another;
Autumn moon and spring wind passed by at ease.
Then my brother enlisted, my aunt died;
Days and nights went by, my beauty faded.
Before my gate, carriages grew cold and few;
Aged, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit, thinks little of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, I guard this empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moon, cold river water.

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted from my horse at the inn, while my guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to be heard.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moon in a misty expanse.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
The music stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to show her face;
Adding wine and relighting the lamp, we set the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerged,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the strings and plucked them a few times;
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, was subdued and full of longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brow lowered, carelessly her fingers moved on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, she brushed and plucked;
First she played 'Rainbow Skirts,' then 'Liu Yao.'
The low strings roared like a sudden shower,
The high strings whispered like secret talk.
Loud and soft, mingling together,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among flowers,
Or a hidden spring choking under ice.
The icy spring freezes, the strings snap and cease;\nThe sound, blocked, halts for a while.
Yet a deeper sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose;
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then, like a silver vase bursting, water gushed forth;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed.
At the song's end, she drew the pick across the center;
The four strings at once split like tearing silk.
The boats east and west were silent as the grave;
Only the autumn moon in the river's heart shone white.
Muttering to herself, she tucked the pick among the strings;
Straightening her clothes, she rose with a solemn face.
She spoke: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
When I made up, the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to lavish me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins snapped as we beat time;
My blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and merriment;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed by in vain.
My younger brother left for the army, my aunt passed away;
Days and nights wore on, and my beauty faded.
Fewer horses stopped at my gate;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
He values profit and cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I guard our empty boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the bright moon and cold water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth;
In my dream, I wept, tears streaking my rouge." 

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Now hearing these words, I sighed again, deeply moved.
We are both wanderers at the end of the world;
Why need we have met before to understand each other? 

Since last year, I left the imperial capital;
Banished and sick, I lie in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and has no fine music;
All year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the river, on low, damp ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my house.
What do I hear here from dawn to dusk?
Only cuckoos crying blood and gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower-filled spring mornings or moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, impossible to enjoy.
Tonight, hearing the music of your pipa,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are awakened.
Do not refuse—sit and play another song;
For you, I will compose a 'Song of the Pipa.'
Touched by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
The mournful tune was not like the one before;
The whole audience heard it again and wept into their sleeves.
Among the guests, who wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet.""}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the river’s head by Xunyang, night we send a guest, 
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver, chill. 
Host dismounts, guest remains on board; 
We raise a cup to drink—but no music plays. 
Not drunk, yet sad to part—the parting bleak, 
As moon sinks deep in river, vague and wide. 

Suddenly, from water, pipa music sounds— 
Host forgets to leave, guest won’t depart. 
Following the sound, we ask in silence: “Who plays?” 
Pipa halts, the player hesitates to speak. 
We move our boat near, invite her to come forth, 
Add wine, turn lamps up, break the feast again. 

A thousand calls, a hundred urging, she appears, 
Still holding pipa half-concealing face. 
She turns the axle, plucks two or three tones— 
Before a tune is shaped, emotion stirs. 
Each string suppressed, each note a hidden thought, 
Like one who speaks of lifelong unfulfilled dreams. 

Bowed head, hands drift on strings, one after another, 
Spilling all hearts’ endless sorrows. 
Gently pressing, slowly rubbing, finger flicks, 
First *Rainbow Skirts*, then *Sixth Yi*. 
The deep strings roar like sudden stormy rain, 
The thin strings whisper soft as private talk. 

Roar and murmur mixed in jumbled notes, 
Large pearls and small drop on jade dish. 
Soft, smooth, like bird’s call through flowered shade, 
Then choked, like spring under ice, hard to pass. 
Ice-cold spring, strings freeze and stall— 
Silence holds fast, sound paused for breath. 

Yet deeper grief, unseen resentments rise— 
This silence more eloquent than sound. 
Silver jar bursts, liquid gushes out, 
Iron cavalry charge, swords clash loud. 

When final stroke sweeps through the heart of string, 
Four strings snap open—like silk torn apart. 
East and west boats hush, no voice within— 
Only the moon white above river’s core. 

Hesitating, he lays down the pick, slips it back, 
Straightens his robe, composes solemn face. 

“I was born in the capital city's heart, 
My home lies beneath Xia Ma Ling. 
At thirteen I mastered pipa fully, 
Named first among the teaching guild. 
After my song, even master musicians bowed; 
After my makeup, Qiu Niang envied me. 

Five-Dynasty youths vied to throw silken robes, 
One song earned me countless red scarves. 
Tortoise-topped silver comb broke with beat, 
Crimson skirt stained with wine from dance. 

Year after year, laughter, joy returned— 
Autumn moons, spring breezes, passed unmarked. 
My brother left for war, my aunt died young, 
Day fades, dawn comes—my looks have long decayed. 

Door grows cold, few riders now ride by, 
Old, I married a merchant, took his name. 
Merchants prize profit, scorn goodbyes— 
Last month off to Fuliang to buy tea. 

He came and went, I stay at river mouth, 
Empty boat round which moonlight pools, 
Cold river flows. At midnight, I dream of youth— 
Dreaming, weeping, tears stain red across my face. 

I’ve heard your pipa music, sighed already— 
Now hearing this, I sigh once more. 
We’re both lost souls beneath the same sky— 
Why need we know each other before? 

I left the capital last year, exiled here, 
Lying sick in Xunyang, far from court. 
Xunyang lies remote, no music ever— 
Whole years pass without strings or bamboo. 

Near Pien River, land low, damp and wet— 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow round my home. 
What do I hear day and night? 
Cuckoos bleed, apes cry mournfully. 

On spring mornings, blossom days, or autumn nights, 
Often I pour wine, drink alone. 
Are there no rustic songs, no village flutes? 
But croaked, shrill, harsh—hard to bear. 

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s speech, 
It feels like listening to heavenly music—ears briefly clear. 
Do not refuse, sit again, play one more piece— 
For you, I’ll make a new *Pipa Song*. 

Moved by my words, long she stands still— 
Returns to seat, tightens strings, faster now. 
Her playing colder now than before— 
All, hearing again, hide their weeping. 

Who wept most in the circle? 
The green-sleeved magistrate’s robe—wet with tears."}

When maples turn and reeds sway, autumn’s rustling sigh. 
The host dismounts, the guest embarks; we lift our wine, 
But no lute or flute is there to make the evening fine. 
Half-drunk, we part in gloom, our parting joy undone, 
The river wide with moonlight, merging sea and sky as one. 
Suddenly from the water floats a lute’s soft strain— 
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his train. 
We trace the sound and ask, “Who plays?” The music dies; 
She hesitates to speak, as if her heart were wise. 
We shift our boats nearer, invite her to appear; 
Add wine, relight the lamps, and start the feast anew with cheer. 
After a thousand calls she comes, her face half-hid 
By the pipa she cradles, as if behind a veil she slid. 
She twists the pegs, plucks strings, two or three notes before 
A melody is born—yet feeling pours out evermore. 
Each string is muted, choked with thought, each note a sigh, 
As if telling a life of dreams that never could fly. 
Brow low, she plays on idly, letting heartstrings speak, 
Pouring out all the unbounded sorrows she can’t keep. 
Light strokes, slow rubs, a sweep, a flick—first “Rainbow Skirt” she plays, 
Then “Six Yao” in the twilight’s haze. 
The large strings rumble like a sudden heavy rain, 
The small strings whisper like a secret, soft and plain. 
The rumbles and the whispers interweave and run— 
Like pearls, both large and small, that fall on a jade dish, one by one. 
Then like orioles among flowers, liquid and bright, 
Or a choked spring beneath the ice, that struggles for its light. 
The ice-cold spring runs stiff; the strings congeal and break, 
Sound frozen, silent—no more music can awake. 
Yet in that silence a hidden sorrow starts to grow: 
Sometimes the soundless hush speaks deeper than the notes we know. 
Then—a silver flask shatters, water gushing free, 
Armored horsemen charge, swords and spears ring wild with glee. 
The song ends with a sweep across the strings’ own heart— 
Four strings crackle once, like silk that’s torn apart. 
The boats to east and west fall still, not a word is said, 
Only the river’s heart and autumn moon, white and spread. 
Slowly she tucks the plectrum in, adjusts her dress, 
Rises with solemn face, her composure all the less. 
She speaks: “I was a girl of Chang’an’s capital, 
My home lay beneath Toad Hill, near the city wall. 
At thirteen I mastered the pipa’s art, 
My name topped the foremost rank of the court’s school of art. 
When I finished a song, even masters bowed in awe, 
And when I dressed, even the famous beauties would feel raw 
With envy. The young lords of Wuling competed to send 
Red silk as reward—no count of what they’d spend. 
Jeweled combs struck time till they shattered in the fray, 
My crimson silk skirt stained with wine in the fray. 
Year after year we laughed and sang, the spring and autumn flew, 
The moon and wind passed by, and we thought nothing new. 
Then my brother left for war, my aunt passed away, 
Dawn turned to dusk, and my beauty began to fade to gray. 
Before my gate the horses dwindled, the crowds grew few; 
In old age I married a merchant, and my youth was through. 
The merchant values profit more than parting’s pain, 
Last month he floated down to Fuliang to buy tea again. 
I wait alone by the river in our empty boat, 
The moon bright round me, the water cold, and I remote. 
Deep in the night I dream of my youth’s bright days, 
Wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face’s haze.” 
Hearing her pipa I had already sighed in vain, 
Now hearing her tale I sigh again, a deeper pain. 
We are both outcasts at the edge of the world’s long lane— 
Why must we have met before to share this common strain? 
Last year I left the imperial capital’s bright scene, 
To live in exile, sick, in Xunyang’s quiet green. 
Xunyang is remote; no music graces the air, 
Whole year I hear no string or flute, no melody to share. 
I live near the river, low and damp, and around my home 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo in tangled thickets roam.

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。

我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River’s edge I bid a guest good-bye,
When maples turn and reeds sway, autumn’s rustling sigh.
The host dismounts, the guest embarks; we lift our wine,
But no lute or flute is there to make the evening fine.
Half-drunk, we part in gloom, our parting joy undone,
The river wide with moonlight, merging sea and sky as one.
Suddenly from the water floats a lute’s soft strain—
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his train.
We trace the sound and ask, “Who plays?” The music dies;
She hesitates to speak, as if her heart were wise.
We shift our boats nearer, invite her to appear;
Add wine, relight the lamps, and start the feast anew with cheer.
After a thousand calls she comes, her face half-hid
By the pipa she cradles, as if behind a veil she slid.
She twists the pegs, plucks strings, two or three notes before

Each string is muted, choked with thought, each note a sigh,
As if telling a life of dreams that never could fly.
Brow low, she plays on idly, letting heartstrings speak,
Pouring out all the unbounded sorrows she can’t keep.
Light strokes, slow rubs, a sweep, a flick—first “Rainbow Skirt” she plays,
Then “Six Yao” in the twilight’s haze.
The large strings rumble like a sudden heavy rain,
The small strings whisper like a secret, soft and plain.
The rumbles and the whispers interweave and run—
Like pearls, both large and small, that fall on a jade dish, one by one.
Then like orioles among flowers, liquid and bright,
Or a choked spring beneath the ice, that struggles for its light.
The ice-cold spring runs stiff; the strings congeal and break,

Yet in that silence a hidden sorrow starts to grow:
Sometimes the soundless hush speaks deeper than the notes we know.
Then—a silver flask shatters, water gushing free,
Armored horsemen charge, swords and spears ring wild with glee.
The song ends with a sweep across the strings’ own heart—
Four strings crackle once, like silk that’s torn apart.
The boats to east and west fall still, not a word is said,
Only the river’s heart and autumn moon, white and spread.
Slowly she tucks the plectrum in, adjusts her dress,
Rises with solemn face, her composure all the less.
She speaks: “I was a girl of Chang’an’s capital,
My home lay beneath Toad Hill, near the city wall.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa’s art,
My name topped the foremost rank of the court’s school of art.
When I finished a song, even masters bowed in awe,
And when I dressed, even the famous beauties would feel raw
With envy. The young lords of Wuling competed to send
Red silk as reward—no count of what they’d spend.
Jeweled combs struck time till they shattered in the fray,
My crimson silk skirt stained with wine in the fray.
Year after year we laughed and sang, the spring and autumn flew,
The moon and wind passed by, and we thought nothing new.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt passed away,
Dawn turned to dusk, and my beauty began to fade to gray.
Before my gate the horses dwindled, the crowds grew few;
In old age I married a merchant, and my youth was through.
The merchant values profit more than parting’s pain,
Last month he floated down to Fuliang to buy tea again.
I wait alone by the river in our empty boat,
The moon bright round me, the water cold, and I remote.
Deep in the night I dream of my youth’s bright days,
Wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face’s haze.”
Hearing her pipa I had already sighed in vain,
Now hearing her tale I sigh again, a deeper pain.
We are both outcasts at the edge of the world’s long lane—
Why must we have met before to share this common strain?
Last year I left the imperial capital’s bright scene,
To live in exile, sick, in Xunyang’s quiet green.
Xunyang is remote; no music graces the air,
Whole year I hear no string or flute, no melody to share.
I live near the river, low and damp, and around my home
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo in tangled thickets roam.
What do I hear from morn to night? The cuckoo’s bloody cry,
The gibbons’ mournful howl beneath the endless sky.
On spring river’s flowered morn or autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone, with no delight.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to cheer?
They croon and clatter, raw and harsh, and hurt the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, like fairy music bright,
And for a moment my ears are cleared, my spirit light.
Do not refuse—sit down once more and play again;
For you I’ll turn this song into “Song of the Pipa,” a lay of pain.”
Moved by my words she stands long, then sits and tunes the string,
The pitch grows faster, sharper, with a desperate sting.
The new song, mournful, unlike the one we heard before,
Makes everyone who listens cover their face and weep once more.
Who weeps the most among the guests at this sad end?
The River Prefect’s blue official robe, soaked to the bend."}

When maples turn and reeds sway, autumn’s rustling sigh.
The host dismounts, the guest embarks; we lift our wine,
But no lute or flute is there to make the evening fine.
Half-drunk, we part in gloom, our parting joy undone,
The river wide with moonlight, merging sea and sky as one.
Suddenly from the water floats a lute’s soft strain—
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his train.
We trace the sound and ask, “Who plays?” The music dies;
She hesitates to speak, as if her heart were wise.
We shift our boats nearer, invite her to appear;
Add wine, relight the lamps, and start the feast anew with cheer.
After a thousand calls she comes, her face half-hid
By the pipa she cradles, as if behind a veil she slid.
She twists the pegs, plucks strings, two or three notes before
A melody is born—yet feeling pours out evermore.
Each string is muted, choked with thought, each note a sigh,
As if telling a life of dreams that never could fly.
Brow low, she plays on idly, letting heartstrings speak,
Pouring out all the unbounded sorrows she can’t keep.
Light strokes, slow rubs, a sweep, a flick—first “Rainbow Skirt” she plays,
Then “Six Yao” in the twilight’s haze.
The large strings rumble like a sudden heavy rain,
The small strings whisper like a secret, soft and plain.
The rumbles and the whispers interweave and run—
Like pearls, both large and small, that fall on a jade dish, one by one.
Then like orioles among flowers, liquid and bright,
Or a choked spring beneath the ice, that struggles for its light.
The ice-cold spring runs stiff; the strings congeal and break,
Sound frozen, silent—no more music can awake.
Yet in that silence a hidden sorrow starts to grow:
Sometimes the soundless hush speaks deeper than the notes we know.
Then—a silver flask shatters, water gushing free,
Armored horsemen charge, swords and spears ring wild with glee.
The song ends with a sweep across the strings’ own heart—
Four strings crackle once, like silk that’s torn apart.
The boats to east and west fall still, not a word is said,
Only the river’s heart and autumn moon, white and spread.
Slowly she tucks the plectrum in, adjusts her dress,
Rises with solemn face, her composure all the less.
She speaks: “I was a girl of Chang’an’s capital,
My home lay beneath Toad Hill, near the city wall.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa’s art,

With envy. The young lords of Wuling competed to send
Red silk as reward—no count of what they’d spend.
Jeweled combs struck time till they shattered in the fray,
My crimson silk skirt stained with wine in the fray.
Year after year we laughed and sang, the spring and autumn flew,
The moon and wind passed by, and we thought nothing new.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt passed away,
Dawn turned to dusk, and my beauty began to fade to gray.
Before my gate the horses dwindled, the crowds grew few;
In old age I married a merchant, and my youth was through.
The merchant values profit more than parting’s pain,
Last month he floated down to Fuliang to buy tea again.
I wait alone by the river in our empty boat,

Deep in the night I dream of my youth’s bright days,

Hearing her pipa I had already sighed in vain,
Now hearing her tale I sigh again, a deeper pain.

To live in exile, sick, in Xunyang’s quiet green.

Makes everyone who listens cover their face and weep once more.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host alighted from his horse, the guest was on the boat;
He lifted his cup to drink, but there was no music.
Half-drunk, not merry, we grieved at the coming parting,
As we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player was slow to reply.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
Adding wine, relighting the lamps, we reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings, a note or two;
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
She lowered her brows, and carelessly, she went on playing,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly touching, slowly twisting, she swept and plucked,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The thick strings roared like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin strings whispered like private words.
Roars and whispers, mingled and mixed,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,

The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,

Then, like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.

The four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats to the east and west, all was silent;

Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.

Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's troupe.

Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
And wakes weeping, her tears staining her rouge-streaked cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
And now I live, sick and exiled, in Xunyang.
This place is remote, and there is no music;
All year, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the low, damp banks of the Pen River,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

The cuckoos weep and gibbons howl.

And I will dedicate to you a "Song of the Pipa."

Then sat back, tightened her strings, and the tempo grew faster.

Everyone in the seat who heard it again covered their face and wept.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Nai Shang, then the Liuyao.

The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.

Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Day by day, her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.

I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I sighed again, full of sorrow.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the capital of the Son of Heaven,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa,
Like listening to divine music, my ears came alive.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
I will compose a Pipa Song for you.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the sounds before,
All who heard it covered their faces and wept.
Who wept the most among the guests?
Jiangzhou's scribe, his blue robe wet with tears."}
