At Xunyang's riverbank, I bid farewell to a guest by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
We raise our wine, but no music plays with us.
Drunk, we cannot find joy in sorrow's parting,
As moonlight bathes the river in hazy silence.
Suddenly, a pipa sound floats upon the water;
My host forgets to return, my guest won't depart.
I seek its source, softly ask who plays;
The pipa stills—hesitant to speak.
We move our boat closer, invite her to meet;
Add wine, turn up lamps, restart the banquet.
After many calls, she appears at last,
Still holding her pipa half-concealing her face.
She turns the axle, plucks strings twice or thrice,
Before any tune, emotion already fills the air.
Each string mourns; each note reflects deep thought—
As if narrating a life unfulfilled.
Lowering her eyes, she plays on steadily,
Speaking all her heart's endless sorrows.
Softly stroking, slowly plucking, touching and picking—
First 'Feather Dress,' then 'Six Ya.'
The thick strings rattle like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rattling, whispering, a jumble of sounds—
Like large and small pearls dropping on jade.
Smooth as a bird skims through flowers,
Low-pitched like spring water frozen beneath ice.
Cold, stagnant, the strings freeze in place;\nSilence falls, as if sound has vanished.
Yet another hidden sorrow and hatred grows—
This silence speaks louder than sound.
Suddenly, a silver bottle cracks—water spurts out;
A cavalry charge, swords and spears clash.
When the melody ends, the pick strikes the heart of the strings—
Four strings snap once, like silk torn apart.
East and west ships fall silent, no word spoken;
Only the autumn moon shines white on the river's heart.
After a pause, she rests the pick in the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, composes her face.
She says: 'Born in the capital city, my home was under the Xiamaling hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the teaching bureau's troupes.
After playing, even the master musicians were amazed;
After makeup, I was envied by every beauty.
Young nobles vied to offer me silken gifts—
One song earned me countless red scarves.
Silver hairpins broke from rhythmic beat;
Crimson robes stained with wine, spilled by dance.
Happy laughter year after year, spring blossoms, autumn moons—
All passed carelessly.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days pass, nights pass—my looks fade.
My door grows cold, few visitors ride by;
Old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit more than parting—
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I remain, guarding an empty boat;
Moonlight circles the ship, the river is cold.
Deep into the night, I dream of youth,
Dreaming cries, tears staining my red-smeared cheeks.
Hearing this pipa, I sigh deeply;
Now hearing these words again, I'm moved even more.
We're both lost souls adrift on distant shores—
Meeting? Why must we have known before?
I left the capital last year, exiled, bedridden in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, no music to be found;
Whole years gone without a trace of strings or bamboo.
Near Panyang, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.
What do I hear day and night here?
Cuckoos bleeding red, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring mornings, flower-filled days, autumn nights with moonlight,
I often pour wine, drink alone.
Are there no village songs or rustic flutes?
But their noise is harsh, hard to endure.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's voice,
It feels like celestial music—my ears briefly brightened.
Don't refuse—sit and play one more tune;
For you, I'll compose this 'Song of the Pipa Player.'
Moved by my words, she stood a long time,
Then sat down, tightened the strings—the pitch grew urgent.
The sorrowful sound no longer matches what came before;

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang's ferry head, seeing a guest off at night,
The maple leaves and reeds shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest boards the boat.
We lift our cups to drink, but there is no music.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting,
As we leave, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to go; the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops; she hesitates to speak.
We move the boat near and invite her to meet;
Add wine, relight the lamps, and reopen the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges,
Still hugging the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three notes;
Before the tune is formed, emotion is already there.
Each string sobs with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brows low, casually she plays on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, strumming and picking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Minor tunes.
The large strings rumble like sudden rain,
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Loud and soft, mixed and played together,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
Or a choked spring flowing under ice.
Cold and sluggish, the strings freeze and stop;
Frozen, unable to pass, the sound briefly halts.
A hidden sorrow and secret hate arise;
At this moment, silence is better than sound.
Suddenly, a silver vase breaks, water bursts forth;
Armored cavalry charges out, swords and spears clash.
The song ends; she draws the拨 across the center;
Four strings snap at once like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, no one speaks;
Only the river's heart shows the white autumn moon.
Muttering, she tucks the拨 among the strings;
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, composing her face.
She speaks: "I was originally a girl of the capital,
My home was below the Toad Mound.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music School.
When I finished, even masters were convinced;
When dressed up, I was envied by beauties.
The young men of Wuling competed to give gifts;
For one song, red silk was countless.
Silver hairpins beat time till they shattered;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring wind passed by at ease.
My brother went to the army; my aunt died;
Day and night passed, and my youth faded.
Before my door, carriages grew sparse and cold;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
He values profit and lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I guard the empty boat at the river's mouth,
Around the boat, bright moon and cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, my makeup ruined by tears."
I had already sighed upon hearing the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply moved.
Both of us are people lost at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I hear no sound of strings and flutes.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here from morning to night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful call.
On flower mornings and moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa's voice;
It is like immortal music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please do not refuse; sit and play another song,
And I will compose a Pipa Song for you.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time;
Then sits and tightens the strings, which turn urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the sound before,
All the seats weep again upon hearing it.
Who weeps the most among the guests?
The official from Jiangzhou—his blue gown is wet."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays.

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part,
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises,
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?”
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless.
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last,
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes—
No tune yet, but feeling already flows.

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing,
Like one speaking of a lifetime of sorrow and thwarted destiny.

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers,
Telling all the sorrows in her heart.

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting—
First *Fei Huang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down,
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk.

Clashing, mingling, interweaving—
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls.

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear,
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass.

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard.

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out.

When the final stroke cuts across the heart,
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart.

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs,
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart.

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings,
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity.

My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute,
Named first among the Imperial School’s best.

After my songs had silenced even masters,
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me.

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years.

Year after year, laughter and joy,
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed.

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast.

Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me.

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years.

Year after year, laughter and joy,

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast.

Cuckoos bleeding red in the trees, monkeys wailing.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, sweeping, then picking— 
First *Feiye*, then *Liuyao* she sings. 
The thick strings roar like sudden rain, 
The thin ones whisper like private talk. 

Cacophony of clatter, mingled tones— 
Like pearls tumbling onto jade plates, clear and bright. 
Softly gliding, like a bird's song through blossoms, 
Low and choked, like spring water beneath ice. 

The icy spring grows cold, the strings grow stiff and still— 
Silence comes, when sound seems to fade away. 
Yet deeper sorrow, hidden hate, now rise— 
In that silence, all is louder than sound. 

Then, a silver jar bursts open—water sprays forth— 
A cavalry charge erupts, swords and spears clash. 
When music ends, the pick strikes center, drawn sharp— 
Four strings cry out as if tearing silk apart. 

East and west ships fall silent, breathless, still— 
Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river's heart. 

After a pause, she leans down, places the pick within the strings, 
Adjusts her clothes, composes her countenance. 

She says: "I was born in the capital city, 
My home lay beneath the Frog-Mound Lane. 
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, 
Named first among the Imperial Music House. 

After every piece, even the wise teacher bowed; 
After every makeup, the famed Qiuming envied me. 
Nobles young and bold would vie to shower me with gifts— 
One song, one red silk, countless times given. 

Gold-studded combs shattered from rhythm’s beat, 
Crimson robes stained with wine spilled from laughter. 
Years pass in joy and mirth, summer and winter slip by— 
Spring mornings, autumn nights, I pour wine alone. 

No mountain songs, no village flutes? 
Their harsh cries are hard to bear, impossible to enjoy. 

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
It feels like heavenly music—my ears awake. 

Do not refuse—sit again and play one more piece— 
For you, I’ll compose this *Pipa Song*. 

Moved deeply by my words, she stands for long— 
Then sits back, tightens the strings, and plays faster. 

Her music now is colder, sadder than before— 
All at the table weep again, covering their faces. 

Who among us sheds the most tears today? 
The Jiangzhou magistrate, with green robe drenched in sorrow."}

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's head I see a guest off by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I dismount; the guest boards the boat.
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no string or pipe.
Drunk without joy, we grieve at parting;
At parting, the vast river holds the moon.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Seeking the sound, I quietly ask who plays—
The pipa stops; she hesitates before speaking.
We move the boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamp, and open the feast again.
After a thousand calls, she at last comes out,
Half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds—
Before the tune is formed, feeling already lives.
String upon string, muted and low, each note brims with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, at her ease, she plays on and on,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow rubbing, sweeping and flicking—
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The heavy strings rumble like driving rain;
The light strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering mingle as she plays—
Great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers;
Like a muffled spring trapped under ice.
The cold water congeals, the strings grow stiff,
The stiffness blocks the current; the sound rests a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret恨 rises—
In this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver vase breaks, water bursts forth;\nArmored horsemen charge out, swords and spears clash.
At the song's end she sweeps the拨 across the center;
Four strings at once tear like a bolt of silk.
Boats east and west are silent, no one speaks;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart shines white.
Musing, she tucks the拨 among the strings,
Straightens her robes, rises, composes her face.
She speaks: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home lay below Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Music Academy.
After each song the master musicians were won;
When dressed, even Qiu Niang envied me.
The young lords of Wuling competed to send me gifts;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs struck time till they broke;
Blood-red skirts were stained and spoiled with wine.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
Autumn moons, spring winds, I wasted them at ease.
My brother went to war; my aunt passed away;
Dawns and dusks wore on, and my beauty faded.
Before my gate, fewer horses, the place grew cold;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit over parting;
Last month he floated to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I guard this empty boat alone,
The moon bright around me, the river cold.
In the deep night I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face."
I had sighed already at the pipa's sound;
Hearing these words, I sigh again, and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the world's edge—
Why must we have met before to meet tonight?
Since last year I left the capital,
I lie sick and exiled in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote; there is no music here—
All year I have not heard string or pipe.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear instead?
The cuckoo crying blood, gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower mornings in spring, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech,
Like listening to immortal music—my ears, for a moment, are cleared.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
And I will compose a Pipa Song for you.
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits back, quickens the strings, and they grow urgent.
Sorrowful—nothing like the sound before;
The whole room hears it again and weeps.
Who in this company weeps the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou—his blue gown is wet."}

The host forgets to leave, the guest delays his bound.

We follow the sound, softly ask who plays,
The music stops, she hesitates to speak her ways.
We move our boats close, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight the lamps, and feast anew, clear.
After countless calls, she finally comes out,
Still clutching her pipa, half her face hid about.

She turns the pegs, plucks strings a time or two,
No tune yet, but feeling flows before it’s through.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought confined,
As if telling of a life, unfulfilled, resigned.
Brow low, she plays on, hands free and light,
Telling all the endless matters of the night.
Gently pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, plucking,
First “Rainbow Garment,” then “Six Yao” humming.

The large strings roar like sudden, driving rain,
The small strings whisper like a soft refrain.
Roar and whisper, tangled in their sound,
Like pearls, big and small, on jade plates bound.
Like orioles warbling, gliding under flowers,
Or a choked spring, trapped beneath ice’s powers.
The icy spring freezes, strings snap and cease,
Frozen, blocked, the sound finds brief release.
A hidden sorrow, a silent hatred, grows,
In that silence, deeper than any music flows.
Then, like a silver vase, shattering, water bursts forth,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring forth.
At the end, she draws the plectrum across the heart,
All four strings split as one, like tearing silk apart.

On boats east and west, all sits in hushed array,
Only the autumn moon, white in the river’s sway.
She ponders, inserts the plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her robes, rises, her face composed, she sings:
“I was born in the capital’s heart,
My home below Toad Hill, a gentle start.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art,
First among the musicians, fame did start.
My tunes made even skilled players bow,
And beauties like Qiu Niang would envy vow.
Young men from five tombs vied with gifts for me,
A single song brought silks, beyond count, for me.
Jeweled combs snapped in time, their fragments flew,
My blood-red skirts were stained with splashing brew.
Year after year, in laughter, we would spend,
Spring breezes, autumn moons, time without end.
But my brother left for war, my aunt passed away,
Dusk gave to dawn, and youth began to decay.
No more carriages at my door, few visitors came,
Now old, I married a merchant, bearing his name.
He values profit over our parting’s pain,
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang for tea’s gain.
Alone at the river’s mouth, I guard the empty boat,
The moon shines bright, the river water cold, remote.
In the deep of night, I dream of my youth’s bright days,
And wake in tears, my makeup washed in crimson ways.”

I sighed upon hearing her pipa’s song,
And hearing her tale, I sighed along.
Both of us, lost souls at the world’s far ends,
Why must we have met, who were never friends?
Last year, I left the capital’s bright gleam,
Exiled and sick, to Xunyang, a distant dream.
This place is remote, no music graces the year,
No strings or flutes, only silence, clear.
I live by the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, a lonely camp.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk’s low hum?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbon’s mournful drum.
On flower-filled spring days or autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone of its blights.

Their crude, discordant sounds, hard to salute.
But tonight, hearing your pipa’s speech so bright,
It’s like celestial music, my ears take flight.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play once more,
For you, I’ll write this “Song of the Pipa,” a store.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and plays with a wilder smile.
The tune, so mournful, unlike the sound before,
The whole assembly weeps, hearing it once more.
Among the guests, whose tears fell most that night?
The Jiangzhou official, his blue robe soaked in light."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge, seeing off a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts; the guest stands in his boat;
He raises his cup to drink, yet no lute or zither plays.
Half-drunk, uncheered, we grieve at our parting soon;
As we part, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water comes a pipa's sound—
The host forgets to go home, the guest forgets to depart.
Following the sound, I ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, and she is slow to answer.
I move my boat nearer and invite her to meet us;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and reopen the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still cradling her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings, a note or two;
Before the tune is formed, emotion is already there.
Each string a murmur, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
She lowers her brows and plays on, carelessly,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly touching, slowly twisting, she sweeps and plucks;
First the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Little Ones.
The thick strings roar like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roars and whispers, mingled and mixed,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Then, like a spring choking, struggling under ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings congeal and break;
When they break and fail to sound, the music pauses for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In that moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Then, like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
The song ends with a stroke across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats to the east and west, all is silent;
We only see the bright autumn moon in the river's heart.
She ponders, puts down her plectrum, tucks it between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.
She says she was once a girl from the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's troupe.
After each song, even the best players were impressed;
Each time she made up, the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.
Her ornate comb would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The spring winds and autumn moons were wasted.
Then her brother went to the army, and her aunt died;
Dusk came and morning went, and her beauty faded.
Before her gate, carriage tracks grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She waits alone at the river mouth in an empty boat,
Surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
And wakes weeping, her tears staining her rouge-streaked cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
And now I live, sick and exiled, in Xunyang.
This place is remote, and there is no music;
All year, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the low, damp banks of the Pen River,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can be heard here, morning and night?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbon's mournful howl.
On days of spring river and flowers, or autumn moon and night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their raucous, grating sound is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
Is like hearing immortal music; my ears are suddenly cleared.
Do not refuse, but sit and play one more song,
And I will dedicate to you a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back, tightens her strings, and the tempo grows faster.
The mournful notes are not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seat who hears it again covers their face and weeps.
Who weeps the most among all the guests?
The Xunzhou official, whose blue gown is wet with tears."}

Where maples and reeds shivered in autumn's chill.
I dismounted; he boarded the boat.
We raised our cups—no lute, no flute to fill
The empty air. Drunk, yet joyless, we faced the parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon's pale gleam—
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's cry.
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot his dream.
We followed the sound, asked softly who played so,
The music stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat near, invited her to show her face,
Poured wine, relit the lamps, set the banquet again.
After a thousand calls, she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her cheek with the screen.
She tuned the strings, plucked two or three notes—
Before a melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string a suppressed sigh, each note a deep thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled despair.

Pouring out the endless things within her heart.

She tucked the拨 among the strings, sighed long,

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's head I see a guest off by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn.
The host dismounts, the guest is on his boat;
He lifts his cup to drink, but no lute or strings.
Drunk without joy, we grieve at parting;
At farewell the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly from the water comes a lute's sound;
The host forgets to go, the guest stays.
Following the sound, I ask in whispers who plays;
The lute stops, she hesitates to speak.
Moving our boat near, we invite her to meet;
Wine is refilled, lamps relit, the feast reopened.
After a thousand calls she finally comes,
Still holding her lute half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings three or two sounds;
Before the melody forms, feeling already fills.
Every string suppressed, every sound full of thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.
Brows low, she idly plucks on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Yao.
The large strings rumble like sudden rain;
The small strings murmur like whispered words.
Rumbles and murmurs mixed and strummed together,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smoothly under flowers,
Like a choked spring trickling under ice.
Ice-cold water, the strings freeze and cease;
Frozen, blocked, the sound rests for a while.
A separate hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rise;
At this moment, silence is better than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water bursting;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears ringing.
At the song's end she sweeps the拨 across the center;
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
The boats east and west are silent, no one speaks;
Only the river's heart, the autumn moon, white.
Thoughtfully she puts the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands with solemn face.
She says: I was originally a girl of the capital,
My home was under Hail Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the lute,
My name was listed first in the Music Academy.
When I finished a song, even the masters admired;
When I dressed up, even Qiu Niang envied.
The young men of Five Tombs competed to send gifts;
For one song, red silk past counting.
Gold-headed silver combs broken keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy;
Autumn moon and spring wind passed idly.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Evening went, morning came, my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew few, horses cold;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit, lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Coming and going, I guard the empty boat alone;
Around the boat, bright moon, cold river water.
Deep in night I suddenly dream of youthful things;
In dreams I weep, my makeup streaked with tears.
I heard the lute and already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
Both of us are people lost at the edge of the sky;
Why must we have met before to know each other?
Since last year I left the imperial capital;
Exiled and ill, I lie in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, has no music;
All year I hear no lute or string sounds.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;\nYellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons mourning.
Spring river, flower mornings, autumn moon nights;
Often I take wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your lute's language;
Like hearing celestial music, my ears briefly bright.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song;
For you, I will write a Song of the Lute.
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits back, quickens the strings, they turn urgent.\nSad and mournful, not like the sound before;
The whole company hearing again, all weep.
Among the guests, whose tears fell most?
The Jiangzhou司马, his blue gown wet."}

Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there was no zither or flute to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, grimly about to part,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she played on with casual ease,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.

First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.

The thin strings whispered like private talk.

Four strings together, like tearing silk.

Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.

Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.

Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.

One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.

Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.

Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.

The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge, I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reeds tremble in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards the boat,
We raise our cups to drink, but no lutes or flutes float.
Drunk, yet not merry, we part in sorrow's gloom,
As the vast river swallows the moon's fading bloom.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his bound.
Following the sound, we ask who plays the tune,
The pipa stops; she hesitates, as if in a swoon.
We move our boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight the lamps, and hold a banquet here.
After countless calls, she finally comes,
Still clutching her pipa, half-hiding her face's blooms.
Turning the pegs, she plucks two or three strings,
Not yet a melody, but emotion already clings.
Each string's suppressed sigh, each note a deep thought,
As if telling a life of dreams dearly bought.
Brow low, she plays on, her fingers tracing a stream,
Telling all the endless sorrows of her dream.
With light strokes and slow rubs, she strums and picks,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Little Yangko" tricks.
The low strings rumble like a sudden rain,
The high strings whisper like a secret's bane.
Rumble and whisper, a chaotic blend,
Like pearls, great and small, on a jade plate descend.
Like orioles singing soft through flower-laden boughs,
Or a choked spring struggling under icy sloughs.
The icy spring freezes, the strings snap and cease,
A silence where hidden sorrows find release.
Then, a silver vase shatters, water bursts and flies,
Armored cavalry charges, swords and spears arise.
The song ends with a sweep across the heart,
Four strings crackle as if tearing silk apart.
All boats, east and west, are hushed and still,
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart remains, pale and chill.
Pensively, she tucks the pick between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, her face regaining composure's wings.
She says, "I was once a girl from the capital's pride,
My home was by toad-hill, where the shadows hide.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
My name stood first in the Music Academy's chart.
My playing once made even masters bow,
And when adorned, I was envied by beauties' vow.
Young lords of five tombs vied for my favor's sign,
A red silk scarf for each song, their gifts unconfined.
Jeweled combs broke as they clapped to my tune,
My blood-red silk skirts were stained by spilled wine's boon.
Year after year, in laughter we passed our days,
Spring winds and autumn moons, in careless haze.
My brother left for war, my aunt died in her prime,
Dusk turned to dawn, and my beauty slipped its time.
Before my door, horses grew few, the crowds grew thin,
Old, I married a merchant, a life of trade and sin.
He values profit over our parting's tears,
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang's spheres.
He comes and goes, leaving me to guard an empty boat,
The moon shines bright, the river's cold, a lonely float.
In the deep night, I dream of my youthful years,
Wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears tracing sorrow's fears."
I sighed upon hearing her pipa's song,
And hearing her tale, I sighed again, all along.
Both of us, exiles on the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met to know this shared dearth?
Since last year, I left the capital's bright scene,
Exiled and sick, I lie in Xunyang's demeane.
Xunyang is remote, no music graces my ear,
All year, I hear no lute or flute's sound clear.
I live by the low-lying Penjiang's damp ground,
Reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk's mournful sigh?
The cuckoo's blood-curdling cry, the gibbons' wail high.
On flower-filled spring days, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often drink alone, seeking solace in fights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They're harsh and grating, hard to bear, the truths.
Tonight, I hear your pipa's words, so clear and bright,
Like fairy music, my ears see light.
Please, don't refuse, sit and play another tune,
For you, I'll write this "Pipa Ballad" to croon.
Moved by my words, she stands for long, then sits and plays,
Her strings quicken, her tune takes a sadder maze.
Sadder still than before, the mournful strain,
All in the audience weep, overwhelmed by pain.
Who wept the most among us, tears falling free?
The Jiangzhou Sima, my blue robe soaked, was he."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays.

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part,
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises,
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?”
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless.
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last,
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes—
No tune yet, but feeling already flows.

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing,
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers,
Telling all the sorrows in her heart.

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting—
First *Fei Huang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down,
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk.

Clashing, mingling, interweaving—
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls.

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear,
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass.

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard.

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out.

When the final stroke cuts across the heart,
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart.

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs,
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart.

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings,
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity.

She says: “I was born in the capital city,
My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute,
Named first among the Imperial School’s best.

After my songs had silenced even masters,
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me.

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years.

Year after year, laughter and joy,
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed.

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast.
Old age creeps in with every dawn and dusk.

Front gate now lonely, horses and riders few—
In my twilight years, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care for profit, not for parting—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the river bank,
Moon circles the boat, cold waters rise.

Late at night, I dream of youth—
Waking, I weep, tears streaking my painted face.

Hearing her lute, I sigh deep—
And hearing her tale, I sigh again.

We are both lost souls, far from home,
Why need we have met before to feel this kinship?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, lacking music—
All year long, no strings or bamboo pipes.

Near Pien River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.

What sounds do I hear day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding red in the trees, monkeys wailing.

On spring mornings, blooming flowers, autumn nights under moonlight—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the riverbank of Xunyang, I bid farewell to a guest one night,
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays.

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part,
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises,
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?”
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless.
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last,
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes—
No tune yet, but feeling already flows.

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing,
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers,
Telling all the sorrows in her heart.

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting—
First *Fei Huang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down,
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk.

Clashing, mingling, interweaving—
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls.

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear,
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass.

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard.

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out.

When the final stroke cuts across the heart,
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart.

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs,
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart.

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings,
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity.

She says: “I was born in the capital city,
My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute,
Named first among the Imperial School’s best.

After my songs had silenced even masters,
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me.

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years.

Year after year, laughter and joy,
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed.

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast.
Old age creeps in with every dawn and dusk.

Front gate now lonely, horses and riders few—
In my twilight years, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care for profit, not for parting—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the river bank,
Moon circles the boat, cold waters rise.

Late at night, I dream of youth—
Waking, I weep, tears streaking my painted face.

Hearing her lute, I sigh deep—
And hearing her tale, I sigh again.

We are both lost souls, far from home,
Why need we have met before to feel this kinship?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, lacking music—
All year long, no strings or bamboo pipes.

Near Pien River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.

What sounds do I hear day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding red in the trees, monkeys wailing.

On spring mornings, blooming flowers, autumn nights under moonlight—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no folk songs, no village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, discordant—hard to bear.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s words,
It’s like listening to celestial music—my ears clear.

Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece—
I will rewrite your story as a *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands still a long while—
Then sits again, tightening the strings, playing faster.

Her music now is more sorrowful than before—
Everyone in the circle, hearing again, covers faces, weeping.

Who shed the most tears in this room?
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his blue robe wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays.

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part,
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises,
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?”
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless.
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last,
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes—
No tune yet, but feeling already flows.

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing,
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers,
Telling all the sorrows in her heart.

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting—
First *Fei Huang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down,
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk.

Clashing, mingling, interweaving—
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls.

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear,
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass.

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard.

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out.

When the final stroke cuts across the heart,
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart.

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs,
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart.

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings,
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity.

My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute,
Named first among the Imperial School’s best.

After my songs had silenced even masters,
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me.

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years.

Year after year, laughter and joy,
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed.

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast.
Old age creeps in with every dawn and dusk.

Front gate now lonely, horses and riders few—
In my twilight years, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care for profit, not for parting—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the river bank,
Moon circles the boat, cold waters rise.

Late at night, I dream of youth—
Waking, I weep, tears streaking my painted face.

Hearing her lute, I sigh deep—
And hearing her tale, I sigh again.

We are both lost souls, far from home,
Why need we have met before to feel this kinship?

Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted; my guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, but there was no lute or string to drink to.

And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.

Added wine, relit the lamps, and began the banquet anew.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.

Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and flicked the strings with grace,
First playing Rainbow Skirt, then Liù Yāo.

The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.
The roaring and whispering, the complex interplay,
Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, the notes were fluid,
Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
The sound was blocked, and for a moment, it was silent.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the end of the tune, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent,
Only the bright autumn moon on the river could be seen.

Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn expression.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
After she finished a song, even the masters were impressed,
When she dressed up, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to give her gifts of silk,
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Her jeweled hairpins would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy followed year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes were passed by in leisure.

As days and nights passed, my youth faded.

The boat surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of my youth,
And woke weeping in my makeup, my tears staining my red railing.

And hearing her words, I sighed again from deep within.

Why must we have met to feel this kinship?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River, seeing a guest off at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she'd speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Yao."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the Xiama Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the Music Bureau's troupe.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her crimson silk skirt was often stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk turned to dawn, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over love, and they were often parted;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the capital's jade stairs,
Exiled and sick, I lie in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On a spring river morning or an autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their harsh and discordant sound is hard to bear.
To hear your pipa tonight is like hearing celestial music,
My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Deeply moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and the tempo grows more urgent.
Mournful and bleak, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats, hearing it again, weeps.
Of all the people here, whose tears fell the most?
The River Prefect, whose dark blue robe was soaked with tears."}

On the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off at night,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.

more wine was brought, the lamps relit, and the feast began anew.

still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.

it seemed to tell of a life of unfulfilled hopes.

telling of all the countless troubles in her heart.

The low strings roared like a sudden downpour,

The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and broke,

at that moment, silence was better than sound.

Thoughtfully, she put the plectrum between the strings,

At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,

When she finished a song, even the best players were impressed;
when she made herself up, even the famous beauties were jealous.
The young men from the five noble tombs competed to give her gifts;
for one song, they gave countless bolts of red silk.
Her jeweled pin and silver comb were smashed to pieces as they beat time;
her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, there was only laughter and joy,
the autumn moon and spring breeze passed by without a thought.

Visitors became rare, horses and carriages few,
and in her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;

She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
and in her dream, she weeps, her tears staining her rouge-streaked face.

hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper still.
We are both people cast to the ends of the earth;
why must we have known each other before to meet?

the sound stopped, unable to pass through.

straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.

the autumn moon and spring breeze passed by without a thought.

On the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off at night,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there were no lutes or flutes.
We grew drunk, but not merry; a sad farewell was coming.
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, we asked secretly who was playing.
The pipa stopped; words came slowly, with hesitation.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
more wine was brought, the lamps relit, and the feast began anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes;
before the tune was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and brooding;
it seemed to tell of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, she played on, skillfully and readily,
telling of all the countless troubles in her heart.
Light pressing, slow rolling, stroking and picking,
first "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Young."
The low strings roared like a sudden downpour,
the high strings whispered like private talk,
roaring and whispering, all mixed together,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing sweetly under the flowers,
like a choked-up spring struggling under the ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and broke,
the sound stopped, unable to pass through.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, was born;
at that moment, silence was better than sound.
Then a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
as if an armored cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
all four strings at once, like a piece of silk being torn.
The boats east and west were silent and speechless;
only the white autumn moon in the river's heart could be seen.
Thoughtfully, she put the plectrum between the strings,
straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was a woman from the capital,
whose home was at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's ranks.
When she finished a song, even the best players were impressed;
when she made herself up, even the famous beauties were jealous.
The young men from the five noble tombs competed to give her gifts;
for one song, they gave countless bolts of red silk.
Her jeweled pin and silver comb were smashed to pieces as they beat time;
her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, there was only laughter and joy,
the autumn moon and spring breeze passed by without a thought.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
dusk came, morning went, and her youth began to fade.
Visitors became rare, horses and carriages few,
and in her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;
last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
and in her dream, she weeps, her tears staining her rouge-streaked face.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper still.
We are both people cast to the ends of the earth;
why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
and was exiled and fell ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is a remote place with no music;
all year long, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,

my ears are suddenly cleansed and enlightened.

On the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off at night,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there were no lutes or flutes.
We grew drunk, but not merry; a sad farewell was coming.
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, we asked secretly who was playing.
The pipa stopped; words came slowly, with hesitation.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
more wine was brought, the lamps relit, and the feast began anew.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes;
before the tune was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and brooding;
it seemed to tell of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, she played on, skillfully and readily,
telling of all the countless troubles in her heart.
Light pressing, slow rolling, stroking and picking,
first "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Young."
The low strings roared like a sudden downpour,
the high strings whispered like private talk,
roaring and whispering, all mixed together,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing sweetly under the flowers,
like a choked-up spring struggling under the ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and broke,
the sound stopped, unable to pass through.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, was born;
at that moment, silence was better than sound.
Then a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
as if an armored cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
all four strings at once, like a piece of silk being torn.
The boats east and west were silent and speechless;
only the white autumn moon in the river's heart could be seen.
Thoughtfully, she put the plectrum between the strings,
straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was a woman from the capital,
whose home was at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's ranks.
When she finished a song, even the best players were impressed;
when she made herself up, even the famous beauties were jealous.
The young men from the five noble tombs competed to give her gifts;
for one song, they gave countless bolts of red silk.
Her jeweled pin and silver comb were smashed to pieces as they beat time;
her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, there was only laughter and joy,
the autumn moon and spring breeze passed by without a thought.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
dusk came, morning went, and her youth began to fade.
Visitors became rare, horses and carriages few,
and in her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;
last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat,
surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
and in her dream, she weeps, her tears staining her rouge-streaked face.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper still.
We are both people cast to the ends of the earth;
why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
and was exiled and fell ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is a remote place with no music;
all year long, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my house.
What can one hear here, morning and evening?
Only the cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbons' mournful howl.
On a spring river with flowers, or an autumn night with moon,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are so harsh and grating, they are hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, is like hearing immortal music;
my ears are suddenly cleansed and enlightened.
Please do not refuse; sit again and play another song,
and I will compose a "Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
then sat back and tightened the strings, which grew more urgent.
It was mournful, not like the sound before;
the whole audience heard it again, and wept.
Who in the audience shed the most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's head, I see a guest off by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismount, the guest steps into the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but no strings play.
Drunk without joy, we grieve at parting;
At parting, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
I forget to go home, the guest delays his setting out.
Seeking the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, she hesitates to speak.
We move our boat near, invite her to meet;
Add wine, relight the lamps, begin the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last comes out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before the melody forms, the feeling is already there.
Each string, each note, sighs with dark restraint;
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled desires.
Eyes lowered, fingers idle, she plays on and on,
Telling all the heart's unbounded matters.
She gathers, rolls, brushes, and picks;
First the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Minor.
The great strings rumble like sudden rain;
The small strings murmur like whispered secrets.
Rumbling and whispering, tangled and plucked,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly under flowers,
Or a spring choked, flowing under ice.
The icy spring freezes, the strings snap tight;
The snap blocks the flow, the sound pauses.
A separate sorrow, a hidden resentment rises;
At this moment, silence is more than sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water spraying;\nLike armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
Four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, no one speaks;
Only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.
Musing, she puts the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composes her face.
She says, 'I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was below Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name topped the first rank of the Teaching Bureau.
My playing once made the masters bow;
My beauty, once made the courtesans jealous.
The young lords of Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I knew not how many bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs beat time till they broke;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy;
The autumn moon and spring wind passed without a thought.
My brother went to war, my aunt died;
Dusk came and went, my youth grew old.
Before my door, carriages grew cold and rare;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
The merchant prizes profit, lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, I guard this empty boat;
The moon shines around the boat, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep, my tears streak my rouge.'
I had sighed already at her pipa;
Hearing her story, I sigh again and again.
We are both men lost at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the capital;
Demoted, ill, I dwell in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I have not heard strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful cry.
On flower-moon spring days, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, grating sound is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
Is like hearing immortal music, my ears briefly cleared.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song;
For you, I will compose a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time;
Then sits, tightens the strings, the pitch grows urgent.\nDesolate, unlike the sound before;
The whole company, hearing it again, weeps.
Who among us weeps the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with tears."}

He dismounts; I board the boat; we lift our cups to drink, 
But no lute nor flute to aid the time, we pause and think. 
Drunk, yet our spirits low, we part in sorrow's gloom, 
The vast river swallows the moon, sealing our doom. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound we hear, 
The host forgets to leave, the guest delays to steer. 
I sought the source and softly asked who played that tune, 
The music stopped, but words came slow, as if too soon. 
I moved my boat to hers and asked her to appear, 
Refilled the wine, relit the lamp, and gathered near. 
After a thousand calls, she finally appears, 
Holding her pipa, half her face veiled by her fears. 
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, three notes or two, 
Before the melody begins, emotion bursts through. 
Each string a sigh, each note a thought of long regret, 
Like telling tales of a life's unfulfilled debt. 
Brows low, her fingers glide, she plays on and on, 
Spilling the heart's infinite tales before the dawn. 
She brushes and kneads, picks and flicks with gentle art, 
First "Song of Flowery Skies," then "Dance of the Small Heart." 
The heavy strings roar like a sudden, driving rain, 
The light strings whisper like secrets told in pain. 
The loud and soft, the mingled chords, in chaos dance, 
Like pearls, great and small, falling in silver sequence. 
Then like an oriole singing smooth beneath the bloom, 
Then like a choked spring, struggling past winter's gloom. 
The ice-cold spring, the strings congeal, the sound is bound, 
All motion stops, and silence holds the very ground. 
A different sorrow, a hidden hate, begins to rise, 
In this moment, silence speaks far more than sound implies. 
Like a silver vase shattering, water bursting free, 
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears in glee. 
The song ends with a stroke across the strings' wide space, 
Four strings one sound, like tearing silk in one embrace. 
The boats around us, all are hushed, not one word said, 
Only the river's heart shows the white autumn moon overhead. 
Thoughtfully, she tucks the plectrum, straightens her robe, 
And rises with a solemn, dignified globe. 
She tells us she was once a maiden of the capital's fame, 
Her home lay by the Toad Mound, a familiar name. 
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa's every art,

Her blood-red silk skirt, stained and spoiled with wine's embrace that night.

The autumn moon, the spring breeze, passed with nothing new.

Morning came, evening went, and youth began to fade.

The dashing youths of Wuling competed to bestow gifts,
For one song, countless rolls of red silk the lift.
Jeweled combs snapped in time with the beat,
Crimson skirts were stained by spilled wine, oh so sweet.

Spent idly with spring breezes and autumn moonlight.

As days and nights flew by, my youth began to decay.
Fewer horses at my door, the crowds grew thin,

He values profit over parting, light as air,

I wait for him by the river mouth, in an empty boat,

Deep in the night, I dream of my youthful days,
Wake crying, my makeup washed away in crimson ways."

We are both lost souls at the edge of the world, pale.
Why must we have known each other before we meet?
I left the capital last year, sick and in retreat,
Exiled to Xunyang, bedridden and low.
This place has no music; all year, no strings to know.
I live by the Pen River, low and damp,

The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked in plight."}

Like orioles gliding under flowers, the notes are smooth;
Like a muffled spring beneath ice, they are hard to pass.
The cold spring freezes; the strings seem to congeal,
Congealed, they block the way, and the sound stops for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret hate, is born;
At this moment, silence is better than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water bursts forth;
Like armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clash.
At the song's end, she draws the pick across the center;
The four strings snap together like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all is silent;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart is white.
Pondering, she tucks the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She speaks: 'I was once a girl from the capital,
Living below Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name headed the list of the foremost troupe.
My playing would make even the best musicians admire me;
My beauty often made the famous courtesans envious.
The young blades of Wuling competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
Silver hairpins beat time until they broke;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
The autumn moons and spring winds were passed in vain.
My brother went to the army; my aunt died;
Days and nights went by, and my looks faded.
Before my gate, carriages grew few, horses were rare;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit and lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the bright moon, the cold river.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep, my tears staining my rouge.'
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
We are both men cast adrift at the end of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the capital's bright scene,
An exile, ill, I dwell in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote; there is no music here;
All year I hear no sound of strings and flutes.
I live near the Pen river, in low, damp ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here from morning to night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons mourning.
On flower-moon spring days and autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their crude, jarring notes are hard to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
It is like hearing immortal music; my ears are briefly cleared.
Do not refuse; sit, and play another song,
And I will write for you a 'Song of the Pipa.'
Touched by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits back, quickens the strings, which grow more urgent.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
