座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River one autumn night, seeing a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted; my guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, but there was no lute or string to drink to.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow,
And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and began the banquet anew.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows and casual fingers, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and flicked the strings with grace,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.
The roaring and whispering, the complex interplay,
Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, the notes were fluid,
Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
The sound was blocked, and for a moment, it was silent.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the end of the tune, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent,
Only the bright autumn moon on the river could be seen.

Musing, she put the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn expression.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
After she finished a song, even the masters were impressed,
When she dressed up, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to give her gifts of silk,
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Her jeweled hairpins would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy followed year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes were passed by in leisure.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
As days and nights passed, my youth faded.
Few horses and carriages stopped at my door,
And in my old age, I married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for our parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, leaving me to guard this empty boat,
The boat surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of my youth,
And woke weeping in my makeup, my tears staining my red railing.

I had sighed when I heard the pipa's music,
And hearing her words, I sighed again from deep within.
Both of us are people cast to the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met to feel this kinship?
I left the capital last year, and was banished to this sickbed in Xunyang.
This place is remote and has no music,
I have not heard the sound of strings all year long.
Living near the marshy river, the land is low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What can I hear here, morning and night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons howling in sorrow.
On a spring morning with flowers, or an autumn night with the moon,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are too crude and jarring to listen to.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
Is like hearing the music of immortals; my ears are enlightened.
Do not refuse, but sit and play one more song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat and tightened her strings, the tempo growing faster.
The mournful notes were not like the ones before,
And the whole audience, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Among the guests, whose tears fell the most?
The tears of the Master of Jiangzhou soaked his blue robe."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted; my guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, but there was no lute or string to drink to.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow,
And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and began the banquet anew.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows and casual fingers, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and flicked the strings with grace,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.
The roaring and whispering, the complex interplay,
Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, the notes were fluid,
Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
The sound was blocked, and for a moment, it was silent.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the end of the tune, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent,
Only the bright autumn moon on the river could be seen.

Musing, she put the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn expression.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
After she finished a song, even the masters were impressed,
When she dressed up, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to give her gifts of silk,
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Her jeweled hairpins would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy followed year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes were passed by in leisure.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
As days and nights passed, my youth faded.
Few horses and carriages stopped at my door,
And in my old age, I married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for our parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, leaving me to guard this empty boat,
The boat surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of my youth,
And woke weeping in my makeup, my tears staining my red railing.

I had sighed when I heard the pipa's music,
And hearing her words, I sighed again from deep within.
Both of us are people cast to the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met to feel this kinship?
I left the capital last year, and was banished to this sickbed in Xunyang.
This place is remote and has no music,

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge I see a guest off by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn light.
I dismount, the guest boards the boat;
We raise our cups, but no lute or flute plays.
Drunk without joy, we part in sorrow;
At parting, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa—

Following the sound, I ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops; she hesitates to answer.
We move the boat nearer, invite her to meet;
Add wine, relight the lamps, reopen the feast.

Each string sobs, each note sighs,

Brow low, fingers casual, she plays on,

Light pressing, slow twisting, plucking and flicking,
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Minor.'
The big strings roar like sudden rain,
The small strings whisper like private speech.\nRoars and whispers interweave,
Like pearls, big and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,

A hidden sorrow, a dark resentment rises—

Four strings cry out as if tearing silk.

Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.

Autumn moons and spring winds passed by in ease.

Dawns and dusks wore my youth away.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

Their crude, grating sound is hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech—
Like celestial music, my ears brighten at last.
Do not refuse; sit and play once more,
And I will turn your song into a 'Pipa Ballad.'
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits back, quickens the strings—now faster,急.
Sadder, sadder than before,

The maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest boards his boat.
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music.
Drunk, we cannot be merry; sadly we must part.
At parting, the vast river is drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa.
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask in a low voice: who is playing?
The pipa stops; she hesitates to speak.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to meet.
We add wine, relight the lamps, and begin the feast again.
After a thousand calls, she finally comes out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings a few times,
Before the tune begins, there is already feeling.
Each string, each note, is heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled dreams.
She lowers her brows, plays on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things in her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, strumming and picking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, tangled together,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then a choked flow of springs, frozen under ice.
The ice-cold spring chills the strings to a halt;
The sound stops, blocked and frozen for a time.
A secret sorrow, a hidden regret, is born.
In this moment, the silence is more than the sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly broken, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the end of the song, she sweeps the拨 across the center;
The four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all is silent and still;
Only the autumn moon in the river's heart, white and bright.
Pensive, she puts the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says: I was a girl of the capital,
My home was near Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Teaching Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, the beauties were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.\nJeweled combs broke as we beat time;
My crimson skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, we laughed and sang,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed by in vain.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died.
Day turned to night, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, horses and carriages grew rare.
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit, not our time together.
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
The moon is bright around the boat, the river water cold.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake, crying, my tears staining my rouge.
I sighed when I heard her pipa,
And hearing her words, I sighed again.
We are both people, lost at the edge of the world.
Why must we have met before to understand?
Since last year, I left the capital,
Demoted and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I hear no string or wind.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On flower-viewing mornings, moonlit autumn nights,

Maple leaves and reeds rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest stays aboard the boat;
Toasting with wine, yet no music plays.
Drunk but not joyful, sad as we part,
As dusk descends, the river drowns the moon in its mist.
Suddenly, from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets his return, the guest halts his voyage.

She winds the axle, plucks the strings twice or thrice;

Each note mournful, each tone filled with memory,
Like lamenting a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, fingers glide one after another,
Telling all the heart’s unspeakable sorrows.
Gently stroking, slowly pressing, gliding and lifting,

The deep strings thunder like a stormy downpour;
The high ones whisper soft as private talk.
Thunder and whisper interweave in chaotic play,

Then, in that stillness, deeper grief blooms.

An iron cavalry charges — swords and spears clash.

Hearing her tale, I sigh once more.
We’re both exiled souls at the world’s edge —
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Exiled here, bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang’s isolated, without music;
All year long, no string or bamboo sounds.
Near Pien River, damp and low-lying,

All seated, hearing again, we all cry out in grief.
Who wept most in this gathering?
The Jiangzhou magistrate, his blue robe soaked in tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds rustle in autumn's chill.
I dismount to welcome him; he stays on board—
We raise our cups, but no music plays.

Drunk, we can't find joy in parting,
as dusk descends, moonlight floods the river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: "Who's playing?"
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like pearls tumbling on jade plates.

Now clear as a bird skims through blossoms,
Now choked as springs flow under ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
Then silence speaks more than sound.

A silver jar breaks—water gushes forth,
Armored cavalry charges, swords and spears clash.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
a blood-red silk skirt stained by spilled wine.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breeves passed carefree.

My brother departed for the army, my madam died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, grating, hard to bear.

Yet tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly bright.

Please, don’t refuse—sit once more to play,
I'll compose a poem for you: *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits, tightens the strings—now the music quickens.

Her new melody is colder than before—
All seated weep anew, eyes veiled in tears.

Who weeps the most among us all?
The River Chief of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

In rustling reeds and maples deep, the autumn sighs.
The host dismounts; the guest boards boat; to drink we raise,
No lute or fiddle's sound to grace those parting days.
All drunk, but joyless, we prepare to leave in sorrow,
The vast river drinks the moon, a parting on the morrow.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa's notes we hear,
The host forgets his homeward way; the guest delays his pier.
We ask the player softly, "Who makes music there?"
The pipa stops; she hesitates, she doesn't dare.
We move our boats together, invite her to appear,
Pour wine, relight the lamps, and start the feast once more.
After calls and pleas, she finally comes to sight,
Still hugging her pipa, half her face from us in light.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings, two or three notes at first,
A tune not yet formed, but emotion is already nursed.
Each string's suppressed, each note a sigh, a pensive sound,
As if telling of a life where fortunes were not found.
Brows low, she idly plays, and lets the music flow,
Telling of all the countless things that in her heart did grow.
She plucks and strums, she rolls her fingers, now slow, now fast,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Little Yangtze," from the past.
The great strings rumble like a sudden, driving rain,
The small strings whisper like a soft, secret refrain.
Rumbling and whispering, a complex, tangled sound,
Like pearls, both large and small, on a jade plate, falling round.
Like orioles, their speech, in flowers, is smooth and clear,
Then choked, like springs beneath ice, so hard to hold so near.
The icy spring runs cold and slow, the strings are stiff and tight,
The sound is blocked, a silence comes, the music stops its flight.
A deeper melancholy, hidden sorrow, starts to grow,
This moment's silence speaks more than the notes we've learned to know.
Then, like a silver vase that shatters, water bursts in flight,
Or armored horsemen charge, with swords and spears in clanging might.
The song ends, a sweep of the拨 across the strings' own heart,
Four strings at once, a single tear, as silk is torn apart.
In boats to east and west, all sit in silent awe,
And see the autumn moon, white in the river's central maw.
Pensive, she puts the拨 back, straightens her clothes with grace,
And with a solemn face, she turns to show her history's trace.
She says she was a girl from the capital's bright scene,
Her home was near the Toad Mound, where life had once been keen.
At thirteen, she had mastered pipa's art's command,
Her name was listed first among the court's performing band.
When she finished a song, the skilled masters were impressed;
When her makeup was complete, the autumn beauties were depressed.
The young nobles of Wuling competed for her favor's sign,
For one song's worth of red silk, their gifts I can't define.
Her silver comb would break with time to the beat's own sound,
Her blood-red silk skirt would be stained with the spilled wine's round.
Year after year, in laughter and in song, did she pass by,
The autumn moon, the spring wind, were wasted, and went by.
Her brother left for the army, her aunt she saw no more,
As evenings came and mornings went, her youthful looks she wore.
Before her gate, the horses' hooves grew sparse, the crowds grew thin,
And now, grown old, she married a merchant, deep within.
The merchant values profit, and cares little for good-bye,
Last month, he went to buy his tea in Fuliang, and I
Am left to guard this empty boat, here at the river's mouth,
The moon shines bright around the boat, the river's cold, in truth.
In the deep night, she dreams of her youth's days gone by,
And wakes from crying, with red tear-stains upon her cheek, and I
Heard her pipa and sighed, and hearing these words, I sigh once more,
We are both lost souls, adrift; why must we have met before?
I left the capital last year, and fell ill in this town,
Exiled to Xunyang, a place with no music's renown.
This place is remote, with no music's sweet, familiar sound,
All year, I hear no strings or flutes, no joy is to be found.
I live near the Pan river, in this damp and lowly place,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the space.
What can I hear here, morn and eve, but cuckoos' bloody cries,
And gibbons' mournful howls, beneath these vast and empty skies?
On flower mornings in spring, on moonlit nights in fall,
I often take my wine, and drink it all alone, and call
For songs. Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes to play?
They're harsh, and crude, and difficult to listen to, and stray.
But tonight, I heard your pipa's voice, and my ears were made bright,
Like listening to the music of the gods, a moment's light.
Do not refuse, but sit and play one more song for me,
And I will write a "Pipa Xing" for you, to set you free.
Moved by my words, she stands for long, then sits and tunes her strings,
The pitch is higher, and the tempo faster as it swings.
More mournful than the sound before, it's full of pain and grief,
And all who hear it in this place are moved to silent relief.
And who among us weeps the most, with tears that fall like rain?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's head, I see a guest off by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn light.
The host dismounts, the guest steps on the boat;
We raise our cups, but no lute or flute to float.
Drunk without joy, we part in grief and gloom;
The river floods with moonlight at our parting's room.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound—
The host forgets to leave, the guest stays, bound.
We ask in whispers who may play this strain;
The music stops; she hesitates to explain.
We move our boat near hers and bid her come;
Relight the lamps, bring wine, and make the feast resume.
Called a thousand times, at last she comes outside,
Half hiding her face behind the pipa's side.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings three, two, one—
Before the tune, a feeling's breathed and done.
Each string, subdued, each note, a sigh of thought,
As if her life's unfulfilled grief she sought.
Brow low, at ease, she plays on, string by string,
Telling the heart's unending everything.
She gathers, twists, and brushes, then picks fast—
First 'Rainbow Garment,' then 'Six Threads' in haste.
The low strings roar like sudden, rushing rain;
The high strings whisper, soft as private pain.
Now loud, now soft, in tangled, crossing flight—
Like pearls, great and small, falling on jade bright.
Like orioles singing smooth beneath the flowers,
Or a cold spring choked beneath frozen bowers.
The ice-cold spring congeals, the strings grow still;"The sound, blocked up, breaks off against her will.
A deeper sorrow, hidden hatred, springs—
At this moment, silence out-sings all things.
Like a silver vase that cracks and water bursts,
Or armed horsemen with clashing swords and spears.
The song ends; her pick sweeps across all four;
One sound, like tearing silk, from shore to shore.
In boats east and west, all is hushed, no word;
Only the autumn moon on the river, seen, is heard.
Pensive, she tucks the pick behind the strings;
Adjusts her clothes, rises, and composure brings.
She says: 'I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was by Hama Hill, near the canal.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
Ranked first in the Music Bureau's every part.
My playing made the masters bow in awe;
My beauty made the famous courtesans draw
The envy of their eyes. Young gallants vied
To shower me with gifts; for one song, untied
Red silks unnumbered. Hairpins, combs of silver, beat
In time to music, broke. My crimson skirt,
Wine-stained, was turned in dance. Year after year,
Laughter and spring breezes, all held dear,
Were spent and wasted. Then my brother went to war,
My aunt died; day by day, my youth grew poor.
Before my gate, fewer and fewer steeds;
I married, old, a merchant, for my needs.
He values profit, not our parting's pain;
Last month he left for Fuliang, to buy tea's grain.
I wait alone in our boat at the river's mouth,
Around the boat, the moon, the water, cold as drouth.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth's days,
And wake, crying, my tears streaking my face's haze.'
I sigh to hear her pipa, and now, to hear her tale,
I sigh again, and my heart cannot but fail.
Both of us, lost souls at the edge of the sky—
Why must we have met to know this, you and I?
Since last year I left the capital's bright scene,
To lie, demoted, sick in Xunyang's demesne.
Xunyang is remote; there's no music here,
All year, no sound of strings or flutes to cheer.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
With yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, a damp.
What do I hear from morning until night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbons' plight.
On spring river days, or autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone in flights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?\nThey're harsh, discordant, hard on ears and suits.
But tonight, to hear your pipa's words, is like
Hearing immortal music, my ears quick.
Don't refuse—sit, play one song more for me;
I'll write a 'Song of the Pipa,' for all to see.
Moved by my words, she stands a long, long while;
Then sits, tightens her strings, and with new fire
Plays a more mournful tune than all before;
The whole assembly weeps, and weeps some more.
Who weeps the most among us, you may ask?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe, a mask."}

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,

Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn light.
I dismounted; my guest stepped aboard the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was neither lute nor flute.
Drunken, but not merry, we prepared to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moonlight in the dark.
Suddenly from the water came a lute’s sound,
I forgot to go back, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a whisper who was playing,
The lute stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambitions.
She lowered her brows and played on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly she strummed, slowly she plucked, swept and flicked,
First the “Rainbow Skirt,” then the “Six Yao” tune.
The high strings roared like sudden rain in the sky,
The low strings whispered like secret words.
Roaring and whispering, they mingled and crossed,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and snapped,
The sound was blocked, and for a while there was silence.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—
In that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.

All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.

Only the white autumn moon in the river’s heart was seen.

Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.

Her home was beneath Toad Hill.

Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.

When dressed, she was envied by the courtesans.

For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.

Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.

The autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died,
Dawn and dusk went by, her beauty faded.
Few carriages and horses stopped at her door,
In old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

The moon shines bright around her, the river water is cold.

Hearing her words, I sighed again, with deeper grief.

maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn’s chill. 
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat; 
raising a cup to drink, yet no strings or pipes to play. 
Drunk but unable to find joy, sorrowful as we part— 
as we depart, the river mirrors moonlight, vast and gray. 

Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa— 
the host forgets to return, the guest halts his sail. 
Searching for the source, I ask softly, “Who plays?” 
The pipa falls silent, hesitant words unsaid. 
I steer my boat near hers, invite her to appear— 
add wine, turn up lamps, reopen the feast again. 

Countless calls bring her forth at last, 
still holding the pipa half-concealed. 
She turns the axle, plucks the strings—three or four notes— 
before any tune is formed, emotion already flows. 

Each string, subdued; each note, a sigh— 
as if recounting a life unfulfilled. 
Bowing her head, fingers move by instinct, 
telling all that lies within her endless heart. 

Gently brushing, slowly rubbing, sliding, then plucking— 
first *Ní Cháng*, then *Liù Yāo*. 
The thick string roars like sudden rain, 
the thin string whispers like private talk. 

Roar and whisper interweave, 
great pearls and small falling on jade plate. 
Now the bird sings smoothly beneath blossoms, 
now a spring runs low beneath frozen stream. 

Cold spring chokes, strings freeze in silence— 
then silence itself breaks, a pause held long. 
Another sorrow, hidden, deepening, 
in this stillness, silence speaks more than sound. 

A silver bottle cracks—water spurts out; 
a cavalry charge bursts through with swords and spears. 
When the final stroke strikes the center of the string, 
four strings snap once: like cloth torn wide. 

East and west boats fall utterly silent— 
only see the autumn moon white over the river’s heart. 

After a pause, she rests the pick, slides it into the strings, 
adjusts her clothes, rises with composed face. 

She says: “Born originally in the capital city, 
my home lay beneath the Frog-Mound Lane. 
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art, 
ranked first among the Imperial School’s top band. 

After one song, even the master bowed in praise; 
after each makeup, the lady Qiu would envy me. 
Five-Border youths vied to toss silk scarves— 
a single tune could earn ten, twenty lengths. 

Silver hairpins shatter with every beat; 
crimson gowns stained by wine, spilled and grimed. 
Year after year, laughter comes and goes— 
spring moons and autumn winds pass casually. 

My brother left for war, my aunt died— 
days fade, mornings vanish, youth departs. 
The gate grows cold, fewer riders now come— 
old, I married a merchant. 

Merchants care only for profit, not for farewells— 
last month, he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea. 
He came and went, leaving me here alone— 
around the empty boat, moonlight and icy water shine. 

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s bright days— 
awake sobbing, makeup streaked red across my face. 

I heard the pipa, sighed already— 
and hearing her tale, I sighed again. 

We are both wanderers far from home, 
meeting need not mean we knew before. 

I left the capital last year, 
exiled, ill, lying in Xunyang town. 
Xunyang is remote, lacks music— 
throughout the year, no silken bamboo sounds. 

Near Pénjiang, land low and damp— 
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around. 
What do I hear day and night? 
Crows cry blood, apes wail through the dusk. 

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moon— 
often I pour wine, drinking solitarily. 
Are there no mountain ballads, no rustic flutes? 
Their cries are harsh, grating, hard to bear. 

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
like listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear. 

Do not refuse—sit again, play one more tune— 
I will compose this song for you, called “Pipa Xíng.” 

Moved by my words, she stands long, then sits back, 
tightens the strings—the music quickens. 

The tone now mournful, not as before—

Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, he boarded the boat; we raised our cups,
But there were no pipes or strings to go with the wine.
Drunk without joy, we faced the sad parting,
When the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot to go back; my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked softly, "Who plays?"
The music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to show her face,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three notes,
Before the tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brows lowered, she went on playing, her fingers moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking,
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, tangled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and bright,
Then like a choked spring flowing under ice.
The ice-cold spring made the strings stiff and mute,
The sound stopped, blocked, and paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, an unspoken grievance, arose—
At that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then a silver vase shattered, water bursting forth,
Armored cavalry charging, swords and lances clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke at the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.
All around, boats fell silent, not a word,
Only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river.
She put down the plectrum, tucked it among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After a song, even the finest players were humbled;
Her beauty made the autumn beauties jealous.
Young lords from the five tombs competed to shower her with gifts,
One song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs broken in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Spring winds and autumn moons passed by in vain.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk came, dawn went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, horses grew scarce, visitors rare;
In her old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river in an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold water.
Deep in the night, she dreamed of her youth,
And woke crying, her rouge-stained tears streaking her face.
I had sighed already at her pipa,
But hearing her words, I wept again, soft and low.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished and sick, I live in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year round, not a sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,

The Vice-Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose dark blue robe was soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River one autumn night, seeing a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted; my guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, but there was no lute or string to drink to.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow,
And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and began the banquet anew.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows and casual fingers, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and flicked the strings with grace,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.
The roaring and whispering, the complex interplay,
Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, the notes were fluid,
Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
The sound was blocked, and for a moment, it was silent.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the end of the tune, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent,
Only the bright autumn moon on the river could be seen.

Musing, she put the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn expression.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was enrolled in the foremost division of the Music Bureau.
After she finished a song, even the masters were impressed,
When she dressed up, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to give her gifts of silk,
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Her jeweled hairpins would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy followed year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes were passed by in leisure.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
As days and nights passed, my youth faded.
Few horses and carriages stopped at my door,
And in my old age, I married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for our parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, leaving me to guard this empty boat,
The boat surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of my youth,
And woke weeping in my makeup, my tears staining my red railing.

I had sighed when I heard the pipa's music,
And hearing her words, I sighed again from deep within.
Both of us are people cast to the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met to feel this kinship?
I left the capital last year, and was banished to this sickbed in Xunyang.
This place is remote and has no music,
I have not heard the sound of strings all year long.
Living near the marshy river, the land is low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What can I hear here, morning and night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons howling in sorrow.
On a spring morning with flowers, or an autumn night with the moon,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are too crude and jarring to listen to.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
Is like hearing the music of immortals; my ears are enlightened.
Do not refuse, but sit and play one more song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat and tightened her strings, the tempo growing faster.
The mournful notes were not like the ones before,
And the whole audience, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Among the guests, whose tears fell the most?
The tears of the Sima of Jiangzhou soaked his blue robe."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold. 
I dismount; my guest remains on board. 
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays. 

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part, 
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river. 
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises, 
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat. 

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?” 
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless. 
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear, 
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast. 

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last, 
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face. 

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes— 
No tune yet, but feeling already flows. 

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing, 
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams. 

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers, 
Telling all the sorrows in her heart. 

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting— 
First *Fei Huang*, then *Liu Yao*. 

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down, 
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk. 

Clashing, mingling, interweaving— 
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls. 

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear, 
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass. 

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs— 
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard. 

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth, 
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out. 

When the final stroke cuts across the heart, 
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart. 

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs, 
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart. 

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings, 
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity. 

She says: “I was born in the capital city, 
My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley. 

At thirteen, I mastered the lute, 
Named first among the Imperial School’s best. 

After my songs had silenced even masters, 
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me. 

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts— 
One song earned me countless red silks. 

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm, 
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years. 

Year after year, laughter and joy, 
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed. 

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast. 
Old age creeps in with every dawn and dusk. 

Front gate now lonely, horses and riders few— 
In my twilight years, I wed a merchant. 

Merchants care for profit, not for parting— 
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea. 

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the river bank, 
Moon circles the boat, cold waters rise. 

Late at night, I dream of youth— 
Waking, I weep, tears streaking my painted face. 

Hearing her lute, I sigh deep— 
And hearing her tale, I sigh again. 

We are both lost souls, far from home, 
Why need we have met before to feel this kinship? 

I left the capital last year— 
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town. 

Xunyang is remote, lacking music— 
All year long, no strings or bamboo pipes. 

Near Pien River, land low and damp, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door. 

What sounds do I hear day and night? 
Cuckoos bleeding red in the trees, monkeys wailing. 

On spring mornings, blooming flowers, autumn nights under moonlight— 
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the riverbank of Xunyang, I bid farewell to a guest one night, 
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold. 
I dismount; my guest remains on board. 
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays. 

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part, 
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river. 
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises, 
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat. 

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?” 
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless. 
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear, 
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast. 

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last, 
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face. 

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes— 
No tune yet, but feeling already flows. 

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing, 
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams. 

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers, 
Telling all the sorrows in her heart. 

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting— 
First *Fei Huang*, then *Liu Yao*. 

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down, 
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk. 

Clashing, mingling, interweaving— 
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls. 

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear, 
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass. 

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs— 
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard. 

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth, 
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out. 

When the final stroke cuts across the heart, 
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart. 

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs, 
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart. 

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings, 
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity. 

She says: “I was born in the capital city, 
My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley. 

At thirteen, I mastered the lute, 
Named first among the Imperial School’s best. 

After my songs had silenced even masters, 
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me. 

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts— 
One song earned me countless red silks. 

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm, 
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years. 

Year after year, laughter and joy, 
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed. 

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast. 
Old age creeps in with every dawn and dusk. 

Front gate now lonely, horses and riders few— 
In my twilight years, I wed a merchant. 

Merchants care for profit, not for parting— 
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea. 

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the river bank, 
Moon circles the boat, cold waters rise. 

Late at night, I dream of youth— 
Waking, I weep, tears streaking my painted face. 

Hearing her lute, I sigh deep— 
And hearing her tale, I sigh again. 

We are both lost souls, far from home, 
Why need we have met before to feel this kinship? 

I left the capital last year— 
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town. 

Xunyang is remote, lacking music— 
All year long, no strings or bamboo pipes. 

Near Pien River, land low and damp, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door. 

What sounds do I hear day and night? 
Cuckoos bleeding red in the trees, monkeys wailing. 

On spring mornings, blooming flowers, autumn nights under moonlight— 
Often I pour wine, drinking alone. 

Are there no folk songs, no village flutes? 
But their cries are harsh, discordant—hard to bear. 

Tonight, hearing your lute’s words, 
It’s like listening to celestial music—my ears clear. 

Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece— 
I will rewrite your story as a *Pipa Xing*. 

Moved by my words, she stands still a long while— 
Then sits again, tightening the strings, playing faster. 

Her music now is more sorrowful than before— 
Everyone in the circle, hearing again, covers faces, weeping. 

Who shed the most tears in this room? 
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his blue robe wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest is already in his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she'd speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole, smooth beneath the flowers,
A choked spring, difficult to flow beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the toad mound.

Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her blood-red silk skirt was often stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
My fellow pupil left for the army, my matron died;
Dusk turned to dawn, and her youthful looks passed away.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over ties of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,

Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,

My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.

For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Deeply moved by my words, she stands for a long while,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。

间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the riverbank of Xunyang, at night I bid farewell to a guest—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy drunk, I mourn as we part—
Parting in twilight, moon mirrored in the vast river’s sweep.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a lute—
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I softly ask who plays—
The music stops, hesitant, as if about to speak.
I move my boat near, urge them to appear;
Add wine, turn lamps, relight the feast once more.

After many calls, she finally emerges,
Still cradling her lute half-hiding her face.

She turns the peg, plucks a few strings—
Before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string choked down, each note full of longing—
As though recounting an unfulfilled life.
Bowing low, fingers glide, one by one,
Filling the air with sorrows never spoken.

Gently brushing, slowly teasing, sweeping, lifting—
First *Nightsong of the Rainbow Skies*, then *Sixth Lament*.

The deep strings roar like sudden rain,
The light ones whisper like secrets shared.
A jumble of loud and soft tones—
Like pearls dropping on jade plates, clattering clear.

Now a bird's voice slips through blossoms, smooth and sweet,
Then a hidden spring flows beneath ice, slow and strained.

Cold spring chokes, strings frozen—silence breaks—
No sound for breath, yet silence speaks.

Suddenly, a silver jar shatters, water bursts forth—
A warhorse charges, swords clash, steel sings.

When the final stroke cuts across the heart of the strings,
Four strings explode like torn silk.

From east to west, boats grow still—
Only the moon white over the river’s heart.

Lost in thought, she sets down the pick, slides it into the strings,
Smooths her robe, straightens, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
Lived beneath the Hare-Mound Lane.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute;
Name listed first among the Imperial Troupe.

After my song, even master musicians bowed—
After my makeup, even Qiuniang envied me.

Young men from the Five Hills vied to give me gifts—
One song earned me endless red silks.

Silver hairpins struck the beat till broken,
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine.

Happy years pass, year after year—
Autumn moons, spring breezes, all slipped away.

Brother went to war, aunt passed on,
Days pass, nights fade—my beauty fades too.

Empty gate, few horsemen now,
Old, I married a merchant, bound by trade.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewells—
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone—my empty boat drifts here,
Moonlight circles, cold river surging.

Deep in night, I dream of youth—
Weeping in sleep, tears streaked red down my cheeks.

Hearing this lute, I sighed already—
Now hearing these words, my spirit grieves anew.

We’re both lost souls, cast far from home—
Why must we know each other before we feel kinship?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang.

Xunyang is remote, no music heard—
Whole years pass without a flute or string.

Near Pien River, ground low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow round my door.

What sounds do I hear every dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their souls, apes wailing their grief.

On spring mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain ballads, no village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, unbearable to hear.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s song—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly clear.

Do not refuse, sit again—
Let me compose this lute’s tale—for you.

Moved deeply by my words, she stands silent—
Then sits, tightens the strings, makes them quicken.

Her music now is less like before—
Sad, sorrowful, no longer calm.

All seated weep anew, hiding our faces in shame.

Who shed the most tears here tonight?
The Governor of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked through."}

Name listed first among the Imperial Troupe.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy drunk, I mourn as we part—
Parting in twilight, moon mirrored in the vast river’s sweep.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a lute—
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I softly ask who plays—
The music stops, hesitant, as if about to speak.
I move my boat near, urge them to appear;
Add wine, turn lamps, relight the feast once more.

After many calls, she finally emerges,
Still cradling her lute half-hiding her face.

She turns the peg, plucks a few strings—
Before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string choked down, each note full of longing—
As though recounting an unfulfilled life.
Bowing low, fingers glide, one by one,
Filling the air with sorrows never spoken.

Gently brushing, slowly teasing, sweeping, lifting—
First *Nightsong of the Rainbow Skies*, then *Sixth Lament*.

The deep strings roar like sudden rain,
The light ones whisper like secrets shared.
A jumble of loud and soft tones—
Like pearls dropping on jade plates, clattering clear.

Now a bird's voice slips through blossoms, smooth and sweet,
Then a hidden spring flows beneath ice, slow and strained.

Cold spring chokes, strings frozen—silence breaks—
No sound for breath, yet silence speaks.

Suddenly, a silver jar shatters, water bursts forth—
A warhorse charges, swords clash, steel sings.

When the final stroke cuts across the heart of the strings,
Four strings explode like torn silk.

From east to west, boats grow still—
Only the moon white over the river’s heart.

Lost in thought, she sets down the pick, slides it into the strings,
Smooths her robe, straightens, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
Lived beneath the Hare-Mound Lane.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute;
Name listed first among the Imperial Troupe.

After my song, even master musicians bowed—
After my makeup, even Qiuniang envied me.

Young men from the Five Hills vied to give me gifts—
One song earned me endless red silks.

Silver hairpins struck the beat till broken,
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine.

Happy years pass, year after year—
Autumn moons, spring breezes, all slipped away.

Brother went to war, aunt passed on,
Days pass, nights fade—my beauty fades too.

Empty gate, few horsemen now,
Old, I married a merchant, bound by trade.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewells—
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone—my empty boat drifts here,
Moonlight circles, cold river surging.

Deep in night, I dream of youth—
Weeping in sleep, tears streaked red down my cheeks.

Hearing this lute, I sighed already—
Now hearing these words, my spirit grieves anew.

We’re both lost souls, cast far from home—
Why must we know each other before we feel kinship?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang.

Xunyang is remote, no music heard—
Whole years pass without a flute or string.

Near Pien River, ground low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow round my door.

What sounds do I hear every dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their souls, apes wailing their grief.

On spring mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain ballads, no village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, unbearable to hear.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s song—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly clear.

Do not refuse, sit again—
Let me compose this lute’s tale—for you.

Moved deeply by my words, she stands silent—
Then sits, tightens the strings, makes them quicken.

Her music now is less like before—
Sad, sorrowful, no longer calm.

商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River, seeing a guest off at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she’d speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the toad mound.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the court's musicians' troupe.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her blood-stained silk skirt was often stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk turned to dawn, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over love, and they were often parted;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the capital's jade stairs,
Exiled and sick, I lie in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On a spring river morning or an autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their crude, grating sound is hard to bear.
To hear your pipa tonight is like hearing celestial music,
My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Deeply moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and the tempo grows more urgent.
Mournful and bleak, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats, hearing it again, weeps.
Of all the people here, whose tears fell the most?
The River Prefect's, whose blue robe was soaked with tears."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
I dismount to greet the traveler on his boat;
We raise our wine but no music plays to fill the air.

Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting—
At parting, the river is vast, moonlight soaking the waves.

Suddenly, from the water’s edge, a lute’s sound arises—
The host forgets he should return, the guest halts his sail.

Following the music, I ask softly who plays,
The lute falls silent, hesitates before words begin.

I move my boat near, inviting her to come see—
Add wine, adjust the lamp, relight the feast anew.

After countless calls, she appears at last,
Still holding the lute half-hidden by her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune is formed, emotion already flows.

Each string suppressed, each note full of longing—
As if recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing her head, fingers glide one after another,
Speaking through music every secret heart has known.

Softly stroking, slowly pressing, flicking, pulling—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao* she performs.

The bass strings roar like sudden rain,
The treble whispers like lovers’ secrets.

A jumble of loud and soft, clear and muffled:
Like great pearls and small ones falling on jade bowls.

Now smooth as a bird's song through blossoms,
Now choked like spring water beneath frozen ice.

Cold springs grow still, strings freeze in silence—
Then silence swells, louder than any sound.

Then—like a silver vase shattering, water spurts out,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.

When the final stroke cuts the heart of the string,
Four strings snap once—a sound like tearing silk.

All boats in east and west lie still, speechless—
Only the moon white above the river’s heart remains.

She pauses, thinking, slips the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

She says: "I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog-Wharf Lane.

At thirteen I mastered the lute,
Ranking first in the imperial Music Bureau.

After my performance, even the master praised me—
Each time dressed up, the courtesans envied me.

Young nobles vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned more crimson scarves than I could count.

Silver hairpins cracked from rhythm’s beat,
Crimson gowns stained with wine spilled in joy.

Year after year, laughter and delight—
Autumn moons, spring breezes pass carelessly by.

My brother left for war, my aunt passed away—
Days turn to years, beauty fades with time.

The gate grows cold, fewer horses come and go—
Old now, I married a merchant, took his name.

Merchants value profit, scorn farewells—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone and left me alone on the river shore—
Moonlight circles the empty boat, cold water chills.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s past—
Waking, I weep, paint and tears streak my face.

Hearing this lute, I sigh—then hear again,
And sigh deeper still at her sorrowful tale.

We’re both exiles, lost on life’s distant shores—
Why must we have met before to understand?

I left the imperial capital last year,

Xunyang is remote, no music here—
Whole years pass without a single string or flute.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays.

Unhappy in my drunkenness, I must part,
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a lute's sound rises,
My host forgets to return; the guest halts his boat.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who plays?”
The lute falls silent—hesitating, speechless.
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—she comes at last,
Still half-concealed, holding her lute before her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—a few soft notes—
No tune yet, but feeling already flows.

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing,
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bending low, she plays with gentle fingers,
Telling all the sorrows in her heart.

Softly stroking, slowly twisting, pressing, lifting—
First *Ni Chang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick string roars like storm-rain rushing down,
The thin string whispers like secret, private talk.

Clashing, mingling, interweaving—
Pearls large and small fall upon jade bowls.

Glimmering, like a bird’s song through blossoms—sliding clear,
Then choked, like water beneath ice—hard to pass.

The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
For a moment, no sound, yet all feels heard.

Then—like a silver flask bursting open, water gushes forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears ring out.

When the final stroke draws the pick across the middle,
Four strings cry out as if silk were torn apart.

East and west boats hush—no voice stirs,
Only the moon gleams white in the river’s heart.

Silent, I drop the pick into the strings,
Adjust my clothes, compose my face, regain dignity.

She says: “I was born in the capital city,
My home lay beneath the Frog-Beach Alley.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute,
Named first among the Imperial School’s best.

After my songs had silenced even masters,
Every time I dressed, Jiaoniang envied me.

Young men from five noble districts vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered to beat the rhythm,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with years.

Year after year, laughter and joy,
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time passed unnoticed.

My brother enlisted, my aunt died—the days fade fast.
Old age creeps in with every dawn and dusk.

Front gate now lonely, horses and riders few—
In my twilight years, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care for profit, not for parting—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the river bank,
Moon circles the boat, cold waters rise.

Late at night, I dream of youth—
Waking, I weep, tears streaking my painted face.

Hearing her lute, I sigh deep—
And hearing her tale, I sigh again.

We are both lost souls, far from home,
Why need we have met before to feel this kinship?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, lacking music—
All year long, no strings or bamboo pipes.

Near Pien River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.

What sounds do I hear day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding red in the trees, monkeys wailing.

On spring mornings, blooming flowers, autumn nights under moonlight—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no folk songs, no village flutes?
But their cries are grating, jarring—hard to bear.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s words,
It’s like listening to celestial music—my ears clear.

Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece—
I will rewrite your story as a *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands still a long while—
Then sits again, tightening the strings, playing faster.

Her music now is more sorrowful than before—
Everyone in the circle, hearing again, covers faces, weeping.

Who shed the most tears in this room?
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his lowly blue-green robe wet with tears."}
