座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's head I see a guest off by night;
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest boards the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there is neither pipe nor string.
Drunk without joy, in gloom we part;
At parting, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to go, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops; she hesitates to speak.
We move our boat nearer and invite her to show herself;
More wine is brought, lamps relit, the feast begins again.
After a thousand calls, at last she comes out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, three or four sounds;
Before the tune is formed, feeling is already there.
Every string, every note is choked with thought,
As if telling of a life of broken hopes.
Knitting her brows, she plays on carelessly,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, a sweep, a pluck—
First the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Minor tune.
The great strings rumble like sudden rain;
The small strings murmur like whispered words.
The rumbling and the whispering interweave,
Like pearls, great and small, dropping on a jade plate.
Then orioles warble, gliding smooth beneath the flowers;
Then a choked spring struggles under ice.
The icy spring freezes; the strings congeal and break;
The break cuts off—silence falls.\nA secret sorrow, a hidden resentment rises:
Just here, the silence is more moving than sound.
Then—like a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
Like armored riders charging out, swords and spears clashing—
At the song's end she sweeps the拨 across the center;
Four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, without a word;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart, white.
Musing, she tucks the拨 back among the strings,
Straightens her robes, rises with a solemn face.
She tells me: "I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was below Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Music Academy.
When I finished a song, even the master players were humbled;
When I dressed up, the beauties envied me.
The young gallants of Wuling competed to send me gifts;
One song earned me silks past counting.
I beat time with a jeweled comb till it broke,
My crimson skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
Autumn moon and spring breeze I wasted without care.
My brother went to war, my aunt grew old and died;
Days went by, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew few, saddles sparse;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my rouge-stained tears streaking my face."
I had sighed already over her pipa;
Now, hearing her words, I sigh again, again.
Both of us are lost souls at the edge of the world—
Must we have met before for this meeting to matter?
Since last year I left the capital,
A sick exile in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, with no fine music;
All year, no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
Morning and evening, what sounds do I hear here?
The cuckoo crying blood, gibbons mourning.
On flower-bright spring days, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my cup and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak,
It is like hearing the music of immortals—my ears come alive.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
And I will write for you a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
Then sits back, tightens the strings—they grow faster,
More mournful than before.
The whole room, hearing it again, hides their tears.
Who wept the most among all the guests?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue robe was wet."}

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn air.
I had dismounted, my guest was in the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to accompany us.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in sorrow;
The parting scene was vast and misty, the river flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
We added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the banquet.
After a thousand entreaties she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune began, emotion was already there.
Each string, each phrase was heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled aspirations.
With lowered brows she played on and on,
Telling all the countless things in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First she played “Rainbow Skirts,” then “Six Yao.”
The thick strings clattered like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
The clattering and whispering were interwoven;
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers,
Like a hidden stream choking under ice.
The icy stream froze, the strings grew stiff and snapped;\nThe snap broke off, and for a moment the sound ceased.
A separate sorrow and hidden resentment rose;
At this moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Suddenly a silver vase seemed to burst, water gushing forth;\nArmored cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end, with a sweep she struck the center;
All four strings at once, like tearing silk.
The boats east and west were silent;
Only the autumn moon, white at the river’s center, could be seen.
Pensively she tucked the plectrum into the strings,
Adjusted her garments, and composed her expression.
She said, “I am originally from the capital city,
My home was near Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed first in the Music School.
After each performance, even the finest musicians admired me;
When dressed up, I was often envied by the courtesans.
The young gallants of the Five Tombs would vie to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
My jeweled hairpins snapped as I kept time;
My blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of joy followed another,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed idly by.
My younger brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Morning after evening, my beauty faded.
The horses and carriages before my door grew sparse;
Growing old, I became a merchant’s wife.
The merchant valued profit and lightly bore separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone on the empty boat at the river’s mouth;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the water cold.
In the deep night I suddenly dream of my youth;
I wake weeping, my makeup streaked with tears.
I sighed when I first heard the pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again.\nBoth of us are people adrift at the end of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital;
Banished and ill, I lie in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry and the gibbon’s mournful howl.
On spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moon,
Often I take my wine and drink alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
Their crude, grating sound is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are briefly revived.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
Sorrowful and mournful, unlike the sound before;\nThe whole audience, hearing it again, wept.
Among those weeping, who wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet with tears."}

And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.

After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,

Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,

Telling all the endless matters in her heart.

The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.

Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.

Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.

A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the Xunyang River's edge, seeing a guest off at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she'd speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the toad mound.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the court's musicians' troupe.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her crimson silk skirt was stained where wine was knocked over.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
But my younger brother left for the army, my madam died,
Dusk turned to dawn, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prizes profit, and thinks little of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the capital's jade stairs,
Exiled and bedridden in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On a spring river morning or an autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their squeaks and squawks are hard to endure.
To hear your pipa tonight is like hearing celestial music,
My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Touched by my words, she stands a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and the tempo grows more urgent.
Mournful and bleak, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats, hearing it again, weeps.
Of all the people here, whose tears fell the most?
The River Prefect's, whose blue official's robe was wet with them."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the riverbank of Xunyang, at night, I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting—
At parting, the vast river mirrors the moon in haze.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises,
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.

I search for the voice, whispering, 'Who plays?'
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast.

She’s called a thousand times before she comes,
Still holding her pipa half-hiding her face.

Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion is there.

Each string low, each note heavy with grief,
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Head lowered, fingers drift in steady motion,
Her playing speaks all that her heart holds.

Lightly brushing, slowly plucking, sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Lian*, then *Liu Yao*.

The great strings roar like sudden rain,
The small ones whisper like private talk.

Roar and whisper entwine in a mingled stream—
Pearls large and small fall on jade plates.

Like a bird skims through blossoms, smooth and light,
Like spring water beneath ice, choked and tight.

Cold springs stall, strings freeze into silence—
Silence hangs, brief, profound.

Then another hidden sorrow, deep resentment—
In this stillness, louder than sound.

A silver jar shatters, liquid bursts forth,
A cavalry charge rushes out—sword and spear sing.

When the final stroke draws a line across the heart of the strings,
Four strings snap once—a rip like tearing silk.

East and west boats lie quiet, no word spoken—
Only the river's heart glows white with autumn moon.

After a pause, he rests the pick on the string,
Straightens his clothes, composes his face.

'I was born a girl in the capital city,
Lived under the terrace where frog-dragons dwell.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first among the court troupe.
After each performance, even the masters were awed.
My beauty stirred envy in the old courtesan.

Young nobles vied to buy my trinkets—
One song earned me endless red sashes.

Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm,
Red silk gowns stained by wine, soaked through.

Year after year, laughter, joy, same as ever—
Spring rivers, blooming flowers, moonlit nights pass carelessly.

My brother left to war, my aunt died;
Days pass, mornings fade—my looks grow dim.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses or riders—
Old, I married a merchant.

Merchants care only for profit, not parting—
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Now, alone, I guard an empty boat by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills with cold.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Waking, tears streak down my cheeks in red lines.

Hearing this pipa, I sigh already—
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.

We’re both exiled souls far from home,
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship?

I left the imperial capital last year—
Exiled, living in pain, here in Xunyang.

This place is isolated, no music to be found,
Whole years pass without a single note of string or flute.

Near Pien River, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.

What sounds do I hear daily, morning and night?
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing in sorrow.

In spring, at dawn when flowers bloom, in autumn nights with moonlight,
I often pour wine alone, drinking to myself.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But their harsh cries are unbearable to hear.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It’s as if listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.

Please don’t refuse—sit again, play one more tune—
I’ll compose a poem for you, 'Pipa Xing.'

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits again, tightens the strings, speeds up the beat.

The music now is colder, less like the earlier tone—
All in the audience weep, covering their faces.

Who shed the most tears in this room?
The Jiangzhou magistrate, his blue robe wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn gloom.
I dismounted; my guest stepped aboard the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was neither lute nor flute.
Drunken but joyless, we were about to part in sorrow,
When the vast river swallowed the moonlight in the dark.
Suddenly from the water came a lute’s sound,
I forgot to go back, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a whisper who was playing,
The lute stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambitions.
She lowered her brows and played on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly she strummed, slowly she plucked, swept and flicked,
First the “Rainbow Skirt,” then the “Six Yao” tune.
The high strings roared like sudden rain in the sky,
The low strings whispered like secret words.
Roaring and whispering, they mingled and crossed,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and snapped,
The sound was blocked, and for a while there was silence.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—
In that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song’s end she swept the plectrum across the center,
All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all sat in hushed awe,
Only the white autumn moon in the river’s heart was seen.
Musing, she put the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home was beneath Toad Hill.
At thirteen she had mastered the lute,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After her songs, even music masters admired her,
When dressed, she was envied by the courtesans.
Young gallants from the Five Tombs competed to send her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Silver hairpins with jeweled tips were snapped while beating time,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed,
The autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting—
At parting, the vast river mirrors the moon in haze.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises,
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.

I search for the voice, whispering, "Who plays?"
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast.

She’s called a thousand times before she comes,
Still holding her pipa half-hiding her face.

Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion is there.

Each string low, each note heavy with grief,
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Head lowered, fingers drifting, playing on,
Her playing speaks all that her heart holds.

Lightly brushing, slowly plucking, sliding, lifting—
First *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The great strings roar like sudden rain,
The small ones whisper like private talk.

Roar and whisper entwine in a mingled stream—
Pearls large and small fall on jade plates.

Like a bird skims through blossoms, smooth and light,
Like spring water beneath ice, choked and tight.

Cold springs stall, strings freeze into silence—
Silence hangs, brief, profound.

Then another hidden sorrow, deep resentment—
In this stillness, louder than sound.

A silver jar shatters, liquid bursts forth,
A cavalry charge rushes out—sword and spear sing.

When the final stroke draws a line across the heart of the strings,
Four strings sound as one—a crack like torn silk.

East and west boats lie quiet, no word spoken—
Only the river's heart glows white with autumn moon.

After a pause, he rests the pick on the string,
Straightens his clothes, composes his face.

"I was born a girl in the capital city,
Lived under the terrace where frog-dragons dwell.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first among the court troupe.
After each performance, even the masters were awed.
My beauty stirred envy in the old courtesan.

Young nobles vied to buy my trinkets—
One song earned me endless red sashes.

Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm,
Red silk gowns stained by wine, soaked through.

Year after year, laughter, joy, same as ever—
Spring rivers, blooming flowers, moonlit nights pass carelessly.

My brother left to war, my aunt died;
Days pass, mornings fade—my looks grow dim.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses or riders—
Old, I married a merchant.

Merchants care only for profit, not parting—
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Now, alone, I guard an empty boat by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills with cold.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Waking, tears streak red down my cheeks.

Hearing this pipa, I sigh already—
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.

We’re both lost souls far from home,
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship?

I left the imperial capital last year—
Exiled, living in pain, here in Xunyang.

This place is isolated, no music to be found,
Whole years pass without a single note of string or flute.

Near Pien River, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.

What sounds do I hear daily, morning and night?
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing in sorrow.

In spring, at dawn when flowers bloom, in autumn nights with moonlight,
I often pour wine alone, drinking to myself.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But their crude, jarring notes are hard to bear.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It’s as if listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.

Please don’t refuse—sit again, play one more tune—
I’ll compose a poem for you, “Pipa Xing.”

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits again, tightens the strings, speeds up the beat.

The music now is colder, less like the earlier tone—
All in the audience weep, covering their faces.

Who shed the most tears in this room?
The Jiangzhou magistrate, his blue robe wet with tears."}

Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home lay by the Hami Tomb in Chang'an.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young gallants from the Wuling district vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirt was often stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
With days and nights passing, her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit and thought little of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the capital's jade stairs,
Exiled and sick, I lie in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On a spring river morning or an autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their crude, grating sound is hard to bear.

My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Deeply moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and the tempo grows more urgent.
Mournful and bleak, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats, hearing it again, weeps.
Of all the people here, whose tears fell the most?
The Assistant Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue official's robe was wet with them."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds sway in autumn's chill.
I dismount to welcome him; he stays aboard the boat—
We raise our wine but no music plays.

Drunkenness brings no joy, only sorrow as we part,
The wide river mirrors the moon with misty glow.
Suddenly, on the water, a lute's voice arises—
I forget to return, my guest won't depart.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who is playing?”
The music stops, hesitant, like words half-spoken.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn lamps back up, renew the feast.

Countless calls bring her out at last,
Still holding the lute, half her face concealed.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—just a few notes—
Before the tune begins, emotion already stirs.

Each string sighs, each note bears deep thought,
As though speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing low, she plays with steady hands,
Pouring out endless sorrows from her heart.

Softly brushing, slowly plucking, sliding, lifting—
First "Feather-Robed Dance," then "Six-Yao."

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like lovers' secrets.

A jumble of loud and soft, a mingling of sounds,
Like pearls rolling on jade bowls, bright and clear.

Now, a bird sings smoothly through the flowers,
Now, a spring under ice struggles, constrained.

The icy spring grows cold, the strings stiffen, stop—
Silence holds fast, breath suspended.

Then new depths of hidden grief arise,
In that silence, more than any music speaks.

Suddenly, a silver jar cracks—water bursts forth,
Then iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.

At end, she draws the pick across the center string—
Four strings cry out as if torn silk rends.

East and west boats fall silent as stone,
Only the moon above the river's heart gleams white.

She pauses, then sets down the pick, tucks it into the strings—
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the imperial city, lived beneath the Crab Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the lute, named first in the Music Academy.
After each performance, even the masters were awed.
My beauty stirred envy in the old courtesan known as Qiu Niang.

Five-Great-Grave youths vied to shower me with silks—
One song earned me countless lengths of red brocade.
Silver hairpins broke with each beat of rhythm,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.

Laughter and joy year after year,
Spring blossoms, autumn moons—time passed without care.

But then my brother joined the army, aunt died,
Days fade, years pass, beauty dims.

Door now empty, few horses come—
Old, I married a merchant.

He values profit, lightly sees parting—
Last month left for Fuliang to buy tea.

Now he’s gone, I guard an empty boat alone,
Moonlight circles round me, river cold.

Deep in night, I dream of youth—
Awakening, weeping, tears streaked red across my face.

Hearing her lute, I sigh; hearing her tale, I weep again.

We're both castaways on life's far shore—
Why must we have met before to know this pain?

I left the emperor’s court just last year,
Now exiled, sick, in Xunyang's remote town.

Xunyang lies so far from music’s reach,
Whole years pass without a single string or flute.

Near Panshui River, the land damp and low,
Hemp and bitter bamboo grow wild around my home.

What sounds fill day and night here, I ask?
Crows bleeding their hearts, apes wailing mournfully.

On spring mornings, in moonlit nights,
Often I pour wine, drink alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But their rough, grating tones I cannot bear.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s words,
It feels like heavenly music—my ears suddenly clear.

Do not refuse another song,
Let me rewrite this tale for you: "Song of the Lute."

Moved by my words, she stands still long—
Then sits, tightens the strings, plays faster, sharper.

Her music now is sadder than before,
All seated hear it once again, all weep.

Who among us shed the most?
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his green robe soaked with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted; my guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, but there was no music to drink to.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow,
And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and began the banquet anew.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows and casual fingers, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and flicked the strings with grace,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.
The roaring and whispering, the complex interplay,
Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, the notes were fluid,
Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and ceased,
The sound was blocked, and for a moment, it was silent.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.

The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent,
Only the white autumn moon in the river's heart could be seen.

Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn expression.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.

Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau.

When she dressed up, even Qiuniang herself was jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to give her gifts of silk,
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Her jeweled hairpins would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy followed year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes were passed by in leisure.

As days and nights passed, my youth faded.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.

Half-drunk, not merry, we grieved at the coming parting,
As we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player was slow to reply.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
Adding wine, relighting the lamps, we reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings, a note or two;
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
She lowered her brows, and carelessly, she went on playing,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly touching, slowly twisting, she swept and plucked,
First the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Little Ones."

The thin strings whispered like private words.
Roars and whispers, mingled and mixed,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.

The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
And when they broke, the sound paused for a time.

In that moment, the silence was more powerful than sound.

The four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.

We only saw the bright autumn moon in the river's heart.

Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.

Living at the foot of Toad Hill.

Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's troupe.
After each song, even the best players were impressed;
Each time she made up, the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.
Her ornate comb would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.

The spring winds and autumn moons were wasted.
Then her brother went to the army, and her aunt died;
Dusk came and morning went, and her beauty faded.
Before her gate, carriage tracks grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang.

Surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.

And wakes weeping, her tears staining her rouge-streaked cheeks.

Hearing her story, I sighed again, and again.

Why must we have known each other before to meet?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River, on a night I saw a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host alighted from his horse, the guest was on the boat;
He lifted his cup to drink, but there was no music.
Half-drunk, not merry, we grieved at the coming parting,
As we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player was slow to reply.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
Adding wine, relighting the lamps, we reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings, a note or two;
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
She lowered her brows, and carelessly, she went on playing,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly touching, slowly twisting, she swept and plucked,
First the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Little Ones."
The thick strings roared like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin strings whispered like private words.
Roars and whispers, mingled and mixed,
Like large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Then, like a spring choking, struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
And when they broke, the sound paused for a time.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, was born;
In that moment, the silence was more powerful than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Then, like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
The song ended with a stroke across the center;
The four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats to the east and west, all was silent;
We only saw the bright autumn moon in the river's heart.
She pondered, put down her plectrum, and tucked it between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said she was once a girl from the capital,
Living at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's troupe.
After each song, even the best players were impressed;
Each time she made up, the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.
Her ornate comb would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The spring winds and autumn moons were wasted.
Then her brother went to the army, and her aunt died;
Dusk came and morning went, and her beauty faded.
Before her gate, carriage tracks grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She waits alone at the river mouth in an empty boat,
Surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
And wakes weeping, her tears staining her rouge-streaked cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
And now I live, sick and exiled, in Xunyang.
This place is remote, and there is no music;
All year, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the low, damp banks of the Pen River,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can be heard here, morning and night?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbon's mournful howl.
On days of spring river and flowers, or autumn moon and night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their raucous, grating sound is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
Is like hearing immortal music; my ears are suddenly cleared.
Do not refuse, but sit and play one more song,
And I will dedicate to you a "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened her strings, and the tempo grew faster.
The mournful notes were not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seat who heard it again covered their face and wept.
Who wept the most among all the guests?
The Xunzhou official, whose blue gown was wet with tears."}

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.

Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau's troupe.
After each song, even the best players were impressed;
Each time she made up, the famous courtesans were jealous.
The young men of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.
Her ornate comb would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The spring winds and autumn moons were wasted.
Then her brother went to the army, and her aunt died;
Dusk came and morning went, and her beauty faded.
Before her gate, carriage tracks grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She waits alone at the river mouth in an empty boat,
Surrounded by the bright moon and the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
And wakes weeping, her tears staining her rouge-streaked cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, and again.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
And now I live, sick and exiled, in Xunyang.
This place is remote, and there is no music;
All year, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the low, damp banks of the Pen River,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What can be heard here, morning and night?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbon's mournful howl.

I often take my wine and drink alone.

The Xunzhou official, whose blue gown was wet with tears."}

Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting—

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises,
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.

I search for the voice, whispering, "Who plays?"
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld.

Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast.

She’s called a thousand times before she comes,
Still holding her pipa half-hiding her face.

Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion is there.

Each string low, each note heavy with grief,
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Her playing speaks all that her heart holds.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises,
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.

I search for the voice, whispering, "Who plays?"
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast.

She’s called a thousand times before she comes,

Before a tune begins, emotion is there.

Her playing speaks all that her heart holds.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups, but there was no lute or string to drink to.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow,
And as we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.

Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and began the banquet anew.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody was formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and laden with thought,
As if telling of a life's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows and casual fingers, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and flicked the strings with grace,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."

The thin strings whispered like a secret conversation.
The roaring and whispering, the complex interplay,
Were like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding through flowers, the notes were fluid,
Like a spring choked under ice, they were choked with sorrow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke,
The sound was blocked, and for a moment, it was silent.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment were born in that silence,
For at that moment, the silence was more powerful than the sound.

Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
At the end of the tune, she swept the plectrum across the center of the strings,
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
In the boats around us, all was silent,
Only the bright autumn moon on the river could be seen.

Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn expression.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
After she finished a song, even the masters were impressed,
When she dressed up, even the autumn beauties were jealous.
The young lords of Wuling competed to give her gifts of silk,
For one song, the red silk they gave was beyond counting.
Her jeweled hairpins would break as she beat time,
Her blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy followed year after year,
The autumn moons and spring breezes were passed by in leisure.

As days and nights passed, my youth faded.
Few horses and carriages stopped at my door,
And in my old age, I married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for our parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

The boat surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamt of my youth,
And woke weeping in my makeup, my tears staining my red railing.

I had sighed when I heard the pipa's music,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On Xunyang River's edge I see a guest off on an autumn night,
maple leaves and reed-blooms rustling in the chill.
I dismount; my friend boards the boat.
We raise our cups to drink, but there's no music.
Drunk without joy, we grieve at parting—
the vast river swallowing moonlight at farewell.
Suddenly, pipa music drifts across the water.
I forget to go home; my guest delays his boat.
We seek the sound, softly ask who plays—
the music stops; she hesitates to answer.
We move our boat nearer, invite her out;
add wine, relight the lamps, and feast again.
After a thousand calls, she emerges at last,
half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs, plucks a string or two—
before the tune begins, feeling already stirs.
Each string, each note, is muted with longing,
as if telling of a life of thwarted desire.
Brow lowered, she plays on absently,
saying all the heart's unbounded things.
Light pressing, slow rubbing, sweeping and picking—
first the Rainbow Skirt, then the Little Branch.
Thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling, whispering, all tangled together,
like pearls, large and small, dropping on a jade plate.
Then orioles singing under flowers, smooth and quick,
then a spring choked off under ice.
The icy spring stiffens, the strings freeze and snap—
the stuck notes break off; the sound rests a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rises:
here, silence speaks more than sound.
Then—like a silver vase bursting, water bursting forth,
like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing!
The tune ends; she draws the pick across the center—
four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.
All boats around are silent;
only the autumn moon on the river's heart is white.
She tucks the pick among the strings, straightens her clothes,
composes her face and begins to speak:
"I used to live in the capital, at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
and took first place in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even masters were humbled;
when I dressed up, even famous beauties were jealous.
Young men from wealthy towns would vie to shower me with gifts—
for one song, I'd get uncounted bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped keeping time;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year—
spring breezes and autumn moons passed idly by.
My brother left for the army; my aunt died.
Dusk after dawn, my beauty faded.
Fewer horses waited at my door;
grown old, I married a merchant.
My husband values profit over parting—
last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait for him alone on an empty boat,
moonlight all around, the river cold.
In the deep night I dream of my youth—
I wake weeping, my ruined makeup streaked with tears."
Her words make me sigh; her tale makes me grieve.
Both of us are lost souls at the edge of the world—
why must we have known each other before to meet like this?
Last year I left the capital,
exiled and sick, to this town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote—no music here;
year-round, I never hear strings or flutes.
By the river, the land is low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo crowd my house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons mourning.
On flower-mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
I take my wine and drink alone.
It's not that there are no hill songs or village flutes—
but their squawking, grating noise is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
it's like celestial music; my ears come alive at last.
Don't refuse—sit and play one more.
For you, I'll turn this into a Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
then sits back, tightens the strings—now faster,
more sorrowful than before.
Everyone around us weeps into their sleeves.
Who weeps the most among us all?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.  
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;  
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.  

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,  
The moment of departure sinks into misty moonlight on the river.  
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s sound arises—  
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.  

I search for the voice, whispering in silence: "Who is playing?"  
The pipa falls silent, hesitates before speaking.  
I move my boat near, invite the player to meet—  
Add wine, adjust lamps, relight the feast.  

Hundred calls bring her forth at last—  
Still clutching her pipa half-concealed by her face.  

She turns the axle, plucks the strings three or four times—  
Before a tune begins, emotion already spills.  

Each string mourns, each note reflects sorrow—  
As if recounting unfulfilled life’s regrets.  
Bowing her head, fingers glide one after another,  
Speaking all that heart can hold.  

Gently brushing, slowly plucking, stroking, then lifting—  
First *Fei Shang*, then *Liu Yao* she played.  

The thick strings roar like urgent rain,  
The thin ones whisper like private talk.  
Crashing, chattering, interwoven sounds—  
Like pearls falling into jade bowls.  

A lark’s song glides through flowers smooth and clear,  
A spring beneath ice struggles, choked and weak.  

The cold spring slows, strings freeze, silence breaks—  
Silence long, then sudden stillness.  

Another hidden grief, another secret hate emerges—  
In this silence, more than sound is heard.  

Then silver jar cracks, liquid bursts free—  
Iron cavalry charge, swords and spears clash loud.  

When final stroke sweeps across the heart of the instrument,  
Four strings ring once, like silk torn apart.  

East and west ships fall utterly still—  
Only the moon above the river’s heart shines white.  

She pauses, sighs, places the pick back in the strings—  
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.  

“I was born in the capital city,  
Living down at the Crab Lane.  
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,  
Name listed first in the imperial troupe.  

After my performance, even master players would praise me;  
After my makeup, the famed Autumn Lady grew jealous.  

Five-gentleman youths vied to gift me silk—  
One tune, a flood of crimson scarves, lost in count.  

Gold hairpins shattered to the beat,  
Crimson skirts stained with wine spilled in revelry.  

Year after year, laughter and joy passed—  
Autumn moons, spring breezes, all left untouched.  

My brother joined the army, my aunt passed away;  
Days fade, nights pass, beauty dims.  

Door now empty, no horsemen come near—  
Old now, I married a merchant.  

Merchants care for profit, not parting farewells—  
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.  

He's gone and left me here alone on the shore—  
Moon circles the boat, the river runs cold.  

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—  
Waking to cry, tears streak red across my face.  

I hear this pipa, and I sigh—  
Now hearing these words again, I’m moved to deeper grief.  

We both are wanderers cast far from home,  
Why must we have met before to know?  

I left the imperial capital last year—  
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang.  

Xunyang lies remote, lacking music—  
Whole years pass without ever hearing strings or bamboo flutes.  

Near P’en River, land low and damp—  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.  

From dawn to dusk, what do I hear?  
Cuckoos bleeding their songs, apes crying in misery.  

On spring mornings, under blossoms, or autumn nights beneath the moon—  
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.  

Are there no rustic songs or village flutes?  
But their sounds grating, harsh, unbearable to endure.  

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech—  
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly brightened.  

Do not refuse—please play one more tune—

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。

钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the riverbank of Xunyang, at night I bid farewell to a guest—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill.
My host dismounts; my guest remains on board.
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in our drunkenness, we part in sorrow,
As moonlight sinks into the vast, misty river.
Suddenly from the water, a lute’s cry pierces the air—
My host forgets to leave, my guest halts his voyage.

I search for its source, whispering softly: "Who plays?"
The lute falls silent, hesitates before words begin.
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight lamps, open feasts anew.

Thousands of calls bring her forth at last—
Still half-hiding her face behind the lute.
She turns the shaft, plucks strings three or two—
Before melody forms, emotion already flows.

Each string subdued, each note filled with thought—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.
Bending head, hands move steadily,
Unfolding all the heart’s endless sorrows.

Gently plucking, slow strumming, flicking, lifting—
First *Feiye*, then *Liuyao* she plays.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin ones whisper like secret talk.
Cacophony mingled, overlapping—
Large pearls and small pearls fall upon jade plates.

A sparrow skims through flowers, voice slippery,
A brook gurgles under ice, struggling to flow.
Cold spring chokes, strings freeze in silence—
Silence breaks, as if breath held long.

Another sorrow stirs, deep hatred hidden—
In this stillness, sound speaks louder than sounds.

Then silver bottle shatters, waters burst free—
Horsemen charge, swords and spears clash with might.

When the final stroke draws across the heart of the lute,
Four strings snap once: like silk torn apart.

East and west ships are hushed, silent as stone—
Only the moon above the river's heart shines white.

After a pause, he slams the pick back into the strings,
Adjusts his clothes, composes his face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home beneath the Crab-Leg Alley.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute—
Ranked first in the Imperial Academy’s troupe.

After each song, even the master praised me;
After each makeup, the jade-faced beauty envied me.

Young lords vied to throw crimson silks—
One song, countless lengths of red cloth.

Silver hairpins broke with beat;
Crimson robes stained with wine, now tattered.

Laughter and joy year after year,
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carelessly.

My brother joined the army; my aunt died.
Days fade, mornings vanish—the face grows old.

Door now empty, no horses, few visitors—
So I married, grown, a merchant’s wife.

Merchants value profit, scorn parting—
Last month, off to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left and came again, but I stay alone—
Moon circles the boat, cold river chills the night.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Waking, crying, tears streak red down my cheeks.

I hear this lute, and sigh; I hear her tale—
And sigh again, deeper, more intense.

We both are wanderers lost on distant shores—
Why must we have met before to know?

I left the imperial capital last year—
Now exiled, sick, trapped in Xunyang’s remote town.

Xunyang is far from music, barren of art—
For whole years, not a single string or flute has sounded.

Near Panyang, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear each morning, each night?
Cuckoos bleeding blood, apes wailing mournfully.

On spring mornings, flower-dappled nights, autumn moonglow—
I often pour wine, drink alone.

Are there no folk songs, no village flutes?
But their harsh cries cannot be endured.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s speech—
It’s like listening to celestial music, ears suddenly bright.

Do not refuse—stay, play another piece—
Let me compose for you this *Song of the Lute*.

Moved by my words, she stands in silence long—
Then sits, tightens the strings, the music quickens.

Now the notes ache, unlike what came before—
All guests, hearing again, cover their faces and weep.

Who among us sheds the most tears?
The Jiangzhou Magistrate, his green robe soaked with salt."}

Autumn moons, spring breezes, all slipped away. 

My brother went to war, my aunt passed on— 
Days fade, nights pass; my beauty fades too. 

Door now quiet, few riders pass by— 
Old, I married a merchant, a life of trade. 

Merchants care for profit, not for parting— 
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea. 

He left, and here I stay, alone aboard the boat— 
Moonlight circles, cold waves embrace the shore. 

Deep in the night, I dream of youth— 
Awake crying, tears staining my rouge-smeared cheeks. 

Hearing this lute, I weep, already moved— 
Now hearing these words, I weep again. 

We are both castaways beneath the same sky— 
Why must we have met before to feel this kinship? 

I left the imperial capital last year— 
Exiled, ill, in Xunyang City I lie. 

Xunyang is remote, no music heard— 
Whole years pass without a note of string or flute. 

Near Pien River, land low and damp—

What do I hear day and night among them?

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? 
But their sounds are harsh, grating—hard to bear. 

Tonight, hearing your lute, I feel celestial music— 
My ears are clear, as if heaven has opened. 

Do not refuse—sit and play another song— 
For you I’ll compose *Song of the Pipa*. 

Moved by my words, she stands long silent— 
Then sits down, tightens the strings, speeds the rhythm.

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River, seeing a guest off at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she’d speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the toad mound.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the court's musicians' troupe.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her blood-red silk skirt was often stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk turned to dawn, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over love, and they were often parted;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the capital's jade stairs,
Exiled and sick, I lie in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On a spring river morning or an autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their crude, grating sound is hard to bear.
To hear your pipa tonight is like hearing celestial music,
My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Deeply moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and the tempo grows more urgent.
Mournful and bleak, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats, hearing it again, weeps.
Of all the people here, whose tears fell the most?
The River Prefect's, whose blue official's robe was wet with them."}

The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: 'Who's playing?'
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like pearls tumbling on jade plates.

Now clear as a bird skims through blossoms,
Now choked as springs flow under ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
Then silence speaks more than sound.

A silver jar shatters—water bursts forth,
Warhorses charge, blades clash in the wind.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

'I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
Crimson robes stained by wine and sweat.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carefree.

My brother left for war, my aunt died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, grating, hard to bear.

Yet tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly bright.

Please, don’t refuse—sit once more to play,
I'll compose a poem for you: *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits, tightens the strings—now the music quickens.

Her new melody is colder than before—
All seated weep anew, eyes veiled in tears.

Who weeps the most among us all?
The River Chief of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

Deep strings thunder like rushing rain, high strings whisper like secret talk.

Now, a bird’s smooth trill through blossoms; now, a brook choked beneath ice. 
Cold and brittle, the strings freeze—then silence falls, as if all sound has ceased.

A silver bottle shatters, spilling liquid in bursts; a cavalry charge breaks through, swords clashing in fury. 
At the final stroke, the pick strikes the center string—four strings snap together like tearing silk. 
All boats along the banks fall silent—only the moon above the river’s heart shines pure white. 
Lost in thought, she drops the pick into the strings, adjusts her dress, and composes herself with dignity. 
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath Hama Ridge.

Young men from noble families vied to shower me with gifts—each song earned red silk beyond count. 
My silver hairpin broke on rhythm-strikes; my crimson skirt stained with spilled wine.

But now my brother has gone off to war, my aunt has died; days fade, and my beauty fades too. 
My gate grows empty, horses and riders few. 
Older now, I married a merchant. 
He values profit over parting, left last month for Fuliang to buy tea. 
He’s gone—he returns only to leave me guarding an empty boat in this harbor. 
By moonlight circling the vessel, the river runs cold. 
Late at night, I dream of youth—awake weeping, tears staining my makeup across the cheeks. 
Hearing her lute, I sigh deeply. Then hearing her story, I sigh again, even more. 
We are both castaways from distant shores—why must we have met before to feel such kinship? 
I left the capital last year, exiled, ill, living in remote Xunyang.

Do not refuse to play another piece! I will compose this song for you—the Lute Ode.

The music now feels colder than before—every listener weeps anew.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn mist.
I dismount, the guest boards the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but no lute or flute.
Drunk without joy, we sadly part,
When parting, the vast river fills with moonlight.
Suddenly a lute is heard upon the water;
I forget to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask who plays;
The music stops, and words come slow.
Moving the boat near, we invite her out;
More wine, lamps relit, the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion is already there.
Each string muffled, each note full of thought,
As if telling a life of thwarted ambition.
Brow low, casually she plays on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Strumming, rolling, sweeping, picking,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao."

The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, mixed and woven,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath flowers,
Like a choked spring under ice.

The blockage, the silence, the music’s pause.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rises;
At this moment, silence is more than sound.
Like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ends, the pick sweeps across the center,
Four strings sound as one, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are quiet, no one speaks;
Only the white autumn moon in the heart of the river.

Adjusts her clothes, stands up, and composes her face.

Lived at the foot of Toad Hill.

Her name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
After a tune, even the best players admired her;
When dressed, even Qiu Niang envied her.
Rich youths competed to lavish gifts;
One song earned her countless red silks.
Jeweled pins, silver combs broken in keeping time;
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and gaiety,
Autumn moons, spring winds, passing without care.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dusk to dawn, dawn to dusk, her beauty faded.
Before her door, fewer horses and carriages;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit, not parting;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Around the boat, the bright moon, the cold river water.
Deep in the night, she dreams of her youth;

Hearing her words, I sighed again.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.

Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,
The moon submerged in misty waves reflects our sorrow.
Suddenly, on water’s surface, a pipa’s cry—
My host forgets his way home, my guest halts his voyage.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who is playing?”
The pipa stops—the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn down the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas—she comes at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turns the peg, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air.

Each note suppressed, each tone laden with memory,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady hands,
Saying all that heart could hold—endless, deep.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Yang*, then *Liu Yao* she performs.

The light strings whisper like secret talk.

Like pearls tumbling into jade.

Low and choked as spring water beneath ice.

Silence breaks, sound lingers, then stops.

In this stillness, silence sings more than sound.

A cavalry charge, blades clash, weapons scream.
