My beauty stirred envy from the old courtesan.

One song would win me red silk—countless times!

Gold-tipped combs broke on rhythm’s beat,
Red brocade gowns stained with wine and blood.

Spring breezes, autumn moons, passed as mere common days.

But then my brother left to war, my aunt died—
Days pass, nights fade, my beauty fades too.

Worn out, I wed a merchant.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,
The moon submerged in misty waves reflects our sorrow.
Suddenly, on water’s surface, a pipa’s cry—
My host forgets his way home, my guest halts his voyage.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who is playing?”
The pipa stops—the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn down the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas—she comes at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turns the peg, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air.

Each note suppressed, each tone laden with memory,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady hands,
Saying all that heart could hold—endless, deep.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Yang*, then *Liu Yao* she performs.

The heavy strings roar like sudden rain,
The light strings whisper like secret talk.
Cacophony mixed—both loud and soft—
Like pearls tumbling into jade.

Smooth as a bird glides through flowers,
Low and choked as spring water beneath ice.

Ice-cold spring chokes, strings freeze in silence—
Silence breaks, sound lingers, then stops.

Another sorrow, hidden hate arise—
In this stillness, silence sings more than sound.

A silver bottle shatters, water bursts forth,
A cavalry charge, blades clash, weapons scream.

When music ends, she strikes the strings straight through the heart—
Four strings ring once, like silk torn apart.

Eastward and westward boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river’s heart.

After a pause, she rests the pick in the string,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the court musicians.

After each piece, even masters stood in awe—
My beauty stirred envy from the old courtesan.

Five noble youths vied for my attention,
One song would win me red silk—countless times!

Gold-tipped combs broke on rhythm’s beat,
Red brocade gowns stained with wine and blood.

Year after year, laughter, joy returned—
Spring breezes, autumn moons, passed as mere common days.

But then my brother left to war, my aunt died—
Days pass, nights fade, my beauty fades too.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses come—
Worn out, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care only for gold, not goodbyes—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

Left here alone by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the empty boat, the river chills my bones.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s lost days—
Dreaming, I weep, tears staining rouge across my face.

Hearing your pipa made me sigh;
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.

We’re both lost souls adrift on distant shores—
Why must we have met before to know each other?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.

All year long, no strings or flutes are sung.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick round my door.

I often pour wine, drunk and alone.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。

莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I bid farewell to a guest—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,
The moon submerged in misty waves reflects our sorrow.
Suddenly, on water’s surface, a pipa’s cry—
My host forgets his way home, my guest halts his voyage.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who is playing?”
The pipa stops—the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn down the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas—she comes at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turns the peg, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air.

Each note suppressed, each tone laden with memory,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady hands,
Saying all that heart could hold—endless, deep.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Yang*, then *Liu Yao* she performs.

The heavy strings roar like sudden rain,
The light strings whisper like secret talk.
Cacophony mixed—both loud and soft—
Like pearls tumbling into jade.

Smooth as a bird glides through flowers,
Low and choked as spring water beneath ice.

Ice-cold spring chokes, strings freeze in silence—
Silence breaks, sound lingers, then stops.

Another sorrow, hidden hate arise—
In this stillness, silence sings more than sound.

A silver bottle shatters, water bursts forth,
A cavalry charge, blades clash, weapons scream.

When music ends, she strikes the strings straight through the heart—
Four strings ring once, like silk torn apart.

Eastward and westward boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river’s heart.

After a pause, she rests the pick in the string,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

“I was born in the imperial city, lived by the Frog Terrace Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the court musicians.

After each piece, even masters stood in awe—
My beauty stirred envy from the old courtesan.

Five noble youths vied for my attention,
One song would win me red silk—countless times!

Gold-tipped combs broke on rhythm’s beat,
Red brocade gowns stained with wine and blood.

Year after year, laughter, joy returned—
Spring breezes, autumn moons, passed as mere common days.

But then my brother left to war, my aunt died—
Days pass, nights fade, my beauty fades too.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses come—
Worn out, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care only for gold, not goodbyes—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

Left here alone by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the empty boat, the river chills my bones.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s lost days—
Dreaming, I weep, tears staining rouge across my face.

Hearing your pipa made me sigh;
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.

We’re both lost souls adrift on distant shores—
Why must we have met before to know each other?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.

Xunyang lies remote, no music heard,
All year long, no strings or flutes are sung.

My house near Panyang, damp and low,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick round my door.

What do I hear day and night?
Crows bleeding their voices, apes wailing in grief.

On spring mornings, autumn nights,
I often pour wine, drunk and alone.

Are there no mountain ballads, village flutes?
Yet how harsh, how grating—no ear can bear them.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It feels like heavenly music—my ears wake up, clear.

Don’t refuse one more song—I’ll rewrite this poem for you.

Moved by my words, she stands still long—
Then returns to sit, tightens the strings, quickens the pace.

Her tones now mournful, unlike before—
All in the audience weep again, hiding faces.

Who weeps most here?
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his green robe soaked in tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I bid farewell to a guest—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,
The moon submerged in misty waves reflects our sorrow.
Suddenly, on water’s surface, a pipa’s cry—
My host forgets his way home, my guest halts his voyage.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who is playing?”
The pipa stops—the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn down the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas—she comes at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turns the peg, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air.

Each note suppressed, each tone laden with memory,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady hands,
Saying all that heart could hold—endless, deep.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Yang*, then *Liu Yao* she performs.

The heavy strings roar like sudden rain,
The light strings whisper like secret talk.
Cacophony mixed—both loud and soft—
Like pearls tumbling into jade.

Smooth as a bird glides through flowers,
Low and choked as spring water beneath ice.

Ice-cold spring chokes, strings freeze in silence—
Silence breaks, sound lingers, then stops.

Another sorrow, hidden hate arise—
In this stillness, silence sings more than sound.

A silver bottle shatters, water bursts forth,
A cavalry charge, blades clash, weapons scream.

When music ends, she strikes the strings straight through the heart—
Four strings ring once, like silk torn apart.

Eastward and westward boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river’s heart.

After a pause, she rests the pick in the string,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

“I was born in the imperial city, lived by the Frog Terrace Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the court musicians.

After each piece, even masters stood in awe—
My beauty stirred envy from the old courtesan.

Five noble youths vied for my attention,
One song would win me red silk—countless times!

Gold-tipped combs broke on rhythm’s beat,
Red brocade gowns stained with wine and blood.

Year after year, laughter, joy returned—
Spring breezes, autumn moons, passed as mere common days.

But then my brother left to war, my aunt died—
Days pass, nights fade, my beauty fades too.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses come—
Worn out, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care only for gold, not goodbyes—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

Left here alone by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the empty boat, the river chills my bones.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s lost days—
Dreaming, I weep, tears staining rouge across my face.

Hearing your pipa made me sigh;
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.

We’re both lost souls adrift on distant shores—
Why must we have met before to know each other?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.

Xunyang lies remote, no music heard,
All year long, no strings or flutes are sung.

My house near Panyang, damp and low,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick round my door.

What do I hear day and night?
Crows bleeding their voices, apes wailing in grief.

On spring mornings, autumn nights,
I often pour wine, drunk and alone.

Are there no mountain ballads, village flutes?
Yet how harsh, how grating—no ear can bear them.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It feels like heavenly music—my ears wake up, clear.

Don’t refuse one more song—I’ll rewrite this poem for you.

Moved by my words, she stands still long—
Then returns to sit, tightens the strings, quickens the pace.

Her tones now mournful, unlike before—
All in the audience weep again, hiding faces.

Who weeps most here?
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his green robe soaked in tears."}

My beauty stirred envy from the old courtesan.

One song would win me red silk—countless times!

Red brocade gowns stained with wine and blood.

Spring breezes, autumn moons, passed as mere common days.

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I bid farewell to a guest—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn tremble with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,
The moon submerged in misty waves reflects our sorrow.
Suddenly, on water’s surface, a pipa’s cry—
My host forgets his way home, my guest halts his voyage.

Following the sound, I whisper, “Who is playing?”
The pipa stops—the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn down the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas—she comes at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turns the peg, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air.

Each note suppressed, each tone laden with memory,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady hands,
Saying all that heart could hold—endless, deep.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Yang*, then *Liu Yao* she performs.

The heavy strings roar like sudden rain,
The light strings whisper like secret talk.
Cacophony mixed—both loud and soft—
Like pearls tumbling into jade.

Smooth as a bird glides through flowers,
Low and choked as spring water beneath ice.

Ice-cold spring chokes, strings freeze in silence—
Silence breaks, sound lingers, then stops.

Another sorrow, hidden hate arise—
In this stillness, silence sings more than sound.

A silver bottle shatters, water bursts forth,
A cavalry charge, blades clash, weapons scream.

When music ends, she strikes the strings straight through the heart—
Four strings ring once, like silk torn apart.

Eastward and westward boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river’s heart.

After a pause, she rests the pick in the string,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

“I was born in the imperial city, lived by the Frog Terrace Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the court musicians.

After each piece, even masters stood in awe—
My beauty stirred envy from the old courtesan.

Five noble youths vied for my attention,
One song would win me red silk—countless times!

Gold-tipped combs broke on rhythm’s beat,
Red brocade gowns stained with wine and blood.

Year after year, laughter, joy returned—
Spring breezes, autumn moons, passed as mere common days.

But then my brother left to war, my aunt died—
Days pass, nights fade, my beauty fades too.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses come—
Worn out, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care only for gold, not goodbyes—
Last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.

Left here alone by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the empty boat, the river chills my bones.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s lost days—
Dreaming, I weep, tears staining rouge across my face.

Hearing your pipa made me sigh;
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.

We’re both lost souls adrift on distant shores—
Why must we have met before to know each other?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.

Xunyang lies remote, no music heard,
All year long, no strings or flutes are sung.

My house near Panyang, damp and low,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick round my door.

What do I hear day and night?
Crows bleeding their voices, apes wailing in grief.

On spring mornings, autumn nights,
I often pour wine, drunk and alone.

Are there no mountain ballads, village flutes?
Yet how harsh, how grating—no ear can bear them.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It feels like heavenly music—my ears wake up, clear.

Don’t refuse one more song—I’ll rewrite this poem for you.

Then returns to sit, tightens the strings, quickens the pace.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she'd speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the toad mound.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the court's musicians' troupe.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her blood-red silk skirt was often stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
But my brother left for the army, my aunt died,
Dusk turned to dawn, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her door, the horses and carriages grew sparse;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over love, and they were often parted;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays and goes, guarding the empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon bright around the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream, she weeps, her tears smearing her rouge in streaks.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
Both of us are souls, cast to the ends of the earth;
To meet like this, why must we have been old friends?
Since last year, I left the capital's jade stairs,
Exiled and sick, I lie in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, with no fine music;
All year, I hear no sound of lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What can I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On a spring river morning or an autumn moonlit night,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their crude, grating sound is hard to bear.
To hear your pipa tonight is like hearing celestial music,
My ears, for a moment, are cleared and bright.
Please, do not refuse, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Deeply moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, and the tempo grows more urgent.
Mournful and bleak, not like the sound before;
Everyone in the seats, hearing it again, weeps.
Of all the people here, whose tears fell the most?
The River Prefect's, whose blue official's robe was wet with them."}

My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.

She’s called a thousand times before she comes,

Before a tune begins, emotion is there.

Each string low, each note heavy with grief,

Her playing speaks all that her heart holds.

Pearls large and small fall on jade plates.

Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm,

Spring rivers, blooming flowers, moonlit nights pass carelessly.

maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest steps aboard.
He raises his cup to drink, but there is no music.
Drunk, yet not merry, they part in gloom—
and at parting, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
the host forgets to go home, the guest delays his departure.

He moves his boat closer and invites her to appear;
more wine is poured, the lamps relit, the feast renewed.
Only after a thousand calls and entreaties does she come out,
still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings a few times—
before a tune is formed, feeling is already there.
String after string, muted and brooding, note after note, full of longing,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, she plays on and on at her ease,
availing all the endless things within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twining, a sweep, a flick—
first the Rainbow Skirt Garment, then the Six Yao dance.
On the heavy strings, a rush like driving rain;
on the light strings, a murmur like whispered secrets.
The rush and murmur, mingled and crossed,
like great pearls and small falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smoothly beneath the flowers,
then a stifled stream struggling under ice.
The icy spring grows cold and astringent; the strings seem to congeal;
congealed, blocked, the sound pauses for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, arises—
here, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver vase shatters, water bursts forth;
iron cavalry charge out, blades and spears clash.
The tune ends; with the拨 she draws a line across the center—
all four strings snap at once like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are hushed and wordless;
only the autumn moon, white in the middle of the river, is seen.
Musing, she lays the拨 among the strings,
straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says she was originally a girl of the capital,
whose home lay below Hama Hill.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa,
her name listed first in the Teaching Bureau.
When she finished a song, even skilled masters were won over;
when she made herself up, the beauties envied her.
The young men of the Five Tombs competed to shower her with gifts;
for one song, skeins of red silk—no one knew how many.
Silver hairpins struck time and shattered;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed by unregarded.
Then her brother went off to the army, her aunt died;
night went and morning came, and her beauty faded.
The horses and carriages before her door grew few and cold;
growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit and makes light of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone she waits at the river mouth in an empty boat;
around it the bright moon, the river water cold.
Deep in the night she suddenly dreams of her youth,
and wakes weeping, her painted tears streaking red across her face.

hearing these words, I sigh again, over and over.
Both of us are people lost at the ends of the earth—
why must we have known each other before to meet?

a sick exile in the city of Xunyang.

all year I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
with yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the riverbank of Xunyang, at night, I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers in autumn, stillness trembling.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
Raising a cup for drinking, yet no strings or pipes sound.
Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting—
At parting, the vast river mirrors the moon in haze.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises,
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved.
I search for the voice, whispering, "Who plays?"
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast.
She’s called a thousand times before she comes,
Still holding her pipa half-hiding her face.

Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion is there.
Each string low, each note heavy with grief,
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled.
Head lowered, fingers drift in steady motion,
She played on, as if telling all she had kept deep inside.
Lightly brushing, slowly plucking, sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Lian*, then *Liu Yao*.

The heavy strings crash like urgent rain,
The thin strings murmur like hushed words.
Roar and whisper entwine in a mingled stream—
Pearls large and small fall on jade plates.

A warbler’s call, smooth sliding through the flowers,
Like spring water beneath ice, choked and tight.
The icy spring grows cold and choked—the strings freeze silent,
A pause, then nothing.

Then another hidden sorrow, deep resentment—
In silence, more is said than in sound.

Suddenly, iron cavalry bursts forth—swords and spears ring out,
Four strings strike at once—a rending of silk, sharp and loud.
East and west boats lie quiet, no word spoken—
Only the autumn moon above the river’s heart lies bright.

After a pause, he rests the pick on the string,
Straightens his clothes, composes his face.

"I was born a girl in the capital city,
Lived under the terrace where frog-dragons dwell.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first among the court troupe.
After each performance, even the masters were awed.
My beauty stirred envy in the old courtesan.

Young nobles vied to buy my trinkets—
One song earned me endless red sashes.
Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm,
Red silk gowns stained by wine, soaked through.

Year after year, laughter, joy, same as ever—
Spring rivers, blooming flowers, moonlit nights pass carelessly.
My brother left to war, my aunt died;
Days pass, mornings fade—my looks grow dim.

Front gate grows cold, no more horses or riders—
Old, I married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, not parting—
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Now, alone, I guard an empty boat by the river’s mouth,
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills with cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Waking, tears streak red down my cheeks.

Hearing this pipa, I sigh already—
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We’re both lost souls far from home,
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship?

I left the capital last year—exiled, confined here in Xunyang, ill and idle.
This place is isolated, no music to be found,
Whole years pass without a single note of string or flute.

Near Pien River, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.
What sounds do I hear daily, morning and night?
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing in sorrow.

In spring, at dawn when flowers bloom, in autumn nights with moonlight,
Often I pour wine and drink alone.
Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But their harsh cries are unbearable to hear.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It’s as if listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.
Please don’t refuse—sit again, play one more tune—
I’ll compose a poem for you, “Pipa Xing.”

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits again, tightens the strings, speeds up the beat.
The music now is colder, less like the earlier tone—
All in the audience weep, covering their faces.

Who shed the most tears in this room?
The Jiangzhou magistrate, his blue robe wet with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the riverbank of Xunyang, at night, I see a guest off—
maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver.

The host dismounts; the guest remains on board.
Raising wine to drink, no strings or pipes to play.

Drunk but not joyful, grief shadows our parting—
as we depart, the river swallows the moon in haze.

Suddenly, from water’s surface, pipa sounds arise—
the host forgets to return, the guest stays still.

Following the sound, I ask softly: who plays?
The music halts; voice hesitates, half-formed.

I move my boat near, urge them to appear—
add wine, turn lamps, restart the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred invitations, then she comes—
still clutching her pipa, half-face veiled.

She turns the axis, plucks a few notes—
before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string suppresses, each note breathes longing—
as though recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing low, fingers wander, playing on—
telling all that hearts can never speak.

Lightly touching, slowly pressing, brushing, lifting—
first "Feiyan," then "Liuyao."

The deep strings roar like sudden rain,
the thin ones whisper like private talk.

Roar mingling with whisper, crash with hush—
large pearls and small, falling on jade plates.

Like a bird skims through flowers, its voice slips smooth,
like a spring choked under ice, slow and strained.

Cold springs freeze, strings lock tight—
silence thickens, sound ceases.

Yet beneath it, hidden sorrows rise—
in this silence, more than sound is heard.

A silver jar cracks open, water bursts forth—
a cavalry charge, swords and spears scream.

At last, the final stroke across the heart of the strings—
four strings snap at once, like tearing silk.

East and west boats fall silent—
only the white moon above the river’s heart remains.

After brief pause, he pushes the pick back into the strings,
adjusts his robes, rises, composes himself.

"I was born a woman of the capital city,
my home beneath the Frog-Mound Lane.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
ranked first in the Imperial Academy's troupe.

After every performance, even the master praised me—
each beauty I painted made the courtesans jealous.

From noble youths, they vied to shower me with silken gifts—
for one song, a red scarf, a hundred times over.

Tinsel hairpins shattered with rhythm’s beat,
crimson skirts stained by wine, spilled and torn.

Laughter year after year, joy beyond reckoning—
every passing autumn moon and spring breeze drift by unheeded.

My brother marched off to war; my aunt passed away;
days fade, nights pass, my face grows dim.

My gate grows cold, horses and riders rare—
at last I married a merchant, old and worn.

The merchant cares for gain, not farewell—
last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stay here in empty boat—
moonlight circles, the river runs cold.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
awake weeping, tears streak red down my cheeks.

I’ve heard the pipa and sighed already—
now hearing these words, sighs multiply.

We, both castaways on life’s far shore, need not have met before.

I left the imperial capital last year—
exiled, ill, in Xunyang town.

Xunyang lies remote, no music anywhere—
whole years go past without a single string or flute.

Near Panyang River, land low and damp—
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.

What do I hear day and night in this place?
Cuckoos bleeding red, apes wailing in sorrow.

On spring mornings, flower-lit days, autumn nights with moon—
often I pour wine, drunk alone.

Are there no mountain songs? No village flutes?
But their tones are harsh, grating, hard to bear.

Now, tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
like listening to celestial music, ears suddenly clear.

Do not refuse—sit again and play another piece—
for you, I’ll compose a Pipa Ode.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence—
then sits, draws the strings tighter, speed increases.

The music now, so chill, so unlike before—
all in the hall, hearing it again, veil their weeping.

Who sheds the most tears among us all?
The River-Jiang Prefect, his green robe soaked through."}

The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
To raise a cup for a drink, but no lute or song.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieve at parting;
At leave-taking, the vast river is steeped in the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his sailing.
Seeking the sound, we ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, as if she'd speak but hesitates.
We move our boat nearer, invite her to show her face;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and the feast begins anew.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerges,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, two or three sounds;
Before a melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string, each note, a suppressed, thoughtful sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted hopes.
With lowered brows, she plays on, skillfully and freely,
Telling of countless things within her heart.
A gentle strum, a slow twist, a sweep, and a flick,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Little Ones."
The big strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whisper like a private conversation.
Loud and soft, in a complex, interwoven weave,
Like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbling oriole glides beneath the flowers,
A choked spring struggles beneath the ice.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings seem to freeze,
The freezing blocks the flow, and the sound pauses for a spell.
A different, hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born;
In this moment, the silence is more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth,
Like an armored cavalry charging, blades and spears ringing.
The song ends with a sharp sweep across the center;
The four strings crack as one, like tearing silk.
In boats to the east and west, all are silent and still,
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river, is seen.
Pensively, she tucks her plectrum among the strings,
Smoothes her clothes, rises, and assumes a solemn face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home was by the toad mound.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name ranked first in the court's musicians' troupe.
When she finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
With her makeup done, she was envied by the beauties.
Young men from the five aristocratic tombs vied for her favor,
For one song, the red silk rewards were beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs would break to the beat,
Her crimson silk skirt was stained where wine was knocked over.
One year of laughter followed the next,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.

大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds sway in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard—
We raise our cups, yet no music plays.

Drunk, we can't find joy in parting,
As dusk descends, moonlight floods the river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: "Who's playing?"
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Though not yet in tune, emotion already flows.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade platter,
Clear as rain on stone, bright as chimes in air.

Now like springwater struggling beneath frozen stone—
A voice half-sung, barely heard, held back by ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
In that stillness, all is said—
More than sound can ever tell.

A silver jar shatters—water gushes wide,
Then sudden cavalry charges, spears flashing in storm.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
Crimson robes stained by wine and sweat.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breeves passed carefree.

My brother left for war, my aunt died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the court last year, cast out from high seat—
Exiled, sick, chained to Xunyang’s silent streets.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their songs are crude, their flutes discordant—
No ear can bear such noise.

Yet tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly bright.

Please, don’t refuse—sit once more to play,
I'll compose a poem for you: *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits, tightens the strings—now the music quickens.

Her new melody is colder than before—
All seated weep anew, eyes veiled in tears.

Who weeps the most among us all?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his green gown soaked through."}

Each string, each note is choked with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she plays on carelessly,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, sweeping and plucking,
First the Rainbow Skirt Dance, then the Six Yao tune.
The bass strings rumble like a sudden rain;
The treble strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, tangled and strung,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding beneath the flowers,
Or a spring choked under ice.
The icy spring freezes; the strings grow numb;
umb, the sound stops for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, arise;
At this moment, silence is more than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly broken, water bursting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clanging.
The song ends; the pick sweeps across the center;
Four strings at once, like tearing silk.
East and west, boats and pavilions, all are silent;
Only the river's heart, the autumn moon, shines white.
She ponders, puts the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, stands up with a solemn face.
She says she was a girl from the capital,
Her home was near Hama Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Music Academy.
After a song, even masters admired her;
When dressed, she was envied by every courtesan.
The young lords of Wuling competed to gift her;
For one song, she received countless red silks.
Gold and silver hairpins beat time till they broke;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
The autumn moon and spring wind passed by in vain.
Her brother went to war; her aunt died;
Morning came and evening went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, carriages grew rare and cold;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit, not parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the bright moon, the cold river water.
In the deep night, she suddenly dreams of her youth;
In her dream, she weeps, her tears staining her rouge.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
We are both outcasts at the edge of the world;
Why must we have met before to know this feeling?

Banished and ill, I live in Xunyang.

I live near the Pen River, low and damp;

And I will write for you a Song of the Pipa.

Then sits, adjusts the strings, and they grow急.

Drunk but unable to rejoice, my heart grows sad as we part,
As dusk descends, moonlight bathes the river in misty gloom.
Suddenly, a lute's sound floats upon the water—my host forgets to return, the guest delays departure.
I follow the music, silently asking who plays;
the lute falls silent, hesitant words on the lips.
We steer the boat closer, inviting her to appear;
we add wine, relight lamps, and reopen our feast.
After many calls, she finally emerges, half-hiding her face behind the lute.
She turns the tuning peg, plucks the strings with three or two notes—before any melody forms, emotion already speaks.

Bowing her head, fingers glide smoothly across the strings, weaving tales of endless sorrows.
Gently brushing, slowly plucking, stroking, then lifting—the piece begins as 'The Rainbow Skirt,' then shifts to 'Sixth Flute.'

or a spring beneath ice, flowing choked, barely audible.
Cold springs grow stiff, strings freeze, the music halts abruptly—silent for a moment.

A silver bottle shatters, water spurts forth; iron cavalry charge, swords clash.
At the end, the final stroke cuts straight through the center; four strings resound like tearing silk.
Boats on east and west lie silent, nothing stirs—only the moon, white over the river's heart.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute, ranked first in the Imperial Academy.
After every performance, even master musicians bowed in respect;
After every makeup, beauties like Autumn Mother envied me.
Young lords from the Five Tombs vied to buy my gifts; one song would earn countless red silks.
Silver hairpins shattered from vigorous beat; crimson gowns stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Year after year, laughter returned, years passed like springtime breezes and autumn moons.
But then my brother left for war, my aunt passed away; days pass, beauty fades.
Now the gate lies cold, few riders come; at last, I married a merchant.

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the riverbank, watching the moon circle my empty boat,

Hearing her lute, I sigh deeply; hearing her story, my spirit trembles more.
We are both exiles, cast down far from home—why must we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year, now stranded, ill, in Xunyang City.

Tonight, hearing your lute's speech—like listening to celestial music, my ears momentarily brighten.
Please, don’t refuse to play another tune—for you, I will compose this poem 'The Lute Player.'

Who shed the most tears among us all? The governor of Jiangzhou, his green robe soaked with salt."}

今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "Night at Xunyang River, seeing off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn.
The host dismounts, the guest boards the boat;
He lifts his cup to drink—no lute or string.
Drunk, yet not mirthful, sad at parting,
At parting, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his going.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops—she hesitates to speak.
Moving the boat near, we invite her to appear;
More wine, lamps relit, the banquet resumes.
After a thousand calls, she at last comes out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
Turning the pegs, plucking strings, two or three notes,
Before the tune begins, feeling is already there.
Each string, each note, choked with thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, fingers pressing, she plays on,
Telling all the heart’s unending matters.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, picking,
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The great strings roar like sudden rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Loud and soft, crossed and mixed, they mingle—
Large pearls, small pearls, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing beneath flowers, smooth and flowing,
Like a hidden spring, choking under ice.
The icy spring, cold and stiff, the strings freeze;
Frozen through, the sound halts for a time.
A separate sorrow, a hidden resentment, rises—
At this moment, silence is more than sound.
A silver vase suddenly breaks, water gushing;\Iron cavalry charges out, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ends—she draws the pick across the center;
Four strings at once, like tearing silk.
East boats, west boats, all silent, hushed;
Only the autumn moon, white on the river’s heart.
Meditating, she tucks the pick among the strings,
Straightens her robe, rises, composes her face.
She says: “I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was beneath Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
After I played, even masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, even beauties were jealous.
The young lords of Five Tombs competed to gift me;
For one song, silks beyond counting.
Ornamented combs smashed as we beat time;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song;
Autumn moons, spring breezes, spent at ease.
My brother went to the army, my aunt has died;
Evenings went, mornings came, my beauty faded.
Before my gate, horses grew sparse and cold;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant prizes profit, lightly parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone at the river’s mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moon, cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep—tears streak my powder-red cheeks.”
I heard the pipa and sighed already;
Hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
Both of us are lost souls at the edge of the world;
Why must we have met before to meet tonight?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Lying ill, banished to Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year, I hear no lute or string.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear here, morning and night?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons mourning.
Spring river, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, hard to listen to.

It is like immortal music, my ears briefly enlightened.

For you, I will compose a Pipa Ballad.

Then sits back, quickens the strings—they turn urgent.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds sway in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard—
We raise our cups, yet no music plays.

Drunk, we can't find joy in parting,
As dusk descends, moonlight floods the river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: "Who's playing?"
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Though not yet in tune, emotion already flows.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade platter,
Clear as rain on stone, bright as chimes in air.

Now like springwater struggling beneath frozen stone—
A voice half-sung, barely heard, held back by ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
In that stillness, all is said—
More than sound can ever tell.

A silver jar shatters—water gushes wide,
Then sudden cavalry charges, spears flashing in storm.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
Crimson robes stained by wine and sweat.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carefree.

My brother left for war, my aunt died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the court last year, cast out from high seat—
Exiled, sick, chained to Xunyang’s silent streets.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their songs are crude, their flutes discordant—
No ear can bear such noise.

Yet tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly bright.

Please, don’t refuse—sit once more to play,
I'll compose a poem for you: *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits, tightens the strings—now the music quickens.

Her new melody is colder than before—
All seated weep anew, eyes veiled in tears.

Who weeps the most among us all?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his green gown soaked through."}

同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

Maple leaves and reeds sway in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard—
We raise our cups, yet no music plays.

Drunk, we can't find joy in parting,
As dusk descends, moonlight floods the river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: "Who's playing?"
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Though not yet in tune, emotion already flows.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade platter,
Clear as rain on stone, bright as chimes in air.

Now like springwater struggling beneath frozen stone—
A voice half-sung, barely heard, held back by ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
In that stillness, all is said—
More than sound can ever tell.

A silver jar shatters—water gushes wide,
Then sudden cavalry charges, spears flashing in storm.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
Crimson robes stained by wine and sweat.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carefree.

My brother left for war, my aunt died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the court last year, cast out from high seat—
Exiled, sick, chained to Xunyang’s silent streets.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Before the tune begins, emotion stirs. 

Each string is hushed, each note mournful— 
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled. 

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace, 
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow. 

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts— 
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the Riverbank at Xunyang, I bid farewell to guests one autumn night,
Maple leaves and reeds rustle in the chill of fall.
I dismount, my guest remains on board;
We raise a cup to drink—but no music plays.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful as we part,
As dusk descends, the river swallows the moon's pale light.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa music floats—
The host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.
Following the sound, I whisper, 'Who plays?' The music pauses,
Trembling, words almost spoken.
I steer our boat near, urging her to appear;
We pour more wine, adjust the lamps, relight the feast.
After many calls, she finally appears,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the peg, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion fills the air.
Each note is mournful, each tone full of longing,
Like tales of unfulfilled dreams, life’s unspoken pain.
Bending low, fingers glide with quiet grace,
She pours out all her heart’s endless sorrows.
Gently pressing, softly twisting, brushing, lifting—
First playing 'Feiying', then 'Liuyao' with flair.
The deep strings thunder like rushing rain,
The thin ones chirp like whispers in the dark.
Harmonious, complex, overlapping sounds—
Like pearls tumbling onto jade bowls, bright and clear.
A bird sings through blossoms, smooth and sweet;
A spring runs under ice—slow, choked, hard to breathe.
Cold springs freeze, strings halt in silence;
Then silence breaks, yet stillness speaks louder than sound.
A silver jar shatters—water bursts forth;
Iron horse charges, swords clash, war cries rise.
At last, the final stroke across the heart of the string—
Four strings snap as one, like silk torn apart.
East and west boats stand silent, speechless,
Only the river’s heart glows white with autumn moonlight.
Doubtfully, she rests the pick, slides it back into the strings;
Adjusts her clothes, composes her face, stands to speak.
'Since childhood, I was born in the capital city,
My home lay beneath the Crab Hill, where shadows dwell.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa—ranked first in the Imperial School.
After each song, even masters would bow in respect;
With makeup done, I'd draw envy from the famed Qiumei.
Fancy youths fought for my red scarves—countless they gave;
Silver hairpins shattered with every beat;
Crimson silk gowns stained by wine and tears, tossed aside.
Year after year, laughter, joy—I let time pass without care,
But now my brother left for war, my aunt died too;
Days fade, mornings shift—the beauty of youth grows old.
Front gate empties, horses rare—my loneliness grows vast;
In later years, I married a merchant, lost to trade.
He values profit, hates parting—last month he sailed to Fuliang
To buy tea. Now I wait here, alone on the river’s edge,
Moonlight circles my boat, the river cold as frost.
At midnight, I dream of youthful days—
Waking in tears, my rouge streaks down my cheeks like blood.
Hearing this pipa tale, I sigh deeply;
And now that I hear these words again, I tremble.
We’re both castaways on distant shores—why must we have met before?
Since last year, I’ve left the imperial capital,
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, no music ever heard;
Full years go by—no string or bamboo flute is heard.
Near Pienjiang, land dips, damp and low;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow thick around my door.
What do I hear each morning and evening there?
Cuckoos scream blood-red, apes wail in grief.
Spring mornings, flower-filled days, autumn nights with moonlight—
Often I pour wine, alone, drinking to myself.
Are there no rustic songs? No village flutes?
But their rough, grating tones are unbearable to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa music—
It feels like heavenly melodies, ears suddenly clear.
Please don’t refuse—sit again, play one more piece;
For you, I’ll compose this poem: 'The Pipa Player.'
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits again, tightening the strings—now faster, sharper.
Her music grows sorrowful, no longer as before;
All in the audience weep anew, eyes hidden in shame.
Who among us sheds the most tears tonight?
The Jiangzhou Magistrate, his green robe soaked in salt."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill. 
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays. 

Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting—
At parting, the vast river mirrors the moon in haze. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises, 
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved. 

I search for the voice, whispering, "Who plays?" 
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld. 
I move my boat near, invite her to appear, 
Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast. 

She’s called a thousand times before she comes, 
Still holding her pipa half-hiding her face. 

Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion is there. 

Each string low, each note heavy with grief, 
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled. 

Head lowered, fingers drift in steady motion, 
Her playing speaks all that her heart holds. 

Lightly brushing, slowly plucking, sliding, lifting—
First *Fei Lian*, then *Liu Yao*. 

The great strings roar like sudden rain, 
The small ones whisper like private talk. 

Roar and whisper entwine in a mingled stream—
Pearls large and small fall on jade plates. 

Like a bird skims through blossoms, smooth and light, 
Like spring water beneath ice, choked and tight. 

Cold springs stall, strings freeze into silence—
Silence hangs, brief, profound. 

Then another hidden sorrow, deep resentment—
In this stillness, louder than sound. 

A silver jar shatters, liquid bursts forth, 
A cavalry charge rushes out—sword and spear sing. 

When the final stroke draws a line across the heart of the strings, 
Four strings snap once—a rip like tearing silk. 

East and west boats lie quiet, no word spoken—
Only the river's heart glows white with autumn moon. 

After a pause, he rests the pick on the string, 
Straightens his clothes, composes his face. 

"I was born a girl in the capital city, 
Lived under the terrace where frog-dragons dwell. 

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first among the court troupe. 
After each performance, even the masters were awed. 
My beauty stirred envy in the old courtesan. 

Young nobles vied to buy my trinkets—
One song earned me endless red sashes. 

Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm, 
Red silk gowns stained by wine, soaked through. 

Year after year, laughter, joy, same as ever—
Spring rivers, blooming flowers, moonlit nights pass carelessly. 

My brother left to war, my aunt died; 
Days pass, mornings fade—my looks grow dim. 

Front gate grows cold, no more horses or riders—
Old, I married a merchant. 

Merchants care only for profit, not parting—
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea. 

Now, alone, I guard an empty boat by the river’s mouth, 
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills with cold. 

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Waking, tears streak red down my cheeks. 

Hearing this pipa, I sigh already—
Now hearing these words, I sigh again. 

We’re both lost souls far from home, 
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship? 

I left the imperial capital last year—
Exiled, living in pain, here in Xunyang. 

This place is isolated, no music to be found, 
Whole years pass without a single note of string or flute. 

Near Pien River, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house. 

What sounds do I hear daily, morning and night? 
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing in sorrow. 

In spring, at dawn when flowers bloom, in autumn nights with moonlight, 
I often pour wine alone, drinking to myself. 

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes? 
But their harsh cries are unbearable to hear.

Bowing her head, she plays on steadily, pouring out infinite sorrows from her heart.

Cold springs grow stiff, strings freeze, silence reigns—then all sound ceases.

My jeweled hairpins broke from rhythm’s beat, my crimson skirts stained by spilled wine.

When my brother joined the army and my aunt passed away, days slipped by, my youth faded. 
Our door grew cold, few riders came—now, old and worn, I married a merchant. 
He values profit more than people, left last month to buy tea in Fuliang.

In deepest night, I dream of youthful days—wake screaming, tears streaking red down my painted cheeks.

We are both castaways on this distant shore—why must we have met before to know such kinship?

My dwelling lies close to the Pianjiang River, low-lying, damp—yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. 
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
We raise our wine, but no music plays. 
Drunk yet unable to find joy, we sorrow as we part— 
In twilight's haze, the river drowns the moon. 
Suddenly, a lute’s voice floats from the water— 
My host forgets to return, my guest holds back from departure. 
Following the sound, I whisper quietly: 'Who is this player?' 
The music stops; she hesitates, almost speaks. 
I move my boat close, urging her to come, 
Add wine, turn up the lamps, and reopen the feast. 
A thousand calls, a thousand entreaties—then she appears, 
Still holding her lute half-concealing her face. 
She turns the axle, strikes a few strings— 
Before any tune, emotion already stirs. 
Each string trembles with suppressed grief, each note sings of longing, 
As if recounting a life unfulfilled. 
Bowing low, she plays with gentle touches, 
Telling all her unspoken sorrows. 
Lightly plucking, slowly pressing, brushing, then picking— 
First playing 'Rainbow Skirts,' then 'Six Ya.' 
The heavy strings roar like sudden rain, 
The light ones whisper like private talk. 
A clashing mix of loud and soft, 
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on jade. 
Now clear, like swallows gliding beneath blossoms; 
Now choked, like spring water struggling under ice. 
Cold springs freeze, strings grow tight and stop; 
Silence follows—yet silence speaks louder than sound. 
Sudden crack! A silver pot bursts, water gushes out; 
Then cavalry charges, swords and spears clash. 
At last, the final stroke across the heart of the strings— 
Four strings snap together like torn silk. 
East and west, boats fall silent, no word spoken— 
Only the moon white over the river's heart.

Adjust my clothes, straighten my face, compose myself.

My home lies beneath the frog mound. 
At thirteen I mastered the lute;
I belonged to the first troupe of the Imperial Conservatory.
After each performance, even the finest master was speechless in awe;
After every makeup, the famed Qiuniang would envy me. 
Fancy youths from the Five Tombs vied to shower me with silks;
One song, countless red lengths of cloth. 
Silver hairpins shattered on the beat;
Crimson skirts stained with wine from dancing.

Then my brother went off to war, my aunt passed away;
Days pass, mornings fade, my beauty fades.

Old now, I married a merchant.

He left, I guard an empty boat by the river mouth,

Suddenly, a pipa melody floats from the water’s edge—my host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure.

I move my boat near, inviting her to appear—adding wine, turning lamps, again we open our feast.
After countless calls, she emerges at last, still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tunes the axis, plucks the strings three or two times—before a single note, emotion already flows.
Each string veiled, each tone laden with sorrow, as if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady fingers, telling all within her heart, endlessly.

Cold, sluggish water chokes the strings into silence—stillness breaks the sound for a breath.

A silver bottle bursts, spilling liquid forth; iron cavalry charges, swords clash with thunder.

Young lords vied to give me silken gifts—each song earned me endless lengths of red silk.
Gold-tipped hairpins shattered from rhythmic beats; crimson skirts splashed with wine from drunken revelry.
Year after year, laughter returned, and time passed with spring moons and autumn breezes.

My host dismounts, the guest remains on board; I raise my cup to drink yet no music plays. 
Drunk, I cannot find joy—the parting is sad, with the river shrouded in moonlight. 
Suddenly, a lute sound drifts from the water—my host forgets to return, the guest holds back from departure. 
I search for the voice, softly asking: 'Who plays?' The lute stops, hesitant to speak. 
I move my boat near, urge them to meet, add wine, relight lamps, restart the feast. 
After many calls, she appears at last, still holding her lute half-covering her face. 
She turns the axis, plucks a few strings—before any melody begins, emotion stirs. 
Each string is heavy, each note full of sorrow, as though narrating a life unfulfilled. 
Her eyes downcast, fingers moving slowly, she plays, pouring out endless grief. 
Gently caressing, lightly rubbing, pressing, then plucking—first she plays 'Fei Hua,' then 'Liu Yao.' 
The deep strings roar like sudden rain, the light ones whisper like private words. 
A jumble of loud and soft notes—great pearls, small pearls, clattering on jade. 
Like a bird’s smooth song through blossoms, or a hidden spring choked under ice. 
Cold springs, icy tension—strings stop, silence breaks like frozen thread. 
Another quiet sorrow, another hidden hate—this silence surpasses all sound. 
Like an iron jar shattering, splashing water pours forth; like cavalry charging, swords clash. 
At end, the pick strikes the heart of the strings—a single crack, like tearing silk. 
East and west boats fall silent; only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river’s heart. 
With pause, she leans the pick into the strings, adjusts her clothes, stands straight, composes herself. 
She says: 'Born a woman of the capital city, living beneath the Xiamama Ridge. 
At thirteen, I mastered the lute, ranked first among the Imperial Music Bureau. 
After playing, even master musicians admired me; after dressing, beauties envied me. 
Young nobles vied to give gifts—each song earned red silk by the yard. 
Silver hairpins snapped to rhythm, crimson skirts stained with wine. 
Laughter and joy year after year—autumn moons, spring breezes pass carelessly. 
My brother went to war, my aunt passed away; mornings and nights, beauty fades. 
Front gate now cold, fewer horses, fewer visitors—old, I wed a merchant. 
Merchants value profit, scorn partings—last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea. 
Now he leaves me alone in this empty boat at the river mouth, moonlight circling, the river cold. 
Deep in night, I dreamt of youth—awakened, weeping, tears streaming red through my painted face. 
Hearing her lute, I sigh; hearing her tale, I sigh again. 
We are both lost souls adrift in distant lands—why need we have met before? 
Since last year, I left the imperial capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang City. 
Xunyang remote, no music—whole years without the sound of strings or flutes. 
Near Panyang, land low and damp, bitter reeds and bamboo grow around our homes. 
What sounds fill day and night here? Cuckoos cry blood-red, apes wail mournfully. 
On spring mornings and autumn evenings, I often pour wine, drinking alone. 
Is there no folk song or rustic flute? But their sounds are harsh, unbearable. 
Tonight, hearing your lute’s speech, it feels like celestial music—ears newly opened. 
Do not refuse to play us one more piece—I will rewrite these thoughts into a 'Song of the Lute.' 
Moved by my words, she stands stunned, then returns, tightens the strings—now they grow urgent. 
Her music now chills, unlike before—everyone in the hall covers their faces, weeping. 
Who sheds the most tears among this crowd? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his green robe soaked."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers tremble in autumn's chill.
I dismount; my guest remains on board;
We raise a cup to drink—but no music plays.
Drunk without joy, heartbroken as we part,
In twilight’s hush, the river swallows moonlight whole.
Sudden, from the water, a pipa melody rings—
My host forgets to leave; the guest won’t depart.
Following the sound, I whisper, 'Who plays?'
The music pauses; hesitating, she speaks no word.
I urge our boat near, invite her to appear,
Refill wine, turn up lamps, relight the feast once more.
A thousand calls bring her forth at last,
Still clutching the pipa half-concealing her face.
She turns the axle, plucks strings three or four times—
No tune yet formed, but emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, each tone filled with longing,
As if narrating a life of unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing low, hands gliding, she plays on—
All hidden sorrows poured out, endlessly.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing, lifting—
First 'Feather Dress,' then 'Sixth Yāo' she begins.
The deep strings roar like sudden rainstorm,
The thin ones murmur like private whispers.
Harmonious chaos: great pearls and small,
Dancing across jade plates in clattering streams.
Smooth as a bird slipping through blossoms,
Low and choked, like spring water beneath frozen ice.
Cold and strained, the strings freeze in silence,
Silence thickens—then, a pause that speaks volumes.
Another sorrow stirs, an unseen hatred grows—
This stillness exceeds all sound in depth.
Like a silver bottle shattering, waters burst forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash loud.
When the piece ends, the pick strikes center—the chord—
Four strings ring out, sharp as tearing silk.
East and west boats fall silent; not a breath heard,
Only the moon above the river's heart, white as bone.
After a pause, she leans down, inserts the pick into string,
Straightens her clothes, composes her features anew.
She says, 'I was born in the capital city,
Lived beneath Hāmá Ling, where the frog-pond stands.
At thirteen, I mastered pipa, ranked first
In the imperial teaching guild’s foremost troupe.
After each performance, even the master praised me;
Beauty so fierce, the courtesan Qiu Niang envied.
Young men from the five hills vied to give me gifts—
One song earned red silks beyond count.
Jade hairpins shattered with beat, blood-red robes stained with wine.
Year after year, laughter and joy passed as days,
Spring’s bloom, autumn’s moon—flitting through like mist.
Then brother went to war; auntie passed away;
Days pass, nights pass—my beauty fades.
Front gate deserted, horses few, riders thin;
Older now, I wed a merchant, lost my name.
Merchants value profit, scorn partings—
Last month he left for Fúliáng to buy tea.
Now I stay behind at the river’s mouth, alone,
Moonlight circling the boat, cold river chills the night.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s bright past—
Dreaming, I weep, tears staining my rouge-darkened face.
Hearing your pipa, I sigh long and deep;
And hearing these words, my spirit shakes again.
We’re both exiles far from home, strangers in this world—
Why need we have known before to feel such kinship?
I left the capital just last year, banished, sick,
Living in exile in Xunyang City, remote and poor.
This place is isolated—no music to be heard,
Whole years pass without even a lute or flute sound.
Near Pénjiang, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What sounds can I hear each day, from dawn till dusk?
Cuckoos scream blood, apes cry mournfully.
On spring mornings, flower-filled days, autumn nights,
I often pour wine alone, sipping to solitude.
Are there no rustic songs? No village flutes?
But their harsh, grating tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech, it feels like listening
To heavenly music—ears suddenly clear and bright.
Don’t refuse—one more song! Let me remake this poem
For you, titled 'The Pipa Player.'
Moved by my words, she stands in silence long,
Then sits back, tightens strings, quickening the pace.
The music now grows colder, less like earlier tones—
Everyone in the hall, hearing it afresh, covers their faces in tears.
Who among us sheds the most tears tonight?
The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe is soaked through with grief."}
