Maple leaves and reed flowers stirred in autumn's chill.
Host dismounted, guest aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music played.
Drunk but not joyful, sad as we part—
Parting under moonlight drowned in river mist.
Suddenly, on water, pipa music rose—
Host forgot to return, guest held his course.
Following the sound, I asked in silence who was playing,
Music paused, player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat near, invited her to appear;
Added wine, turned up lamps, relit the feast.
Called again and again before she came forth—
Still holding her pipa half-concealed by face.
Tuning the axis, plucking strings two or three times,
Before a tune began, emotion stirred.
Each string suppressed, each note full of yearning—
As if recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Head down, fingers moving slowly, one after another,
She poured out all that heart could hold, unsaid.
Lightly stroking, gently rubbing, then lifting, pressing again—
First 'Feather Dress,' then 'Sixth Yao' she played.
Loud strings clattered like sudden rain,
Soft strings whispered like lovers’ secrets.
Clatter mingled with whisper, sharp with soft;
Big pearls, small pearls, falling on jade plates.
Between them, birdsong slips through blossom shadows;
Low, choked sounds, like spring water beneath ice.
Cold springs slow, strings freeze and cease;
Silence follows, broken, brief.
Yet deeper sorrow, hidden hatred rise now—
This stillness speaks more than any sound.
A silver bottle cracks, liquid bursts forth;
Iron cavalry charge, swords clash, spears shout.
When the piece ended, the pick struck center—
Four strings snapped at once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fell silent, breathless,
Only the river’s heart glowed white with autumn moon.
After a pause, he laid down the pick, slipped it into strings;
Adjusted clothes, straightened posture, composed his face.
She said: ‘I was born in the capital city,
My home lay beneath the Frog-Mound Lane.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa, named among first ranks
Of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After my piece, even master musicians bowed;
After each makeup, Qiu Niang envied me.
Five-generations youths vied to give me gifts—
One song earned crimson silks, countless times.
Silver hairpins shattered with rhythm’s beat;
Crimson skirts stained from wine spilled in joy.
Happy years, laughing ones—past, forgotten, same as spring moons and autumn breezes.
Young brother went to war, aunt died,
Day after day, my looks wore thin.
Front gate cold, few horses or riders,
Now old, married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, leave easily—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I stay at river mouth, empty boat alone;
Moon circles the ship, river water chills with cold.
Deep in night, suddenly dream of youth—
Dreaming, weeping, tears streak red across my face.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed already;
Hearing these words, again I grieved deeply.
We’re both lost souls afar from home—
Why should we have met before to know?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, no music heard;
Whole year long, no strings nor bamboo flutes.
Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What do I hear day and night here? Only
Cuckoos bleeding, apes mournfully crying.
In spring, mornings by blossoms; in autumn, nights beneath moon—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Surely there are mountain songs, village flutes?
But their jarring tones, harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa voice—
Like listening to celestial music, ears brightened briefly.
Don’t refuse—sit again and play one more tune,

Moved deeply by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, speeded up the notes.
Now the music shivered—no longer as before;
All present, hearing again, buried faces in tears.
Who wept most among the listeners?

The host dismounts, the guest remains on board; raising wine, yet no music plays.
Drunk, not joyful, filled with sorrow as we part—the river merges with the moon, vast and dim.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa floats across the water, the host forgets to return, the guest halts their journey.
I search for its source, whispering softly: 'Who is playing?' The pipa ceases, hesitant to speak.
I move the boat near, invite the player to meet, pour more wine, turn the lamp back on, restart the feast.
After many calls, she finally appears, still holding the pipa half-covered by her face.
She turns the axle, plucks the strings—three or four notes, though no tune formed, already emotion flows.
Each string is low, each note full of longing, as if narrating a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady fingers, pouring out endless thoughts from her heart.
Gently caressing, slowly rubbing, brushing, then plucking—first she plays 'Feathered Robe,' then 'Six Ya.'
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain, the thin ones whisper like private words.
Thundering, whispering, mixed together—large pearls and small, falling on jade dishes.
Smooth as a swallows' song slipping through blossoms, muffled deep beneath ice-cold springs.
Cold, icy, the strings freeze—silence follows, all sound stops momentarily.
Another hidden sorrow, another quiet hate arises—here, silence speaks louder than sound.
Like a silver bottle shattering, water bursts forth; like iron cavalry charging, swords clash in battle cries.
At the end, she draws the plectrum sharply across the center—four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.
From east to west, the boats grow silent, only the autumn moon shines over the river's heart.
She pauses, leans back, inserts the plectrum into the strings, adjusts her clothes, composes her face.
She says: 'I was born a lady of the capital city, my home lies beneath the Frog Mound Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy.
After each performance, even masters were impressed; after every beauty made, the old courtesan envied me.
Young men from wealthy families vied to give me silks—each tune earned countless red sashes.
With ivory hairpins, I beat time so hard they cracked; my crimson skirts turned red with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter and joy passed—spring breezes, autumn moons, all taken lightly.
My brother went off to war, my aunt passed away; days pass, my youth fades.
My door now rarely sees riders or horses—aged, I married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, not for parting—last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes, but I remain guarding an empty boat, the moon circling it, the river cold.
Late at night, I dream of my youthful days—crying in dreams, tears streaming down my cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply; hearing her story, I sigh again.
We are both lost souls, scattered far from our homes—why need we have met before?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick and confined in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music; year-round, no sounds of strings or bamboo.
Near Pienjiang, the land is low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear each morning and night? Cuckoos bleeding in blood, apes crying mournfully.
On spring mornings, flower-filled days, or autumn nights bright with moonlight—I often pour wine alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? But their sounds are harsh, unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, it’s like listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.
Please don’t refuse to play one more piece—for you, I’ll compose this poem called 'Pipa Song.'

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds sway in autumn's chill.
I dismount to welcome him; he stays on board—
We raise our cups, but no music plays.

Drunk, we can't find joy in parting,
As dusk descends, moonlight floods the river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: "Who's playing?"
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like pearls tumbling on jade plates.

Now clear as a bird skims through blossoms,
Now choked as springs flow under ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
Then silence speaks more than sound.

A silver jar shatters—water bursts forth,
Warhorses charge, blades clash in the wind.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
Crimson robes stained by wine and sweat.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carefree.

My brother left for war, my aunt died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, grating, hard to bear.

Yet tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly bright.

Please, don’t refuse—sit once more to play,
I'll compose a poem for you: *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits, tightens the strings—now the music quickens.

Her new melody is colder than before—
All seated weep anew, eyes veiled in tears.

Who weeps the most among us all?
The River Chief of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the river of Xunyang, at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reeds sway in autumn's chill.
I dismount to welcome him; he stays on board—
We raise our cups, but no music plays.

Drunk, we can't find joy in parting,
As dusk descends, moonlight floods the river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound,
The host forgets to return, the guest won't leave.

We search for its source, whispering softly: "Who's playing?"
The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

A thousand calls, a hundred entreaties—she appears at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.

She tunes the axis, plucks two or three strings—
Before the tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string is hushed, each note mournful—
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, she plays with quiet grace,
Singing all her heart's endless sorrow.

Gently she strokes, slow she rubs, then scrapes and lifts—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The light ones murmur like lovers' whispers.

Crisp and mingled, they pour forth—
Like pearls tumbling on jade plates.

Now clear as a bird skims through blossoms,
Now choked as springs flow under ice.

Cold, still, the strings freeze, silence hangs—
Then silence speaks more than sound.

A silver jar shatters—water bursts forth,
Warhorses charge, blades clash in the wind.

The final stroke across the heart of the strings—
Four chords snap once, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats fall silent,
Only the autumn moon gleams on the river’s heart.

She pauses, then drops the pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I was born in the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Hill.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the imperial music school.

After every piece, even masters were baffled;
After every makeup, Miao was envious.

Young nobles vied to offer silks—
One song earned me countless red scarves.

Silver hairpins shattered to the beat,
Crimson robes stained by wine and sweat.

Year after year, laughter shared,
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carefree.

My brother left for war, my aunt died—
Days fade, beauty fades with them.

Now front gate grows cold, horses and riders few,
Old, I married a merchant, lost my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not farewell—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone now, leaving me alone on the riverbank,
Moonlight circles my boat, cold waves lap.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking to weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face.

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply—
And hearing these words, I tremble again.

We are both castaways on this vast earth—
Why need we know each other before?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard,
Year-round, no strings nor flutes echo.

Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our home.

What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Crows crying blood, apes wailing in grief.

Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their cries are harsh, grating, hard to bear.

Yet tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly bright.

Please, don’t refuse—sit once more to play,
I'll compose a poem for you: *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits, tightens the strings—now the music quickens.

Her new melody is colder than before—
All seated weep anew, eyes veiled in tears.

Who weeps the most among us all?
The River Chief of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

From east to west, all boats lie still, speechless—

My host forgets to return, the guest refuses to depart.

I search for the source, softly asking who is playing;
The pipa falls silent, hesitates before words begin.

I move my boat near, inviting the player to see me—
Add wine, turn up lamps, renew the feast once more.

After many calls, she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa half-concealed by her face.

She turns the axis, plucks the strings three or four times—

Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing low, fingers glide steadily across the strings—
All the hidden sorrows of her heart unfold.

Gently pressing, slowly twisting, brushing, then flicking—
First "Feathered Robe," then "Sixth-Yao."

The thick string roars like sudden rain,
The thin string whispers like private talk.

Big pearls and small pearls falling on jade plates.

Or a stream choked beneath ice, struggling to flow.

Cold springs grow still, strings freeze in silence—
Then silence swells, louder than sound itself.

A silver pitcher shatters, liquid spurts forth—
A cavalry charge breaks through, swords and spears clash.

At last, the melody ends—she strikes the strings with a flourish,
Four strings crash together like tearing silk.

From east to west, all boats lie still, speechless—
Only the moon above the river’s heart shines white.

She pauses, musing, then slips the pick into the strings—

After each performance, even the finest master would bow in respect—
After every makeup, the famed Qiu Nang would envy my grace.

Five-gentleman youths vied to gift me silken robes—
One song earned me more than countless bolts of red silk.

Gold hairpins shattered from rhythmic beat,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter, spring and autumn passing freely—
But then my brother joined the army, my aunt passed away.

Days vanish, nights pass, my beauty fades.

Front gate grows cold, few horses or riders come—
Now old, I wed a merchant.

He values profit, cares not for parting—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

Since then, I've stayed at the riverside, guarding an empty boat—
Moonlight circles the ship, the river chills the night.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth again—

I dismount; my guest remains aboard the boat. We raise our wine, yet no music plays.
Drunk, we cannot feel joy—sadness stains parting, as moonlight drowns in the vast river.
Suddenly, on the water, a lute’s sound emerges: I forget to return, my guest won’t depart.
I search for the source in silence, asking softly who dares play. The music ceases, hesitant to speak.
We shift the boat near, invite her forth. Add wine, relight lamps, rekindle the feast.
After many calls, she finally appears, still half-concealing her face behind the lute.
She turns the axle, plucks two or three notes—before any tune begins, emotion stirs.
Each string sighs, each note bears sorrow, as if telling lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing low, fingers glide with ease—her heart poured out through endless strings.
Gently brushing, slowly rubbing, then flicking and lifting—first 'The Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Liu Yao.'
Thick strings clash like sudden rain, thin strings whisper like secret talk.
Clashing, whispering—a cascade of pearls on jade plates!
Like a bird skimming through blossoms, its song smooth and clear;
Like brookwater choked beneath ice, barely flowing, hard to hear.
Cold springs freeze—the strings grow tight, then halt. Silence reigns, brief but profound.
Another sorrow, hidden hate stir—now, silence speaks louder than sound.
A silver bottle bursts—spurted liquid floods; iron cavalry charges—sword and spear cry out.
At last, the final stroke across the heart of the strings—four strings shatter like torn silk!
East and west boats fall silent—only the autumn moon floats above the river's heart.
In thought, she rests her pick in the strings, adjusts her clothes, composes her face.
She says: 'I was born a city girl, in Hama Ling, where my home stood.
At thirteen, I mastered the lute—my name ranked first in the Imperial School.
After every performance, even the great artists bowed in awe; after every makeup, the beauty Qiuniang envied me.
Young nobles vied to flatter me, each tune worth countless red silks.
Tinsel hairpins shattered to the beat; crimson robes stained by wine spill.
Year after year, laughter and joy pass—autumn moons, spring breezes, all wasted.

He’s gone—only empty ship at the river mouth. Moon circles the boat, the water chills the night.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth—awaken weeping, makeup streaked red and wet.
Hearing this lute, I sigh deeply. Hearing her words again, I’m moved to tears.
We’re both castaways on distant shores—why need we have met before to understand?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the riverbank of Xunyang, at night, I see a guest off, 
Maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn stillness trembling. 
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
To raise a cup for drinking, yet no strings or pipes sound. 

Unhappy drunk, I face a sorrowful parting— 
At parting, the vast river mirrors the moon in haze. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises, 
My host forgets to return, my guest stays unmoved. 

I search for the voice, whispering, "Who plays?" 
The pipa stops—hesitating, speech withheld. 
I move my boat near, invite her to appear, 
Add wine, turn back the lamp, renew the feast. 

She’s called a thousand times before she comes, 
Still holding her pipa half-hiding her face. 

Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice— 
Before a tune begins, emotion is there. 

Each string low, each note heavy with grief, 
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled. 

Head lowered, fingers drift in steady motion, 
She played on, as if telling all she had kept deep inside. 

Lightly brushing, slowly plucking, sliding, lifting— 
First *Fei Lian*, then *Liu Yao*. 

The heavy strings crash like urgent rain, 
The thin strings murmur like hushed words. 

Roar and whisper entwine in a mingled stream— 
Pearls large and small fall on jade plates. 

A warbler’s call, smooth sliding through the flowers, 
Like spring water beneath ice, choked and tight. 

The icy spring grows cold and choked—the strings freeze silent, 
A pause, then nothing. 

Then another hidden sorrow, deep resentment— 
In silence, more is said than in sound. 

Suddenly, iron cavalry bursts forth—swords and spears ring out, 
Four strings strike at once—a rending of silk, sharp and loud. 

East and west boats lie quiet, no word spoken— 
Only the autumn moon above the river’s heart lies bright. 

After a pause, he rests the pick on the string, 
Straightens his clothes, composes his face. 

"I was born a girl in the capital city, 
Lived under the terrace where frog-dragons dwell. 

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first among the court troupe. 
After each performance, even the masters were awed. 
My beauty stirred envy in the old courtesan. 

Young nobles vied to buy my trinkets— 
One song earned me endless red sashes. 

Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm, 
Red silk gowns stained by wine, soaked through. 

Year after year, laughter, joy, same as ever— 
Spring rivers, blooming flowers, moonlit nights pass carelessly. 

My brother left to war, my aunt died; 
Days pass, mornings fade—my looks grow dim. 

Front gate grows cold, no more horses or riders— 
Old, I married a merchant. 

Merchants care only for profit, not parting— 
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea. 

Now, alone, I guard an empty boat by the river’s mouth, 
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills with cold. 

Deep in the night, I dream of youth— 
Waking, tears streak red down my cheeks. 

Hearing this pipa, I sigh already— 
Now hearing these words, I sigh again. 

We’re both lost souls far from home, 
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship? 

I left the capital last year—exiled, confined here in Xunyang, ill and idle. 

This place is isolated, no music to be found, 
Whole years pass without a single note of string or flute. 

Near Pien River, land low and damp— 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house. 

What sounds do I hear daily, morning and night? 
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing in sorrow. 

In spring, at dawn when flowers bloom, in autumn nights with moonlight, 
Often I pour wine and drink alone. 

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes? 
But their harsh cries are unbearable to hear. 

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
It’s as if listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear. 

Please don’t refuse—sit again, play one more tune— 
I’ll compose a poem for you, “Pipa Xing.” 

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence, 
Then sits again, tightens the strings, speeds up the beat. 

The music now is colder, less like the earlier tone— 
All in the audience weep, covering their faces. 

Who shed the most tears in this room? 
The Jiangzhou magistrate, his blue robe wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn light.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat,
They raise their cups, but no lute or zither note.
Drunk without joy, they part in gloom,
The vast river reflects the moon.
Suddenly, a lute's sound from the water's expanse,
The host forgets to leave, the guest delays his dance.
Following the sound, they ask who plays so,
The lute stops, she hesitates, as if to say no.
They move their boat near, invite her to appear,
More wine is served, lamps relit, the feast held bright and clear.
After a thousand calls and entreaties, she finally appears,
Still holding her lute, half-hiding her face in fears.
She tunes the strings, plucks them twice, three times,
Before the melody, her feelings chime.
Each string a sigh, each note a thought,
As if her life's frustrations were sought.
She lowers her brow, plays on with ease,
Telling all the endless heart's unease.
With a gentle touch, a slow caress, a sweep, a strum,
First "Rainbow Garment," then "Little Yangtze."
The great strings roar like a sudden rain,
The small strings whisper, a soft refrain.
Roar and whisper, a tangled, complex sound,
Like pearls, great and small, falling to the ground.
Like orioles singing, smooth beneath the flowers,
Then like a choked spring, flowing under icy bowers.
The ice-cold spring, the strings congeal, the sound is lost,
A pause, a silence, at any cost.
A hidden sorrow, a silent grief arises,
In this silence, more than any sound comprises.
Then a silver vase shatters, water bursts,
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears at their worst.
The song ends, she draws a line across the strings,
Four strings at once, like tearing silk, a final sting.
Boats to the east and west are silent, still,
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart is seen from the hill.
Pensive, she tucks the plectrum, straightens her dress,
Her face composed, with solemnness.
She says, "I was a girl of the capital's domain,
Lived at the foot of Toad Hill's plain.
At thirteen, my lute playing was complete,
My name first in the Music School's elite.
When my song ended, even masters were impressed,
My beauty, once made up, made the autumn queens depressed.
Young men from five noble tombs vied for my favor with gifts,
For one song, silks of red, an uncounted lift.
Silver combs, studded with jewels, beat time and broke,
Blood-red silk skirts, stained with wine, as they spoke.
Year after year, of laughter and delight,
I let the autumn moons and spring winds pass light.
My brother went to war, my mother passed away,
Dusk and dawn, my youthful looks began to decay.
Guests grew few, horses at my door were rare,
I grew old, and married a merchant, in despair.
He values profit, not our parting's ache,
Last month, to Fuliang, for tea, he did take.
Back and forth, I guard this empty boat alone,
The moon bright, the river cold, around me thrown.
In the deep night, I dream of my youth's old ways,
And wake to tears staining my rouge's red blaze."
Hearing her lute, I had already sighed,
Hearing her words, I could no longer hide.
Both of us, castaways at the world's end,
Why must we have met, to know and befriend?
I left the capital last year, demoted, ill,
Exiled and sick, in Xunyang town, at will.
This place is remote, with no music to my ear,
I hear no strings or flutes for the whole year.
I live by the Pei River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, around my camp.
What do I hear, from morning till night's deep?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, the gibbon's mournful weep.
On spring river flower-days, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine, and drink alone in the heights.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
They are harsh and jarring, like mocking, discordant types.
But tonight, hearing your lute's speech so clear,
It is like hearing celestial music, banishing my fear.
Please do not decline, sit and play one more tune,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Lute" in this room.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings, her playing wild.
The mournful sound, unlike the one before,
The whole gathering hears it, and weeps, as they pour.
Who in this room weeps the most, so deep?
The Jiangzhou official, his blue robe wet with his weep."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

At parting, the river's moon mirrors our sorrow.
Suddenly on the water, a pipa's sound emerges;
The host forgets his return, the guest pauses his departure.
I follow the sound, quietly asking who plays;
The pipa stops—hesitant, almost speechless.

Adding wine, turning lamps, relighting the feast.

Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.

Before even beginning the tune, emotion stirs.
Each string murmurs low, each note carries memory,

Pouring out endless griefs within her heart.

Silence fills the void—no sound, yet more than sound.

Iron cavalry charges, swords clash, weapons flash.

Four strings snap as one, like silk torn apart.

Each string suppressed and muffled, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Bowing her brows, she played on, note after note,
Telling all the countless things within her heart.
She plucked, rubbed, and picked, gently and slowly,
First the *Nishang*, then the *Liuyao*.
The large strings clattered like heavy rain,
The small strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, the strings in tangled play,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Orioles warble smoothly in the flowers,
Then the spring stream chokes beneath the ice.

Frozen and silent, the sound pauses for a time.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the bank of the Xunyang River, at night, I bid farewell to a guest; maple leaves and reed flowers tremble in autumn's chill.
I dismount, my host, while the guest remains aboard the boat; raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays.
Drunk, I cannot find joy—only sorrow as we part; as we depart, the river stretches into a vast moonlit haze.
Suddenly, from the water’s surface, a pipa melody echoes—my host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.
Following the sound, I ask softly, 'Who is playing?' The pipa pauses, its player hesitates to speak.
We move our boat near, inviting her to come forth; add wine, relight the lamp, and begin the feast anew.
After countless calls, she finally appears, still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.
She turns the shaft, plucks the strings in three or two notes—before a tune begins, emotion already stirs.
Each string suppressed, each note a sigh, as if recounting a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, she plays with steady fingers, pouring out endless thoughts within.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, stroking, then lifting—the first piece is 'The Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Liu Yao.'
The thick strings roar like sudden rain, the thin strings whisper like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft notes interweave: great pearls and small pearls fall upon jade dishes.
Like a bird gliding through blossoms, the music flows smooth and bright; like a spring beneath ice, it struggles, choked and low.
Cold springs grow sluggish, strings freeze, the music stops—brief silence follows.
Yet another kind of hidden sorrow emerges—this silence speaks more than sound ever could.
A silver bottle cracks open, water gushes forth; cavalry bursts through, swords and spears clash.
At the final stroke, the pipa's pick strikes the heart of the instrument—it sounds like silk tearing.
East and west boats fall silent, nothing but the moon white over the river's heart.
After a pause, he lays down the pick, slides it into the strings, adjusts his clothes, and composes his face.
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, lived at the foot of Hama Ling.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After a piece, even master musicians would be amazed; after makeup, every courtesan envied me.
Young men from noble families vied to give me silken robes—each song earned a flood of red silk.
Gold-tipped hairpins shattered with rhythm; crimson skirts stained with wine from dancing.
Year after year, laughter, joy, time passes—autumn moons and spring breezes, all wasted.
My brother left for war, my aunt died; days pass, my beauty fades.
Our gate grows cold, few horses and riders now come; old, I married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, not goodbyes—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He departs, leaving me alone on this empty boat by the river mouth; the moon circles us, the river chills with cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth—crying in sleep, tears streaking my painted face.
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply; hearing her story again, I sigh once more.
We are both castaways far from home—why need we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, lacking music; for whole years, no string or bamboo sound reaches my ears.
Near Panshui, the land is low and damp; yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear day and night? Crows crying blood, apes lamenting in mournful cries.
On spring mornings or autumn nights, often I pour wine alone, drinking to myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? They’re harsh, grating, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa music, it feels like heavenly tunes—my ears clear for a moment.
Please, don’t refuse to play one more piece—for you, I’ll compose this 'Pipa Song.'
Moved by my words, she stands a long while in silence, then returns to her seat, tightens the strings—now the music grows urgent.
The tone now is not as before—its sadness surpasses earlier strains. All in the hall weep with grief.
Who sheds the most tears here? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his green robe soaked with tears."}

Takes care with her clothes, gathers her composure.

The host dismounts, the guest remains on board; raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays to accompany us. Though drunk, we cannot rejoice—our sorrow deepens as we part. In that vast twilight, the river mirrors the moon, dim and broad. Suddenly, from the water comes the sound of a pipa; the host forgets to return, the guest holds back his departure. We search for the source by listening, softly asking who is playing. The pipa stops—words hang unspoken. We move our boat near, inviting the musician to appear. Wine is poured again, lamps adjusted, and a banquet rekindled. After much urging, she emerges, still half-hiding her face behind the pipa. With a turn of the axis and a few plucks, even before the melody begins, emotion fills the air. Each string whispers sorrow, each note mourns unfulfilled dreams. Bowing her head, she plays with steady hands, pouring out endless thoughts. Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding and picking—she first plays 'Fei Lian', then 'Liu Miao'. The thick strings roar like sudden rain, the thin ones whisper like private talk. A jumble of sounds—the large pearls drop onto jade plates, the small ones scatter like beads. Like a bird gliding through flowers, its song smooth and sweet, then like a strained spring under ice, choked and hard to flow. The icy spring grows cold, the strings stiffen, then fall silent, a pause suspended. Yet within silence, a hidden sorrow stirs—this quiet speaks more than any sound could. Then, a silver bottle bursts, spilling liquid forth; a cavalry charge breaks through, swords and spears clang. When the final stroke strikes the center of the pipa, four strings explode like tearing silk. East and west boats hush, utterly still. Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river’s heart. After a long pause, she lowers her pick into the strings, arranges her clothes, straightens her posture, gathers herself. She says: 'I was born in the capital city, lived at the foot of Hama Ling. Young nobles vied to give me silken robes—my songs brought countless gifts. My jeweled hairpin shattered to rhythm, my crimson silk skirts stained by wine. Year after year, laughter and joy passed as easily as the moon and spring breeze. But when my brother marched off to war and my aunt died, my beauty faded with each day. Doors grew cold, fewer horses came. Now old, I married a merchant. He values profit, not parting. Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea. Left here alone at the river mouth, I guard an empty boat. Under the moonlight circling the ship, the water chills the night. Late one night, I dreamed of my youth—awoke crying, tears streaming down my face. I heard this pipa, sighed deeply; hearing her story, I sighed again. We are both lost souls adrift on the same desolate earth—why must we have met before to feel such kinship? I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, ill, living in Xunyang. Far from the world, Xunyang lacks music—year-round, no string or bamboo sounds. Near Panshui, the land lies low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home. What do I hear morning and evening? Crows crying blood-red, gibbons mourning. On spring mornings, flower-filled days, autumn nights glowing with moonlight—I often pour wine alone. Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? But their croaks and screeches are unbearable to hear. Now, tonight, hearing your pipa words, it feels like listening to heavenly music—my ears briefly clear. Please, don’t refuse to play one more piece—for you, I will compose these lines: 'The Pipa Song.' Moved by my words, she stands in silence for a long time, then sits down, tightens the strings, and plays faster. Her music now is sadder than before—every listener covers their eyes in tears. I dismounted to greet the guest on board; we raised our cups but no music played to cheer us.
Half-drunk, we could not celebrate—sadness filled our hearts as we parted, the river lost in misty moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water's surface, came the sound of a pipa—my host forgot to return, the guest halted his journey.
I sought the source in silence, whispered, 'Who plays?' The pipa paused, then faltered in reply.
We rowed closer, invited her to meet us, added wine, relit the lamps, and began again.
After many calls, she finally appeared, still half-concealing her face behind the pipa.
Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice, no melody yet—yet emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed, each note laden with longing, as though speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she played with steady fingers, weaving through endless tales unheard.
Gently stroking, slowly pressing, brushing, lifting—first 'Rainbow Skirts', then 'Sixth Dancer'.
The bass strings roared like sudden rain, the treble whispered like private words.
A jumble of deep and soft tones—pearls spilling onto jade plates.
Like a bird gliding through blossoms, its voice smooth and clear; like a hidden spring choked under ice, strained and labored.
Cold springs congeal, strings freeze, silence grips—the pause holds more than sound can say.
Then, a silver jar bursts—liquid spurts forth; iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash.
At last, the final stroke across the heart of the string—four strings shatter like torn silk.
East and west boats fell silent, only the moonwhite expanse of the river’s heart revealed.
She paused, leaned pensively, inserted the pick into the strings, adjusted her robes, and composed herself.
'I was born a city girl, my home beneath the Toad Pond Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the Imperial Academy's great troupe.
After each performance, even masters would bow in awe; after each makeup, beauty queens would envy me.
Young nobles vied to shower me with silken ribbons—a single song might earn dozens.
My hairpins of jade and silver shattered with beat; red silk gowns stained with wine spilled by laughter.
Year in, year out, joy turned to routine—spring mornings, autumn nights, moments passed carelessly.
My brother left for war, my aunt passed away; days slipped by, my beauty faded.
Now, my door is lonely, horse and rider few; old, I married a merchant.
Merchants seek profit, scorn parting—last month he sailed off to Fuliang to buy tea.
He departs, leaving me alone aboard an empty boat, moonlight circling me, the river cold.
Deep into the night, I dreamt of youth—awakened, weeping, tears streaming down my painted cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed; hearing her tale, I sighed again, deeply moved.
We are both castaways far from home—why must we have met before to feel this kinship?
I left the capital last year, exiled, sick and confined to Xunyang City.
Xunyang remote, no music ever heard—whole years without flute or zither’s sound.

Drunk but unable to rejoice, we sorrowed as we parted—on a vast, misty river reflecting the moon.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa rose from the water; I forgot to return, my guest refrained from departing.
Following the sound, I softly asked who played—who paused, hesitating before speaking.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me; added wine, turned the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerged, still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.
She tuned the axis, plucked a few chords—before any melody began, emotion stirred.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with yearning—like one recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she continued playing slowly, expressing all the sorrows in her heart.
Gently stroking, lightly pressing, sliding, then picking—she first played 'Fei Shang,' then 'Liu Yao.'
The deep strings roared like heavy rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft notes—large pearls and small pearls dropping onto jade plates.
Like a bird gliding through blooming flowers, its song smooth; like a stream beneath ice, struggling to flow.
Cold springs choked, strings frozen silent—then silence stretched, broken only by inner sorrow.
In that moment of silence, more was said than words could express.
Like a silver bottle shattering, water bursting forth; like cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the end, the pick struck the center, four strings resounding as if silk tore apart.
East and west boats fell utterly still; only the autumn moon gleamed over the river's heart.
After a pause, she laid down the pick into the strings, adjusted her clothes, and composed her look.
She confessed: 'I was born a girl in the capital city, living beneath the Hama Ling Hill.
At thirteen, I’d mastered the pipa; my name ranked among the top troupe of the Imperial Academy.
After my performance, even the best musicians would bow in admiration; after dressing, I’d be envied by all the courtesans.
Young men from the five noble districts vied to gift me silken robes—each song earned me countless lengths.
My gold hairpins shattered to rhythm, my crimson skirts stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Year after year, joy followed joy—spring blossoms, autumn moons, passed carelessly.
But when my brother joined the army and my aunt passed away, days slipped by as my beauty faded.
Once-busy gate now cold, horses and riders few; old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit, disdain parting—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I remain here at the river’s mouth, guarding an empty boat. Around it, moonlight bathes the cold waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth—awaking, my tears streak through painted makeup.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply; hearing her story, I sighed again.
We are both castaways on this distant earth—a meeting need not have been predestined.
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled and bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music; for whole years, no lute or bamboo flute has sounded.
Near the Pien River, the land is low and damp—the yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my home.
What sounds do I hear day and night? Cuckoos bleeding their hearts, apes grieving in sorrow.
On spring mornings, autumn nights, I often pour wine and drink alone.
Is there no folk song or village flute? But they’re harsh and grating—hard to endure.
Tonight, hearing your pipa tune, it feels like listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.
Don’t refuse—sit again and play another piece—for you, I’ll compose this poem 'Pipa Xing.'
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence, then sat back, tightening the strings—now the music grew urgent.
The tone now mournful, unlike what came before—every listener covered their eyes in tears.
Among all those present, who shed the most? The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe was soaked with tears."}

As we depart, the vast river mirrors the moon, dim and cold.
Suddenly, a lute's melody floats across the water—
My host forgets to return, the guest refuses to depart.
I search for its source, whispering softly: 'Who is playing?'
The lute falls silent; she hesitates before speaking.
I steer the boat closer, invite her to appear—
Add wine, relight the lamps, restart the feast.
With many calls, she finally emerges, still half-hiding behind the lute.
She turns the axis, plucks the strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion already spills forth.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing—
As if narrating a life of unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, fingers move steadily, one phrase after another—
Pouring out endless sorrows from her heart.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, flicking, sliding—
First *Nayi Shang*, then *Liuyao* she plays.
Thick strings roar like sudden rain, thin ones hiss like private whispers.
A jumble of loud and soft, deep and light—
Like pearls tumbling into jade plates, clear and bright.
Smooth as birds singing through flowerbeds, sweet and free—
Yet strained like springs beneath ice, choked and slow.
Cold spring water stifles, strings grow tense and break—
Silence reigns, the sounds pause, then cease.
Another sorrow stirs in secret, unseen—
In that silence, more speaks than words could ever say.
A silver bottle shatters, water bursts forth—
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash in thunder.
When the last stroke strikes, the pick slashes straight through the center—
Four strings cry out once, like silk torn apart.
East and west boats fall silent, not a sound—
Only the moon above the river’s heart, white and stark.
After a pause, he slides the pick back into the strings,
Adjusts his clothes, composes himself, gathers his countenance.
She says: 'I am from the capital city originally,
My home lies beneath the Frog-Mound Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the lute—my name stood first
Among the palace musicians’ elite.
After every performance, even the master would bow in awe,
My beauty drew envy from the famed Lady Qiu.
Young men from the Five Hills vied to offer me silken robes—
One song, countless red scarves, lost in the crowd.
Tinsel hairpins shattered from rhythmic beating,
Crimson skirts stained by wine spilled in revelry.
Laughter year after year, spring flowers and autumn moons pass unnoted.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt passed away;
Days fade, nights pass—my face grows old.
My door now stands empty, few riders come—
Now old, I married a merchant.
He values profit, ignores parting’s pain—
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since then, I’ve waited here alone at the river bank,
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills with cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth again—
Waking, I weep, tears streak my painted face.
Hearing her lute, I sigh deeply—then hear her tale, and sigh anew.
We are both exiled souls on this distant shore—
Why must we have met before to feel so close?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Now confined, ill, in Xunyang town.
Xunyang’s remote, no music ever heard—
All year long, no strings or bamboo flutes resound.
Near Panyang, land low and damp—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.
What sounds do I hear day and night here?
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring mornings, autumn nights—often I pour wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their harsh cries are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your lute, it feels like heaven’s music—
My ears open wide, just for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece—
For you, I will rewrite this *Pipa Xing*.
Moved by my words, she stands silently for long—
Then sits down, tightens the strings, and plays faster.
Now the tones are colder, sharper than before—
All present, listening once more, cover their faces and weep.
Who among them weeps the most?

Gently stroking, slowly rubbing, flicking, plucking again—first 'Feather Dress,' then 'Six Ya.'
Loud strings roared like sudden rain, soft strings whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft notes—the large pearls, small pearls, falling on jade plates.
Between them: a swift bird's song through blossoms, a strained spring under ice, hard to pass.
Cold, stagnant springs made the strings freeze—frozen silence, then a brief pause.
Yet another sorrow, hidden hatred stirred—here, silence spoke louder than sound.
A silver bottle cracked—water gushed forth; iron cavalry burst forward, swords and spears clashing.
At end, the plectrum struck the center of the strings—four strings rang out as if torn silk.
East and west boats fell silent, only the autumn moon shining white upon the river’s heart.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the palace troupe.
After my performance, even the master musician would bow; my beauty provoked jealousy from Qiu Niang.
Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give me silken gifts—each song earned me countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-tipped combs shattered to rhythm, crimson silk robes stained with wine and blood.
Year after year, laughter and joy passed like spring moons and autumn breezes.
My brother enlisted in war; my guardian died. Each day, my face grew old.

Merchants care more for profit than for parting; last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He’s gone, leaving me alone on the riverbank—moonlight circles the boat, cold water chills the shore.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the bank of Xunyang River, I bid farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising a cup to drink, no music plays to cheer.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful as we part,
At parting, the vast river reflects the moon's dim glow.
Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.
I search for the voice, whispering to ask who plays,
When the pipa falls silent, hesitant to speak.
We move our boat nearer, inviting the player to meet,
Add wine, turn up the lamp, reopen the feast.
After many calls, she appears at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the axle, plucks the strings three or two times;
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air.
Each string mourns, each note brims with longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled and full of grief.
Bowing her head, fingers move on, note by note,
Pouring out endless sorrows from her heart.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, flicking, sliding,
First playing 'Rainbow Skirts,' then 'Sixth Yao.'
The heavy strings thunder like a sudden storm,
The light ones whisper like private, intimate talk.
Thunder and whisper intermingle in a rush,
Like large and small pearls falling on jade plates.
Amidst the flitting birds' songs through blossoms,
A low, choked murmur flows beneath icy springs.
Cold springs freeze, strings grow tight and still,
The music halts — silence deepens, unbroken.
Another hidden sorrow stirs, unseen,
This silence speaks more than any sound ever could.
Sudden as a silver bottle bursting open,
Water gushes forth; a cavalry charge roars,
Swords and spears clashing in battle’s cry.
At the piece’s end, the pick strikes center stage;
Four strings resound once, like silk torn apart.
Boats both east and west lie silent as death;
Only the autumn moon glows white upon the river’s heart.
With hesitation, she rests the pick into the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, straightens her face, composes herself.
She says: 'Born a girl of the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Hare-Moth Alley.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa’s art,
Named first among the Imperial Academy’s ranks.
After my performance, even skilled masters praised me;
My makeup made others jealous, the famed Autumn Lady.
Young nobles vied to offer silk and gold,
A single song earned countless red silks.
Tinsel hairpins shattered with every beat,
Crimson skirts stained with wine from wild revelry.
Joy one year, laughter the next — years pass like springtime blooms and autumn moons.
My brother went off to war, my foster mother died;
Days pass, mornings fade — my beauty fades too.
Front gate now quiet, few horses or riders pass;
Old and worn, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit, scorn separations;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He came and went at the river mouth, leaving me alone,
Beside the boat, the moonlight cold, the river chill.
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youthful days;
Awakening, I weep, tears streaking through my painted face.
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply;
Now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both lost souls beneath the same sky,
Meeting need not mean we’ve known before!
I left the imperial capital last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
Whole years pass without a single string or flute.
Near the Pien River, the land is damp and low,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.
What sounds do I hear day after day?
Cuckoos bleeding blood, apes mourning in the night.
In spring, flowers at dawn, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I pour wine myself, drinking alone.
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes?
But their harsh cries are unbearable to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s speech,
It feels like listening to heavenly music — my ears brighten instantly.
Do not refuse to play another piece;
For you, I will compose this 'Pipa Song.'
Moved deeply by my words, she stands a long time,
Then sits down, tightens the strings — the music grows urgent.
The sound now bleak, unlike what it was before;
All present, hearing it again, cover their eyes in tears.
Who weeps most here? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his green robe soaked wet."}

今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the moonlit bank of Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest at night, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn's chill.
I dismounted while my guest boarded the boat; raising a cup to drink, no music played—no strings or flutes.
Drunk but sad, we parted in gloom, with the river reflecting the moon in vast, dim silence.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa, so poignant that host forgot to return, guest ceased to depart.
I listened for the source, softly asking who played—who paused, hesitating before replying.
We drew our boat near, inviting her to meet; poured more wine, turned up the lamp, remade the feast.
After many calls, she emerged, still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.
She tuned the axis, plucked a few notes: already emotion stirred before the melody began.
Each string sighed, each note spoke of sorrow—like one recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she played on steadily, as if pouring out endless heartaches.
Gently pressing, slowly brushing, gliding and plucking, starting with 'Fei Chang,' then 'Liu Yao.'
The deep strings roared like heavy rain, the light strings whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft, like pearls tumbling on jade plates.
Like a bird skimming through blossoms, its song smooth and sweet, yet beneath, a brook flows under ice—strained, hard to pass.
Cold springs congeal, strings stiffen, then fall silent, a pause suspended.
Yet deeper sorrow and hidden resentment arise—this silence speaks louder than sound.
Like a silver pitcher shattering, splashing liquid forth, or cavalry breaking through, swords and spears clashing.
At the last stroke, the pick struck center, four strings cried out as if torn silk.
East and west boats fell utterly still, only the autumn moon on the river’s heart gleamed white.
After a pause, she placed the pick down, tucked it into the strings, smoothed her robes, and composed herself.
She said: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath Hama Ling’s hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the imperial music bureau.
After a performance, even the best teacher admired me; after makeup, beauties envied me.
Young lords from the Five Tombs vied to gift me silken robes—each song earned countless red silks.
My jeweled hairpins shattered with rhythm, my crimson skirts stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Year after year, laughter followed, and the seasons passed carelessly—autumn moons, spring mornings.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt died; days slipped, my beauty faded.
Front gate grew cold, no more saddled horses; old now, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit over partings—last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he has gone, leaving me guarding an empty boat by the river mouth, bathed in moonlight, chilled by the cold river water.
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youthful days; woke crying, tears streaking red down my painted cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply; hearing her tale, I sighed again.
We are both exiled souls on distant shores—why need we have met before?
I left the imperial capital last year, demoted, bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music; whole years go by without a single note of strings or bamboo.
Near Pienjiang, the land low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.
What sounds do I hear day and night? Crows bleeding blood, gibbons wailing in anguish.
In spring, dawn among blossoms; in autumn, nights beneath the moon—I often pour wine alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? But their rough cries are unbearable to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, it feels like heavenly music—my ears briefly brightened.
Do not refuse to play another piece—for you I will compose this 'Pipa Poem.'
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence, then sat back, quickened the strings, and intensified the playing.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of Xunyang River, at night, I bid farewell to guests—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
Raising a cup to drink, yet no music stirs the air.

Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful as we part,
As dusk descends, the river swallows the moon's pale light.

Suddenly, a lute’s cry rises from the water—
The host forgets to leave; the guest halts his journey.

I seek the sound, whispering, "Who plays?"
The lute falls silent, hesitates to speak.

We move our boat near, urge her to appear—
Add wine, turn up the lamps, open the feast again.

After countless calls, she appears at last,
Still half-hiding her face behind the lute.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings—three or four notes—
Before any tune begins, emotion fills the air.

Each string mourns; each note recalls deep thoughts—
As if recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing her head, fingers flow one after another,
Speaking all that heart has long held in silence.

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, then sliding and lifting—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao* she plays.

The bass strings roar like sudden raindrops,
The treble whispers like secrets in private talk.

A jumble of loud and soft, high and low—
Like pearls tumbling upon jade plates.

Now clear, like a bird's song through blooming flowers,
Then choked, like spring water beneath frozen ice.

Cold streams grow stiff; strings freeze in tense stillness—
Silence deepens, sounds suspended for a breath.

Yet deeper sorrows, hidden resentments rise—
In this silence, more than sound is heard.

Then, a silver jar cracks, liquid spurts forth—
Horsemen charge, blades clash, weapons ring.

When the final stroke strikes the lute’s heart,
Four strings snap once—like silk torn apart.

East and west ships fall silent, breathless,
Only the autumn moon glows white on the river’s core.

She pauses, musing, then slides the pick back into the strings—
Straightens her clothes, composes her face.

"I am by origin a woman of the capital city,
My home lies beneath the Frog Moat’s old wall.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute’s art,
Named first among the Imperial Music Academy.

After every piece, even masters stood amazed—
After every makeup, all the courtesans envied me.

Five noble youths competed to shower me with gifts—
One melody earned me endless silken robes.

Silver hairpins shattered at the beat,
Red silk skirts stained with wine from wild revelry.

Year after year, laughter and joy passed—
Autumn moons and spring breezes slipped away.

My brother left to join the army; my aunt died—
Days pass, mornings fade, beauty fades too.

Door now empty, riders few;
Older, I wed a merchant, bound to trade.

Merchants care for profit, scorn parting—
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He’s gone, leaving me alone on the riverbank—
Moon circles our boat, the water chills the night.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s days—
Crying in sleep, tears streak through rouge-smeared cheeks.

I’ve heard your lute and sighed already—
Now hearing these words, my soul trembles again.

We’re both castaways on life’s far shore—
Why must we have met before to recognize one another?

I left the capital last year, exiled, ill in Xunyang—
This place, remote, lacks music; none hear strings all year.

Near Pienjiang, the land is damp and low—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around the house.

What do I hear day and night?
Cuckoos crying blood; apes wailing in despair.

Spring mornings with blossoms, autumn nights under moonlight—
Often I pour wine and drink alone.

Are there no mountain ballads, no village flutes?
But their crude strains are hard to bear.

Tonight, hearing your lute’s voice,
It’s as if celestial music rings in my ears.

Don’t refuse—sit down again, play one more piece—
I’ll compose for you, a song called *Pipa Xing*.

Moved by my words, she stands in silence long—
Then returns to sit, tightens the strings, quickening the pace.

Her music grows colder now, not like before—
All in the audience weep, covering their faces.

Who sheds the most tears in this room?
The Jiangzhou Magistrate’s blue robe is wet with grief."}

Maple leaves and reeds rustle in autumn's chill.
I dismount; my guest remains aboard the boat.
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Drunk but not joyful, sad as we part,
as we part, the river laps under a moon lost in haze.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s sound—a melody that stilled the host, made the guest delay his departure.
Following the music, I softly ask who plays—
The music halts; the player hesitates, reluctant to speak.

I move the boat near, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight lamps, renew the feast again.

After countless calls, she finally emerges—
Still clutching her pipa, half her face concealed.

She turns the axis, plucks a few strings—
Before the tune is formed, emotion fills the air.

Each string suppressed, each note brimming with sorrow—
As if lamenting a life unfulfilled.

Head lowered, hands drift gently, playing on,
Unfolding all the heart’s endless griefs.

Lightly plucking, slowly pressing, brushing, lifting—
First "Feiwei," then "Liuyao" played without pause.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The thin ones whisper like private talk.

Crash and whisper, interwoven, overlapping—
Like pearls tumbling onto jade plate.

Then, birds glide through blossoms, voice clear and slippery;
A brook gurgles beneath ice, struggling, hard to pass.

Ice-cold springs choke; the strings freeze, silence breaks—
No sound for a moment, yet deeper than sound.

Then, a silver jar shatters—water bursts forth!
A cavalry charge roars—steel and blades clash.

At song’s end, the pick slashes straight down the heart—
Four strings cry out at once, like silk torn apart.

East and west boats fall silent;
Only the autumn moon gleams above the river’s heart.

Doubtful, she leans the pick into the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, composes her face.

She says: "I was born in the city’s core,
Lived at Hama Ling, where the crickets sing.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art,
My name ranked first in the Imperial Academy.

When I finished a piece, even the master bowed to me;
After makeup, even Qiumiang envied my grace.

Young nobles vied to offer silken gifts—
One song, a score of red scarves never counted.

Tinsel hairpins broke with beat; crimson robes stained by wine.

Joy repeated year after year,
Spring mornings, autumn nights—time slipped away.

But my brother joined the army, auntie died—
Day fades, dawn comes, beauty wanes.

Door grows cold—the horsemen come less often.
Old now, I wed a merchant.

Merchants care only for profit, scorn parting—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, leaving me alone on this river mouth,
Moonlight circles the boat, the river chills.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Crying in dreams, tears streaking through rouge.

Hearing her pipa, I sighed; hearing her tale, I sighed again.
We are both castaways on distant shores—
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship?

Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled to sickness in Xunyang City.

Xunyang lacks music—no year passes without silence;
Near Pienjiang, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.

What do I hear every morning and evening here?
Cuckoos scream blood-red; apes mourn in the wild.

In spring’s morning glow or autumn’s moonlit night,
I often pour wine, drinking alone.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Yet these sounds, harsh and jarring, cannot please.

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s song—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly clear.

Do not refuse, sit again and play one more piece—
I’ll compose it, call it “The Pipa Song.”

Moved deeply by my words, she stands a long while—
Then sits back, tightens the strings, the tune sharpens.

Her music now grows sadder than before—
All seated hear it, all cover their eyes and weep.

Who among them sheds the most?
Jiangzhou’s governor—his green robe soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the moonlit bank of Xunyang River, I bid farewell to guests at night, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn's chill.
My host dismounted, my guest stayed on the boat; raising a cup to drink, no music played to guide the tune.
Drunk but not happy, sorrowful as we parted—parting under a vast, moon-washed river lost in mist.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa: my host forgot to return, my guest refused to depart.
I sought the voice in silence, whispered, 'Who plays?' The pipa paused, speech hesitated.
I moved my boat near, invited her to come forth; added wine, turned up the lamp, reopened our feast.
After many calls, she appeared at last, still half-concealing her face behind the pipa.
Turning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice—before any melody began, emotion already filled the air.
Each string choked down, each note full of longing—like an unspoken life of thwarted dreams.
Bowing her head, fingers moving steadily, she played—pouring out infinite sorrows from her heart.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, gliding, lifting, starting with 'Feather-Robe' then moving to 'Six-Zhao'.
The bass strings roared like heavy rain, the treble whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft notes, large pearls and small ones falling onto jade plate.
Now a swift lark's song through blossoms, now a stifled brook beneath ice—hard to pass.
Ice-cold spring halts the strings, silence tightens—then pause, a fleeting hush.
Another sadness, hidden wrath—here, silence speaks louder than sound.
A silver bottle bursts, water gushes out; iron cavalry charges, swords clash.
At song's end, the pick struck hard at center string—four strings rang once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fell silent, only the moon above the river’s heart, white and clear.
Hesitating, he laid down the pick, inserted it into the strings, adjusted his clothes, straightened his posture.
She said: 'Born originally in the capital city, my home was beneath the Hare-Mound Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After playing, even master musicians admired me; after dressing, the Lady Qiu jealously envied me.
Young men from Five-Legend Hills vied to send gifts—each song earned countless red silks.
Silver hairpins shattered on beat, crimson robes stained by spilled wine.
Happy one year, happy another—spring moons, autumn breezes passed carelessly.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died; days and nights brought faded looks.
Door grew cold, horses and riders rare—now old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit, scorn goodbyes—the month before, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I stay here with empty boat—moonlight circling, river water cold.
Deep in night, I dream of youth again—waking, crying, tears staining rouge-dyed cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed already—now hearing her words, I sighed more.
We are both castaways on distant lands, why need we have met before to know each other?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, bedridden in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard—whole years without a single note of strings or bamboo.
Near Pien River, the land low and damp—yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow all around.
Day and night, what do I hear? Cuckoos bleeding their song, gibbons mournfully howling.
In spring, dawn flower-views; in autumn, moonlit nights—I often pour wine alone.
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? But they're harsh, discordant—hard to bear.
Tonight hearing your pipa lines, it feels like listening to heavenly music—my ears suddenly brightened.
Don't refuse to sit again and play another piece—for you, I'll compose this 'Pipa Ode'.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence—then sat down, tightened the strings, making them sharper.
The tones were now sadder than before—every guest, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among them wept most? The Jiangzhou governor—his green robe soaked with tears."}

间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid farewell at night,
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays.
Drunk, I cannot find joy—the parting is sad,
As we depart, the river mirrors the moon’s dim glow.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s melody rings;
The host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.
I search for the sound, whispering to ask who plays,
But the pipa falls silent, hesitant to speak.
I move my boat near, inviting the player to meet,
Add wine, turn back the lamp, relight the feast.
A thousand calls bring her forth at last,
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face.
She turns the axis, plucks the strings three or four times—
No tune yet, but emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
Like lamenting a lifetime unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, she plays on with steady fingers,
Speaking through music every sorrow deep within.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, stroking, then plucking;
First playing 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Sixth Yáo.'
The heavy strings roar like sudden rain,
The light ones whisper like private talk.
Crashing, chattering, interwoven sounds—
Like pearls large and small pattering on jade.
Between them, a warbler's song glides through flowers,
A spring stream choked beneath ice, hard to pass.
Cold springs grow sluggish, strings freeze in silence;
Silence swells, then breaks, as if all sound had ceased.
Another hidden sorrow, silent hatred stirs—
In that stillness, meaning surpasses voice.
Then, a silver jar bursts, splashing liquid forth;
A cavalry charge erupts—sword and spear cry out.
At the piece’s close, the pick strikes center, drawn across—
Four strings ring once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall silent, no word spoken,
Only the moon white over the river’s heart.
She pauses, sighs, slips the pick into the string,
Straightens her clothes, lifts her face with solemn grace.
She says: 'I was born in the capital city,
My home lay beneath the Frog Turtle Terrace.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first
Among the Imperial Music Bureau’s finest.
After a performance, even the master teacher admired me;
After makeup, every beauty envied me.
Young men from noble families vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me endless crimson silks.
Silver hairpins shattered with rhythm’s beat;
Red silk gowns stained by wine spilled on their folds.
Happy laughter year after year, with spring and autumn winds passing by.
Now my brother’s gone to war, my aunt has passed away;
Days fade, mornings pass—my beauty fades too.
Front gate grows cold, few horses, fewer riders;
Old now, I married a merchant man.
Merchants care more for profit than for parting;
Last month he left for Fu Liang to buy tea.
He’s gone, and I remain here in the riverside mooring,
Moonlight circling my empty boat, the river cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Awake crying, tears streaking red through paint.
Hearing this pipa, I sigh deeply;
Heard again, my soul trembles with fresh grief.
We are both castaways in the world’s vast exile;
Meeting need not mean we’ve known before!
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled, sick, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, no music heard;
All year long, no sound of strings or bamboo.
My home near Pien River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear day and night among these? 
Cuckoos weep blood, apes mourn in the mountains.
In spring, I pour wine on flower-filled mornings;
In autumn, under moonlit nights, I drink alone.
Is there no mountain song, no rustic flute?
But their crude cries make ears ache to listen.
Tonight hearing your pipa’s words so clear,
It feels like hearing celestial music—ears brighten for a time.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more piece;
For you, I’ll compose this poem titled 'Pipa Song.'
Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
Then sits down, tightens the strings—now they grow swift and keen.
Her music now is sadder than before;
All present weep again, as though hearts were torn.
Who among them sheds the most tears?
The Jiangzhou governor’s blue robe is soaked through with wet."}

Suddenly, from the water’s surface, a pipa’s voice arises—my host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure.
I seek its source, whispering softly: 'Who is playing?' The pipa pauses, then hesitates to speak.
I move the boat closer, urge the player to appear; pour more wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast once more.
After countless calls, she finally emerges, still holding her pipa half-concealed by her face.
She turns the axis, plucks the strings—just a few notes, already stirring emotion.
Each string, low and suppressed, each note a sigh, as if recounting a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, fingers glide steadily across the strings—her heart laid bare in every tone.
Gently smoothing, slowly pressing, touching, picking—she begins with 'The Feathered Robe,' then shifts to 'Sixia.'
The bass strings thunder like sudden rain; the treble whispers like private talk.
