Maple leaves and reeds with autumn's chill.

The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in our drunkenness, we must part—
Parting in a misty haze, where moonlight pools on the river.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s melody floats,
The host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.

Following the sound, I ask in silence—who plays?
The pipa stops, the player hesitates to speak.

I urge the boat near, invite her to appear—
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

Hundred calls, thousand invitations, she appears at last,
Still shielding half her face with the pipa.

She turns the axis, plucks the strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune forms, emotion already speaks.

Each note suppressed, each tone full of sorrow,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing low, she plays with steady fingers—
All her heart’s troubles sung without words.

Gently stroking, slowly pressing, lifting, then picking—
First "Feather Dress," then "Sixth Yāo."

The thick string roars like rainstorm’s sudden rage,
The thin string whispers like lovers’ secret talk.

A jumble of loud and soft, swift and slow—
Like pearls tumbling deep into jade dishes.

Now, a lark’s voice glides through blossoms, smooth and light,
Then, a hidden spring struggles beneath frozen ice.

The icy stream chokes, the strings freeze in silence—
A pause, no sound, but deeper feelings rise.

Silence louder than sound: a hidden grief, a secret wrath.

Then—like a silver jar shattering, water bursts forth,
Or cavalry charges, swords and spears clash in thunder.

At song’s end, the pick slashes across the heart of the string—
Four strings cry out once, like silk ripped apart.

East and west boats fall silent, breathless,
Only the moon above the river’s heart shines white.

After a long pause, she rests her pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

She says: "Born in the capital city, my home was by Hámá Líng.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Troupe.

After one piece, even the great teachers bowed in awe;
Each beauty made me their envy, each day adorned.

Fifth-Generation youths vied for gifts,
One song earned countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered with the beat,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with mud.

Year after year, laughter and joy pass as if nothing—
Autumn moons and spring breezes drift by unnoticed.

My brother joined the army, my aunt passed away;
Days fade, nights pass—my beauty dims.

Door now quiet, few riders come and go;
Old, I married a merchant, sold my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not parting—
Last month, he went to Fúliáng to buy tea.

He left, and I stay behind, guarding an empty boat,
Moon circles the hull, river cold, night deep.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days—
Waking, I weep, tears streaking through rouge.

Hearing this pipa, I sigh—then hear these words again,
And sigh more deeply still.

Why should we know each other to feel such kinship?

All year long, no strings nor bamboo flute to hear.

Maple leaves and reeds with autumn's chill.

The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in our drunkenness, we must part—
Parting in a misty haze, where moonlight pools on the river.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s melody floats,
The host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.

Following the sound, I ask in silence—who plays?
The pipa stops, the player hesitates to speak.

I urge the boat near, invite her to appear—
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.

Hundred calls, thousand invitations, she appears at last,
Still shielding half her face with the pipa.

She turns the axis, plucks the strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune forms, emotion already speaks.

Each note suppressed, each tone full of sorrow,
As if revealing lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing low, she plays with steady fingers—
All her heart’s troubles sung without words.

Gently stroking, slowly pressing, lifting, then picking—
First "Feather Dress," then "Sixth Yāo."

The thick string roars like rainstorm’s sudden rage,
The thin string whispers like lovers’ secret talk.

A jumble of loud and soft, swift and slow—
Like pearls tumbling deep into jade dishes.

Now, a lark’s voice glides through blossoms, smooth and light,
Then, a hidden spring struggles beneath frozen ice.

The icy stream chokes, the strings freeze in silence—
A pause, no sound, but deeper feelings rise.

Silence louder than sound: a hidden grief, a secret wrath.

Then—like a silver jar shattering, water bursts forth,
Or cavalry charges, swords and spears clash in thunder.

At song’s end, the pick slashes across the heart of the string—
Four strings cry out once, like silk ripped apart.

East and west boats fall silent, breathless,
Only the moon above the river’s heart shines white.

After a long pause, she rests her pick into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, composes her solemn face.

She says: "Born in the capital city, my home was by Hámá Líng.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Troupe.

After one piece, even the great teachers bowed in awe;
Each beauty made me their envy, each day adorned.

Fifth-Generation youths vied for gifts,
One song earned countless red silks.

Gold hairpins shattered with the beat,
Crimson skirts soaked in wine, stained with mud.

Year after year, laughter and joy pass as if nothing—
Autumn moons and spring breezes drift by unnoticed.

My brother joined the army, my aunt passed away;
Days fade, nights pass—my beauty dims.

Door now quiet, few riders come and go;
Old, I married a merchant, sold my youth.

Merchants care only for profit, not parting—
Last month, he went to Fúliáng to buy tea.

He left, and I stay behind, guarding an empty boat,
Moon circles the hull, river cold, night deep.

Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days—
Waking, I weep, tears streaking through rouge.

Hearing this pipa, I sigh—then hear these words again,
And sigh more deeply still.

We both are wanderers, cast down far from home—
Why should we know each other to feel such kinship?

I left the capital last year, exiled, ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, barren of music—
All year long, no strings nor bamboo flute to hear.

Near Pénjiāng, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my dwelling.

What sounds greet us morning and night?
Crows weeping blood, apes wailing mournfully.

In spring, flowers bloom at dawn; in autumn, moonlit nights—
Often, I pour wine, alone, drinking to myself.

But they’re harsh, grating—hard to bear.

Then sits again, tightens the strings, plays faster.

Her music now, so sorrowful, no longer as before—
All in the audience weep anew.

The Jiangzhou Magistrate’s green robe is wet with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the moonlit bank of Xunyang River, I bid farewell to guests at night, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn's chill.
My host dismounted, my guest remained on board; raising a cup to drink, yet no music played through the strings.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful as we parted, the river reflecting moonlight in its vast, hazy glow.
Suddenly, from the water's surface, came the sound of a pipa—my host forgot to return, my guest halted his departure.
I sought the source in silence, asking softly who was playing; the pipa paused, the player hesitated before speaking.
We moved our boat near, inviting her to come see us, poured more wine, turned up the lamps, reopened the feast.
After many calls, she emerged, still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the peg, plucked the strings three or four times—before a tune began, emotion already filled the air.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing, as if recounting a lifetime unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, she played on steadily, pouring out endless sorrows from her heart.
Gently stroking, slowly rubbing, flicking, then picking again—first 'Feather Dress', then 'Sixth Yao'.
The bass strings roared like sudden rain, the treble whispered like private words.
Cacophonous, mingling notes—like pearls dropping on jade plates.
Like a bird gliding through blooming flowers, smooth and clear; like a spring choked beneath ice, struggling and faint.
The icy spring grows cold, the strings freeze in pause—silence follows, brief but deep.
A hidden sorrow, latent hatred—now, silence speaks louder than sound.
As a silver jar shatters, water bursts forth; like cavalry charging, swords clashing.
At the end, the pick strikes the heart of the string—four strings snap with a sound like tearing silk.
East and west ships fell silent; only the moon over the river's heart, white and bright.
After a pause, she laid down her pick, inserted it into the strings, adjusted her clothes, composed herself.
She said: 'Born in the capital city, lived beneath the Crab-Valley Bridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Music Academy.
After each performance, even the master musicians would bow in awe; after every makeup, the courtesans envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts—each song earned me countless silken robes.
Gold hairpins shattered from beat, crimson gowns stained with wine spilled on the floor.
Happy days, year after year, spent carelessly in spring blossoms and autumn moons.
But now my brother left for war, my aunt passed away; day by day, my beauty faded.
Front gate grew desolate, fewer riders, fewer guests—at last, I married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, care less for parting—last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now I remain alone at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat, under a moon that encircles me, cold as the river.
Deep into the night, I dreamt of my youth—awoke weeping, tears streaking my rouge-red face.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed; hearing her story, I sighed again.
We are both castaways of the world’s edge—why need we have met before to feel this kinship?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled and ill, in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music; year-long, no string or bamboo sounds reach me.
Near Pienjiang, the land lies low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my home.
What do I hear from dawn till dusk? Cuckoo birds bleeding their hearts, apes wailing mournfully.
In springtime mornings, autumn nights, I often pour wine and drink alone.
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? But they are harsh, grating—hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa talk, I feel as if listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to play another piece for me—I will compose a poem in your honor.
Moved deeply by my words, she stood still, then sat down, quickened the strings—now the music turned urgent.
The sorrowful tone no longer matched the earlier sound—everyone in the audience covered their eyes in tears.
Who cried the most among them all? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his green robe soaked with tears."}

I dismount, my guest remains aboard the boat; we raise our wine cups but no music plays.
Drunk yet unable to rejoice, as sorrow stains our parting—beneath a moon drowned in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, a sound of lute emerges from the water: the host forgets to return, the guest no longer departs.
We search for its source, whispering in silence—'Who plays?' The lute falls silent, the player hesitates to speak.
We move our boat nearer, urge her to appear; pour more wine, turn up the lamps, relight the feast.
After many calls, she finally appears—still clutching her lute half-concealed by her face.
She turns the axis, plucks the strings twice or thrice—before a single note, emotion already stirs.
Each string echoes with restraint; each tone carries deep thought—like a life unfulfilled, speaking through pain.
Bowing her head, fingers flow one after another—her heart spills out every secret burden.
A light touch, slow slide, then stroke and flick—first 'Rainbow Skies,' then 'Sixth Elegance.'
The thick string booms like sudden rain; the thin one whispers as though secrets shared in hush.
A jumble of loud and soft, like pearls tumbling on jade—each drop distinct.
Like a bird gliding through flowers, smooth and clear; like a stream beneath ice, choked and strained.
Cold springs halt, strings freeze in silence—then pause, breath held.
Yet deeper grief now rises in the quiet—this silence speaks louder than any sound.
A silver pitcher cracks open—water spurts forth; iron cavalry charges, blades howl.
When final strokes strike center, the four strings snap with a sound like tearing silk.
All boats grow still—no voice—only the moon above the river's heart, pale and white.
He pauses, lowers his pick into the strings, adjusts his clothes, composes his face.
'I am a woman born in the capital city, lived near Hama Ling.
At thirteen, I mastered the lute—my name ranked first among the Imperial Academy's best.
After a performance, even the masters were silenced by my skill;
With beauty made, I was envied by all the courtesans of the era.
Five-generations' sons vied to gift me robes; a single song earned countless silks.
My jeweled hairpin shattered on rhythm's beat; my crimson skirts splashed with wine.
Year after year, laughter rose—spring breezes, autumn moons passed carelessly.
My brother left for war; my aunt passed away. Time slipped—my beauty dimmed.
Front gate grew cold, horses and riders rare—now old, I wed a merchant.
Merchants value profit, scorn departure—last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He’s gone—he leaves me here alone on the riverbank, guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight, the river chills with cold.
Late at night, I dream of youth—awake in tears, my kohl-drenched cheeks stained red.
I hear her lute—and sigh deeply; hear her story again, and weep anew.
We are both castaways on the same broken earth—why should we have met before?
Last year, I left the imperial capital—exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.
This place is remote, without music—whole years pass without string or bamboo.
Near Panyang River, land low and damp, bitter reeds and yellow bamboo sprout around the house.
What sounds fill day and night? Only cuckoos bleeding their cries, apes mournfully weeping.
In spring mornings, under flowered skies, or autumn nights beneath moonlit waves—I often take wine and drink alone.
Are there no folk songs or rustic flutes? Yes—but their rough, grating tones are hard to bear.
But tonight, your lute's music—like heavenly tunes—cleanses my ears, just for a moment.
Do not refuse—sit again and play one more piece—for you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Lute.'

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, at night, I see a guest off, 
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill. 
I dismount; my guest stays on the boat. 
We raise our wine to drink—but no music plays. 

Drunk, we cannot cheer; sad, we part. 
As we bid farewell, the river mirrors a hazy moon. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound— 
I forget to return; my guest halts his departure. 

Following the sound, I softly ask who plays. 
The pipa ceases; hesitating, she would speak. 
I move my boat near, invite her forth— 
Add wine, turn the lamp, reopen the feast. 

Countless calls bring her out at last, 
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face. 

She turns the axis, plucks a few strings— 
Even before the tune begins, emotion is felt. 

Each string suppressed, each note full of longing— 
As if narrating a life unfulfilled. 

Bowing low, she plays with steady fingers, 
Expressing all that lies deep within her heart. 

Lightly stroking, slowly pressing, brushing, lifting— 
First "Feather Dress," then "Sixth Dancer." 

The deep strings thunder like sudden rain, 
The thin strings whisper like private talk. 

Thrumming, mingling, overlapping— 
Great pearls, small pearls, falling on jade. 

Like a bird gliding through blossoms, its song clear, 
Or a spring under ice, struggling, choked, hard to flow. 

Cold springs stall, strings freeze, silence holds— 
The pause itself speaks louder than sound. 

Then—like a silver jar shattering, water bursts out, 
And cavalry charges, blades and spears clash. 

When the final stroke slashes through the heart, 
Four strings cry out as if torn silk. 

East and west ships stand silent— 
Only the autumn moon shines white on the river's heart. 

She pauses, pensively rests her pick; 
Straightens her clothes, composes her face. 

She says: "Born in the capital city, 
My home stood beneath the Toad Hill. 

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art, 
Ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau. 

After each performance, even masters were silenced— 
After each beauty, every jade-faced woman envied me. 

Young men from five noble districts vied to give gifts— 
One song earned me countless red silks. 

Tinsel hairpins shattered on the beat, 
Crimson gowns stained by wine spills. 

Year after year, laughter and joy, 
Spring moons, autumn nights—passed carelessly. 

Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died; 
Days fade, years pass—my beauty dims. 

Door now cold, few riders come— 
Old, I wed a merchant. 

Merchants value profit, scorn parting— 
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea. 

He left, leaving me guarding an empty boat, 
Round the vessel, moonlight glows cold, the river chills. 

Deep in night, I dream of youth again— 
Waking, I weep, tears staining my rouge-laced face. 

Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply— 
Now hearing these words, I groan once more. 

We are both lost souls, far from home— 
Why must we have met before to know each other? 

I left the imperial capital last year— 
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang town. 

Xunyang lies remote, without music— 
All year long, no silk or bamboo sounds. 

Near Pенjiang, the land low and damp, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house. 

What do I hear day and night? 
Cuckoos bleeding, apes wailing mournfully. 

On spring mornings, autumn nights, 
I often pour wine and drink alone. 

Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? 
But their rough cries are unbearable to hear. 

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech, 
It feels like heavenly music—ears suddenly clear. 

Do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece— 
I’ll compose for you this "Pipa Song." 

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence, 
Then sits, tightens the strings—now they grow urgent. 

The sorrowful tones differ from before— 
Every seat, re-listening, weeps anew. 

Who weeps the most among them all? 
The Jiangzhou magistrate—his blue robe soaked with tears."}

My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays to grace the moment.
Drunk, yet unable to find joy, we part in sorrow—beneath a vast, moon-drenched river shrouded in haze.
Suddenly, a lute's sound floats upon the water; my host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure.
I search its source, whispering softly: 'Who is playing?' The music ceases, then hesitates as if about to speak.
I move my boat near, urging her to come forth; add wine, relight the lamp, set the feast again.
After countless calls, she finally appears, still holding her lute half-concealed by her face.
She turns the axis, plucks the strings—three or two notes already brim with emotion.
Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing, as if recounting a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, fingers glide steadily across the strings—her heart laid bare in every movement.
Gently smoothing, slowly pressing, touching, picking—she first plays *Nirvana* then *Sixth Lilt*.
The deep strings thunder like urgent rain; the light strings whisper like secret talks.
A mingled rhythm, chaotic yet clear—a cascade of pearls falling onto jade plates.
Now, a bird sings smoothly through the blossoms; now, a spring gurgles beneath frozen ice—strained, choked, struggling to flow.
Cold water chokes the strings, silence grips them—then all sound pauses abruptly.
Another kind of hidden sorrow stirs inside—this silence speaks more than any sound could say.
Like a silver pitcher shattering, liquid bursts forth; like cavalry charging, swords clash and steel roars.
At last, she ends the piece with a sharp strike across the center—four strings snap into a single cry like tearing silk.
East and west, ships are hushed—no voice stirs, only the moon above the river's heart, pure and white.
She pauses, pensively lowers the pick into the string, adjusts her clothes, composes her face.
She begins: 'I was born in the capital city, lived below the Crab-Lake Lane.
At thirteen, I had mastered the lute—my name ranked first among the imperial troupe.
After each song, even the master musicians had to bow to me; after each makeup, the famed Autumn Lady would envy me.
Five noble youths competed endlessly to present me with silken robes—each song earned me countless lengths.
Silver hairpins shattered from rhythmic beat; crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy repeated year after year, while moon and spring passed carelessly by.
My brother left for war, my aunt passed away—days and nights passed, my beauty faded.
Once bustling, now silent, no more horses at the gate; old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit over parting—last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He’s gone, leaving me alone on this empty boat by the river’s mouth—moonlight circling, cold water reflecting.
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youth—awoke crying, tears streaming down my painted face.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice arose; my host forgot to return, my guest stood still, unwilling to depart.

She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times—before a tune began, emotion already flowed.

Bowing her head, she played on steadily, pouring out infinite sorrows from her heart.
Gently stroking, slowly pressing, flicking and lifting: first 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Sixth Arab'.
The thick strings roared like sudden rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk.

At the final stroke, the pick draws across the heart of the string—four strings snap with a sound like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, not a word spoken—only the river center lit by the autumn moon, white and cold.

After each performance, even master musicians had to bow to me; after every makeup, the beauty Qiumei envied me.
Young men from Wuling vied to shower me with silken robes—I lost count of how many I received.
My jeweled hairpin broke from beating time, my crimson sash stained with wine from laughter.
Year after year, joy followed joy, spring winds, autumn moons passed carelessly.
But now my brother went to war, my aunt died; day after day, my looks faded away.
Front gate grew cold, horsemen rare—old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit more than parting; last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I stayed alone at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat; under the moon, the river chills, endless and cold.
Late at night, I dreamt of youth again—awoke crying, tears staining my rouge-laden cheeks.
I heard the pipa, sighed deeply; hearing her words, I sighed once more.
We are both wanderers cast on distant shores—why must we have met before to feel such kinship?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick, in Xunyang City.

Tonight, hearing your pipa, it feels like listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly brightened.
Do not refuse to play one more piece—let me compose for you this poem: 'Pipa Xing'.
Moved by my words, she stood still long, then sat, tightened the strings, which grew sharper.

Lay beneath the Frog-Mound Lane.

At thirteen, I mastered the lute,
Named first among the Imperial Music Bureau.

After each performance, even masters were amazed;
After every makeup, beauties envied me.

Young nobles vied to toss silken ribbons,
One song, a hundred scarves scattered through the air.

Silver hairpins shattered to rhythm,
Crimson silks stained by wine, torn to rags.

Year after year of laughter, one season fading into another,
Spring breezes, autumn moons passed carelessly.

My brother left for war, my aunt passed away;
Dawn after dusk, my beauty fades away.

Door now cold, few riders, few visitors—
Old, I married a merchant.

Merchants care only for profit, not for parting;
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

Now he’s gone, leaving me alone on this empty boat,
Moonlight circles, rivers grow cold.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s past,
Weeping, my painted tears flow red and long.

Hearing the lute, I sighed, hearing her story too,
And sighed again, deeply, sadly.

Why need we have met before to feel so close?

Exiled, ill, lying in Xunyang City.

Whole years pass without the sound of strings or bamboo.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.  
I dismount; my guest remains on board.  
Raising wine, I wish to drink—but no music plays.  

Unhappy in drunkenness, sad as we part,  
At parting, the vast river reflects a moon lost in haze.  
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arises—  
My host forgets to return; my guest stays unmoved.  

Following the sound, I softly ask: "Who plays?"  
The pipa pauses; words hesitatingly start.  
I move my boat near, invite her to appear,  
Add wine, turn up lamps, renew our feast again.  

After countless calls, she finally appears—  
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face.  

She turns the axis, plucks the strings twice or thrice—  
Before any tune begins, emotion is there.  

Each string suppressed, each note full of longing—  
As if telling of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.  

Bowing low, fingers moving gently and slow,  
She plays, pouring out infinite sorrow in her heart.  

Lightly plucking, slowly pressing, brushing, then lifting—  
First playing 'Fei Cai', then 'Liu Yao' in its style.  

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,  
The thin ones whisper like private talk.  

Cacophony of notes, overlapping, mixed—  
Like large pearls and small ones falling on jade plates.  

Smooth as a bird’s voice slipping through flowers,  
Low and choked, like a spring beneath frozen ice.  

Cold springs grow tight, strings freeze in silence—  
Silence breaks, as if all sound has vanished.  

Another deep sorrow, hidden hatred emerges—  
In this silence, more than sound can say.  

A silver bottle cracks open; liquid bursts forth—  
A cavalry charge, swords and spears clash loud.  

When the final stroke sweeps across the heart of the instrument,  
Four strings ring once, like silk torn apart.  

East and west ships fall silent, not a word spoken—  
Only the autumn moon shines white upon the river's core.  

Pensive, she rests the pick back in the strings,  
Straightens her robes, composes her countenance.  

She says: "I was born in the capital city,  
My home lies beneath the Loach Horse Ridge.  

At thirteen I mastered the pipa,  
Ranked first among the Imperial Academy’s troupe.  

After each song, even the master praised me—  
After each makeup, the beauty Qiuniang envied me.  

Young men from the five noble districts vied to offer gifts—  
One song earned endless silken robes.  

Silver hairpins shattered by rhythm,  
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.  

Year after year, laughter and joy,  
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly.  

My brother joined the army; my aunt passed away—  
Days fade, mornings pass, my beauty fades.  

Now the gate grows cold, few horses come or go—  
Old age forced me into marriage with a merchant.  

Merchants value profit, scorn parting—  
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  

Left behind, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth—  
Moonlight circles the ship, the river chills with cold.  

Midnight, suddenly I dream of youth—  
Crying in sleep, tears streak red across my painted face.  

Hearing her pipa, I sighed already—  
But hearing these words, I sigh again, deeply.  

We are both castaways on life’s distant shores—  
Why need we have met before to understand?  

I left the imperial capital last year—  
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang town.  

Xunyang lies remote, without music—  
All year long, no sound of strings or bamboo.  

Near Pien River, land damp and low—  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.  

What sounds do I hear day and night there?  
Cuckoos bleeding crimson, apes wailing in grief.  

In spring, at dawn; in autumn, under moonlight—  
Often I pour wine alone, to no one else.  

Is there no rustic folk-song, no village flute?  
But their harsh, grating tones are hard to bear.  

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice—  
It’s like listening to celestial music, ears wide awake.  

Do not refuse—sit again and play one more piece—  
I’ll rewrite it for you, as 'The Pipa Song'.  

Moved by my words, she stands speechless long—  
Then sits down, tightens the strings, playing faster.  

The music now mournful, no longer as before—  
All seated hear it again, all cover their eyes in tears.  

Who in this gathering weeps most heavily?  
The Governor of Jiangzhou, his green robe soaked with tears."}

I sought the voice stealthily, asking who played; the pipa ceased, the player hesitated before speaking.

A silver bottle shattered, water gushed forth; then iron cavalry charged, blades and spears clashing.

All boats fell silent; only the river’s heart glowed with autumn moonlight white.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver with cold.
I dismount; my guest remains on board.
We raise our cups to drink, but no music plays.

Though drunk, we feel no joy, only sorrow as we part—
In twilight’s haze, the river holds the moon.
Suddenly, a lute's voice floats from the water:
I forget to return, my guest forgets to leave.

Following the sound, I softly ask who plays—
The lute ceases; silence, then hesitant speech.
I move my boat near, invite her to appear—
Add wine, turn up the lamp, renew the feast.

She is summoned a thousand times, yet still delays—
Still half-concealed, her lute hides her face.

She turns the peg, plucks the strings twice or thrice—
Before a tune begins, emotion stirs.

Each string mourns, each note echoes longing—
As if recounting a life unfulfilled.

Bowing low, fingers glide, one after another—
Her playing speaks all she cannot say.

Gently stroking, slowly plucking, brushing, lifting—
First *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*—a dance of song.

The deep strings crash like sudden rain,
The thin ones whisper like private talk.

Cacophony of tones, sharp and soft interwoven—
Like pearls large and small falling on jade.

Like a bird skimming through blossoms, clear and smooth—
Like a stream beneath ice, choked and strained.

The icy spring grows cold, strings freeze, fall silent—
A pause, then quiet so deep it feels louder than sound.

Then, a silver jar bursts—water gushes forth—
A cavalry charge, swords and spears clash.

At last, the final stroke cuts the heart of the string—
Four chords ring out, like silk torn apart.

East and west, boats lie still—no word spoken—
Only the moon above the river’s heart, white and cold.

After a while, she lowers her pick, slides it back into the strings—
Straightens her robes, composes herself, prepares to speak.

"I was born in the capital city, my home beneath the Frog Ridge.
At thirteen, I had mastered the lute—ranked first in the Imperial Academy.
After each performance, even the masters were silenced by awe.
My beauty drew envy from every lady of renown.

Young nobles vied to shower me with gifts—
One song earned me dozens of crimson silks.

Gold-tipped combs shattered on rhythm sticks,
Red silk skirts stained with wine from wild nights.

Year after year, laughter, joy, carefree days—
Spring mornings, autumn moonlit nights, all passed without notice.

But then my brother left for war, my aunt passed away—
Days fade, years pass, my beauty fades.

The gate grew quiet, no more horses, no more riders—
Old, I married a merchant, took his name.

Merchants care only for gain, not for farewells—
Last month, he traveled to Fuliang to buy tea.

Now, he’s gone—on the river’s mouth, I guard an empty boat—
The moon circles us, the river is cold.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth—
Waking, I cry, my tears streaking red across my face.

Hearing this lute’s tale, I sigh deeply—
And now, hearing her words again, I sigh once more.

We’re both castaways on distant shores—
Why must we have known each other to feel this kinship?

I left the imperial capital last year—
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.

Xunyang lies far from fame, barren of music—
All year long, no strings nor bamboo flute to hear.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.

Only cuckoos bleeding, apes wailing.

It’s like hearing heavenly music, ears suddenly brightened.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. 
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
We raise our wine cups, yet no music plays. 
Though drunk, we cannot celebrate—our sorrow deepens as we part, 
Amidst the misty river, moonlight floods the water. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's melody rings out, 
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure. 
Following the sound, I softly inquire who plays, 
The pipa stops—the player hesitates before replying. 
I move my boat near, inviting her to meet, 
Pour more wine, turn up the lamp, renew our feast. 
After many calls, she finally appears, 
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face. 
She turns the tuning peg, plucks the strings with three or two notes— 
Before a tune is formed, emotion already flows. 
Each string mourns, each note carries longing— 
It seems to tell of a life unfulfilled. 
Bowing her head, fingers move steadily, 
Playing all that lies deep in her heart. 
Gently brushing, slowly plucking, flicking, then picking again— 
First playing 'Feather Dress,' then 'Liu Yao.' 
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain, 
The thin strings whisper like private talk. 
Thunderous and soft, intertwining sounds— 
Like pearls large and small falling on jade. 
Clear and smooth, like a bird’s voice slipping through blossoms, 
Low and stifled, like spring water beneath ice, struggling to flow. 
Cold springs clog the strings, silence fills the air, 
Then stillness settles—momentary pause in music. 
Another kind of sorrow, silent hate arises— 
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sound. 
A silver bottle bursts, water gushes forth, 
Steel cavalry charges, swords and spears clash. 
When the final stroke cuts across the string’s heart, 
Four strings snap once—like silk torn apart. 
East and west ships lie silent, motionless; 
Only the autumn moon glows white upon the river’s heart. 
After a pause, he sets down the pick, inserts it into the strings, 
Adjusts his clothes, composes his face. 
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, 
My home stood beneath the Crab Alley. 
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau. 
After every performance, even masters bowed to my skill; 
After every makeup, beauties envied me. 
Young noblemen vied to lavish gifts— 
One song earned countless lengths of crimson silk. 
Silver hairpins shattered from beat-rhythm strikes, 
Crimson gowns stained with wine from joyful spills. 
Laughing and dancing year after year, 
Autumn moons, spring breezes passed carelessly by. 
My brother went off to war, my aunt passed away; 
Dawn fades, dusk comes—my beauty faded. 
Our gate now empty, few riders passing by; 
Old and worn, I married a merchant. 
Merchants value profit more than parting; 
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea. 
He departs, leaving me alone on the river’s mouth, 
Moonlight circles my boat, cold river chills my soul. 
Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s days past— 
Waking to weep, tears streak red down my painted cheeks. 
Hearing her pipa, I sigh with pity; 
Now hearing her tale, I sigh again and again. 
We are both wanderers in a far-off land, 
Why must we have known each other before to feel such kinship? 
I left the imperial capital last year, 
Exiled, ill, living in Xunyang City. 
Xunyang’s remote, no music to be heard; 
All year long, not a single note of string or bamboo. 
Near Pien River, the ground is damp and low— 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door. 
What do I hear day and night within this place? 
Cuckoos bleeding red, apes mourning in despair. 
On spring mornings, under blooming flowers, 
Or autumn nights with bright moonlit skies, 
I often pour wine and drink alone. 
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? 
But their crude sounds are hard to bear. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
It feels like celestial music—my ears suddenly clear. 
Do not refuse to play another piece— 
For you, I will compose this 'Pipa Song.' 
Moved by my words, she stands in silence, then sits back, 
Tightens the strings—their tone grows sharper, harsher. 
The music now is less like before— 
All seated weep, moved anew by its grief. 
Who sheds the most tears among us all? 
The Jiangzhou magistrate’s green robe soaks wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I bid farewell to a guest, 
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. 
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
I raise a cup to drink, yet no music fills the air. 
Drunk but unable to find joy, sorrow marks our parting— 
As we depart, the river mirrors the moon, vast and dim. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa melody sounds, 
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure. 
Following the sound, I softly ask who plays— 
The pipa stops, as if hesitating before speech. 
I move my boat near, inviting her to meet me, 
Add wine, turn up the lamp, renew our feast. 
After many calls, she comes at last, 
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face. 
She turns the axle, plucks the strings with three or four notes— 
Before a tune begins, emotion already lingers. 
Each string mourns, each note speaks of longing, 
Like one recounting a life unfulfilled. 
Bowing her head, fingers move steadily, 
Conveying all the unspoken sorrows within. 
Gently pressing, slowly picking, brushing, then plucking— 
First playing 'Feather Dress,' then 'Liu Yao.' 
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain, 
The thin ones whisper like private talk. 
Thunderous and soft, interwoven, 
Like pearls large and small falling on jade. 
Clear and smooth, like a bird singing beneath blossoms, 
Muffled and choked, like water flowing under ice. 
Cold spring water chokes, strings grow still, 
Silence deepens, as if sound has ceased. 
Yet more hidden grief, deeper resentment emerge— 
At this moment, silence outshines sound. 
A silver bottle cracks open, water bursts forth; 
A cavalry charge, swords and spears clash. 
At the end, the pick strikes center, a single crack— 
Four strings shatter like torn silk. 
East and west boats fall silent, 
Only the autumn moon shines white over the river's heart. 
He pauses, rests the pick, inserts it into the strings, 
Adjusts clothes, composes countenance. 
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, 
My home lies below the Frog Mound. 
At thirteen I mastered the pipa, 
Ranked first among the palace troupe. 
After every performance, even the master could not deny me; 
After every makeup, the beauty Qiu sang would envy me. 
Young nobles vied for gifts, 
One song earned me countless red silks. 
Gold hairpins shattered with rhythm, 
Crimson gowns stained by wine spilled in revelry. 
Year after year, laughter and joy pass— 
Autumn moons and spring breezes drift unheeded. 
My brother left for war, my aunt passed away; 
Days fade, nights vanish, and my beauty fades. 
Front gate grows cold, horses and riders scarce; 
Old now, I wed a merchant. 
Merchants care only for profit, disdain parting— 
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. 
Now he goes and returns, leaving me alone by the river mouth, 
Moonlight circles the empty boat, the river chills. 
Deep in the night I dream of youthful days— 
Dreaming, I weep, tears staining my painted face. 
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply; 
Hearing her story, I sigh again. 
We are both wanderers far from home, 
Why must we have met before to feel such kinship? 
I left the imperial capital last year; 
Exiled, I lie ill in Xunyang. 
Xunyang is remote, untouched by music; 
All year long, no lute nor bamboo flute is heard. 
Near Pien River, the land low and damp, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house. 
What do I hear day and night here? 
Cuckoos cry blood-red, monkeys wail in sorrow. 
On spring mornings, flower-filled days, or autumn nights beneath the moon, 
I often pour wine alone, drinking in solitude. 
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? 
But their grating tones are hard to bear. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa words, 
It feels like listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly brightened. 
Please don't refuse to sit once more and play another piece— 
For you, I will compose this 'Pipa Song.' 
Moved by my words, she stands still long, 
Then sits back, tightens the strings—now the music grows urgent. 
This new sound, so mournful, no longer matches the old— 
All seated listeners cover their faces and weep. 
Who sheds the most tears in this hall? 
Jiangzhou’s governor, his green robe soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I bid farewell to a guest, maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn's chill.
I dismount, my guest remains on board; raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful as we part, the moon sinks into the misty river under a vast, dim sky.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa rises—my host forgets to return, my guest stays put.
Following the sound, I whisper, asking who is playing? The pipa falls silent, hesitant to speak.
I move my boat near, invite her forth—add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.
She comes at last, after many calls, still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.
She turns the axis, plucks a few strings—before the tune begins, emotion stirs.
Each note veils sorrow, each tone carries memory—like words unspoken for a lifetime.
With lowered brows, she plays on, fingers tracing out endless tales from the heart.
Gently pressing, slowly brushing, gliding, lifting—first *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.
The heavy strings roar like sudden rain, the light ones murmur like private talk.
A jumble of soft and sharp notes—pearls large and small drop on jade plates.
Like a bird slipping through blossoms, clear and smooth; like spring water choked beneath ice, faint and strained.
Cold springs choke, the strings freeze, silence breaks—no sound at all for a moment.
Yet deeper grief and hidden resentment grow—this silence speaks more than sound could ever say.
Like a silver bottle shattering, liquid bursting forth; like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears crying out.
At end, the pick strikes the center—four strings snap once, like silk torn apart.
East and west boats fall utterly still, only the autumn moon shining white upon the river's core.
After a pause, she rests the pick, slides it back into the strings, arranges her robe, straightens her face.
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath the Frog Mound area.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa—ranked first among the Imperial Academy’s finest.
After a single performance, even the master musicians would marvel;
My beauty so often stirred envy from the famed Qiumiang.
Young men of five noble clans vied to offer silken robes—each song earned me countless lengths.
Silver hairpins shattered with rhythm; crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter and joy passed, seasons drifting like wind and moonlight.
My brother joined the army; my aunt passed away; days fade, my beauty dims.
Front gate grows cold, horses and riders rare—I married a merchant in old age.
The merchant cares only for profit, longs to be gone—last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me here, guarding an empty boat; moonlight circles the vessel, the river chills with cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth again—awake, tears streak my painted face.
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply; hearing her story, I sigh even more.
We are both castaways far from home—why must we have met before to feel this kinship?
I left the capital last year, exiled, sick in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, no music to be heard—whole years pass without a single string or bamboo flute.
Near Pien River, the land is low and damp—yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around the house.
What do I hear morning and night? Crows bleeding red, apes mourning through the hills.
On spring mornings, flower-filled days, and autumn nights, I often take wine alone, pouring it out.
Are there no mountain ballads or village flutes? They’re harsh, grating—hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak, it sounds like celestial music—my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece—for you I will compose this poem, *Pipa Xing*.
Moved by my words, she stands motionless for a long time, then sits, tightens the strings—the sounds become urgent.
Now the melody is sharper, less like before—everyone in the circle weeps anew.
Who weeps most here? The Jiangzhou magistrate—his blue robe soaked through."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. 
I dismount to welcome the guest aboard the boat; 
We raise our wine cups, but no music plays. 
Drunk yet unable to enjoy, sorrowful as we part— 
The parting scene is dim, with moonlight soaking the river. 
Suddenly, a lute's sound floats upon the water; 
I forget to return, my guest halts his departure. 
Following the music, I softly ask: 'Who is playing?' 
The lute falls silent—she hesitates, unsure how to speak. 
I move the boat closer, urging her to appear, 
Add wine, turn up the lights, and open the feast anew. 
After many calls, she comes forth at last, 
Still holding the lute half-concealing her face. 
She turns the axis, plucks the strings three or four times— 
Before a tune begins, emotion already fills the air. 
Each note mourns, each tone holds deep memory, 
Like a lifetime’s unfulfilled longing spoken in silence. 
Bending her head, her fingers trace the strings one by one, 
Pouring out endless sorrows from her heart. 
Gently gliding, slow pressing, then sweeping and lifting, 
First playing 'Fei Hua,' then 'Liu Yao' in sequence. 
The thick string roars like a sudden storm of rain, 
The thin string whispers like private, tender speech. 
A jumble of loud and soft, sharp and gentle, 
As if great pearls and small ones fall on jade. 
Smooth and clear, like a bird singing through blossoms; 
Low and strained, like water flowing beneath ice. 
Cold springs choked, strings stiffen and freeze, 
Silence follows, the music cut short. 
Yet another sorrow—silent hate stirs within— 
In that stillness, silence speaks more than sound could. 
Suddenly, a silver jar bursts, waters gush forth, 
Then cavalry charges, swords and spears clang loud. 
At end, the pick strikes center, a sharp slash— 
Four strings snap together, like silk torn apart. 
East and west, boats grow quiet, speechless, 
Only the moon above the river’s heart shines pale white. 
She pauses, ponders, sets the pick back in place, 
Adjusts her clothes, composes herself into solemn grace. 
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, 
My home lies beneath the Frog Crab Slope. 
At thirteen, my lute mastery was complete, 
Numbered among the top ranks of the Imperial Academy. 
After each performance, even master musicians would bow in admiration; 
After makeup, I was envied by all the beauties of the day. 
Young men from the Five Hills vied to give me gifts— 
One song earned me countless red silken robes. 
Gold hairpins shattered from rhythmic beat, 
Crimson skirts stained with wine spilled from joy. 
Laughter filled year after year, while spring wind and autumn moon passed carelessly by. 
But then my brother went off to war, my aunt passed away, 
Days pass, mornings fade, my beauty dims. 
Front gate grows cold, few riders come and go. 
Now grown old, I married a merchant. 
He values profit more than love, having left last month for Fuliang to buy tea. 
Since then, I’ve stayed alone in this boat at the river mouth, 
Moonlight circles it, the river chills with cold. 
Deep in night, I dreamt of youthful days—

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. 
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
We raise our wine cup to drink, but no music plays. 
Though drunk, we cannot celebrate with joy— 
Parting comes, dim and vast, as moonlight soaks the river. 
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa melody drifts through— 
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure. 
I follow the sound, whispering softly: 'Who is playing?' 
The pipa ceases—then hesitates, as if about to speak. 
I move the boat near, invite her to appear, 
Add wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast. 
Countless calls bring her forth at last, 
Still clutching the pipa, half-concealing her face. 
She turns the axle, plucks the strings—three or two notes— 
No tune yet, but emotion already flows. 
Each string low, each note filled with sorrow, 
As if recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams. 
Bowing her head, she picks out the tune with steady fingers, 
Saying all that’s hidden in her heart, without words. 
Gently she strokes, slowly she plucks, then glides and lifts— 
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Sixth Tone.' 
The thick strings roar like sudden rain, 
The thin ones whisper like private talk. 
A jumble of loud and soft, crash and murmur— 
Large pearls and small pearls falling on jade plates. 
Between them, the oriole sings smooth beneath blossoms; 
Then the flow of spring water under ice becomes strained and hard. 
Cold springs grow sluggish, strings freeze and halt— 
Silence hangs, a pause before resuming. 
Another deep grief stirs unseen, 
This silence speaks louder than any sound. 
Like a silver jar splitting open, water gushes forth; 
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clash in thunder. 
At end, her pick strikes the center—the four strings snap once— 
One cry, sharp as silk torn apart. 
East and west ships fall silent, speechless, 
Only the river's heart reflects the white autumn moon. 
She pauses, leans back, slips the pick into the strings, 
Straightens her clothes, composes herself, solemnly serene. 
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, 
Lived beneath the Frog Mound in the lower quarter. 
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, 
Belonged to the first troupe of the Imperial Academy. 
After every piece, even the finest master stood amazed; 
After every makeup, the famed Lady Qiu would envy me. 
Young men from the Five Hills vied for my gifts— 
A single red ribbon, I’d receive countless times. 
Gold hairpins shattered from drumming, 
Crimson robes stained by wine, splashed again and again. 
Year after year, laughter and joy pass— 
Autumn moons, spring breezes, casually spent. 
But when my brother went off to war, my aunt passed away, 
Days and nights pass, my beauty fades. 
The gate grows cold—few riders now come by; 
Old and worn, I wed a merchant. 
Merchants care only for profit, not partings— 
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea. 
He came and went, leaving me alone on the riverbank, 
Moonlight circling my empty boat, cold river water chills. 
Deep in the night, I dream of youth— 
Waking, I weep, my painted tears staining my face. 
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply; 
Now hearing her tale, I sigh again. 
We are both castaways on this distant shore— 
Why must we have known each other before? 
I left the imperial capital last year, 
Exiled here, sick in bed in Xunyang. 
Xunyang lies remote, no music ever heard— 
All year long, never a note of strings or bamboo. 
Near the Pien River, land low and damp— 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo sprout all around. 
What do I hear morning and night among these places? 
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing in grief. 
Spring mornings with flowers, autumn nights with moonlight— 
Often I pour wine alone, seeking solace. 
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes? 
Their sounds are shrill, harsh, unbearable to listen to. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
It feels like listening to divine music—my ears brighten briefly. 
Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece— 
I’ll compose this song for you, called 'The Pipa Song.' 
Moved by my words, she stands still for a long time, 
Then sits down, tightens the strings—now the music grows urgent. 
Her playing is sadder now than before— 
All in the audience weep anew, touched to tears. 
Who in this crowd sheds the most tears? 
The Governor of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked with sorrow."}

My jeweled hairpins shattered to rhythm, crimson gowns stained by wine. Year after year, joy returns, spring and autumn pass carelessly. My brother left for war, my foster mother died. {"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I bid farewell to a guest, 
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill. 
My host dismounts, my guest steps aboard the boat; 
I raise my cup to drink, but no music plays. 
Drunk yet unable to find joy, sorrowful as we part— 
At parting, the river mirrors the moon, vast and dim. 
Suddenly, a lute’s voice rises from the water— 
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure. 
Following the sound, I softly ask: 'Who is playing?' 
The lute falls silent, hesitating before reply. 
I move my boat near, inviting her to meet; 
We add wine, turn up the lamp, reopen the feast. 
After many calls, she appears at last, 
Still holding the lute half-concealing her face. 
She turns the axis, plucks the strings three or four times— 
Before a tune begins, emotion already flows. 
Each string whispers grief, each note carries longing, 
Like one who speaks of lifelong unfulfilled dreams. 
Bowing low, she plays with steady fingers, 
Conveying all the sorrows buried deep within. 
Gently pressing, slowly picking, brushing, then plucking— 
First the 'Feather Dress,' then the 'Sixth Rhythm.' 
The heavy strings roar like a sudden downpour, 
The light ones murmur like lovers' private talk. 
A chaotic mix of crash and whisper— 
As if large pearls and small fall upon jade plates. 
Smooth as a bird flitting through flowered shades, 
Muffled like water under ice, struggling to flow. 
Cold springs stagnate, strings grow still and tight, 
Then silence breaks, a pause that speaks more than sound. 
Suddenly, a silver jug cracks open—water spurts forth; 
A cavalry charge bursts forward, swords clashing, blades baring. 
The final stroke strikes straight through the heart, 
Four strings snap together—a sound like tearing silk. 
East and west boats fall silent, no word spoken— 
Only the river’s heart reflects the white autumn moon. 
He pauses, rests the pick in the strings, adjusts his clothes, 
Straightens his posture, gathers his composure. 
She says: 'I was born in the capital city, 
Lived beneath the Frog Hill, where the alley winds. 
At thirteen, I mastered the lute, 
Ranked first among the palace troupe’s finest. 
After every piece, even masters would bow in awe; 
After every makeup, the beauty Qiuniang would envy me. 
Young noblemen vied to shower me with gifts— 
One song earned red silks, countless in number. 
Tinsel hairpins shattered from rhythmic beating, 
Blood-red skirts stained by wine spilled in revelry. 
Year after year, laughing, dancing— 
Autumn moons and spring breezes pass without care. 
But then my brother left for war, my aunt passed on; 
Days fade, nights pass—my beauty fades too. 
The gate grows cold, few horses stop by; 
Now old, I married a merchant. 
He values profit, treats parting lightly— 
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea. 
Since then, I’ve stayed alone at the river’s mouth, 
Circling my boat, the moon above, the water cold. 
Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s past— 
Dreaming, I weep, my painted tears streaking down my face. 
Hearing this lute, I sigh deeply; hearing her words, 
My heart stirs again, echoing with lament. 
We are both fallen souls, adrift in distant lands— 
Why need we have met before to feel such kinship? 
I left the imperial capital last year, 
Exiled, ill, living in the remote Xunyang. 
Xunyang lies far from the world, no music to hear— 
Whole years pass without a single note of strings or bamboo. 
Our home is near Panyang, damp and low; 
Yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow all around our house. 
What sounds do we hear day and night? 
Cuckoos bleed red, apes mourn in the wind. 
On spring mornings, on autumn evenings, 
Often I pour wine, drinking alone. 
Are there no mountain songs, no rustic flutes? 
They’re harsh, grating—hard to bear. 
Tonight, hearing your lute’s speech, 
It’s as if heavenly music fills my ears, just for a moment. 
Don’t refuse—sit again and play another piece; 
For you, I’ll rewrite the 'Pipa Xing.' 
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence, 
Then sits back, tightens the strings—now the music grows urgent. 
The notes, once gentle, now ache with sorrow— 
All in the hall weep again, moved to tears. 
Who weeps the most here? The Jiangzhou magistrate’s green robe is soaked."}

Cold springs stilled, strings froze—silence momentarily broken. Then deep, hidden griefs arose: this silence spoke louder than sound. Suddenly, a silver bottle shatters, spilling liquid; cavalry charges forth, swords clanging. Each string murmurs sorrow, each note carries memory—like lamenting a life unfulfilled. 
Bowing low, she plays with gentle touch, as if revealing all her heart’s grief. 
Softly caressing, slowly brushing, pressing, then lifting—first the 'Feather Dress,' then 'Six Yāo.' 
The deep strings thunder like stormy rain, the light strings whisper like private talk.

Like a hidden spring choked beneath ice, struggling to flow.

A silver pitcher shatters, splashing water; iron cavalry bursts forth, blades clashing. 
At end, the pick strikes the center, four strings snap once—a sound like tearing silk.

I dismounted while my guest stepped aboard the boat; raising a cup to drink, there was no music to accompany us. 
Drunk but unable to rejoice, we faced sorrowful parting—when we parted, the vast river reflected a moon immersed in misty gloom. 
Suddenly, a sound of pipa rose from the water's surface; the host forgot to return, the guest ceased departure. 
Following the sound, I softly asked who played; the pipa fell silent as if hesitating to speak.

After many calls, she appeared at last, still holding her pipa half-concealed by her face. 
She turned the axle, plucked a few strings, and before the tune began, emotion already rang through. 
Each note veiled, each tone full of longing—like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams. 
Bowing her head, fingers flowing on, she played without pause, conveying all she could not say. 
Gently brushing, slowly picking, gliding and plucking, first playing 'Rainbow Skies,' then 'Six Yao.' 
The thick strings thundered like heavy rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk. 
Thunderous and soft, intermingled sounds: great beads and small beads falling on jade plates. 
Like a bird singing through blossoms, clear and smooth; like a hidden spring struggling beneath ice, choked and strained. 
The icy spring chokes, the strings freeze, silence breaks the flow—briefly suspended. 
Yet another quiet sorrow, another hidden hatred arises: in this stillness, silence speaks louder than sound. 
A silver bottle shatters, water bursts out; cavalry charges forth, blades and spears ring. 
At the end, the pick strikes the heart of the strings—a single cry, like silk torn apart. 
East and west boats fell utterly silent; only the moon above the river's heart remained white. 
Musing, he placed the pick back among the strings, adjusted his clothes, and composed his expression. 
She said: 'I was once a woman from the capital city, living beneath the Frog Hill. 
At thirteen I had mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Academy’s troupe. 
After performing, even the master teacher had to bow to me; after dressing up, every beauty envied me. 
Young nobles vied to give me silk—how many lengths of red silk I received! 
Tinsel-studded hairpins broke upon rhythm; crimson robes stained with wine spilled by laughter. 
Laughing and happy, year after year, spring winds and autumn moons passed carelessly. 
My brother left to join the army, my aunt died; days passed, my looks faded. 
Before my door, horses and riders grew sparse; old now, I married a merchant. 
Merchants value profit more than parting; last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. 
Since then, I’ve stayed here, guarding an empty boat; around me, moonlight, cold river water. 
Deep into night, I dreamt suddenly of youth—crying in sleep, tears staining my painted face red. 
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply; hearing her story again, I sighed even more. 
We are both wanderers lost on distant shores—why must we have met before to feel such kinship? 
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, lying sick in Xunyang. 
Xunyang is remote, lacking music; for whole years, not a single string or bamboo sound. 
Near Pienjiang, the land lies low and damp; bitter reeds and yellow bamboo grow all around my home. 
Throughout day and night, what do I hear? Blood-drenched cuckoos crying, apes grieving in the distance. 
In spring mornings, autumn nights, I often pour wine alone, raising it to myself. 
Are there no mountain songs or rustic flutes? But their cries—guttural, jarring, hard to endure. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech, it feels like listening to celestial music—my ears momentarily brightened. 
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece—for you, I will compose this poem 'Pipa Xing.' 
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence, then sat down, pressing the strings tighter—the music grew urgent. 
The tones were sad, no longer like before; everyone in the hall, hearing again, covered their eyes and wept. 
Who wept the most in the room? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his green robe soaked with tears."}

My host dismounted, my guest stayed on the boat, raising wine to drink—but no music played.
Drunk yet unable to rejoice, heartbroken as we parted, the moon drowned in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa music arose—my host forgot to leave, my guest stood still.
I sought the sound, whispered in dark, asking who played; the music paused, then hesitated to speak.
I moved the boat near, invited her to meet, poured more wine, turned up the lamp, relit the feast.
After many calls, she finally appeared, still holding her pipa half-concealed by her face.
She tuned the axle, plucked two or three notes—before the tune began, emotion stirred.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing, as if telling a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, fingers moving steadily, she played on—in silence, all her hidden sorrows spoken.
Gently stroking, slowly pressing, brushing, then picking—first *Feeling of Clouds*, then *Six Small Beads*.
The bass strings roared like sudden rain, the treble whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft, big pearls and small falling on jade plates.
Now clear, like a bird gliding through blossoms; now choked, like a spring under ice struggling to flow.
Cold water, icy, strings freeze—silence thickens, then breaks into pause.
Another sorrow stirs, unseen, unspoken—one moment of silence surpasses sound.
Like a silver bottle bursting, liquid gushes forth; like cavalry charging, swords and spears clash.
At end, the pick strikes the heart of the string—a single crack, like silk torn apart.
All ships were still, no word spoken—only the autumn moon above the river's heart.
After a long pause, she laid down the pick, slid it back into the strings, straightened her clothes, composed herself.
She said: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath the Frog Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Music Academy.
After a piece, even the master musician bowed in respect; after makeup, even Qiumei envied me.
Young noblemen vied to give me silks—an endless stream, too many to count.
Silver hairpins shattered with rhythm, crimson robes stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Happy years passed, one after another, while spring moons and autumn breezes slipped away.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died; days faded, my beauty dimmed.
Front gate grew cold, horse and rider rare—I married a merchant in old age.
Merchants care for profit, not farewell—last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He’s gone, leaving me alone on the riverbank, watching empty boats; the moon circles the boat, the river chills with cold.

When I heard the pipa, I sighed; now hearing these words, I sighed again.
We are both lost souls beneath the same sky—why must we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick, lying low in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music—whole years pass without a single string or bamboo flute.
Near Pien River, ground low and wet, bitter reeds and tall bamboo grow around the house.

In spring mornings, on autumn nights, I often pour wine alone, drinking by myself.

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, at night I bid farewell to a guest—
Maple leaves and reeds in autumn, trembling with chill.
My host dismounts, my guest remains on board;
Raising wine to drink, yet no music plays.

Unhappy in our drunkenness, we face parting's sorrow—
As we depart, the vast river swallows the moon's glow.

Suddenly from the water comes the sound of a pipa,
My host forgets to return, my guest halts his journey.

I search for the voice, whispering in the dark: "Who is playing?"
The pipa falls silent—hesitant to speak.

We steer our boat near, inviting her to meet us,
Add wine, turn lamps, reopen the feast once more.

Countless calls bring her forth at last—
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face.

She turns the axle, plucks the strings three or two times—
Before the tune begins, emotion already glows.

Each note mournful, each tone filled with longing,
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.

Bowing low, fingers move steadily, endlessly,
She pours out all her heart’s endless sorrows.

Lightly combing, slowly picking, brushing, then plucking—
First the 'Feathered Robe,' then the 'Sixth-Seven.'

The deep strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin ones whisper like private words.

Harmonious clatter mixed with soft chatter—
Like pearls large and small falling on jade plates.

Smooth as a bird's song through blooming flowers,
Grieving as spring water beneath frozen ice.

Cold and choked, the strings freeze in silence—
A pause, then stillness, as if all sound has died.

But another hidden sorrow stirs in the heart—
In that moment, silence speaks louder than sound.

A silver bottle shatters, water sprays forth;
A cavalry charge breaks through—sword and spear cry out.

When the piece ends, the pick strikes the heart of the string—
Four strings snap in one cry, like tearing silk.

East and west boats stand silent, not a word spoken—
Only the moon above the river's heart, white and clear.

Doubtfully, she lays down her pick, slips it into the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands straight, composes her face.

She says: "Born originally in the capital city,
My home once stood beneath Hama Ling's shadow.

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa—
Named in the first rank of the Imperial Music Troupe.

After each performance, even the greatest master would bow in awe;
After each makeup, every beauty envied me.

Young nobles vied to offer silk—
One song earned me countless lengths of red cloth.

Silver hairpins beat time until shattered,
Crimson skirts stained with wine from joyous spills.

Laughter shared year after year,
Springtime and autumn moonlight passed without care.

Then my brother went off to war, my aunt passed away—
Days pass, nights pass, my beauty fades.

The front gate grows cold, no horse nor rider comes—
Now old, I've married a merchant, lost in life's course.

Merchants prize profit, scorn parting—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I remain here, guarding an empty boat—
Moon circles round, the river chills beneath.

Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s days—
Awake in tears, makeup streaks red down my cheeks.

I hear her pipa and sigh deeply—
Now hearing her story, I sigh again, long and low.

We are both castaways on this distant shore—
Why must we have met before to feel kinship?

I left the capital last year—
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang town.

Xunyang lies remote, no music to be heard;
All year long, no sounds of strings or flutes.

Near Pienjiang, the land is damp and low—
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my door.

What do I hear day and night here?
Cuckoos bleeding blood, apes wailing in grief.

On spring mornings, flower-filled days, autumn nights with moonlight—
I often pour wine alone, raising the cup to myself.

Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Yet their harsh, grating tones can't bear to listen.

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech—
It feels like heavenly music, ears suddenly brightened.

Don’t refuse—sit again, play one more piece—
I’ll compose for you this ‘Song of the Pipa.’

Moved by my words, she stands long in thought—
Then sits, tightens the strings, and quickens the pace.

Now the music, though sad, lacks its former tone—
All in the hall weep again, covering our faces.

Who among us shed the most tears tonight?
The Jiangzhou governor’s green robe, soaked through."}

My host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat; raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays.
Drunk but unable to rejoice, sorrowful as we part—parting in a vast, misty river bathed by moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa sounds arise—my host forgets to return, the guest halts his departure.
I search for the sound, whispering to ask who plays; the pipa stops, the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat near, inviting her to meet; I add wine, turn down the lamps, reopen the feast.
After many calls, she finally appears, still holding the pipa half-concealing her face.
She turns the axis, plucks the strings three or two times—before any tune forms, emotion already fills the air.
Each string suppressed, each note laden with longing, as if recounting a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, she plays on, hand after hand, pouring out all her heart's endless sorrows.
Gently strumming, slowly rubbing, flicking and plucking—first the 'Feather Dress,' then the 'Six Ya.'
The thick strings roar like a sudden storm of rain, the thin strings whisper like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft notes mix together, large pearls and small pearls falling on jade plates.
Like a bird gliding through blossoms, smooth and clear; like a stream choked beneath frozen ice, struggling and low.
Cold and stiff, the icy spring refuses to flow—the strings freeze, silence briefly holds.
Then another hidden sorrow and secret resentment rise—here, silence speaks louder than sound.
A silver jar cracks open, water bursts forth; horsemen charge forward, blades and spears clash in battle.
At the end, she sweeps the pick straight across the heart of the strings—four strings cry out once, like silk torn apart.
East and west boats fall silent, not a word spoken—only the river center reflects the white autumn moon.
In thought, she rests the pick back into the strings, adjusts her clothes, raises her composure.
She says: 'I was born a girl of the capital city, lived at the foot of Rabbit Pond Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the teaching bureau’s finest.
After my performance, even master musicians were moved to admiration; after my makeup, beauties of the day envied me.
Young lords from the Five Burials vied to offer silk—each song earned countless lengths of red gauze.
Tinsel-studded hairpins shattered with the beat; crimson skirts stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Happy laughter carried on from year to year, while autumn moons and spring breezes passed unnoticed.
My brother left for war, my aunt passed away; days vanish, my beauty fades with time.
My door grows cold, few horses or riders pass; old now, I married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, scornful of parting—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he's gone, I stay alone in this empty boat by the river mouth, surrounded by moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days, wake crying—makeup streaked with tears, red and smeared.
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply; hearing her words again, my heart aches anew.
We are both wanderers far from home, strangers in this world—why need we have met before to feel so close?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sickly, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, without music—whole years pass without a single strain of zither or bamboo flute.
Near Panshan, land is low, damp; yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow all around my house.
What do I hear day and night in this place? Crows crying blood-red, monkeys wailing mournfully.
