座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I saw a guest off, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn chill.
My host dismounted, my guest was on board; raising a cup to drink, yet no music played.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful as we parted, the parting scene blurred, with moonlight soaking the vast river.
Suddenly, a pipa sound floated over the water—my host forgot to return, my guest delayed departure.
Following the sound, I softly asked who played; the pipa paused, hesitant to speak.
I moved the boat closer, inviting the player to meet; poured more wine, turned up the lamp, began the feast once more.
After many calls, she finally emerged, still holding her pipa half-concealing her face.
She turned the peg, plucked the strings with a few cautious notes—before any melody, emotion already stirred.
Each string heavy, each note filled with longing—like one recounting lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing her head, she played steadily, weaving through endless sorrows within.
Gently stroking, slowly pressing, brushing and lifting, first playing 'Fei Lian', then 'Liu Yao'.
The deep strings roared like sudden rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft, sharp and gentle—like pearls dropping onto jade plates.
Smooth as a bird's song gliding through flowers, choked as a spring under ice struggles to flow.
Cold springs, stiffened strings, silence suspended—then a brief pause, breath held.
Another hidden sorrow, another silent hate—here, silence speaks louder than sound.
Like a silver bottle bursting, splashing liquid forth; like iron cavalry surging, blades and spears clashing.
At the end, the pick swept across the heart of the string—four strings snapped into one cry, like silk tearing apart.
East and west ships fell quiet, no voice—but only the autumn moon white upon the river's heart.
Sighing, she laid down the pick, slid it back into the strings, adjusted her clothes, composed herself.
She said: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath the Xiamama Ling district.
Thirteen years old, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the imperial music school.
After each performance, even the most skilled musicians would bow before me; after every makeup, beauty queens envied me.
Young noblemen vied to throw silken ribbons at my feet—each tune earned countless red silks.
Gold-tipped combs shattered from beating time; crimson skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter returned, the seasons passed carelessly—spring breezes, autumn moons.
Then my brother left for war, my aunt died; days and nights passed, my beauty faded.
Front door grew cold, few riders came; old now, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit more than parting—I left last month, buying tea in Fuliang.
Now I remain alone at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat, surrounded by moonlit water, cold and still.
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youth’s joys—dreaming, crying, tears staining my painted face red and streaked.
Hearing this pipa, I sighed deeply; hearing these words again, I sighed even more.
We’re both lost souls on distant shores—why must we have met before to feel such kinship?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick and confined in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music; all year long, no sounds of strings or bamboo.
Near Pienjiang, low-lying, damp ground; yellow rushes and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear each morning and evening here? The blood-stained cry of cuckoos, the grief-stricken howl of apes.
In spring mornings and autumn nights, often I pour wine alone, drinking to myself.
Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes? But their rough, grating tones are unbearable to hear.
Now, hearing your pipa tonight, it’s as if listening to celestial music—ears suddenly clear.
Please, don’t refuse to sit and play another piece—for you, I will compose a poem: 'The Pipa Song'.
Moved by my words, she stood still a long while, then sat down, tightened the strings, playing faster.
Her music now trembled—not as before—full of sorrow. All present wept again.
Who wept the most among us? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his green robe soaked with tears."}

Bai Juyi

On Xunyang River's head, at night I was seeing off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn rustling and soughing.
The host dismounted, the guest was already on the boat;
We raised our cups, about to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without finding joy, sad, we were about to part;
At parting, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly we heard a pipa's sound upon the water;
The host forgot to return, the guest did not depart.
Seeking the sound, I quietly asked, "Who is playing?"
The pipa's sound stopped; she seemed reluctant to speak.
We moved the boat nearer, inviting her to meet us;
We added wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last came out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings three or four times;
Before the tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Every string, every note, seemed to choke with thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
Lowering her brows, she played on, note following note,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Skirt" and then "Six Minor."
The thick strings roared like a sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled and intermingled,
Like great and small pearls dropping onto a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling softly beneath the flowers,
Or a hidden stream flowing, choked beneath the ice.
The icy spring ran cold, the strings grew stiff and froze;
The freezing blocked the flow, the sound for a while ceased.
A different sorrow, a secret resentment arose;
At that moment, silence spoke more than sound.
Then a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth;\nArmored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the pick across the center;
The four strings together rang like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were silent, no one spoke;
Only the white autumn moon was seen at the river's heart.
Musing, she tucked the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her countenance.
She said, "I was once a girl from the capital,

My crimson silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.

My younger brother went off to the army, my aunt died;
Evenings came and mornings went, and my beauty faded.

Growing old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit and make light of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Xunyang River Head, seeing off a guest by night—
maple leaves, reed flowers, autumn rustling cold.
The host dismounts, the guest is on his boat;
he lifts his cup to drink, but there is no string music.
Drunk without joy, they grieve at parting—
parting, the vast river drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa:
the host forgets to go back, the guest will not depart.
Seeking the sound, he asks softly, "Who is playing?"
The pipa stops; she hesitates before answering.
They move the boat nearer, invite her to appear;
wine is refilled, lamps relit, the feast begins again.
After a thousand calls, only then she comes out,
still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings—two or three sounds;
before a tune is formed, feeling is already there.
String over string, muted and heavy, sound after sound full of thought,
as if telling a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow lowered, idly, in sequence she plays on,
speaking of all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and plucking,
first she plays "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao."
The big strings rumble like sudden rain,
the small strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, tangled and mixed,
like big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth,
like a hidden stream choking under ice.
The ice-cold stream, the strings freeze and stop;
frozen, the sound cannot pass, and for a while it ceases.
Yet another sorrow, a hidden resentment rises:
here, silence is more powerful than sound.
Then—
a silver vase suddenly shatters, water gushing;
an armored charge bursts out, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; the pick sweeps across the center—
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west, no one speaks;
one sees only the autumn moon white on the river.
Pondering, she tucks the pick among the strings,
straightens her clothes, rises and composes her face.
She speaks:
"I was a girl of the capital,
my home was below Homa Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name listed first in the Music Academy.
When I finished a song, even the master musicians were impressed;
when my makeup was done, the court beauties were jealous.
The young gallants of the Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts—
for one song, I don't know how many rolls of red silk.
Ornamental combs of silver beat time till they broke,
crimson skirts were stained and spoiled by wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
autumn moon, spring wind, all passed in idle ease.
My younger brother went off to war, my aunt died;
night went and morning came, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages grew cold, horses few;
growing old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit, not staying together—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone I wait by the river mouth in an empty boat;
around the boat, bright moonlight, river water cold.
Late at night I suddenly dream of my youth,
and wake crying, my makeup streaked with tears."

I had already sighed at the pipa;
now hearing her words, I sigh again and again.
We are both people lost at the edge of the world—
why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the capital,
exiled and ill, I lie in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, with no music:
all year I have not heard strings or flutes.
I live near the river, the land low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, gibbons mourning.
On flower-moon spring days, autumn moonlit nights,
often I take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa words,
like hearing immortal music—my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
and I will compose a "Pipa Song" for you.
Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
then sits back, tightens the strings—the strings grow urgent.
Sad and mournful, not like the sound before:
all the seats, hearing it again, cover their faces and weep.
Among the seats, who weeps the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue gown wet."}

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn trembled with chill. 
The host dismounted, the guest stayed on the boat; 
We raised our wine to drink, yet no music played. 

Unhappy in our drunkenness, we grieved as we parted— 
As we bid farewell, the river spread beneath a moonlit haze. 
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa, 
The host forgot to return, the guest forgot to depart. 

We searched for the sound, whispered questions: "Who plays?" 
The pipa ceased, the player hesitated, reluctant to speak. 
We moved our boat near, invited her to come see us, 
Added wine, turned up the lamps, reopened the feast. 

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas brought her forth at last, 
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face. 

She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times— 
Before a tune began, emotion had already filled the air. 

Each note bore sorrow, each tone held memory, 
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled. 

Bowed head, fingers moving steadily, 
She played, pouring out endless heartache. 

Softly she brushed, slowly she twisted, pressed and flicked— 
First the 'Feathered Robe,' then the 'Sixth's Dance.' 

The bass strings roared like sudden rain, 
The treble hissed like private whispers. 

A jumble of loud and soft, deep and light, 
Large pearls and small tumbling on jade plates. 

Like birds gliding through blossoms, their song smooth and sweet, 
Or a brook choked beneath ice, struggling, gasping, hard to hear. 

Cold, icy water constricts the strings—silence comes, 
The music halts, the pause is full of silence. 

Then another hidden grief, another silent hate— 
In that stillness, silence speaks louder than sound. 

Suddenly, a silver jar bursts—water sprays; 
A cavalry charge breaks out, swords and spears cry aloud. 

At end, the pick strokes the heartstring with a slash— 
Four strings cry out once, as if torn silk. 

East and west boats fell silent, no word spoken— 
Only the moon white in the river’s heart. 

After a long thought, she laid down her pick, tucked it in the strings, 
Straightened her clothes, composed her countenance. 

She said: "I am from the capital city originally, 
My home stood beneath the Hare-Mound Lane. 

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, 
My name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau. 

After every performance, even the master could not deny me; 
My makeup so dazzling, even Qiu-Niang envied me. 

Five noble youths competed to throw their gifts at my feet— 
One song earned me countless silken robes. 

With gold hairpins, I beat time until they cracked; 
My red silk skirts were stained by wine and blood. 

Year after year, joy followed joy— 
Spring moons, autumn breezes passed carelessly. 

But my brother left for war, my aunt passed away; 
Days fled, nights passed, my beauty faded. 

The gate grew cold, horse and rider few— 
Old, I wed a merchant, lost my youth. 

Merchants prize profit, scorn parting— 
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea. 

Since then, I've stayed at the river mouth, alone with my empty boat— 
Moonlight circles the boat, the river water chills. 

Deep in the night, I dreamt of my youthful days— 
Dreaming, I cried, my rouge-stained tears ran down my cheeks. 

Hearing this pipa, I sighed deeply, 
And hearing her words again, I sighed more. 

We're both castaways, far from home, adrift in fate— 
Why must we have met before to know each other? 

I left the imperial capital last year, 
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City. 

Xunyang is remote, no music ever heard— 
Whole years pass without a single string or bamboo flute. 

Near Pien River, the land is low and damp— 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around. 

What sounds do I hear day and night? 
Crows crying blood, apes wailing mournfully. 

On spring mornings, flower-filled days, autumn nights under the moon— 
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.

My ears brighten, just for a moment.

Maple leaves and reeds in autumn trembled with chill. 
The host dismounted, the guest stayed on the boat; 
We raised our wine to drink, yet no music played. 

Unhappy in our drunkenness, we grieved as we parted— 
As we bid farewell, the river spread beneath a moonlit haze. 
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa, 
The host forgot to return, the guest forgot to depart. 

We searched for the sound, whispered questions: "Who plays?" 
The pipa ceased, the player hesitated, reluctant to speak. 
We moved our boat near, invited her to come see us, 
Added wine, turned up the lamps, reopened the feast. 

A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas brought her forth at last, 
Still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face. 

She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times— 
Before a tune began, emotion had already filled the air. 

Each note bore sorrow, each tone held memory, 
Like one lamenting a life unfulfilled. 

Bowed head, fingers moving steadily, 
She played, pouring out endless heartache. 

Softly she brushed, slowly she twisted, pressed and flicked— 
First the 'Feathered Robe,' then the 'Sixth's Dance.' 

The bass strings roared like sudden rain, 
The treble hissed like private whispers. 

A jumble of loud and soft, deep and light, 
Large pearls and small tumbling on jade plates. 

Like birds gliding through blossoms, their song smooth and sweet, 
Or a brook choked beneath ice, struggling, gasping, hard to hear. 

Cold, icy water constricts the strings—silence comes, 
The music halts, the pause is full of silence. 

Then another hidden grief, another silent hate— 
In that stillness, silence speaks louder than sound. 

Suddenly, a silver jar bursts—water sprays; 
A cavalry charge breaks out, swords and spears cry aloud. 

At end, the pick strokes the heartstring with a slash— 
Four strings cry out once, as if torn silk. 

East and west boats fell silent, no word spoken— 
Only the moon white in the river’s heart. 

After a long thought, she laid down her pick, tucked it in the strings, 
Straightened her clothes, composed her countenance.

My home stood beneath the Hare-Mound Lane. 

At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, 
My name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau. 

After every performance, even the master could not deny me; 
My makeup so dazzling, even Qiu-Niang envied me. 

Five noble youths competed to throw their gifts at my feet— 
One song earned me countless silken robes. 

With gold hairpins, I beat time until they cracked; 
My red silk skirts were stained by wine and blood.

Spring moons, autumn breezes passed carelessly. 

But my brother left for war, my aunt passed away; 
Days fled, nights passed, my beauty faded.

Why must we have met before to know each other?

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I saw a guest off, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn's chill.
I dismounted to greet the guest, who remained aboard the boat; raising my cup to drink, there was no music to accompany us.
Drunk but not joyful, sad as we parted—our parting shadowed by the moon floating on the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water’s surface, a pipa melody rang out—so captivating that host and guest forgot to leave.
In silence, I searched for its source: 'Who plays?' The pipa fell still, hesitant to answer.
We moved our boat near, inviting the player to meet us; we added wine, turned up lamps, and reopened the feast.
After many calls, she finally appeared, still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the tuning pegs, plucked a few chords—before even forming a tune, emotion already stirred.
Each string carried sorrow, each note a memory—like lamenting a life unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, she played on without pause, telling all the endless sorrows hidden within.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, sliding, then plucking—first playing 'Feather-Cloth Dance,' then 'Sixth-Step Rhythm.'
The thick strings roared like heavy rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk.
A jumble of thunder and murmurs, large pearls and small dropping onto jade plates.
Then, clear and fluid—the oriole’s song through blossoms; then choked and strained—like a spring beneath frozen ice.
Cold and stagnant, the strings froze; silence fell, as if sound had ceased altogether.
But now a deeper sorrow, silent, yet louder than any sound.
Like a silver pitcher bursting open, spilling liquid; like cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
When the final stroke slashed across the heart of the instrument, four strings sounded once—a rip like tearing silk.
All boats in east and west lay still, speechless—only the autumn moon, white upon the river’s heart.
After a long pause, she laid down her pick, slid it into the strings, straightened her robes, and composed herself.
She said: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath the Crab-Wharf Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After each piece, the master musicians would be silenced by admiration; after each makeup, the courtesan Qiumei would grow jealous.
Young nobles vied to gift me silken robes—countless times, one piece could not keep track.
My jeweled hairpins shattered to the beat; my crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter returned—until spring and autumn moons passed carelessly.
My brother joined the army; my aunt passed away. Days slipped by, my beauty faded.
Our gate grew quiet, horses few—the old woman married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, not for parting—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me here, guarding an empty boat, while the moon circles the hull and the river grows cold.
Deep in the night, I dreamt again of youth—waking to cry, tears staining my rouge-laden cheeks red and streaked.
Hearing my pipa, I sighed; hearing her story, I sighed again—more deeply now.
We are both wanderers beneath the same sky, lost souls—why need we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick and confined in Xunyang City.
Xunyang lies remote, lacking music; whole years pass with no sound of strings or bamboo.
Near Pengjiang, the land is low and damp—yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my home.
What sounds do I hear every day and night? The blood-stained cuckoo's cry, the mournful howl of apes.
On spring mornings and autumn nights, I often pour wine alone.
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? But their grating, awkward music is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak, it felt like listening to celestial music—my ears suddenly brightened.
Do not refuse—sit again and play another piece—for you, I will compose this 'Pipa Poem.'
The words struck her deeply; she stood motionless for a long time, then sat back, hurriedly tightened the strings—and the music quickened.
Now the notes were more piercing, less like before—everyone in the audience wept anew.
Who among them shed the most tears? The Jiangzhou governor’s green robe was wet with sobs."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night, I saw a guest off, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn's chill. 
I dismounted to greet the guest on board; raising my cup to drink, no music played. 
Drunk, I could not feel joy—sad to part as moonlight soaked the vast, misty river. 
Suddenly, a pipa sound floated from the water: the host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his departure. 
I sought the voice, softly asking who was playing. The pipa paused—hesitant to speak. 
We moved the boat near and invited her to appear. We added wine, relit the lamps, reopened our feast. 
After countless calls, she emerged, still holding her pipa half-concealed by her face. 
She turned the axis, plucked a few chords—before any tune began, emotion stirred. 
Each string sighed, each note bore sorrow—like one speaking of lifelong regrets. 
Bending her head, fingers moving steadily, she played on, revealing all her hidden pains. 
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, dragging, then plucking—first *Nayi Chang*, then *Liuyao*. 
The bass strings roared like sudden rain, the treble whispered like private talk. 
A jumble of loud and soft notes—large pearls and small falling on jade plates. 
Now smooth as a bird’s song through blossoms, now choked as water beneath ice. 
Cold springs freeze, strings grow tight, and silence breaks—then pause. 
Another sorrow, another hidden hatred stirs: silence here is louder than sound. 
Like a silver bottle shattering, water bursts forth; like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clash. 
At the end, the pick strikes the heart of the strings—a single crack, like torn silk. 
East and west ships fell silent—only the autumn moon above the river’s heart remained bright. 
She paused, leaned her staff down into the strings, adjusted her clothes, composed her face. 
She said: 'Born a girl of the capital city, my home lay beneath Hama Ling. 
At thirteen, I had mastered the pipa—my name ranked first in the Imperial Academy. 
After each piece, even masters would bow; after each beauty, every jade-faced courtesan envied me. 
Young nobles vied to give gifts—each song earned endless red silks. 
Tinsel combs shattered with rhythm; crimson robes stained with wine spilled. 
Year in, year out, laughter returned—autumn moons and spring breezes passed too easily. 
My brother left for war, my aunt died; time slipped away, my beauty faded. 
Front gate grew cold—fewer horses, fewer riders. At last, I married a merchant. 
Merchants care only for profit, not partings—last month, he journeyed to Fuliang to buy tea. 
He’s gone now, leaving me alone in a boat at the river mouth—moonlight circles me, the river chills. 
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youth—awoke weeping, makeup streaks red across my cheeks. 
Hearing her pipa, I sighed already—now hearing her story, I sighed again. 
We are both lost souls, far from home—why need we have met before? 
I left the capital city a year ago, exiled, sickly, confined to Xunyang. 
Xunyang’s remote, without music—no year passes without silence where strings should play. 
Near Pienjiang, land low and damp—yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around our homes. 
What sounds do I hear day and night? Crows bleeding their song, gibbons mournfully howling. 
Spring mornings with blooming flowers, autumn nights with golden moons—often I pour wine alone. 
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? But their croaks and screeches are hard to bear. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa music—like listening to heavenly melody, my ears suddenly clear. 
Please don’t refuse to sit again and play one more piece—I’ll write a poem for you, called *Pipa Xing*. 
Moved by my words, she stood still long—then sat back, quickened the strings, made them sharper. 
The music now sounded colder than before—everyone in the room wept anew. 
Who among the crowd shed the most tears? The governor of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River head, I saw a guest off on a night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the autumn light.
The host dismounted; the guest was aboard his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to note.
Drunk but not merry, we parted in gloom, sad to part,
At parting, the vast river was steeped in the moon's pale art.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa,
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed his departure, awestruck, in awe.
Following the sound, we softly asked, "Who is playing?"
The pipa stopped; she hesitated to answer, delaying her speaking.
Moving our boat nearer, we invited her to meet,
Adding wine, relighting the lamp, we reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally came out,
Still hugging her pipa, half her face hidden in a shy pout.
Turning the pegs, plucking the strings, three or two notes she strummed,
Before the tune took shape, a feeling had already come.
String after string, muffled and suppressed, each tone a thought,
As if telling of a life, of ambitions unsought.
With lowered brows, she casually continued to play,
Telling of the endless matters in her heart, in disarray.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and flicking with care,
First she played "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao" rare.
The large strings roared like a sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like a secret, soft refrain.
Loud and soft, in tangled harmony they were played,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade tray's cascade.\nLike orioles singing, smooth over flowered ground,
Or like a muffled spring, under ice, struggling to be found.
The ice-cold spring, the strings grew stiff and still,\nTill a pause came, a silence, against the player's will.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, began to rise,
In that moment, the silence spoke louder than any sound's surprise.
Then a silver vase suddenly broke, water and wine burst forth,
An armored cavalry charged out, swords and spears ringing north.
The tune ended; the撥 (plectrum) struck the center of the strings in a sweep,
All four strings together, like tearing silk, a sound so deep.
East and west, boats and pavilions were silent, without a word,
Only the river's heart, the autumn moon, white and unheard.
Thoughtfully, she put the拨 between the strings, and paused,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her expression, composed.
She said, "I was a girl from the capital, my home near Hama Ling,
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, my name in the First Class of the Imperial Singing.
When I finished a song, even the best players would admire,
When I made up, even the famous courtesans would envy the fire.
The young men of the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I received so many red silks, countless shifts.
I beat time with a jeweled comb, till it broke into pieces,
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with wine, as the feast increases.
Year after year, I laughed and played, carefree and gay,
The autumn moon and spring wind passed by, wasted away.
My brother left for the army; my aunt died, gone away,
Day and night passed, and my youthful beauty began to decay.
Before my gate, the horses and carriages grew few and cold,
I grew old, and married a merchant, a story to be told.
The merchant values profit, and lightly parts from his wife,
Last month, to Fuliang, he went to buy tea, away from life.
He comes and goes; I keep the empty boat at the river's mouth,
Around the boat, the bright moon shines, the river water cold, in the south.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youthful years,
In the dream, I cry, my makeup ruined by tears.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed with regret,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deep in my pocket.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world, lost and stray,
Why must we have met before, to understand each other's way?
I left the imperial capital last year, and came to this sickbed, demoted, exiled in Xunyang,
The place is remote, with no music, no sound of strings and pipes, for long.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp, a place of gloom,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my room.
What do I hear, morning and evening, in this lonely place?
The cuckoo's bloody cry, and the gibbon's mournful face.
On spring river days, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine, and drink alone, in solitary lights.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to hear?\nThey are harsh and grating, and difficult for the ear.
Tonight, I hear your pipa's speech, so clear and bright,
Like listening to celestial music, my ears refreshed with light.
Please do not refuse, sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa" soon.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time, in a trance,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played a faster dance.
The mournful sound was unlike the earlier melody's art,
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept, with a broken heart.
Among the audience, whose tears fell the most, the deepest stain?
The Jiangzhou Mayor, whose blue robe was wet with rain.

The original text contains two proper nouns that required verification but for which no supplementary sources were provided in the dialogue:

1. **虾蟆陵 (Hama Ling)** - A place name in Chang'an (modern Xi'an). The character 虾 (xiā) is often written as 蛤 in other contexts, and the standard name is commonly rendered as 蛤蟆陵 or 下马陵. The translation uses the pinyin "Hama Ling" to preserve the ambiguity of the original text's character choice.

2. **六幺 (Liù Yāo)** - The name of a famous Tang dynasty dance tune (also written as 绿腰 or 六鷓). No source was retrieved to confirm the exact title or its musical characteristics. The translation retains the pinyin "Six Yao" rather than attempting to translate the title, preserving the uncertainty.

All other allusions (霓裳 Nishang, 霓裳羽衣曲, 五陵年少, 教坊, 江州司马, etc.) are standard references in Tang poetry and are translated according to their widely accepted meanings.

Key translation choices:
- "天涯沦落人" rendered as "wanderers at the edge of the world" to capture both geographical displacement and social marginalization.
- "呕哑嘲哳" rendered as "harsh and grating" to convey the onomatopoeic quality of the original.
- The final image of the "blue robe wet" (青衫湿) is preserved literally, as the specific color holds biographical significance (白居易 was demoted to a rank associated with blue robes)."}

Maple leaves and reeds rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard the boat,
Raising a cup to drink, but no music plays.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, we part with sorrow,
As dusk descends, the river mirrors the moon's pale glow.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound resounds;
The host forgets to return, the guest halts his departure.
I seek the voice, whispering softly: 'Who is playing?'

We move our boat near, inviting her to come forth,

With countless calls, she finally appears,

She turns the axis, plucks a few strings—

Each note veiled, each tone a sigh,
Like one speaking of lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Bending her head, fingers glide without pause,
Pouring out all that heart holds, endless and deep.
Gently brushing, slowly picking, gliding, then plucking,
First the 'Rainbow Skirts,' then the 'Six Yao' dance.
Loud strings crash like sudden rain,
Soft strings whisper like private talk.
A cacophony of clatter and chime,
Like pearls large and small on jade plates tumbling down.
Now clear, like a bird singing through flowers,
Then choked, like springs beneath ice struggling to flow.
Cold and slow, the strings freeze, silent and still,
This silence between sounds speaks louder than sound.
A silver bottle cracks open—water spurts,
A cavalry charge bursts forth—sword and spear cry out.
At the final stroke, the pick strikes center stage;
Four strings snap once—like silk torn in twain.
Boats east and west fall silent, no word spoken,
Only the moon bright above the river's heart.
After a pause, she lays down her pick, tucks it into the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, composes her face, grows solemn.

My home lies beneath the Crab-Lake Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Ranking first among the imperial school's famed troupe.
After my songs, even the masters would bow in awe,
And in makeup, every beauty envied me.
Young men from five noble districts vied for my favor,
One song earned me red silks beyond count.
My jeweled hairpin shattered with the beat,
My crimson skirt stained with wine from drunken revels.
Year after year, laughter, then another year,
Spring blossoms and autumn moons pass unnoticed.
My brother enlisted, my foster mother died;
Days fade, nights pass—their youth has faded.
Once-busy gate now scarce sees horse or rider;
Old and worn, I married a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, not partings.
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and here I wait alone on the riverside,
Moonlight circles my empty boat, cold waters rise.
At midnight I dream of youthful days,
Dreaming I weep, my makeup streaked with red tears.
Hearing her pipa, I sigh deeply;
Hearing her story, I sigh again.
We are both castaways on life's distant shore,
Why must we have known each other to feel this kinship?
I left the imperial court last year,
Exiled, sick, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, no music to be heard;
For whole years, no lute or bamboo flute ever sounds.
Near the Pien River, land low, damp and wet;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow all around.
What do I hear day and night? Cuckoos bleeding into blood,
Monkeys wailing in sorrow.
In spring when flowers bloom, in autumn under moonlit skies,
I often pour wine alone, seeking solace.

But their harsh cries are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It feels like heavenly music—my ears are briefly enlightened.
Do not refuse; sit again and play one more piece,

Then sits back, quickens the strings, the music grows more urgent.

Who weeps most among us all?

I dismounted to greet the guest, who remained aboard the boat; raising my cup to drink, there was no music to accompany us.
Drunk but unable to rejoice, we faced a sorrowful parting—beneath a moon drowned in the vast, dim river.
Suddenly, from the water’s surface, a pipa melody rang out; I forgot to return, and the guest did not depart.
I followed the sound, silently asking, 'Who is playing?' The pipa ceased, and words hesitated on the lips.
I moved the boat near, inviting a meeting; added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After many calls and pleas, she appeared at last, still holding her pipa half-hiding her face.
She turned the axle, plucked the strings with three or two tentative notes—before any tune began, feeling was already there.
Each note veiled sorrow, each tone carried longing, as if speaking of a life unfulfilled.
Bending her head, her fingers moved on, playing without pause—her heart laid bare in every stroke.
Gently pressing, slowly twisting, brushing, then lifting—first *Nianchang*, then *Liuyao*.
The thick strings roared like heavy rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft, a clatter of large and small pearls falling on jade plates.
Between them, the oriole’s song slips through blossoms—smooth, clear.
Then the spring beneath ice stumbles, choked, barely audible.
Cold springs slow down, the strings freeze, then stop altogether—the silence hangs for a moment.
Yet another kind of hidden grief and silent hatred arises—this silence speaks louder than sound.
Like a silver jar shattering, water bursts forth; like cavalry charging, swords and spears clash.
At the piece’s end, the pick draws across the heart of the strings—a single sharp cry like tearing silk.
East and west boats fell utterly silent; only the river’s heart glowed white with autumn moonlight.
He paused, then lowered his pick into the strings, adjusted his clothes, and composed his expression.

Young men from the Five Hills vied to give me gifts—each song earned me countless lengths of red silk.
My hairpins of jade shattered from rhythm’s beat; my crimson skirts stained with wine from wild dances.
Laughing through years, enjoying spring and autumn alike, time passed carelessly.
When my brother enlisted and my aunt passed away, days faded, and my looks grew worn.

By Bai Juyi

I was seeing a guest off one night at the Xunyang River;
maple leaves and reed-blossom shivered in the autumn chill.
The host had dismounted, the guest was already in his boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without finding joy, we were about to part in sorrow—
splitting apart, the vast river swallowed the moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to go home, the guest could not depart.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
the music stopped, and she seemed slow to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear;
added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand urgings, she finally emerged,
still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings—two, three notes;
before a melody was formed, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was choked with thought,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Eyes lowered, at her ease, she played on and on,
revealing all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly rolling, stroking, then picking—
first she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Little Branch."
The low strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
the high strings whispered like private words.
The rumbling and the whispering, plucked in tangled mingling—
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers;
like a muffled spring, blocked beneath the ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings grew stiff and still;
the stillness jammed, and for a moment the sound died out.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—
in that moment, silence was more powerful than sound.
Then, like a silver vase bursting, water gushing out;
like armored cavalry charging, sabers and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the pick across all four strings—
with one great sound, like silk being torn apart.
In the boats east and west, all were silent;
only the autumn moon over the river could be seen, white.
Muttering to herself, she slipped the pick among the strings,
straightened her garments, rose, and composed her features.
She said: "I was once a girl from the capital,
living near Hama Ling.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the master musicians were impressed;
when I dressed up, the courtesans envied me.
The young men of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts—
for a single song, I don't know how many bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat;
crimson skirts were stained and spoiled with wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
the autumn moons and spring breezes passed by, unheeded.
My younger brother left to join the army, my aunt died;
night followed day, and my youth began to fade.
Before my gate, carriages grew few, the stirrups lay cold;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
But merchants value profit and think little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I wait by the river mouth in an empty boat;
around the boat, the moon shines bright, the river water is cold.
In the depth of night I suddenly dream of my youth,
and wake weeping, my rouge-streaked tears running down my face."

I had sighed already at the sound of the pipa;
hearing her words, I sighed again, deeply moved.
Both of us are people cast adrift at the ends of the earth—
why must we have known each other before to meet like this?
Since last year I took leave of the imperial capital,
banished here, sick in bed, in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, and has no music;
all year I have not heard the sound of strings and flutes.
I live near the Pen River, in low, damp ground;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What is there to hear, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, and gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower-filled spring mornings, on moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating—hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing the words of your pipa,
I feel as if I have heard immortal music, and my ears are briefly cleared.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
and I will compose a "Song of the Pipa" for you.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster—
sad and piercing, not like the sounds before;
everyone in the room, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Who in the room wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue gown soaked with tears."}

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a friend off one night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stepped into his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk yet not merry, we parted in gloom,
At parting, the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and a voice hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet;
We refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerged,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings three or four times;
Before a melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted, filled with longing,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered eyes, casually, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking, then picking,
First she played 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Minor Melodies.'
The large strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The small strings whispered like private talk.
The rumbling and whispering played in tangled harmony,
Like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.\nThen, like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
Then, like a muffled stream trapped beneath the ice.
The icy stream grew cold, the strings congealed and snapped;
The notes froze and broke, and for a time the sound ceased.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, rose;
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging,
The tune ended; she swept her pick across the center;
All four strings cried out as one, like tearing silk.
Across boats to left and right, all sat in hushed silence;
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart shone white.
Thoughtfully she tucked her pick among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, rose, and composed her features.
She said: 'I was once a girl of the capital,
My home was by the Toad Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name stood first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
When I made up, even the famous Qiu Niang envied me.
The dandies of the Five Tombs competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
With jeweled combs and silver hairpins we beat time till they broke;
In blood-red silk skirts we were drenched with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed without a thought.
Then my younger brother went to war, my aunt died;
Morning came and went, and my beauty faded.
Before my gate, horses grew sparse, the place grew cold;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit and think lightly of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the water cold.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, and tears streak my painted face.'
'I had already sighed at the sound of your pipa;
Hearing your words, I sigh again and again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet as kin?'
'Last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill, I lie in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and night?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons' mournful wails.
On flower-filled spring mornings, on moonlit autumn nights,
Often I take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, impossible to bear.
Tonight, hearing the words of your pipa,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are briefly cleansed.
Please do not refuse; sit and play another tune,
And I will compose a 'Song of the Pipa' for you.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and the tempo quickened.
The sound was mournful, unlike the melody before;
The whole assembly wept again as they listened.
Who wept the most among those seated there?
The River Prefecture's Lieutenant—his blue gown was wet with tears."}

Bowing her head, her fingers moved slowly, one after another, telling all the hidden grief within.
Gently pressing, lightly plucking, gliding and flicking—first playing 'The Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Rhythm of the Six Beats.'

Cold, sluggish water froze the strings till they ceased entirely—silence fell, brief and profound.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。

感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I saw a guest off, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in autumn’s chill.
I dismounted, my guest aboard the boat; raising wine for a drink, but no music played to accompany it.
Drunk without joy, heartbroken as we parted, the parting felt dim, the river mirroring the moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa; the host forgot to return, the guest stayed put.
Following the sound, I softly asked who was playing—then the pipa ceased, the player hesitated before speaking.
I moved the boat nearby to invite her to meet; poured more wine, turned the lamp back on, renewed the feast.
After many calls, she finally appeared, still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the axis, plucked a few strings—before any tune began, emotion stirred.
Each string heavy, each note filled with sorrow—like one speaking of lifelong regrets.
Head lowered, fingers moving slowly through the music, she told all the unspoken pains within.
Gently stroking, softly pressing, brushing and lifting, first she played 'Fei Huan,' then 'Liu Yao.'
The deep strings roared like sudden rain, the light ones whispered like private talk.
A chaotic mix of loud and soft, large pearls and small falling on jade plates.
Smooth as a bird glides beneath blossoms, choked as a brook flows under ice.
Cold and icy, the strings stiffen, then stop altogether—silence briefly breaks the air.
Another hidden sorrow stirs, silence now louder than any sound.
Suddenly, a silver vat cracks—water gushes forth; a cavalry charge bursts forth, swords and spears clash.
At the end, the pick strikes center stage—the four strings sound once like tearing silk.
East and west ships fell silent, nothing but the moon white over the river’s heart.
He paused, dropped the pick into the strings, adjusted his clothes, and composed himself.
She said: ‘Born a woman of the capital city, I lived beneath the Xahma Ling district.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked first among the imperial music academy’s troupes.
When I finished a piece, even the great master bowed in respect; after makeup, I was envied by every courtesan.
Young nobles vied to give me gifts, one tune earned me countless lengths of red silks.
Gold hairpins shattered with beat, crimson robes stained with wine spilled.
Year after year, laughter and joy, while spring moons and autumn breezes passed carelessly.
My brother went to war, my aunt died, days passed, and beauty faded.
Front gate grew cold, fewer horses, fewer visitors—I married a merchant in old age.
The merchant cares more for profit than for parting—he left last month to buy tea in Fuliang.
Now he’s gone, I stay behind on the river’s edge in an empty boat, surrounded by moonlight, the river cold.
Late at night, I dreamt again of youth—waking in tears, my makeup streaked red.
Hearing her pipa made me sigh already; hearing her story again, I sighed more deeply.
We’re both fallen souls adrift in distant lands—why must we have met before to feel this kinship?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, lying sick in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music—whole years pass without a trace of string or bamboo.
Near Panshui River, the land low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear day and night here? Crows bleeding blood, apes crying mournfully.
In spring, when flowers bloom at dawn, in autumn, under moonlit nights—I often pour wine alone.
Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? But their sounds are harsh and grating—hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies, it feels like listening to divine music—my ears suddenly clear.
Don’t refuse to play another piece—let me compose a poem for you, called 'Pipa Xing.'
Moved by my words, she stood a long moment—then sat down, tightened the strings, quickened the pace.
Her music now chilled, no longer like before—everyone in the audience covered their eyes, weeping.
Who among us shed the most tears? The governor of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with salt."}

By Bai Juyi



At Xunyang River's head, at night, I see a guest off;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I, the host, dismount; the guest is in the boat.
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music.

Drunk without joy, we grieve at our looming parting;
At parting, the vast river is flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to go home; the guest delays his departure.

Following the sound, I ask softly: who is playing?
The pipa stops; she hesitates to answer.
We move our boat nearer and invite her to meet;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and reopen the feast.

After a thousand calls, she at last emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times—
Before a tune forms, emotion is already there.

Each string, each note, is suppressed and full of thought,
As if she were telling of a life's frustrations.
With lowered brows, she plays on idly,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and flicking,
First “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Yaos.”
The big strings rumble like sudden rain;
The small strings murmur like whispered secrets.

Rumbling and murmuring, played in tangled complexity,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly over flowers;
Like a muffled spring flowing under ice.

The icy spring runs cold, the strings grow stiff and snap;
The snap seals them shut, and the sound pauses for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment, is born—
At this moment, silence is more expressive than sound.

Then, like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water gushing forth;
Like armored cavalry charging out, sabers and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she sweeps the pick across the center;
All four strings snap at once like tearing silk.

In the boats to the east and west, all is silent and still;
Only the autumn moon in the river's heart is white.

Meditatively, she puts the pick back among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, stands up, and composes her face.
She says she was once a girl from the capital,
Living at the foot of Shama Hill.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name topping the first rank of the court troupe.

Her playing once made even the masters bow;
Her beauty was the envy of every courtesan.
The young men of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.

Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat;
Her blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed by unheeded.

Then her younger brother went off to war; her aunt died.
As days and months went by, her youth faded.
Before her gate, horses grew sparse, visitors grew few;
Growing old, she married a merchant.

The merchant values profit and lightly parts from me;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I come and go, guarding this empty boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream, I weep, my makeup ruined, tears streaking my face.

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her story, I sigh again, deeply moved.
We are both wanderers at the ends of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?

Since last year, I left the capital;
I was banished to Xunyang, lying sick.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year, I hear no sound of string or wind.

I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What sounds do I hear here, morning and night?
The cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbon's mournful wail.

On spring river days, on flower-filled mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are crude and grating, hard to listen to.

Tonight, hearing your pipa's words,
It is like hearing celestial music—my ears are briefly enlightened.
Do not refuse; sit and play another piece,
For you, I will compose a “Song of the Pipa.”

Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back, tightens the strings, and the tempo quickens.
The mournful tune is unlike the one before;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wipes away tears.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

I dismounted as host, while the guest remained aboard the boat; raising a cup to drink, yet no music played to accompany us.
Drunk, we could not find joy—our parting was sorrowful, as moonlight merged with the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, a pipa melody echoed across the water—both host and guest forgot to leave.
We followed the sound, whispering, asking who played; the music paused, the player hesitated before speaking.
We moved our boat near, invited her to meet, added wine, turned up lamps, renewed the feast.
After many calls, she finally appeared, still holding the pipa half-covered by her face.
She tuned the axis, plucked a few strings—before any tune began, emotion stirred.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing—like one confessing lifelong regrets.
Head lowered, fingers moved steadily through the music, revealing all the pain unspoken.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, sliding, then plucking—first *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.
The deep strings roared like sudden rain, the thin ones whispered like private speech.
A jumble of loud and soft notes rang out—the large pearls and small ones fell upon jade plates.
Like a bird gliding through blossoms, its song smooth beneath the flowers;
Like a brook choked under ice, struggling to flow, breathless and strained.
Cold springs grow tight—strings freeze, silence fills the air—then pause, the moment suspended.
Yet another kind of hidden sorrow and silent hatred arises: in that silence, more is said than words can hold.
A silver jar shatters—water bursts forth; cavalry charges, swords clashing, steel bares teeth.
At the final stroke, the pick slashed down the heart of the string—four strings sounded once, like silk torn apart.
All boats fell quiet; only the river center showed the white moon shining above.
Hesitating, he placed the pick down, inserted it into the strings, adjusted his robe, straightened his posture, composed his face.
She spoke: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath Hama Ling district.'
'Thirteen years old, I mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Academy’s troupe.'
'After my performance, even master musicians admired me; after makeup, the courtesans envied me.'
'Young men from noble families vied to offer silken headbands—each piece of red silk given, countless times.'
'The gold hairpins struck rhythm until broken; crimson skirts stained with wine from wild dancing.'
'Happy laughter, year after year, passed easily—spring’s blooms, autumn’s moon, time lost without notice.'
'My brother left for war, my aunt died; days passed, years went by, my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, no horses or riders came. I married a merchant in my later years.'
'The merchant values profit over parting—he left last month to buy tea in Fuliang.'
'Now I wait alone on the river’s edge, my boat empty; moonlight circles it, the river chills.'
'Late at night, I dreamt of youth—awoke crying, tears staining my painted face red and streaked.'
'I heard the pipa and sighed already; hearing this tale again, I groaned deeper.
We are both fallen souls on distant shores—why must we have known each other before?'
'I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, bedridden in Xunyang.'
'Xunyang is remote, lacking music—no strings or bamboo sounds all year long.'
'Our home lies near Pienjiang, damp and low; yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.'
'What sounds do I hear day and night among them? The cuckoo bleeds blood, apes cry mournfully.'
'In spring, when flowers bloom at dawn, in autumn, under moonlit nights—I often pour wine, drinking alone.'
'Are there no rustic songs or village flutes? Yes—but their sounds grating, harsh, unbearable to endure.'
'But tonight, hearing your pipa tune, it’s like listening to heavenly music—my ears clear and bright for a moment.'
'Don’t refuse—sit again, play one more tune—for you I’ll compose this poem, “The Pipa Song.”'
Moved deeply by my words, she stood still for a long time, then sat back, tightened the strings, which grew faster and sharper.
Now the sound was less like before—sorrowful, sharp—everyone in the audience covered their faces and wept.
Who among them wept most of all? The governor of Jiangzhou, his green robe soaked with tears."}

Bai Juyi

That night on the riverbank at Xunyang I saw a guest off;
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, my guest was already aboard;
we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in sorrow—
the parting vast and grey, the river drowning the moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
I forgot to go home, my guest forgot to leave.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
the music stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear;
she poured more wine, relit the lamps, and the feast began again.
After a thousand calls, she at last came out,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings—
before a tune began, feeling was already there.
Each string pressed low, each note steeped in thought,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled longing.
Brow lowered, she played on unhurriedly,
saying all the countless things within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, a sweep and then a flick—first the Rainbow Skirt, then the Little Branch.
The great strings roared like driving rain,
the small strings whispered like private speech.
Roar and whisper tangled together,
great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling beneath the flowers, smooth and gliding;
like a hidden spring choking under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings stiffened and broke;
stuck fast, no sound could pass, and the music paused.
Then a deeper sorrow and a secret resentment rose—
silence there proved mightier than sound.
A silver vase suddenly shattered, water bursting forth;
armored horsemen charging out, sabers and spears ringing.
She swept the pick across the strings to end the song—
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were hushed and mute;
only the autumn moon on the river's heart could be seen, white.
Musing, she set the pick among the strings,
straightened her clothes, and rose with a composed face.
"I was born a girl of the capital," she said,
"my home was below Hama Hill.
At thirteen I had mastered the pipa,
my name listed first among the Music Bureau's performers.
After a performance even the finest players would praise me;
dressed up, I was the envy of every courtesan.
Young men from the five tombs competed to shower me with gifts—one song, and I could not count the bolts of red silk.
Silver hairpins snapped in time to the beat,
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
autumn moons and spring winds passed by unheeded.
Then my brother went off to war, my aunt died;
night followed day, and my beauty faded.
Before my door the carriages grew few and cold;
grown old, I married a merchant.
The merchant cares for profit, not for parting—

By Bai Juyi

By the Xunyang River one autumn night I saw a friend off, the reed flowers and maple leaves shivering in the chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat; we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet without joy, we were about to part in sorrow, when the vast river drowned the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa; the host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing; the music stopped, and she seemed reluctant to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet, added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she at last appeared, still hiding half her face behind her pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times; before the tune began, feeling already filled the air.
Each string was muted, each note full of thought, as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
With lowered eyes, she played on carelessly, pouring out the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking, first she played the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Abreast Dance.
The low strings roared like a sudden rain, the high strings whispered like private talk.
The roar and the whisper tangled together, like big pearls and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding among flowers, or a spring choked beneath ice.
The ice spring grew cold, the strings froze and broke; the sound, blocked and halted, ceased for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment were born; in that moment, silence was more than sound.

On the Xunyang River bank at night I saw a friend off;

My host dismounted, the guest was already in the boat;

Drunk, yet not merry, sad at parting,

Then from the water came the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
the music stopped, and she seemed reluctant to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear,
added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls she finally emerged,
still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few notes;
before any tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Every string pressed down, every note filled with thought,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled longing.
With lowered brows she played on, unhurried,
pouring out all the endless things within her heart.
She gathered and rolled, brushed and picked,
first the Rainbow Skirt Dance, then the Six Yao tune.
The low strings roared like a sudden rain,
the high strings whispered like private speech.
Roaring and whispering, tangled together,
like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smoothly among the flowers,
like a muffled spring flowing under ice.
The cold spring froze, the strings congealed and broke;
silence took over where the sound could go no further.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—
then silence spoke more than any sound.
As a silver vase shatters and water bursts forth,
as armored cavalry charges, blades and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept her plectrum across the strings;
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent;
only the river's heart showed the white autumn moon.
Thoughtfully she put down the plectrum and tucked it in,
straightened her clothes and rose with solemn bearing.
She said she had been a girl of the capital,
living below Hama Hill.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
her name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When she finished a song even the masters were impressed;
when she dressed up, the beauties envied her.
The young gallants of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts;
a single song earned her countless bolts of red silk.
Her jeweled comb broke beating time;
her crimson skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Joy followed joy, year after year,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed in idle ease.
Then her younger brother went to war, her aunt died;
night gave way to day and her beauty faded.
Before her gate the carriage tracks grew sparse;
aging, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit and cared little for parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone at the river's mouth in an empty boat,
the moon bright around her, the river water cold.
In the deep night she suddenly dreams of her youth,
wakes weeping, the rouge on her cheeks streaked with tears.
I had sighed already at the pipa's sound;
hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us are lost souls at the ends of the earth—
why must we have met before to know each other?
Since last year I left the capital,
exiled and ailing here in Xunyang.
This place is remote and has no music;
all year I never hear a string or flute.
I live near the Pan River, low and damp,
surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons mourning.
On flowered spring mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude squawking is hard to bear.

like celestial music, my ears made clear again.

and I will turn it into this Pipa Song.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long moment,
then sat back and tightened the strings; they quickened.

everyone in the room wept upon hearing it again.
Who wept the most among us all?
The江州司馬, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

My host dismounts, my guest remains on board; 
raising wine, I would drink—but no music plays. 
Not drunk, yet grief shadows our parting— 
the sea lost in moonlight as we drift apart. 
Suddenly, a pipa's voice from the water: 
my host forgets to return, my guest halts his sail. 
I follow the sound, ask softly who is playing— 
the pipa stops, words hesitate in silence. 
I steer my boat near, invite her to appear, 
add wine, turn up lamps, relight the feast. 
After many calls, she comes—half-hiding her face behind the lute. 
She turns the axis, plucks two or three strings— 
before any tune begins, feeling stirs. 
Each string mourns, each note breathes sorrow— 
like the unspoken ache of a life unfulfilled. 
Bending low, fingers glide through the melody, 
expressing all that heart could not say. 
Softly combing, slowly picking, brushing, flicking— 
first 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Sixth Aria.' 
The deep strings roar like rushing rain, 
the thin ones whisper like private talk. 
Harmonies clash, rush, blend— 
as pearls large and small fall on jade. 
A bird’s song slips through flowers, smooth and light, 
then a hidden spring struggles beneath ice. 
Cold water chokes the strings, they freeze, stop— 
a pause, no sound, but silence speaks louder than sound. 
A silver bottle bursts, liquid gushes out; 
then iron cavalry charges, blades and spears cry. 
At last, the final stroke across the center— 
four strings snap like torn silk. 
East and west ships hush, no word spoken— 
only the moon white over the river’s heart. 
She pauses, leans the pick into the strings, 
adjusts her robes, composes herself. 
She says: I was born in the capital city, 
my home once beneath the Frog-Mound Lane. 
At thirteen, my pipa mastered— 
ranked first in the Imperial Training School. 
After each performance, even masters bowed to me; 
my face adorned, every beauty envied me. 
Nobles’ youths vied to throw gifts— 
one song, endless silks. 
Pearl-studded hairpins shattered with rhythm; 
red silk skirts stained by wine. 
Year after year of laughter, spring and autumn—the time passed easily. 
But my brother went off to war, my aunt died— 
day after day, youth fades. 
My gate grows empty, horses and saddles few— 
old now, I married a merchant. 
He seeks profit, despises parting— 
last month, he sailed to Fuliang, bought tea. 
Now I stay here, alone on the river’s mouth, 
surrounded by moonlight, cold water. 
Deep in night, I dream of youth again— 
awake, sobbing, tears streak my rouge. 
Hearing her pipa, I sigh—
hearing this tale, I sigh again. 
We’re both castaways on life’s distant shore— 
why must we have known before to meet? 
Last year I left the imperial city— 
now exiled, sick, in Xunyang. 
This place is remote, no music heard— 
all year, not a single flute or zither. 
Near Pien River, damp and low— 
cattails and bitter bamboo grow around my house. 
What do I hear at morning and eve? 
Cuckoos bleed, apes wail in pain. 
Spring mornings, flowered nights, autumn moons— 
often I pour wine, drink alone. 
Are there no mountain ballads, no village flutes? 
But their noise grates, hard to endure. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech— 
it sounds like celestial music, ears awaken. 
Do not refuse—sit and play one more piece— 
for you, I’ll compose a poem called ‘Pipa Xing.’ 
Moved by my words, she stands long silent— 
then sits, tightens the strings, the music quickens. 
Now the music grieves—not as before— 
all seated weep, covering faces. 
Who weeps most among us all? 
Jiangzhou’s governor in green robe, wet with tears."}

still holding the lute half-concealing her face.

before the tune begins, emotion already flows.

like a life unfulfilled, yearning for release.

her fingers unfolding endless sorrows.

first 'Feather Dress,' then 'Sixth Yew.'

the thin ones hiss like whispered secrets.

pearls rolling on jade plates, bright and clear.

like a stream beneath ice, choked and strained.

then silence—suspended, breathless.

this silence surpasses all sound.

then cavalry charges, swords clashing in war.

four strings snap once—a sound like torn silk.

only the river’s heart bathed in autumn moonlight.

adjusts her clothes, composes herself.

every makeup made others envious.

a red sash given again and again. 
Silver hairpins shattered by beat, 
drenched in wine, stained with blood-red skirts. 
Year after year, laughter, joy, 
while spring and autumn passed without care.

day after day, my beauty faded.

old now, married a merchant.

the moon circles the empty boat, the river chills.

tears fall, streaking paint across my face. 
Hearing her lute, I sigh—I hear her words, and sigh again. 
We are both lost souls on the same desolate earth— 
why must we have met before to know such pain?

now exiled, ill, living in Xunyang.

My host dismounts, the guest boards the boat; raising wine, we long to drink, yet no music plays.
Drunk, we cannot feign joy as sorrowful parting looms—the vast river mirrors the moon, dim and cold.
Suddenly, a lute’s voice rises from the water—my host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey.
I seek its source, whispering softly—who plays? The lute falls silent, hesitant to speak.
I move my boat near, invite the player to meet; pour more wine, turn up the lamp, relight the feast.
After many calls, she appears, still holding the lute half-concealed by her face.
She turns the axle, plucks two or three strings—before any tune takes shape, emotion stirs.
Each string suppressed, each note laden with longing—as if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams.
Bowing low, she plays on, hand following hand: all her hidden sorrows laid bare.
Lightly pressing, slowly plucking, sweeping then lifting—first *Nights at the Rainbow*, then *Sixth Flute*.
Loud strings crash like sudden rain, soft ones whisper like private talk.
Crash and whisper entwined, pearls rolling on jade—large, small, scattered.
A swift bird’s song glides beneath blossoms, deep, choked, as spring water strains under ice.
Cold and stiff, the strings freeze—silence breaks, sound pauses.
Another grief stirs in silence—no sound now speaks louder than sound.
A silver pitcher shatters—water spurts forth; iron cavalry charges, blades clash.
The final stroke draws across the heart—four strings snap once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall quiet, only the autumn moon shines white on the river's heart.
She rests her fingers, slips them into the strings; adjusts her robe, composes her face.
She says: 'Born a girl of the capital city, home beneath the Frog Hill.
At thirteen, I learned the lute—ranked first among the Imperial Academy’s troupe.
After every piece, even masters bowed in awe; after every makeup, beauty queens envied me.
Young nobles vied to shower me with silken robes—one song, countless lengths;
Tinsel hairpins shattered with rhythm, crimson skirts stained with wine spills.
Happy years pass into next—autumn moons, spring breezes, all brushed aside.
My brother left for war, my aunt passed away—dawn fades, dusk returns, and beauty wanes.
My gate grows cold, horse and rider few—old now, married a merchant.
Merchants care for profit, not parting—last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I stay at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat—moonlight circles us, riverside cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth—awake, crying, tears stain my rouge-stained cheeks.
Hearing her lute, I sigh—then hear her words again, more deeply stirred.
We’re both lost souls adrift on the same desolate shore—why must we have met before?
I left the imperial capital last year—exiled, ill, lying in Xunyang.
Xunyang’s remote, no music heard; whole years pass without strings or bamboo.
Near Pienjiang, land low and damp—yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow thick around my home.
What sounds fill my days and nights? Crows bleeding red, gibbons mourning in the mountains.
On spring mornings, moonlit evenings—often I pour wine alone, to no one.
Are there no folk songs, village flutes? But their cries are harsh, grating—hard to endure.
Tonight, hearing your lute, it’s like listening to celestial music—ears refreshed, even briefly clear.
Do not refuse—sit, play one more piece—for you I’ll compose this lute-sung ballad.
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence—then sits, tightens the strings, quickens the beat.
The music now, sad, bears no likeness to what came before—all present cry anew.
