By Bai Juyi

That autumn night at Xunyang I was seeing a guest off,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the chill.
I had dismounted, my guest was in the boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in gloom—
the river drowned in moonlight at our farewell.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
I forgot to go home, my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I softly asked who played;
the music stopped, as if she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat near and invited her to meet;
added wine, relit the lamps, and feasted once again.
After a thousand calls she finally emerged,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She tuned the strings and played a note or two—
before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted, each note a sigh,
seeming to tell a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered eyes, idly, she went on playing,
recounting all the boundless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow rubbing, sweeping and plucking—
first the Rainbow Garment, then the Six Minor tune.
The low strings roared like sudden rain;
the high strings whispered like private speech.
The roar and whisper interlaced and crossed—
like great pearls and small pearls spilling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
like a muffled spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings congealed and broke;
silence fell where the sound could go no further.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose:
here, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Then—like a silver vase bursting, water gushing forth,
or armored cavalry charging with swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the拨 across all four strings—
one cry, like silk being torn apart.
In every boat around us, no one spoke;
only the autumn moon on the river, white and bright.
Thoughtfully she tucked the拨 among the strings,
straightened her clothes, and rose with solemn grace.
She said she had been a girl of the capital,
living near Hama Hill.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After each song even the finest musicians were humbled;
every time she dressed, the courtesans were jealous.
Young men from Wuling competed to lavish gifts on her;
for one song, bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Jeweled combs snapped keeping time, their ornaments broken;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Laughing one year, then the next—
autumn moons and spring breezes passing by unmindful.
Then her brother went to war, her aunt died;
night followed day, and her beauty faded.
Fewer horses stopped before her door;
grown old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit over parting;
last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone she keeps the empty boat at the river's mouth,
surrounded by bright moonlight and cold water.
Late at night she dreams of her youth,
and wakes weeping, her rouge-streaked tears staining her face.

now hearing her words, I sighed again.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains on board;
Toasting with wine, yet no music plays to fill.
Drunk, we cannot rejoice—sorrow marks our parting,
As dusk descends, the river mirrors a vast moon.
Suddenly, from water’s depths, a lute’s sweet sound arises;
The host forgets his way home, the guest halts his departure.
Following the melody, I softly ask who plays;
The lute falls silent—words delay, then fade away.
I urge the boat closer, invite her to appear,
Add wine, turn lamps high, renew the feast again.
After many calls, she comes at last,
Still holding the lute half-concealed by her face.
She turns the axle, plucks the strings three or four times—
Before a tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each note veiled, each tone a sigh; it seems to tell
Of lifelong struggles, dreams unfulfilled.
Bowing her head, fingers move with quiet grace,
Pouring out endless sorrows from her heart.
Gently brushing, slowly pressing, flicking, sliding,
First she plays 'Fei Cai,' then 'Liu Yao'—the old dance tunes.
The deep strings thunder like a stormy downpour;
The light ones whisper soft as lovers' talk.
A clash of thunder and whispers, mingling loud and clear,
Big pearls and small spill like gems upon jade.
Like a bird gliding through blossoms, voices smooth and bright;
Like cold spring water choked beneath ice, a stifled cry.
Ice-cold springs, tense strings, silence reigns in pause,
Then, in that stillness, deeper grief emerges—more powerful than sound.
A silver pitcher cracks—water bursts forth;
Iron cavalry charge, swords and spears ring out in war.
When the final stroke cuts through the heart, the strings snap with a shriek;
Four strings crash once, as if silk tore apart.
East and west boats fall hushed, silent as stone;
Only the moon above the river's heart shines white.
After a pause, she lays her pick aside,
Adjusts her robe, composes her face, then speaks:

At thirteen, I learned the pipa to perfection;
My name was listed first among the Imperial Academy’s stars.
After each piece, even the master praised me;
After each makeup, the beauties envied me.
Young nobles vied to shower me with silk;
One song brought me more red sashes than I could count.
Tinsel hairpins shattered with each beat;
Crimson gowns stained with wine, turned crimson with blood.
Year after year, joy and laughter passed like seasons,
Spring blooms, autumn moons—all drifted by without care.
But now my brother has gone to war, my aunt is dead;
Days pass, nights pass—my beauty fades.
My front gate is empty, few horsemen come;
Old and worn, I married a merchant man.
He values profit, not reunion—just last month,
He sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he’s gone—on the river mouth I guard an empty boat,
Moonlight circles around me, the river runs cold.
Deep in the night, I dream of youth’s days,
Dreaming I weep, my painted tears streak red and wet.
Hearing this lute, I sigh—then hear her words again;
How deeply moved! And now I know: We’re both exiles,
Far from home, lost souls—why need we have met before?
I left the imperial capital last year;
Exiled and ill, I’ve lived in Xunyang City ever since.
Xunyang lies remote, scarce music to be heard;
For year on year, no string nor bamboo sounds near.
Near Pienjiang, where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my home.
What sounds do I hear each day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding their hearts, apes wailing in pain.
In spring, when flowers bloom, or autumn moon beams bright,
I often pour wine alone, drinking to solitude.
Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But their harsh cries make me want to flee.
Tonight, hearing your lute tones, my ears feel heavenly,
As if listening to gods’ music—briefly awake!
Do not refuse another tune, for your sake,
I shall compose a poem called 'The Pipa Player.'
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then returns, quickens the strings—now the music grows fast.
The sorrowful notes no longer match the earlier ones;
All seated, hearing again, we all cover our faces in tears.
Who weeps the most among us? The Jiangzhou magistrate’s green robe—wet with tears."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, my friend stepped into his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or flute.
Drunk, yet not merry, we parted in gloom,
And the vast river swallowed the moon as we said goodbye.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a lute;
I forgot to go home, my friend delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat near and invited her to meet;
Poured more wine, relit the lanterns, and the banquet began again.
After a thousand calls, she finally came out,
Still hugging her lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked three or two strings;
Before a tune was formed, emotion already filled them.
Every string choked with feeling, every note steeped in thought,
As if telling the sorrows of a life unfulfilled.
Brow lowered, she casually plucked on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Light strokes, slow twists, sweeps and flicks—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
The thick strings roared like a sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled in play,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly under blossoms,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring froze, the strings snapped in silence;
The silence broke, and the sound paused for a while.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose;
In that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
She ended the tune with a sweep across the center;
Four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fell silent;
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river.
Pensively she tucked the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living below Toad Hill.
At thirteen she mastered the lute,
Ranked first in the Music Academy.
When her tune ended, even masters were impressed;
When her makeup was done, even beauties were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, the red silk gifts were beyond counting.
Silver combs with jeweled pins shattered to keep the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Moonlit autumns and spring winds passed lightly.
Then her brother left for the army, her aunt died;
Dusk came and went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door the carriages grew few and cold;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone at the river mouth in an empty boat,
The moon bright around her, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth;
In the dream she weeps, her tears cutting red lines through her makeup.
Hearing the lute, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill to this city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbons’ mournful howl.
On flower-filled spring days, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Not that there are no mountain songs or village flutes—
The harsh, grating sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your lute’s language,
As if hearing celestial music, my ears briefly clear.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
For you, I’ll turn this into a *Song of the Lute*.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and quickened the pace.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole audience wept as they listened again.
Who among us wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "One night by the Xunyang River I was seeing off a friend,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, my friend stepped into his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or flute.
Drunk, yet not merry, we parted in gloom,
And the vast river swallowed the moon as we said goodbye.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a lute;
I forgot to go home, my friend delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat near and invited her to meet;
Poured more wine, relit the lanterns, and the banquet began again.
After a thousand calls, she finally came out,
Still hugging her lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked three or two strings;
Before a tune was formed, emotion already filled them.
Every string choked with feeling, every note steeped in thought,
As if telling the sorrows of a life unfulfilled.
Brow lowered, she casually plucked on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Light strokes, slow twists, sweeps and flicks—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
The thick strings roared like a sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled in play,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly under blossoms,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring froze, the strings snapped in silence;
The silence broke, and the sound paused for a while.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose;
In that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
She ended the tune with a sweep across the center;
Four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fell silent;
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river.
Pensively she tucked the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living below Toad Hill.
At thirteen she mastered the lute,
Ranked first in the Music Academy.
When her tune ended, even masters were impressed;
When her makeup was done, even beauties were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, the red silk gifts were beyond counting.
Silver combs with jeweled pins shattered to keep the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Moonlit autumns and spring winds passed lightly.
Then her brother left for the army, her aunt died;
Dusk came and went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door the carriages grew few and cold;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone at the river mouth in an empty boat,
The moon bright around her, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth;
In the dream she weeps, her tears cutting red lines through her makeup.
Hearing the lute, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill to this city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbons’ mournful howl.
On flower-filled spring days, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Not that there are no mountain songs or village flutes—
The harsh, grating sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your lute’s language,
As if hearing celestial music, my ears briefly clear.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
For you, I’ll turn this into a *Song of the Lute*.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and quickened the pace.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole audience wept as they listened again.
Who among us wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "One night by the Xunyang River I was seeing off a friend,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, my friend stepped into his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no lute or flute.
Drunk, yet not merry, we parted in gloom,
And the vast river swallowed the moon as we said goodbye.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a lute;
I forgot to go home, my friend delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, and she hesitated to reply.
We moved our boat near and invited her to meet;
Poured more wine, relit the lanterns, and the banquet began again.
After a thousand calls, she finally came out,
Still hugging her lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked three or two strings;
Before a tune was formed, emotion already filled them.
Every string choked with feeling, every note steeped in thought,
As if telling the sorrows of a life unfulfilled.
Brow lowered, she casually plucked on and on,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Light strokes, slow twists, sweeps and flicks—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
The thick strings roared like a sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, tangled in play,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly under blossoms,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring froze, the strings snapped in silence;
The silence broke, and the sound paused for a while.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment, arose;
In that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
She ended the tune with a sweep across the center;
Four strings cracked as one, like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fell silent;
Only the autumn moon, white in the heart of the river.
Pensively she tucked the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her robes, rose, and composed her face.
She said she was once a girl of the capital,
Living below Toad Hill.
At thirteen she mastered the lute,
Ranked first in the Music Academy.
When her tune ended, even masters were impressed;
When her makeup was done, even beauties were jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower her with gifts;
For one song, the red silk gifts were beyond counting.
Silver combs with jeweled pins shattered to keep the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Moonlit autumns and spring winds passed lightly.
Then her brother left for the army, her aunt died;
Dusk came and went, and her beauty faded.
Before her door the carriages grew few and cold;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone at the river mouth in an empty boat,
The moon bright around her, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth;
In the dream she weeps, her tears cutting red lines through her makeup.
Hearing the lute, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, deeper.
Both of us are wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill to this city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no lute or flute.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo’s bloody cry, the gibbons’ mournful howl.
On flower-filled spring days, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Not that there are no mountain songs or village flutes—
The harsh, grating sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your lute’s language,
As if hearing celestial music, my ears briefly clear.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
For you, I’ll turn this into a *Song of the Lute*.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and quickened the pace.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole audience wept as they listened again.
Who among us wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

Still hugging her lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked three or two strings;

For one song, the red silk gifts were beyond counting.

Moonlit autumns and spring winds passed lightly.

The moon bright around her, the river water cold.

The maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
The Host dismounted while the guest boarded the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but no lute or strings were there.
Drunk without joy, we prepared to part in sorrow,
At parting, the vast river was soaked in the moon.
Suddenly we heard the sound of a lute upon the water,
The Host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, we asked in whispers who was playing,
The lute stopped, and she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat near hers and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted again.
After a thousand calls she finally emerged,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before the melody began, the emotion was there.
Each string sounded suppressed, each note filled with thought,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, she played on with ease,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly strummed, slowly rubbed, plucked and picked,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Little Orchard."
The thick strings roared like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
The roaring and whispering mingled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Sometimes like orioles singing smoothly beneath the flowers,
Sometimes like a spring choked under the ice.
The ice-cold spring froze, the strings seemed to snap,
Snapped and blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment rose,
At this moment, silence was better than sound.
Suddenly, a silver bottle broke, water gushing out,
Armored horsemen charging, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended with a stroke across the center,
Four strings sounded as one, like tearing silk.
The boats east and west were silent in awe,
Only seeing the autumn moon pure white in the river's heart.
Thoughtfully she put the plectrum among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was originally a girl of the capital,
Living below the Hama Ling.
At thirteen she mastered the lute,
Her name was listed in the First Division of the Imperial Bureau.
After playing, even the best players admired her,
When dressed, she was envied by all the famed beauties.
The Youth of Wuling competed to shower her with gifts,
For one song, silk scarves were countless.
Silver combs with gold ornaments were broken to keep time,
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed by in vain.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died,
Evenings turned to mornings, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, carriages grew rare and cold,
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting,
Last month he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She comes and goes at the river mouth, guarding the empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth,
Waking from crying, her tears streaked her red makeup.
I had sighed upon hearing the lute,
Hearing her words, I sighed again.
We are both drifters at the end of the world,
Why must we have known each other before to meet?

Exiled and ill in Xunyang city.

All year round one hears no sound of strings.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the riverbank of Xunyang, late at night I saw a guest off, with maple leaves and reed flowers trembling in the autumn chill.
I dismounted to greet the guest, who remained aboard the boat; raising a cup to drink, yet no music played to accompany us.
Drunk but unable to rejoice, we faced sorrowful parting—our farewells blurred beneath the moon reflected in the vast, silent river.
Suddenly, from the water’s surface, a pipa melody arose—my host forgot to return, my guest paused mid-departure.
I searched for its source, softly asking, 'Who is playing?' The sound ceased as if hesitating to speak.
I moved my boat closer, invited the player to come forth, added wine, turned down the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After many calls, she finally appeared, still holding the pipa half-concealed by her face.
She tuned the axis, plucked a few hesitant notes—before even forming a tune, emotion was already there.
Each note veiled sorrow, each tone carried longing—like one speaking of a life unfulfilled.
Bending her head, her fingers moved on, playing without pause, revealing all the endless sorrows in her heart.
Gently touching, slowly pressing, gliding and flicking: first the 'Feathered Garment,' then the 'Six Yao.'
The thick strings thundered like heavy rain, the thin ones whispered like private talk.
A cacophony of overlapping sounds: great beads and small beads tumbling upon jade plates.
Like a bird's song slipping through blossoms, smooth and bright; like a hidden spring choked beneath ice, struggling to flow.
Ice-cold springs slowed, strings stiffened into silence—then silence itself held breath.
Another deep, hidden grief stirred—this silence surpassed any sound.
A silver bottle shattering, water gushing forth; a cavalry charge, swords and spears clashing.
At the end, the pick struck the center of the strings—four strings rang out as if tearing silk.
Eastward and westward boats fell utterly still, not a word spoken—only the autumn moon white above the river's heart.
Thoughtful, I placed the pick down among the strings, adjusted my clothes, composed myself, and raised my expression.
She said: 'I was born in the capital city, lived beneath the Frog-Mound Lane.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, ranked among the first in the Imperial Academy.
After a performance, even the master musician could not help but praise me; after dressing, I’d be envied by the famed Madame Qiu.
Young men from noble families vied to shower me with gifts—each song earned countless red silks.
My jeweled hairpins shattered with rhythmic beat; my crimson skirts stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Year after year, laughter and joy passed—autumn moons and spring breezes slipped away carelessly.
My brother left for war, my aunt died; days fled, and youth faded.
Front gate grew cold, horse and rider few—old now, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit, care little for parting—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He has been gone, leaving me alone on the shore, my boat empty—moonlight circling, river cold around me.
Deep in the night, I dreamt of youth—awoke weeping, makeup streaked red across my cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply; hearing her tale again, I felt even more sorrow.
We are both wanderers lost far from home—why must we have met before to understand?
I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, bedridden in this remote Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music—whole years pass without hearing string or bamboo.
Near Penvi River, the land is low and damp—yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my dwelling.
What do I hear day and night among these? Crows crying blood, apes mourning in grief.
In spring mornings, in autumn nights, I often pour wine alone.
Are there no hill songs or rustic flutes? But their jarring, shrill tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa music, it feels like listening to celestial melodies—my ears suddenly clear.
Please don’t refuse—sit once more and play another piece—for you I’ll compose this poem, 'Pipa Xing.'
Moved by my words, she stood silent for a long time—then sat back, tightened the strings, which grew sharper.
Her music now sounded sadder than before—every seat filled with tears.
Who shed the most tears here? The Jiangzhou magistrate, his blue robe soaked with salt."}

At Xunyang River's edge I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but no music greets our throat.
Drunk, yet not cheered, we grieve at parting near,
The vast river swallowed by the moon, cold and clear.
When suddenly from the water a pipa's strain,
The host forgets to leave, the guest stays on the plain.
We seek the sound and softly ask who plays,
The music stops; she hesitates, half lost in daze.
Our boats we move aside, invite her to appear,
More wine we pour, relight the lamps, and hold the feast once more.
After a thousand calls she finally appears,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face in tears.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings, three or four sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion already resounds.
Each string a sigh, each note a dream,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled, a broken dream.
With lowered eyes, she idly plays on and on,
Telling all the heart's unbounded woes and endless song.
With light strokes and slow pinches, plucking and flicking away,
First she plays "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Yao" at play.
The low strings rumble like sudden rain,
The high strings whisper like secrets in the lane.
The rumble and whisper intertwine in the flight,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate bright.
Like orioles singing swift beneath the flowers' bloom,
Or a muffled spring flowing beneath the ice's gloom.
The icy spring freezes, the strings' sound dies away,
The flow stops, the sound ceases, and silence holds its sway.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief now grows,
At this moment, silence is sweeter than sound that flows.
Then—like a silver vase bursting, water rushing out,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords and spears in a shout.
The tune ends with a sweep across the strings' heart,
Four strings crack as one, like silk being torn apart.
In boats east and west, all sit in hushed dismay,
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart is seen to sway.
Pensively she tucks her pick among the strings,
Adjusts her garments and rises, her solemn bearing rings.
She speaks: "I was once a girl of the capital's fame,
My home was by Homa Tomb, near the river's name.
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Ranked first among the Music Bureau's performers' part.
When I finished a song, even masters bowed in praise,
When I dressed up, the beauties were jealous of my days.
The dandies of Wuling competed to lavish me with gifts,
For one song, countless rolls of red silk my casket lifts.
Jeweled combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine, oh so sweet.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed, careless and light.
But my brother went to war, my aunt passed away,
Day and night went by, and my youth's glow did decay.
Before my gate, fewer and fewer horses tied,
I married, grown old, a merchant as my guide.
The merchant values profit over love's embrace,
Last month he left for Fuliang to trade in tea's grace.
Alone at the river's mouth I guard an empty boat,
The moon bright around me, the river water cold afloat.
Deep in the night, I dream of my youthful past,
I wake crying, my tears staining my rouge-stained mask." 

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed in pain,
Hearing her words, I sigh again, again and again.
We are both lost souls at the edge of the sky;
Why must we have met before to greet each other's sigh?
Since last year I left the capital's bright scene,
Demoted and sick, I lie in Xunyang, where I've been.
This place is remote, with no music to be found,
Year-round, no sound of strings or flutes can be heard around.
I live near the river, the land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my camp.
What do I hear from morning till night's deep breath?
Only cuckoos crying blood and gibbons' mournful death.
On spring river days and autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone in the light.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes to hear?"Their cracked, jarring sounds are harsh upon the ear.
But hearing your pipa tonight is like hearing celestial strains,
My ears, for a moment, are cleared of all their pains.
Please do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
I will compose 'Song of the Pipa Player' for you, to last long." 

Moved by my words, she stands for a long time in thought,
Then sits back, tightens the strings, and plays with all she's got.
The mournful notes are not like the sounds before,
The whole audience, hearing it again, weeps, wanting more.
Among the weeping, who weeps the most, pray tell?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue gown is soaked in the swell."}

One autumn night at Xunyang River I was seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the chill.
I dismounted, my guest boarded the boat;

Drunk without cheer, we parted in gloom—
the parting moonlight drowned in the vast river.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
forgotten was my going home, the guest delayed his departure.
Seeking the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
the pipa stopped, as if loath to speak.
I moved my boat nearer and invited her to appear;

After countless calls she at last came out,

She tuned the pegs, plucked the strings—two, three notes;
before a melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string a sigh of suppressed sorrow, each note a thought,
as if telling the unfulfilled wishes of her life.
Brow lowered, at ease she played on and on,
voicing all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow kneading, sweeping, picking—
first the Rainbow Garment, then the Six-Folds.
On the thick strings, a patter like sudden rain;
on the thin, a whisper like private speech.
Rain and whisper interwoven in the playing—
like great pearls and small falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly under flowers,
then like a choked stream beneath the ice.
The ice-stream grew cold, the strings seemed frozen,
frozen, blocked—the sound rested for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose:
then, silence spoke more than sound.
Then—like a silver vase bursting, water gushing,
or iron cavalry charging, swords and lances clanging—
at the end she swept the拨 across the middle of the strings;
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
In boats east and west, all sat in hushed silence;
only the autumn moon on the river, white and bright.
Thoughtfully she tucked拨 the拨 between her strings,

At thirteen I mastered the pipa,

When I finished a song, even masters were impressed;
dressed up, I was envied by the courtesans.
The young men of Wuling competed to lavish gifts on me;
for one song, bolts of red silk past counting.

crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed another,
autumn moons and spring winds passed by unheeded.
My brother went to the army, my aunt died;
night and day went by, my beauty faded.

old, I married a merchant.

I live near the marshy lowlands of Pen River,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

The cuckoo's bloody cries, the gibbons' mournful howls.
On flower-laden spring days, moonlit autumn nights,

Tonight, hearing your pipa,
is like hearing celestial music—my ears at last find light.
Do not refuse; sit and play once more,
and I will compose a Song of the Pipa for you.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
then sat back, tightened the strings—faster, more urgent.
The mournful sound unlike what came before;
all who sat there wept into their sleeves.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "The River Jiang, on a moonlit night, I bid farewell to my guest; maple leaves and reeds in autumn shiver. The host dismounts, the guest remains on the boat; raising a cup to drink, yet no music plays. Drunk, we can't find joy in parting, as we leave amidst the moon reflected in the vast river. Suddenly, the sound of a pipa floats across the water, the host forgets to return, the guest halts his journey. Following the sound, I softly ask who plays; the pipa stops, hesitating to speak. I move my boat near theirs, inviting a meeting, adding wine, turning lamps back on, and renewing the feast. After many calls, she finally appears, still holding her pipa half-concealing her face. Tuning the axle and plucking the strings with a few strokes, before any tune begins, emotion already fills the air. Each string is suppressed, each note filled with sorrow—like expressing a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams. Lowering her eyes, she continues playing, her fingers gliding smoothly, telling all the endless matters within her heart. Lightly brushing, slowly pressing, dragging and plucking—all beginning with 'Rainbow Skirt' then 'Six Yao'. The thick strings sound like heavy rain, the thin ones whisper like private talk. A jumble of loud and soft notes, like large and small pearls falling onto jade plates. Intermittent, like a swallow's song through blossoms, or a choked spring beneath ice. Cold, icy springs slow down, strings stiffen and stop, the silence brief but profound. Another kind of hidden sorrow arises, where silence speaks louder than sound. Suddenly, a silver bottle bursts, water gushes forth; iron cavalry charges forth, swords and spears clash. At the end, the pick strikes the center, four strings sound at once like torn silk. East and west boats fall silent, only the autumn moon shines upon the river’s heart. She pauses, leans the pick into the strings, composes herself, straightens her clothes, and solemnly assumes her demeanor. She says: 'I was born in the capital city, living at the foot of the Toad Hill. At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, my name listed among the first in the Imperial Music Academy. After finishing a piece, even the master musician admired me; after styling my hair, I was envied by Qiu Niang. Young men from the Five Tombs district vied to give me gifts; one song earned me countless lengths of red silk. My jeweled hairpin shattered with the rhythm, crimson robes stained with wine spilled. Years pass in laughter and joy, while spring moons and autumn breezes drift by carelessly. My brother went off to war, my foster mother passed away; day after day, my beauty fades. The gate grows cold, fewer horses and riders come by; old, I married a merchant. Merchants value profit more than parting; last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea. He departed, leaving me guarding an empty boat by the river mouth, surrounded by moonlight, with cold river water. Deep in the night, I dream of my youthful days, crying in my makeup, tears streaming down my cheeks. Hearing this pipa story, I sigh deeply; hearing these words again, I'm moved even more. We are both lost souls adrift in the world, why must we have met before to understand? I left the imperial capital last year, exiled and ill, living in Xunyang. Xunyang lies remote, without music; for a whole year, I’ve heard no strings or bamboo. Near Pienjiang, land low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home. What sounds do I hear at dawn and dusk? Crows bleeding their voices, apes mourning. On spring mornings with flowers, on autumn nights under the moon, I often pour wine alone. Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? Yet they’re harsh and shrill, hard to endure. Tonight, hearing your pipa, it feels like heavenly music, my ears suddenly clear. Please don’t refuse to play another piece—for you, I’ll compose this 'Pipa Song'. Moved by my words, she stands motionless for a long while, then sits down, quickening the strings, which grow sharper. The sorrowful tones now differ from before; everyone in the audience covers their faces, weeping. Who among the crowd sheds the most tears? The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe is wet."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "SEEING A GUEST OFF AT Xunyang River one autumn night,
The maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the cold.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
They raised cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk without joy, they parted in sorrow;
At parting, the river was a blur of moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, they asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to answer.
They moved their boat nearer and invited her to appear;
They added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few strings;
Before the melody formed, feeling already filled them.
Each string, each note, was muted and pensive,
As if telling a life of unfulfilled desires.
Brow lowered, idly her fingers kept moving,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
She plucked and stroked, swept and picked—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
The low strings roared like sudden rain;
The high strings whispered like private talk.
The roaring and whispering wove together,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among flowers,
Or a spring choking under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and stopped;
Frozen and blocked, the sound ceased for a time.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment arose—
In that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then a silver vase burst, water gushing forth;
Armored cavalry charged, swords and spears ringing.
The song ended: she drew the pick across the center;
All four strings snapped at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent;
Only the autumn moon over the river shone white.
Pensive, she tucked the pick among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said: “I was once a girl of the capital,
Living at the foot of Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first among the performers of the court.
When I finished a song, even master players were impressed;
When I made up, even famous beauties were jealous.
The young nobles of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Ornamental combs and silver hairpins snapped to the beat;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter and joy,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed us by.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Dawn came and dusk went, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit and care little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I wait by the river mouth in my empty boat;
Around the boat, the moon is bright, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
I wake weeping, my makeup streaked with tears.”
I had sighed at hearing her pipa;
Hearing her words, I sighed again.
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
Since last year I left the capital;
I have lived in exile, sick, in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pan River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling mournfully.
On flower-moonlit spring days or autumn nights,
I often take my cup and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, grating sound is hard to endure.
Tonight, hearing your pipa,
It is like hearing celestial music—my ears come alive.
Do not refuse; sit and play another song,
And I will compose a *Pipa Song* for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat again, tightened the strings, and played faster.
The mournful notes were unlike before;
The whole audience wept upon hearing them again.
Who in the room wept the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River's edge I was seeing off a guest one night,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded his boat;
raising our cups to drink, we had no music.
Drunk, but not merry, we were about to part in gloom—
when we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to go home, the guest forgot to depart.
Following the sound, we softly asked who was playing;
the pipa stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear;
added wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls and entreaties she finally came out,
still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
before the tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Every string, every phrase, was choked with sorrow,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Lowering her eyes, she played on easily and without care,
pouring out all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
she played first "Rainbow Skirts" and then "Six Minor."
The low strings rumbled like a rushing rain,
the high strings whispered like intimate talk.
The rumble and the whisper, mingled and crossed,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly among the flowers,
or a hidden stream choked under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings grew stiff and broke;
the sound, blocked, came to a pause.
A deeper sorrow, a hidden grief arose—
that silence said more than any sound.
Then a silver vase smashed, water bursting forth;
an armored charge, sabers and spears clashing.
At the song's end she drew the pick across all four strings—
with one great sound, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were hushed and speechless;
we saw only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.
Musing, she tucked the pick among the strings,
straightened her clothes, and rose with a solemn face.
She spoke: "I was once a girl of the capital,
living near Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
and my name headed the rolls of the court troupe.
My playing once made the masters bow,
and my beauty was the envy of the courtesans.
Young gallants of Wuling competed to shower me with gifts;
a single song earned me countless bolts of red silk.
Silver pins and combs were broken to keep the beat,
and my crimson silk skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and delight,
the autumn moons and spring breezes passed me by.
My younger brother left for the army, my aunt died;
day by day my beauty faded.
Before my gate the carriages grew few and cold,
and in my old age I married a merchant.
But merchants care more for profit than for parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
So I wait alone by the river in my empty boat,
the bright moon around me, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth,
and wake weeping, my rouge-streaked tears staining my face."
I had sighed already at her pipa;
now, hearing these words, I sighed again.
Both of us are lost souls at the edge of the world—
why must we have met before to understand each other?
Last year I took leave of the capital,
and here, sick and exiled, I dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no fine music;
the whole year round I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the river, on low, damp ground,
where reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild around my house.
What is there to hear, morning and evening?
Only the cuckoo's bloody cry and the gibbons' lament.
On flower-filled spring mornings, moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
It is not that there are no hill songs or village flutes,
but their harsh, grating notes are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
is like hearing the music of heaven—my ears are cleansed.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
and I will write it down for you as "The Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
then sat closer and tightened her strings—they grew faster.
The new strain, so different from before,
made everyone who heard it cover their face and weep.
And of all who wept that night, who wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue robe was soaked with tears."}

That autumn night at Xunyang I was seeing off a guest—
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the chill.
I dismounted, my guest stepped into the boat;

Drunk, with no joy, we parted in sorrow—
and as we parted, the river swallowed the moon in mist.
Then, carried over the water, the sound of a pipa:
I forgot to go home, and my guest delayed his leaving.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing.
The playing stopped; she seemed about to speak, but hesitated.
I moved my boat nearer and asked her to show herself;
we added wine, relit the lamps, and feasted again.
After a thousand calls she finally came out,
half hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings—
before the tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Each string, each note, was muted and brooding,
like telling of a life's thwarted ambitions.
Brows lowered, she played on carelessly,
telling all the countless things within her heart.
Gathering, twisting, stroking, and plucking,
she began with the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six Yao.
The lower strings roared like driving rain,
the higher strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, interlaced in playing—
big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding under the flowers,
then a choked spring struggling beneath ice.
The cold ice, the stiffened strings, broke off—
broke off and stilled, the sound a moment gone.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose:
in that moment, silence spoke more than sound.
Then—like a silver vase shattering, water bursting out,
like cavalry charging, blades and halberds clashing.
The song ended; she swept the pick across the strings—
four strings snapped together like tearing silk.
Boats east and west sat hushed and wordless;
only the autumn moon on the river shone white.
Meditating, she tucked the pick among the strings,
straightened her clothes, and composed her face.
"I was a girl from the capital, she said,
living below the Toad Mound.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
and my name stood first in the teaching quarters.
When I finished a song, even masters were convinced;
when I dressed up, the beauties envied me.
Young men from the five tombs vied for my favors—
one song, and countless bolts of red silk.
Ornamented combs broke beating time;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and song,
the spring moon and autumn breeze went by unnoticed.
My brother left for the army; my aunt died.
Dusks passed, dawns came, and my looks grew old.
Before my door, carriages grew few;
grown old, I married a merchant.
A merchant values profit and thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I keep a empty boat at the river's mouth,
the moon bright around me, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed of my youth,
and woke crying, the rouge on my cheeks in streaks."

I sighed already at the pipa's song;
owing her story, I sighed again.
Both of us are lost souls at the ends of the earth—
why must we have met before to know each other now?
Since last year I left the capital,
exiled and ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music:
all year I hear no strings or pipes.
I live near the Pen River in low, damp ground,
with yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing round my house.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?

On flower-moon spring days and autumn nights,
I often pour my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?

Tonight I heard your pipa's speech—
like hearing immortal music, my ears awoke.
Don't refuse; sit and play one more song,
and I will turn your song into a Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
then sat back and tightened the strings—they grew urgent.
The sound, so mournful, was not like the song before:
all who heard it wept, covering their faces.
Among the weepers, who wept most?
The River Prefect's blue gown was wet."}

Following the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she seemed about to speak but hesitated.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
Added wine, relit the lantern, and reopened the banquet.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, three or two sounds;
Before the tune was formed, the emotion was already there.
String after string, suppressed and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brow, idly, she continued to play,
Telling all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and plucking,
First she played 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Yao.'
The large strings rumble like rushing rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
The rumbling and whispering interlaced,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding over flowers, smooth and sweet;
Then, like a hidden stream flowing under ice, hard to pass.
The icy spring, cold and astringent, the strings congealed and stopped;\nWhen congealed and blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
A different sorrow, a hidden resentment arose;
At this moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Suddenly, a silver vase broke, water and milk gushed forth;
Armored cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept the拨 across the center of the strings;
The four strings together sounded like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all was silent;
Only the autumn moon white in the middle of the river could be seen.
Pondering, she put the拨 back among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, stood up, and composed her countenance.
She said, 'I was a girl from the capital,
My home was below the Hama Tomb.
At thirteen, I learned to play the pipa;
My name was listed in the first rank of the Teaching Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the skilled musicians admired me;
When I made up, even Qiuniang was jealous of me.
The young men of Wuling competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless red silks.
I beat time with my silver hairpin until it broke;
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and merriment,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed in vain.
My younger brother went to the army, my aunt died;
As days and months passed, my beauty faded.
The horses and carriages before my door grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit and lightly parts from his wife;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I keep a lonely boat at the river's mouth;
Around the boat, the bright moon and cold river water.
In the deep night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In my dream, I weep, my tears staining my rouge-streaked face.'

Hearing these words, I sighed again.
Both of us are wanderers at the end of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet?

I was banished and fell ill in Xunyang city.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow thick around my house.

The cuckoo crying blood and the gibbon's mournful cry.
On spring river days with flowers, or autumn moonlit nights,

Their crude and grating sound is hard to listen to.

It is like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly enlightened.

By the Xunyang River one autumn night I was seeing off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.
I dismounted from my horse while the guest boarded the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music to accompany us.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were about to part in sorrow;
The river, vast and hazy, was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly we heard a pipa playing on the water;
The host forgot to return, the guest set not sail.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The music stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet us;
We refilled the wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings three or four times;
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string, each note, was suppressed and full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
She lowered her brows and, with practiced ease, played on,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
With light touches and slow rubs, she strummed and picked,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt" and then "Six Yao."
The low strings roared like sudden rain;
The high strings whispered like private words.
The roar and whisper mingled together,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles gliding among flowers, the notes flowed smoothly;
Then, like a hidden stream under ice, they struggled to pass.
The icy spring grew cold; the strings seemed to freeze;
The sound halted, and for a moment there was silence.
Then, out of hidden sorrow and secret resentment, new music was born;
At that moment, the silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly breaking, water gushed out;
Like armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed.
The tune ended; she drew the pick across the center of the strings;
The four strings rang out as one, like tearing silk.
On east and west, in every boat, all was silent;
Only the autumn moon on the river shone white.
Pensive, she tucked the pick back among the strings;
She straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her countenance.
She said, "I was a girl from the capital,
My home was beneath Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name was listed first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the masters were impressed;
When I dressed up, the other girls were jealous.
The young men of the Five Tombs competed to reward me;
For one song, I received countless rolls of red silk.
Ornaments and silver combs were broken in the beat;
My blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
The spring moons and autumn winds passed by in vain.
My younger brother went to war, my aunt died;
Day by day, my youth and beauty faded.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
Grown old, I married a merchant.
The merchant cared more for profit than for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I wait alone in my empty boat;
Around the boat, the bright moon and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth;
In my dream, I wake crying, my tears staining my pillow."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again.
Both of us are drifters at the end of the world;
Why must we have known each other before to meet with feeling?
Last year I left the capital;\nI was demoted and lay ill in Xunyang.
Xunyang was remote and had no music;
All year I heard no strings or flutes.
I lived near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grew around my house.
What did I hear there, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood and the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river mornings and autumn moon nights,
I would often take my wine and drink alone.
Were there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They were harsh and grating, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa music,
It was like hearing celestial music; my ears were briefly refreshed.
Do not refuse; sit and play one more song,
And I will compose a "Song of the Pipa" for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then she sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sadder and sadder, unlike the sound before;
The whole audience listened again and wept.
Who in this room wept the most?

Suddenly, from the water’s surface, a pipa’s voice arises—my host forgets to return, my guest halts his departure.

A silver vase cracks open, splashing liquid forth; then cavalry charges, swords and spears clashing.

East and west, ships are hushed—only the autumn moon above the river’s heart remains bright.

We both are lost souls adrift on distant shores—why must we have met before to feel this kinship?

My home near Panchiang lies damp and low—yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my dwelling.

On the Xunyang River bank at night I saw a guest off;
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest boarded the boat;
wine was lifted for drinking, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet not merry, we grieved at parting—
when we parted, the vast river was flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
the music stopped, and she seemed slow to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear;
more wine was brought, lamps relit, the feast renewed.
After a thousand calls and ten entreaties she at last came out,
still half hiding her face behind her pipa.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times—
before a tune was formed, feeling was already there.
String after string, muted and sighing, note after note, full of thought,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled longing.
Brow lowered, carelessly and continuously she played,
recounting all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly rubbing, stroking and picking,
first she played "Rainbow Skirts," then "Little Willow."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whispered like private talk.
Roar and whisper, tangled and interlarded,
like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smoothly under the flowers,
like a muffled spring flowing beneath the ice.
The icy spring grew cold and harsh, the strings congealed and broke off;
the sound, choked and blocked, paused for a while.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment rose—
then, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
like armored cavalry charging out, sabers and spears clanging.
At the end of the song she swept the pick across the center;
four strings at once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west were silent, no one spoke;
only the autumn moon on the river's heart, white.
Musing, she set the pick among the strings, straightened her clothes, and rose with a solemn face.
She said she had once been a girl of the capital,
her home near Haima Mound.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa,
her name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When she finished a song, even the best musicians admired her;
when she made herself up, the beauties envied her.
The young men of Wuling competed to lavish gifts on her;
for one song, she received countless red silks.
Jeweled combs snapped to the beat, broken;
crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Joy after joy, year after year,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed without care.
Then her brother went off to war, her aunt died;
night followed morning, and her beauty faded.
Before her door, carriages grew few, horses scarce;
growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and lightly parted from her;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Alone she keeps the empty boat at the river's mouth;
around it, bright moonlight, river water cold.
Deep in the night she suddenly dreams of her youth;
in the dream she weeps, her makeup streaked with red tears.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing her words, I sighed again, deep within.
Both of us are people fallen to the ends of the earth—
why must we have met before to know each other?

a sick exile in Xunyang city.

all year I have not heard strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

like hearing immortal music, my ears briefly cleared.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "Xunyang River head, I saw a friend off by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn light.
I dismounted, my guest stepped aboard the boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but there was neither lute nor flute.
Drunken, but not merry, we prepared to part in gloom,
When the vast river swallowed the moonlight in the dark.
Suddenly from the water came a lute's sound,
I forgot to go back, and my guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a whisper who was playing,
The lute stopped; she hesitated to speak.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to meet,
Poured more wine, relit the lamp, and feasted anew.
After a thousand calls, she at last appeared,
Still holding the lute, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three sounds,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string was muted and brooding, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambitions.
She lowered her brows and played on with ease,
Telling all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly she strummed, slowly she plucked, swept and flicked,
First the "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Six Yao" tune.
The high strings roared like sudden rain in the sky,
The low strings whispered like secret words.
Roaring and whispering, they mingled and crossed,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding smoothly beneath the flowers,
Like a choked spring struggling under ice.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and snapped,
The sound was blocked, and for a while there was silence.
Then a hidden sorrow, a secret grief arose—
In that moment, silence was more eloquent than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the plectrum across the center,
All four strings cracked at once like tearing silk.
In the boats east and west, all sat in hushed awe,
Only the white autumn moon in the river's heart was seen.
Musing, she put the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said she was a girl of the capital,
Her home was beneath Toad Hill.
At thirteen she had mastered the lute,
Her name listed first in the Music Bureau.
After her songs, even the best players admired her,
When dressed, she was envied by the courtesans.
Young gallants from the Five Tombs competed to send her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Jeweled hairpins snapped to the beat, their ornaments broken,
Her blood-red silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed,
The autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.
Her brother went to the army, her aunt died,
Dawn and dusk went by, her beauty faded.
Few carriages and horses stopped at her door,
In old age, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
She waits alone by the river's mouth in an empty boat,
The moon shines bright around her, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
In the dream she weeps, her rouge-streaked tears staining her face.
I had already sighed on hearing the lute,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, with deeper grief.
We are both fallen souls at the ends of the earth,
Why must we have met before to share this bond?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
I have been exiled and ill in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard,
All year long, no sound of strings or flutes.
My home is near the river, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear from morning till night?
Only the cuckoo's blood-curdling cry and the gibbon's mournful howl.
On spring river flower-days, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my cup and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude, discordant noise is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your lute speak,
Is like hearing immortal music, my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Lute."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Mournful and desolate, unlike the sound before,
All who heard it wept, their tears falling.
Who among the guests wept the most?
The Marshal of Jiangzhou, his blue gown soaked through."}

I dismounted while my guest remained on board; raising a cup to drink, yet no music played to accompany us.
Half-drunk, we could not celebrate—sad as we parted, the river blurred under a moon immersed in water.
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa arose: the host forgot to return, the guest no longer set sail.
We followed the sound, whispering, asking who played—who paused mid-speech, hesitant to speak.
We moved our boat near, invited her to join us, poured more wine, turned up the lamps, and began again.
After countless calls, she finally appeared, still holding her pipa half-concealed by her face.
She turned the axis, plucked two or three strings—before any tune was formed, emotion already filled them.
Each string choked back, each note full of longing—like a life unfulfilled, now told in secret.
Bowing her head, fingers moving slowly and steadily, she played on, pouring out endless sorrow.
Lightly brushing, gently rubbing, then sweeping and lifting—first 'Feather-Robe Dance,' then 'Six-Yao.'
The deep strings boomed like sudden rain, the high ones whispered like private talk.
A jumble of loud and soft notes, large pearls and small, falling on jade plates.
Like a bird slipping through blossoms, its song smooth beneath the branches;
like a spring choked beneath ice, its voice stifled, hard to reach.
Cold and sluggish, the strings froze in silence; this pause held breath, a moment hushed.
Then new depths of hidden grief stirred, where silence spoke louder than sound.
As if a silver vase cracked open, liquid burst forth; as if iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashed.
At the music’s end, she drew her pick across the heart of the strings—four strings snapped once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fell silent, nothing but the autumn moon above the river’s heart.
Then, hesitating, she dropped her pick into the strings, adjusted her clothes, and composed herself with solemn grace.

At thirteen, I’d mastered the pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After a single performance, even the master musicians were silenced by my skill; after each makeup, Qiu Niang envied me.

My hairpins of silver and ivory shattered with every beat; my red silk skirts stained with wine spilled in revelry.
Year after year, laughter and joy passed—but so did moonlit springs and wind-warmed autumns, all taken for granted.
My brother left for war; my aunt died. As days passed, my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, the horses and riders few. Now, old, I wed a merchant.
Merchants care only for profit, less for parting—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now, left here at the river’s mouth with an empty boat, the moon circles me, and the river is cold.
In the deep night, I dreamt suddenly of my youth, weeping in sleep, tears streaking red through my makeup.
Hearing this pipa, I sighed deeply. Then hearing these words again, I sighed once more.

I left the imperial capital last year, exiled, sick and bedridden in Xunyang.

Near Penge River, land low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around.

In spring, when flowers bloom at dawn; in autumn, under moonlight—it's often I pour wine alone.

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech, it felt like heavenly music—my ears brightened at once.

I often recall the stream pavilion bathed in sunset glow,
so drunk we lost the road that led us home.
When the revelries had spent themselves, we stumbled back by boat

"Oars! Hurry the oars!" we called, again and again—
and startled from the shoal,
a whole flock of gulls and herons, taking flight."}

{"source": {"title": "江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦", "author": "苏轼", "text": "十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。"}, "translation": "# English Translation

Ten years of life and death, boundless and unknowable—
unspoken, yet never forgotten.

A thousand miles away, her lone grave;
nowhere to pour out this desolation.

Even if we met again, she would not know me now,
my face caked in dust, my temples silvered white.

Last night a ghostly dream brought me back to the old home—
at the small window, she was at her vanity,
combing her hair in the morning light.

We looked at each other and could say nothing at all,
only tears, flowing line after line.

I know that every year the place that breaks the heart
is that moonlit hillside,
where short pines stand against the sky."}

I hear that spring along the Twin Creeks lingers fair —
And think to drift a little boat upon the water there.

But I fear the light skiffs of the Twin Creeks cannot bear
The weight of all this sorrow I would have them carry there."}

{"source": {"title": "江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦", "author": "苏轼", "text": "十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。"}, "translation": "Ten years, life and death, a vast and mute divide —

A lonely grave a thousand miles away,
With no place where I can tell my grief.
Even if we met, you would not know me —
Dust upon my face, temples white as frost.

Last night in a dark dream I suddenly returned home:
By the small lattice window, you were combing your hair.
We gazed at each other, wordless —
And only tears, a thousand lines.
I know, year after year, where my heart breaks:
On the moonlit night, the little pine-covered ridge."}

But even wine and song can't fill the void with mirth.
My belt grows looser yet—I never mourn,
Willing to wither away for her alone."}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。"}, "translation": "#念奴娇·赤壁怀古

The great river surges east,
its waves have scoured away
the luminous heroes of a thousand years.

West of the old ramparts lies,
people say, Red Cliff—
where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms once stood.

Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
fierce waves batter the shore,
rolling up a thousand heaps of snow-white spray.

The land and rivers are a painting—
in that time, how many heroes blazed.

I recall Gongjin in his prime,
Xiao Qiao newly wed,
his bearing fierce and radiant.

Feather fan, silk cap,
amid easy banter and laughter,
the enemy fleet turned to ash and smoke.

My spirit drifts to that old kingdom—
if love were mine to feel, I should be laughed at:
white hairs already crown my brow.

The world is but a dream—
I raise my cup and pour
a libation to the river and the moon."}

The wind has stilled; the fragrant dust— the flowers are gone.  
Too late to comb my hair, I linger on.  
Things remain; the person is gone; all is done.  
I try to speak—but tears come first, and run.  

They say the Twin Streams still hold spring’s beauty bright—  
I think of boating there, to ease my plight.  
But fear those little boats upon the stream  
Cannot bear the weight of so much dream.

{"source": {"title": "江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦", "author": "苏轼", "text": "十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。"}, "translation": "Ten years of death and parting, both lost in a vast void—
Even without dwelling on it, I cannot forget.
A thousand miles away, her lonely grave,
Nowhere to speak of this cold desolation.
Even if we met, she would not know me—
Dust upon my face, temples white as frost.
Last night a faint dream brought me home once more:
A small windowed room, she sat arranging her hair.
We looked at each other, wordless—
Only tears in a thousand lines.
I know the place where hearts have broken year after year:

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
