{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "# A Song of the Pipa

Down by the Xunyang River, I bid a friend good-bye on this night,
Through maple leaves and reed blossoms the autumn wind blows chill and white.
The host dismounts, the guest boards the boat, and raises a cup in vain,
For there is no music, no strings, no song to ease the parting pain.

Too drunk for joy, we part in sorrow as the vast river swallows the moon.
When, suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa is heard—
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure,
And tracing the sound, he calls out: "Who is the player?"
The music stops; the player hesitates before speaking.
He moves the boat closer, invites her out to meet, then
Adds wine, relights the lamp, and reopens the feast.

After a thousand calls and ten entreaties she finally appears,
Still clutching her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings—three, two notes—
Before the tune begins, her feeling already breathes through.
Note after note, subdued and sighing,
Each phrase a lament of a life unfulfilled.
Brow lowered, she plucks on, heedless,
Pouring out all the countless things within her heart.
Light touches and slow rubs, strokes and picks—
First the *Song of Nishang*, then the *Song of Liuyao*.

The great strings rumble like driving rain,
The fine strings murmur like whispered secrets.
Rumbling and whispering, mingled and woven,
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smooth beneath the blossoms,
Like a buried spring struggling beneath the ice.
The cold, hard ice thickens the strings till they nearly break—
The sound congeals, then rests, in silence.

Yet in that silence, a deeper sorrow and hidden resentment arise—
For at this moment, silence speaks more than sound.
Then silver vases crack open, water bursts forth,
Armored cavalry charges with the clash of blades and spears.
She strikes the final chord with a sweep across the heart of the strings,
Four strings ringing at once like splitting silk.
The boats on either side are hushed, without a word—
Only the pale autumn moon in the middle of the river shines.

She lowers her hand, rests the pick among the strings,
Smooths her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She speaks: "I was once a girl of the capital,
Living beneath the Hama Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
First among the ranks of the Imperial Academy.
After my playing, even the best masters praised me,
And when I dressed, the beauties of the court were jealous.
The young lords of the Five Tombs competed to reward me—
One song brought me red silks beyond counting.
Jeweled combs and silver hairpins were broken in the rhythm,
My crimson skirt stained with wine.

Year after year of laughter and glee,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passing all too easily.
Then my younger brother left to serve the army, my aunt died,
And day by day my youth and beauty faded.
Before my door, horses and carriages grew few and cold.
Growing old, I married a merchant.
He loves his trade and thinks little of our parting—
Last month he sailed to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait by the river mouth, guarding this empty boat,
The bright moon circling the deck, the river cold.
Deep in the night, I dream again of my youth,
And wake weeping, the rouge of my tears streaking my face."

I had sighed already at the sound of her pipa,
Now I sigh again at her words of grief.
Both of us, cast away from home at the ends of the earth—
Why must we have met only now?
Since last year, I left the capital,
Banished and ailing to the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote; there is no music here—
Year after year, no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, in low, damp ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing wild around my house.
What do I hear from dawn till dusk? The cuckoo's bloody cry,
The gibbons' howling, mournful and wild.
On spring riverside mornings of flowers, on autumn nights of moon,
I often pour my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs, no village pipes?
Their cracked and mocking notes are hard to bear.

But tonight, hearing your pipa and your voice,
It is like hearing immortal music—my ears restored.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song,
I will compose for you this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stands still for a long time,
Then sits again, tightening the strings till they grow taut and swift—
Not like the sound before, but sharper, more piercing, more heartbroken.
The whole audience weeps anew upon hearing it.
Who among us weeps the most?—

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**Song of the Pipa**

On the autumn night at Xunyang River I saw a guest off, the maples and reeds rustling in the chill.
My host dismounted, the guest aboard the wine-cup raised yet no lute, no strings to fill the hall.
Half-drunk and joyless, we parted in sorrow—out on the water, the river lay steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly from the surface came the cry of a pipa; the host forgot to leave, the guest stayed, not departing.
Following the sound I asked softly who was playing; the music stopped, as if to speak but held back.
We drew our boats near and asked her out, brought wine, relit the lanterns, and feasted again.
After a thousand calls and entreaties she emerged, still cradling her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked a few notes—before any melody began, emotion flowed within.
String over string, veiled and sighing, each note a thought, as if she were telling a life of thwarted ambition.
Brows low, fingers free, she played on without pause, pouring out the countless things within her breast.
Lightly strummed, slowly twisted, swept and flicked—first the Ni Shang, then the Liu Yao.
Great strings rough as driving rain, small strings fine as whispered confidences.
Rough and fine tangled together, great pearls and small falling on a jade plate.
Like an oriole's song slipping through the flowers, like a muffled stream choking beneath the ice.
The ice-cool water stiffened; the strings seemed to freeze—then silence held, and the sound was cut off.
From the hush a hidden grief and silent longing rose—there, silence spoke louder than any sound.
Like a silver pitcher bursting, water spraying; like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The tune ended—she drew the pick across the center; four strings rang as one, tearing silk.
The boats east and west sat speechless, and only the autumn moon in the river's heart shone white.
She pondered, set her pick behind the strings, straightened her robes, and rose with solemn grace.
She said, "I am a woman of the capital, my home was beneath the toad mound.
At thirteen I had mastered the pipa, my name first-ranked in the imperial music hall.
When I finished a song the masters were impressed; when I dressed, autumn beauties envied me.
The young lords of the Five Tombs all bid for my favor—one song and red silk, beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs beat time and broke; blood-red silk skirts were stained with wine.
Year after year of laughter, and the autumn moons and spring breezes slipped away unheeded.
My younger brother left for the army, my elder sister died; dusk came and dawn returned, and beauty faded.
Before my door the horses were few, the guests sparse; grown old, I married a merchant for a wife.
The merchant cares more for profit than parting—for tea he has gone to Fulang this past month.
I wait by the river mouth in an empty boat, the moon bright around me, the water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of my youth, and woke weeping, my rouge-streaked tears staining the pillow."
I had sighed already hearing her pipa; hearing this I sighed and sighed anew.
Both of us, cast away at the ends of the earth—why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial city, banished and sick here in Xunyang.
This land is remote and musicless—no silk, no bamboo the whole year through.
I live near the Pei River, low and damp, surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk? The cuckoo's bloodied cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On flower-bright spring days and moonlit autumn nights, I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village flutes? They squawk and screech, unbearable to hear.
But tonight, hearing your pipa's song, it was like hearing immortal music—my ears cleared at last.
Do not refuse to sit and play once more; for you I'll compose this *Song of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood a long while, then sat back, tightened the strings—faster, tighter still.
Sorrowful now, nothing like the sound before; everyone in the room wept as they listened again.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge, I saw a guest off at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest boarded the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no string or pipe to hear.
Drunk without joy, we parted in bitter sorrow,
At parting, the vast river swallowed the moon.

Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to go home; the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked in a low voice, "Who is playing?"
The pipa stopped; she hesitated to answer.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to meet us,
Added wine, relit the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before the melody began, emotion was already there.
Each string seemed to hide a sigh, each note a thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she played on and on,
Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and picking,
First the *Nishang*, then the *Liu Yao*.

The large strings roared like sudden rain,
The small strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft, intertwined they played,
Like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing, smooth on the flowered branches,
Like a secluded spring, choked under the ice.
The icy spring, cold and astringent, the strings froze,
Frozen and blocked, the sound paused for a while.
A secret sorrow, a hidden resentment rose—
In that moment, silence was more powerful than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept the拨 across the center,
Four strings together, like tearing silk.

East and west, boats and cabins, all were silent,
Only the autumn moon, white, on the river's heart.
She pondered, put the拨 down, tucked it into the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and composed her face.
She said, "I was once a girl of the capital,
Living near Hama Ling.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even the skilled masters admired me;
When I dressed up, the beauties envied me.
The young men of Wuling competed to give me gifts—
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled combs and silver pins shattered to the beat,
Blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, of joy and laughter,
Autumn moons and spring winds, passed by in vain.
My younger brother went to the army; my aunt died,
Evenings came, mornings went, my youth grew old.
Before my gate, carriages grew sparse and cold,
And in my old age, I married a merchant.
The merchant values profit over parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I stay alone by the river mouth in this empty boat,
The boat wrapped in bright moonlight, the river cold.
In the deep of night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
And wake weeping, my rouge-streaked tears staining the rails."

I had sighed upon hearing her pipa,
And sighed again upon hearing these words.
Both of us are wanderers at the end of the world—
Why must we have met before to understand?

Last year I left the capital's imperial city,
Demoted and ill, I dwell in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music,
All year I hear no strings or pipes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk?
The cuckoo's blood-cry, the ape's mournful wail.
On spring river flower-mornings, autumn moon-nights,
I often take wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, grating tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's words,
It is like hearing immortal music, my ears briefly revived.
Do not refuse; sit again and play one more song,
And I will compose a *Pipa Xing* for you.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and they grew急.
The mournful sound was not like the one before,
The whole assembly, hearing it again, wept into their sleeves.
Who in the seats wept the most?
The Xunyang official's blue robe was wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**A Song of the Pipa Player**  

At Xunyang River’s edge, I saw a friend off on a night in autumn;  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill.  
I dismounted, my guest boarded the boat;  
We raised our cups, but no lutes or flutes cheered the parting.  

Drunk, yet still not merry, we parted in gloom—  
The river swallowed the moon, a blur of farewell.  
Suddenly, from the water, the sound of a pipa;  
I forgot to go home, my guest delayed his departure.  

Following the sound, I softly asked, “Who plays?”  
The music stopped; she hesitated to reply.  
We moved our boat nearer, invited her to meet;  
Added wine, relit the lanterns, and feasted anew.  

After a thousand calls, she finally appeared,  
Holding the pipa, half hiding her face.  
She tuned the strings, three or four plucks—  
Before the melody, emotion already stirred.  

Each string, muted and sighing, carried a thought,  
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.  
Lowering her brows, she played on, unforced,  
Speaking of the countless matters in her heart.  

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, strumming and picking,  
First “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Small Dances.”  
The large strings roared like sudden rain,  
The small strings whispered like private talk.  

Roaring and whispering, tangled together,  
Like pearls, great and small, falling on a jade plate.  
Like orioles singing under blossoms, smooth and gliding,  
Or a muffled stream seeping beneath ice.  

The icy spring chilled, the strings froze silent—  
In that silence, a deeper sorrow was born:  
Sometimes, the unsounded note speaks louder.  

Then a silver vase bursts, water gushing forth;  
Armored riders charge, swords and spears clash.  
The song ends, the pick sweeps across the strings—  
Four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.  

In the boats around, no one spoke;  
Only the autumn moon, white on the river’s heart.  
Thoughtfully, she tucked the pick, straightened her robe,  
And composed her face before she spoke.  

“I was once a girl of the capital,  
My home beneath Hachang Hill.  
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,  
Ranked first in the Imperial Music Academy.  

Each performance made the old masters bow;  
Each time I dressed, the court beauties envied.  
Young lords of the Five Tombs vied to shower me with gifts—  
One song, and silks piled high beyond count.  

Golden hairpins, silver combs, struck in time till they broke;  
Crimson skirts, stained with wine, turned to ruin.  
Year after year of laughter and revelry,  
The spring winds and autumn moons passed by, unheeded.  

My younger brother left for the army, my aunt died;  
Day and night, my youth slipped away.  
Before my gate, carriages grew sparse and cold;  
Growing old, I married a merchant.  

But merchants prize profit over parting;  
Last month, he sailed to Fuliang for tea.  
I wait for him alone on this river mouth,  
The moon bright around my boat, the water cold.  

Deep in the night, I dream of my youth—  
In the dream, my tears soak the rouge on my face.”  

I sighed when I heard the pipa;  
Hearing her story, I sighed again.  
We are both wanderers at the edge of the world—  
Why must we have met before to understand?  

Last year I left the capital,  
Sick and exiled to Xunyang.  
Here, the land is remote, with no music;  
All year, I hear no lutes or flutes.  

I live near the low, damp riverbank,  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my hut.  
What do I hear from morning to night?  
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in grief.  

On spring mornings or autumn evenings,  
I often drink alone by the river.  
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?  
They are crude and grating, hard to bear.  

Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,  
It was like celestial music—my ears awoke.  
Please, don’t refuse—sit and play once more;  
I will compose a song for you in return.  

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,  
Then sat and tuned; the strings grew urgent.  
The new tune, mournful, unlike the one before,  
Made everyone in the hall weep in silence.  

Who wept the most among the guests?  
The Xunyang official, whose blue robe was wet with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang Riverhead I saw a guest off by night,
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shivered in autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stayed aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no strings or flutes played.
Drunk, yet not merry, we parted in gloom—
At parting, the vast river drowned the moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his going.
Following the sound, I softly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated to answer.
I moved my boat nearer, invited her to meet;
More wine was brought, lamps relit, the feast spread anew.
After a thousand calls she finally emerged,
Still hugging her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked the strings—a note or two;
Before any tune took shape, feeling already stirred.
String after string, muted and brooding, note after note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow low, unhurried, she went on playing,
Voicing all the endless matters in her heart.
Light gathering, slow rubbing, brushing, picking—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Yao*.
Great strings rumbled like sudden rain;
Small strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, mingled and crossed,
Like great pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles warbling smooth beneath the flowers,
Or a hidden stream choking under ice.
The icy spring turned cold, the strings froze and snapped;
Frozen, blocked, the sound paused for a while.
Then a secret sorrow and hidden grief arose—
In that silence, more than sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water gushing forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
At the song's end she swept the拨 across the center;
All four strings tore as one like splitting silk.
East boats, west pavilions—silent, no one spoke;
Only the river's heart, the autumn moon, white.
Pondering, she tucked the拨 into the strings,
Adjusted her garments, rose with solemn bearing.
She said: "I was once a girl of the capital,
Home was beneath Hama Hill.
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
When a song ended, even the finest masters admired;
When dressed up, the beauties envied me.
Young gallants of the Five Tombs competed to lavish gifts—
One song, countless bolts of red silk.
Silver combs with inlaid shells beat time till they shattered;
Crimson skirts stained and splashed with wine.
Year after year of laughter and revelry,
Autumn moons, spring breezes, squandered idly.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Evenings passed, mornings came, and my looks grew old.
Before my door, carriages grew sparse, horses few;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
Merchants prize profit over parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Back and forth at the river's mouth I guard an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moon, cold river water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of my youth;
In the dream I weep, makeup streaked with tears."
I had sighed already at the pipa's sound;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, "Ah, ah."
Both of us, drifters at the world's end—
Why must we have met before to understand?
Since last year I left the capital's grace,
Lodging sick in Xunyang city.
Xunyang's remote, with no music;
All year, no sound of strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing.
Spring river, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I fetch wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs, no village pipes?
They rasp and squawk, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
It's like hearing immortal music—my ears come alive.
Don't refuse—sit and play once more;
For you, I'll turn it into a *Song of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back and pressed the strings—they quickened.
Mournful, unlike the sound before,
All the seats wept again, each wiping tears.
Who in this room wept the most?
The Xunyang Prefect—his blue gown damp."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang River's edge I saw a guest off that night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stepped aboard his boat;
They raised their cups to drink, but there was no lute or string.
Drunken yet joyless, soon they parted in sorrow,
At parting, the vast river swallowed the moonlight.
Suddenly a pipa's sound drifted across the water—
The host forgot to leave, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, they asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated before replying.
They moved their boat close and invited her to appear;
They added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still cradling the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before a tune began, emotion was already there.
String by string, her notes were muted yet brooding,
Each sound a sigh, as if telling a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Brow lowered, she played on, her fingers moving free,
Pouring out all the boundless matters in her heart.
With light and slow strokes, she plucked and picked,
First the "Rainbow Skirt" dance, then the "Six Yao."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like secret talk.
Roaring and whispering, intertwined they played,
Like pearls large and small falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing beneath the blossoms, smooth and sweet,
Like a hidden stream struggling under ice.
The icy stream grew cold and harsh, the strings seemed to freeze;
Frozen, the sound broke off, and silence took its place.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose—
At that moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Then a silver bottle burst, water and wine spilled,
Iron cavalry charged forth, swords and spears clashing.
She finished the song with one stroke across the strings,
All four strings snapped at once like tearing silk.
On boats east and west, all was silent and still;
Only the white autumn moon at the river's center.
Pensive, she tucked the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said: "I am from the capital, originally,
My home was beneath the Toad Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first in the Music Bureau.
After each song, even the finest players were amazed;
Once made up, even the autumn beauties were envious.
Young lords from the five tombs competed for tribute,
For one song, countless red silk scarves were given.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke to the beat,
Crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter and joy went on,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed by unnoticed.
Then my brother went to the army, my aunt died;
Dawn and dusk came and went, my looks grew old.
Before my door, carriages and horses grew sparse;
Growing old, I married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over parting and love;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
I wait by the river mouth, guarding the empty boat;
The moonlit river water grows cold around me.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of my youth,
In the dream, I weep, my makeup smeared with tears."
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Hearing her words, I sighed again, softly.
Both of us are wanderers at the world's edge—
Why must we have known each other before to meet?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Exiled and ailing, I live in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, with no music to be heard;
All year, I hear no lute or flute at all.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening?
The cuckoo's blood-cry, the gibbon's mournful howl.
On flower-moon spring days and autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and strident, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's words,
Is like hearing celestial music, my ears refreshed.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song,
And I will compose for you "The Pipa Song."
Moved by my words, she stood still for a long time;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and they grew faster.
Mournful and different from her earlier sounds,
All who listened again wept, covering their faces.
Who in the room wept the most?
The Jiangzhou sheriff, his blue robe soaked with tears."}

On the Xunyang River I was seeing off my guest,
When the maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest stayed in the boat,
Raising his cups, he wished to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk, yet not merry, we were parting with heavy hearts,
And as we parted, the vast river seemed to swallow the moon.

Then from the water came the sound of a pipa;
My host forgot to go home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, he secretly asked, "Who is the player?"
The pipa stopped, and she was slow to answer.
We moved our boat nearer and invited her to appear,
Added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls, she at last emerged,
Still clutching her pipa, half-hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, a few notes first,
Before the tune was formed, a feeling was already there.
String after string, bent and muted, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled hopes.
Bowing her head, she played on, without a pause,
Telling the countless things that filled her heart.
Lightly strummed and slowly twisted, plucked and stroked,
First the “Rainbow Skirts,” then the “Six Yao.”

The large strings roared like a sudden, heavy rain,
The small strings whispered like a secret tale.
Loud and soft, the notes wove together,
Like great and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
A warbler's song from the flowers, smooth and clear,
A mountain spring choked under ice, choked and hard to flow.
The icy spring grew cold, the strings froze and broke—
And in that broken silence, a pause.

A deeper sorrow and hidden grief arose;
In that moment, silence was more powerful than sound.
Then a silver pot suddenly shattered, water bursting forth,
Or an armored cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she swept her pick across the four strings;
They cried out as one, like tearing silk.

In the boats to east and west, no one spoke;
Only the white autumn moon in the river's heart was seen.
Thoughtfully, she tucked the pick back among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and stood with a solemn face.
She said she was once a girl from the capital,
Her home at the foot of the Toad Hill.
At thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name first in the ranks of the court's troupe.
After her song, even the masters would be impressed,
And when she dressed up, the other girls would envy her.
Young lords from the five tombs would vie for her favors,
And her red silk scarves for one song were countless.
Her ornate combs and silver hairpins often broke as she beat time,
And her wine-stained crimson skirts were never clean.

Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moons and spring breezes passed without a thought.
Then her brother went to war, her aunt died,
And day by day, her youthful beauty faded.
Her door fell into neglect; the horses were few.
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and thought little of parting;
Last month he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She was left alone at the river's mouth in an empty boat,
The bright moon surrounding her, the water cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth,
Waking with tears of rouge tracing red lines down her face.

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again and again.
We are both wanderers, cast adrift at the world's edge—
Why must we have known each other before now?
I left the capital last year,
Banished to this sickbed in Xunyang.
Xunyang is a remote place with no music;
All year, I never heard the sound of strings.
I live near the Pen River, in low, damp ground,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear from morning to night?
The cuckoo's blood-cry and the gibbon's mournful howl.
On spring days with flowers, on autumn nights with moon,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village tunes?
Their harsh, grating sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
It was like hearing the music of immortals, my ears briefly cleared.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more song,
I will compose this "Song of the Pipa" for you.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened her strings, and played with growing urgency.
The mournful notes were not like the ones before;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept.
In the room, whose tears fell the most?
The riverside official, his blue robe was wet."}

She pauses, tucks the pick among the strings,

Thirteen, I completed my pipa training,
my name heading the first rank of the Music Academy.
My playing once awed even the masters;
when made up, I was envied by every beauty.
Young gallants of the Five Tombs vied to shower me with gifts—
one song, and bolts of red silk past counting.
Jeweled pins and silver combs—shattered as I kept time;
crimson skirts—stained and fouled with wine.
Joyful this year, then joyful again the next,
autumn moon and spring breeze squandered without a thought.
My brother went to serve in arms; my elder died.
Evenings went, mornings came—my youth, my beauty, faded.
Before my gate, stirrups grew cold, carriages thinned.
Grown old, I married—a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, thinks lightly of parting—
last month he floated off to Fuliang to buy tea.
He comes and goes; I guard a lone boat at the river's mouth,
the bright moon circling the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of my younger years—
and weeping in the dream, my tears streak the painted rails."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sighed again—deeper still.
Both of us, drifters at the edge of the world—
what matter if we never knew each other before!

Last year I took leave of the imperial capital,

Xunyang is remote—there is no music here.

大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At night on the Xunyang River we see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards the boat;
They raise cups to drink, but no lute or strings sound.
Drunk, they cannot make merry; soon they part, sad and downcast;
At parting, the river is vast, flooded with moonlight.
Suddenly they hear a pipa from the water;
The host forgets to leave, the guest delays his departure.
They follow the sound and ask softly who is playing;
The pipa stops, and the player hesitates to answer.
They move their boat closer and invite her to appear;
They add wine, relight the lamp, and the banquet resumes.
After a thousand calls she finally emerges,
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune forms, emotion already flows.
String after string, muffled and sighing, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambition.
Brow low, she plays on at will, speaking without end,
Telling all the countless things that fill her heart.
Light touches, slow presses, strokes and flicks;
First "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Minor."
The big strings roar like driving rain,
The small strings whisper like secret talk.
Roaring and whispering, intertwined and mixed,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles gliding beneath blossoms, smooth and sweet,
Like a brook choking under ice, muffled and hard.
Ice-cold spring, the strings stiffen and snap;
Stuck, no sound passes, and the music rests.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grievance arise;
At this moment, silence is more eloquent than sound.
Suddenly a silver vase bursts, water and wine spill forth;
Armored cavalry charge out, swords and spears clash.
At the end of the tune she sweeps the plectrum across the center;
Four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.
On boats east and west, all is silent;
Only the white autumn moon in the river's heart is seen.
Pensive, she sets the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her face.
She says she was a girl of the capital,
Living beneath the Toad Mound.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
First in rank at the Music Academy.
After a tune she won even the masters' praise;
Her beauty made the seasoned courtesans envious.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to shower her gifts;
For one song, red silk gifts were countless.
Silver combs and jeweled pins smashed in keeping time;
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and gaiety,
Spring breezes and autumn moons passed by as nothing.
Then her younger brother left for the army, her aunt died;
Days passed, and her youthful beauty faded.
Before her gate, horses grew rare, visitors few;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant prized profit over parting;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
She stays alone by the river mouth, guarding the empty boat;
The boat is circled by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night she dreams of her youth;
In the dream she weeps, her rouge-streaked tears staining her face.
I sighed hearing the pipa, and sighed again at her words.
Both of us are lost souls at the ends of the earth;
Why must we have met before to recognize each other?
Last year I left the capital, banished and ill to Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music;
All year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What is heard there from dawn to dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in grief.
On flower-filled spring days and moonlit autumn nights,
Often I take wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
They are harsh, cacophonous, hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's voice,
Like celestial music, my ears briefly clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more tune;
For you I compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stands for a long moment,
Then sits again, quickens the strings, and the tempo grows urgent.
Its sorrow is not like the sound before;
All who hear it weep, hands covering their faces.
Who in this room weeps the most?
The Jiangzhou official's blue gown is soaked with tears."}

At Xunyang River's edge I saw a guest off into the night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest was already on the boat;
He raised his cup to drink, but there was no music to be had.
Drunk without joy, we were about to part in sorrow;
When parting, the vast river was flooded by the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to go home, and the guest could not depart.
Following the sound, he asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and she was slow to answer.
He moved his boat nearer, and invited her to meet;
More wine was served, the lamps relit, the feast began again.
After a thousand calls, she finally came out,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before a tune was formed, it was already full of emotion.
Each string, each note, was suppressed and thoughtful,
As if telling of a life of unfulfilled ambitions.
Lowering her brows, she played on and on with ease,
Pouring out all the endless matters in her heart.
Lightly plucking, slowly twisting, stroking and pulling,
First she played "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Little Ones."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like a private conversation.
The roaring and whispering intertwined and mingled,
Like pearls, large and small, falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles' chatter over flowers, smooth and swift,
Like a choked stream flowing under ice.
The ice-cold stream, the strings grew stiff and broke;
The break, the block, and the sound paused for a moment.
A new, hidden sorrow and secret regret arose;
In this moment, silence was better than sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly shattering, water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended, she drew the pick across the center;
The four strings snapped at once, like tearing silk.
In the boats to the east and west, all was silent and still;
Only the white autumn moon over the river's heart was seen.
Thoughtfully she put the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, and rose with a solemn face.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home was at the foot of Toad Hill.
At thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Her name was listed first in the Court's Registry.
After a tune, even the best musicians were impressed,
When she made up, even the beauties were jealous.
Young men from noble families competed for her favors;
For one song, she received countless bolts of red silk.
Ornamental combs and silver hairpins were broken keeping time,
Her crimson silk skirt was stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
The autumn moon and spring breeze passed in vain.
Her younger brother went to the army, and her aunt died;
Dawn after dusk, her beauty faded.
Before her door, carriages and horses grew rare;
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting;
Last month, he went to buy tea in Fuliang.
She waits alone on an empty boat at the river's mouth,
The moon shines around the boat, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of her youth,
She cries in her dream, her makeup tears red on her face.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her words, I sighed again, even more deeply.
We are both wanderers at the end of the world,
Why must we have known each other before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished to a sickbed in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings and flutes.
Living near the Pen River, the ground is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo's cry of blood, the gibbons' mournful wail.
On spring river days with flowers, autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their crude, harsh sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,
It's like hearing immortal music, my ears are momentarily clear.
Please don't decline, sit and play another song,
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, and they grew more urgent.
The mournful sound was not like the one before;
The whole audience, hearing it again, wept in silence.
Of all those in the room, who wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe was wet with tears."}

Dust on my face, frost in my hair.  
Last night, in dream, I returned home,  
Small window, you were combing your hair.  
We gaze at each other, speechless, tears,  
A thousand streams flowing.  
I know the place where sorrow breaks each year—  
Moonlit nights, short pines on the hill."}

Last night, a dream of returning home; by the small window, you were combing your hair.  
We looked at each other in silence, only tears streaming down.  
I know that every year, at the heart-rending spot, on the moonlit night, by the short pines on the hill."}

I linger, leaning on the high tower, as the breeze grows thin and fine,  
Gazing afar, spring’s sorrow deepens—dimly born from the sky’s far line.  
In twilight’s glow, the grasses shroud in misty haze,  
Silent, who can read my heart as I gaze at the balustrade?  

I’d drown in wild abandon, seek one night of drunken bliss,  
Face wine, sing, yet even joy feels hollow, cold, and void.  
My sash grows loose—I never regret;  
For you, I’ve grown gaunt, worn down by grief and endless weight."}

We look at each other, no words—  
Only thousands of tears.  

I know each year, heartbroken,  
On moonlit nights, by Short Pines Ridge."}

Who understands, as I lean silent on the balustrade, this lonely mind?  

I’d drown my wild unrest in one deep drink of wine,  
Sing with wine, raise a cup—but joy feels hollow, empty, unkind.  
Though robes grow loose with time, I will not regret this plight—  
For her, I’ve wasted away, heartbreak etched in every line."}

With feather fan and silk cap, calm in speech—he made the enemy ships turn to ashes in an instant.

Last night, in a dream deep, I suddenly returned home; by the small window, you were combing your hair.  
We looked at each other in silence, only thousands of tears.  
I know every year, the heartbreak spot: moonlit night, short pine hill."}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "A thousand years of rivers and hills,  
No trace of heroes—where’s Sun Zhongmou?  
The pavilions of dance and song,  
All swept away by wind and rain.  

Sunset on grass and trees,  
In common alleys—people say Liu Yu once lived here.  
Recalling those days:  
Steel-clad warriors, war horses thundering,  
Mightily swallowing ten thousand miles like a tiger.  

Yuanjia's reckless campaign,  
Seizing the Wolf's Ridge—  
Only to flee in panic, looking back northward.  

Forty-three years pass;  
Still vivid in sight:  
The fires along the Yangzhou road.  

Who can bear to look back—  
At Buddha’s Temple, where crows cry,  
And drums beat for communal rites?  

Who dares ask—  
Old General Lianpo,  
Can he still eat?"}

纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。

料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。"}, "translation": "Ten years apart in life and death, two endless voids,  
No thought needed, yet the memory clings.  
A thousand miles from my lonely grave—  
No place to voice this sorrow.

Dust-stained face, hair frosted white.  
Last night, a dream returned me home,  
By the small window, you were dressing your hair.  

We gazed in silence, no words spoken,  
Only a thousand tears streaming down.  
I know each year, the heartbreak spot—  
Moonlit nights on the pine-clad hill."}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。"}, "translation": "The great river flows eastward, its waves washing away all the brilliant men of past ages.  
West of the old fort, they say, it's the Red Cliffs where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms held sway.  
Jagged rocks pierce the sky, surging waves crash against the shore, rolling up thousands of heaps of snow.  
The land and rivers are like a painting; how many heroes arose at that time!  
I recall Zhou Yu in his prime, when Xiao Qiao had just married him, his heroic bearing in full bloom.  
With feather fan and silk cap, in calm talk, the warships turned to ash and smoke.  
In spirit I roam my homeland; the tender-hearted would laugh at me, for I have white hair early.  
Life is like a dream; I raise a cup to pour out to the river moon."}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "A thousand years of rivers and hills,  
No trace of heroes—where’s Sun Zhongmou?  
The dance pavilions, singing halls,  
All the elegance once known,  
Washed away by wind and rain.  

Sunset on grass and trees,  
Ordinary alleys where people say  
Li Nu once lived.  
I recall those days:  
Armored troops, iron horses,  
Giant strides devouring ten thousand miles like a tiger.  

Yuanjia’s rashness,  
Foolish pursuit of fame at Langjuxu,  
Only to flee in panic northward.  

Forty-three years—  
Still vivid in my sight:  
The fires along the Yangzhou road.  

How unbearable to look back—  
At Buddha’s Temple,  
Crows cawing, drums beating,  
A crowd in worship.  

Who will ask?  
Old General Lianpo—  
Can he still eat?"}

乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。

Mountains and rivers like a painting, how many heroes then?  
Recalling Gongjin in his prime, Xiao Qiao newly wed, his heroic bearing splendid.  
With feather fan and straw hat, amid laughter, warships turned to ash and smoke.  
My spirit wanders the ancient land, the tenderhearted would laugh at me, already white-haired.  
Life is but a dream, I raise my cup to the river moon."}

舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "A thousand years of rivers and mountains,  
Where heroes once roamed—no trace remains of Sun Zhongmou.  
The dance halls and singing pavilions,  
Their grandeur now all swept by wind and rain.  

Sunset on grass and trees,  
Ordinary lanes where the common folk say:  
Li Tu once lived here.  
I recall those days—  
Steel horses charging, golden weapons gleaming,  
A spirit that swallowed ten thousand miles like a tiger's roar.  

Yuanjia’s rash campaign,  
Haste to conquer Mount Lian,  
Yet fled in panic, fearing northern pursuit.  

Forty-three years have passed—  
Still vivid in my gaze:  
Fires burning along the Yangzhou road.  

How can I bear to look back—  
At the temple of Fu Li,  
Where crows feast and drums beat in sacred frenzy?  

Who dares ask—old General Lianpo,  
Is he still strong enough to eat?"}

The land and rivers like a painting—how many heroes of that time!  
I recall Zhou Yu in his prime, when Xiao Qiao had just been wed, his bearing majestic and full of vigor.  
With feather fan and silk cap, in calm talk, the enemy ships turned to ash and smoke.  
My spirit wanders through the old land; the compassionate would laugh at me for my early white hair.  
Life is but a dream; I raise my cup to the river moon."}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Eternal rivers and mountains—where are the heroes now?  
Where Sun Quan once reigned.  
The halls of dance and song, all grandeur swept by rain and wind.  
Sunset on grass and trees, in common lanes—  
They say Liu Yu once lived here.  

Remember those days: golden spears and iron horses,  
Like a tiger devouring a thousand miles.  

Yuanjia’s rash campaign, sealing Wolf’s Ridge,  
Only earned a hasty retreat north.  

Forty-three years—still vivid in sight,  
The beacon fires on Yangzhou Road.  

Who can bear to look back?  
At Fuli’s shrine, sacred crows and village drums.  

Who asks, "Old Lian Po, can he still eat?""}

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "A Thousand Years of Rivers and Mountains  
Where heroes can no longer be found—  
Where Sun Zhongmou once stood.  

Palaces of dance, stages of song,  
All elegance now swept away by rain and wind.  

Sunset on grass and trees,  
Ordinary lanes where Li Tu once lived.  
I recall those days:  
Steel horses and golden spears,  
A spirit that devoured ten thousand miles like a tiger.  

Yuanjia's hasty campaign,  
Seizing the Wolf's Height,  
Only to flee in panic northward.  

Forty-three years pass—  
In memory still burned:  
The flames along the Yangzhou road.  

How unbearable to look back—  
At the temple of Fuli,  
Crows cawing, drums beating, a godless noise.  

Who dares ask—  
Old General Lianpo?  
Still able to eat, isn't he?"}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。"}, "translation": "Ode to the Red Cliffs — Nian Nu Jiao  
By Su Shi

The great river flows eastward, waves washing away—  
All the brilliant figures of a thousand years.  
West of the old fortress, they say—  
Three Kingdoms' Zhou Yu, at Red Cliffs, once stood.  

Rocks pierce the sky, wild surges crash the shore,  
Whipping up thousands of heaps like snow.  
The land and rivers, a scroll so vivid—  
How many heroes rose in that fleeting moment!  

I recall Gongjin in his prime:  
Xiao Qiao had just married him, radiant and bold.  
With feather fan and silk sash, calm and wise,  
In laughter, enemy ships turned to ashes, gone.  

Lost in spirit among ancient lands,  
My heartfelt sorrow must seem absurd—  
Gray hairs have come too early.  

Life’s but a dream, so I raise my cup—  
To the moon above the river, I pour this wine."}

夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。

Dust on my face, hair turned to frost.

You sat by the small window, fixing your hair.  

We looked at each other, speechless,  
Only thousands of tears streaming down.  

I know each year, where heartbreak pierces most—  
The moonlit night, the short pine hill."}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。

West of the old fort, they say, this is the Red Cliff of the Three Kingdoms, where Zhou Yu once stood.  
Rocks pierce the sky, waves crash on shore, lifting thousand heaps of snow.  
The land and rivers like a painting—how many heroes in that age!  

Remembering Zhou Yu in his prime, when Little Qiao had just been wed, his martial grace bright.  
With feather fan and silk cap, in calm discourse, the enemy ships turned to ash and smoke.  
My spirit roams the ancient land; those with tender hearts would laugh at me,  
For I have gray hair before my time. Life on earth is but a dream—I lift my cup to the river moon."}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。"}, "translation": "The great river flows eastward, its waves washing away all the brilliant figures of ancient times.  
West of the old fortress, they say—this is where Zhou Lang’s Red Cliff stood.  
Cliffs pierce the sky, waves crash against the shore, swirling up thousands of heaps of snow.  
The landscape as splendid as a painting—how many heroic men arose in that age!  
I recall Gongjin in his prime, just married to Xiao Qiao, with majestic bearing and vibrant spirit.  
With feather fan and silk cap, at ease in talk—he brought down the enemy ships, turning them to ashes and smoke.  
In spirit I wander through the lost land; how should the affectionate soul not laugh at me—my hair already grayed too soon?  
Life on earth is but a dream—raise a cup, offering it to the moon over the river."}

heroes nowhere to be found, where Sun Quan once dwelled.  
The dance pavilions and song halls, all grace and elegance,  
swept away by rain and wind.  
At sunset, grass and trees, ordinary lanes and alleys,  
people say Liu Yu once lived here.  
Thinking of those days, golden spears and iron horses,  
swallowing a million miles like a tiger.  
In the Yuanjia era, hastily, Feng Lang Ju Xu,  
only winning a hurried northward glance.  
Forty-three years, looking back, still remember  
the fires of Yangzhou Road.  
How can one bear to look back,  
at Fuli's temple, a scene of sacred crows and community drums?  
Who will ask, "Lian Po is old, can he still eat?""}

Now battered by wind and rain.

Ordinary lanes and alleys—

I recall those days:  
Steel swords clashing, iron horses charging,  
A spirit that swallowed ten thousand miles like a tiger.  

Yuanjia’s hasty campaign,

Still vivid in my sight:  
The fires along the Yangzhou road.

At the temple of Foli,  
Crows flying, drums beating in frenzy.  

Who will ask—  
Old General Lianpo,  
Still able to eat a meal?"}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。"}, "translation": "The river flows eastward, its waves wash away all heroes of ancient times.  
West of the old fortress, it is said to be Zhou Yu's Red Cliff of the Three Kingdoms.  
Rocks pierce the sky, waves crash on the shore, rolling up thousands of snow-white heaps.  
The land is like a painting, so many heroes arose at that time.  
I recall the young Zhou Yu, just married to Xiao Qiao, with vigorous bearing.  
With a feather fan and a silk cap, he laughed and talked, and the warships turned to ashes.  
In my dream of the ancient land, you would laugh at me for my sentiment, as my hair has turned gray too soon.  
The world is but a dream; I raise a cup to the river moon."}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Eternal rivers and peaks, where heroes no longer stay,  
Where Sun Quan once reigned, now lost to time’s decay.  

Dance halls and song stages, all the glory swept away,  
Scattered by rain and wind, as years pass on the way.  

Sunset on grass and trees, in common lanes,  
They say General Ji Nu once called those lanes his own.  

Recall those days, golden spears and iron steeds,  
His might like a tiger, swallowing ten thousand miles.  

Yuanjia’s rash campaign, sealing Wolf’s Ridge high,  
Ended with panic, turning northward, with no cry.  

Forty-three years, still I see the beacon fires  
Along Yangzhou Road, where war once blazed like pyres.  

Can we bear to look back? At Beili’s shrine,  
Divine crows and drumbeats fill the mournful air.  

Who now asks, Old General Lianpo, can he still eat?"}

Yuanjia's hasty campaign, sealing the wolf at Juxu, winning only a hasty retreat north.

How unbearable to look back, beneath Fuli's temple, crows and drums resound.

江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。

Recalling Zhou Yu in his prime, when Xiao Qiao was newly married, his heroic bearing and vigor.  
With feather fan and silk cap, in calm talk, warships turned to ashes.  
In spirit, I roam the old land; the tender-hearted would laugh at me for my prematurely white hair.  
Life is but a dream, I raise a cup to the river moon."}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "Eternal rivers and mountains, no trace of heroes where Sun Zhongmou was.  
The dance halls and singing stages, all grace swept by rain and wind.  
Sunset on grass and trees, in common lanes, where they say Liu Yu lived.  
Recalling those days, golden spears and iron horses, swallowing a million miles like a tiger.  
Emperor Yuanjia's hasty campaign, sealing the wolf's ridge, won only a hurried northern glance.  
Forty-three years later, still in sight, the flames on the Yangzhou road.  
How can I bear to look back? At Fu Li's temple, a clamor of crows and drums.  
Who would ask: "Is General Lianpo old, can he still eat?""}

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "A thousand years of rivers and mountains,  
Where heroes once roamed—no trace remains of Sun Zhongmou.  
The dance pavilions, the singing halls,  
All are swept away by rain and wind.  

Sunset stains the trees and weeds;  
In alleyways ordinary as any,  
They say Li Tu once lived here.  
I recall those days:  
Armored horses, iron warlords,  
Their spirit, a tiger devouring ten thousand miles.  

Yuanjia’s hasty campaign too—  
Seizing Mount Langju, yet fleeing in panic northward.  
Forty-three years have passed;  
Still vivid in my mind:  
The smoldering flames along the Yangzhou road.  

How painful to look back—  
At Buddha's Shrine, where crows cry and drums beat,  
A ghostly feast of gods and men.  

Who now dares ask—  
Old General Lianpo? Still can he eat?"}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "The eternal rivers and mountains, heroes nowhere to be found, at Sun Zhongmou's place.  
Dance halls and singing pavilions, all their grace swept away by wind and rain.  
Sunset on grass and trees, in common lanes and alleys, people say Li Ju once lived here.  
Recalling those days, golden armor and iron horses, swallowing a thousand miles like a tiger.  
Yuanjia rash, sealing the wolf at Juxu, winning only a hasty retreat north.  
Forty-three years later, still remembered in sight, the fires on the road to Yangzhou.  
Hard to bear to look back, at the temple of Fuli, a flock of sacred crows and the community drum.  
Who would ask, Lian Po is old, can he still eat?"}

江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。

Rocks pierce the sky, waves crash on the shore, rolling up thousands of heaps of snow.  
The river and mountains are like a painting; how many heroes arose at that time!  
Recalling Zhou Yu in his prime, when Xiao Qiao had just married, his martial bearing was radiant.  
With feather fan and silk cap, in talk and laughter, warships turned to ashes.  
Dreaming of the old land, my sentiment should laugh at me for my early white hair.  
Life is like a dream; I raise a cup to the river moon."}

Sun Quan once ruled where gallant deeds took root.

Sunset on grass and trees, by lanes where Liu Yu dwelt,
Recall those days: golden spears, iron horses, a tiger’s might consuming a million miles.
Yuanjia’s rash campaign, sealing the wolf at Juxu, gained only a hurried retreat north.
Forty-three years pass, still vivid in sight—the fires along Yangzhou’s road.

故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。

West of the old fortress, they say—this is where Zhou Lang of the Three Kingdoms fought at Red Cliff.  
Rough rocks pierce the sky, surging billows crash against the shore, rolling up thousands of heaps of snow.  
The land lies as beautiful as a painting—how many heroic talents arose in that era!  

I recall the young Gongjin in his prime: just married to Xiao Qiao, with noble grace and vigorous spirit.  
In feather fan and silk cap, he laughed and talked—then the warships burned to ashes, vanishing like smoke.  

My spirit wanders through the ancient realm; the tender-hearted would surely laugh at me—already gray-haired too soon.  
The world is but a dream. I raise my cup, offering wine to the moon above the river."}

舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。

元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。

No trace of heroes—where is Sun Zhongmou?  
The pavilions and singing halls,  
All the elegance now beaten by rain and wind.  

Sunset among grass and trees,  
Ordinary lanes and alleys—  
They say Liu Yu once lived here.  
Recall those days:  
Iron horses and golden spears,  
Power to swallow ten thousand miles like a tiger.  

Yuanjia's reckless campaign,  
Seizing Mount Langjuxu,  
Only to flee in panic northward.  

Forty-three years—  
Still vivid in memory:  
The smoke of war across Yangzhou Road.  

How can I bear to look back—  
At the temple of Fuli,  
Where crows feast and drums ring in worship.  

Who dares ask—  
Old General Lianpo,  
Can he still eat?"}

{"source": {"title": "念奴娇·赤壁怀古", "author": "苏轼", "text": "大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。"}, "translation": "Ode to the Red Cliff, Remembering the Past  
By Su Shi

The great river flows eastward, waves washing away  
All the heroic figures of a thousand years.  
West of the old fortress, they say—  
Three Kingdoms’ Zhou Yu’s Red Cliff, where heroes rose.  

Rocks pierce the sky, thunderous tides crash on the shore,  
Whirlpools rise like thousands of heaps of snow.  
The land and rivers form a picture so bright—  
How many valiant spirits once graced that scene!  

I recall Gongjin in his prime:  
Young Qiao just married him, his spirit radiant, bold.  
With feather fan and silk cap, calm and wise,  
At his mere smile, warships turned to ash and smoke.  

Now, spirit wandering through the ancient realm,  
They’d surely laugh at me—so moved, my hair already gray.  
Life's but a dream; I raise my cup, pour wine to the moon above the river."}

{"source": {"title": "永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古", "author": "辛弃疾", "text": "千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？"}, "translation": "A thousand years of rivers and mountains,  
Where heroes once roamed—no trace remains of Sun Zhongmou.  
The dance pavilions, the singing halls,  
All are swept away by rain and wind, lost to time.  

Sunset glows on grass and trees,  
In common alleys where ordinary folk dwell—  
They say Li Tu lived here.  
Recalling those days,  
Golden spears, iron horses,  
A spirit that devoured ten thousand miles like a tiger.  

Yet Emperor Yuanjia’s campaign was hasty;  
He sought glory at Langjuxu,  
Only to flee in panic northward, heartbroken.  

Forty-three years have passed—  
In memory, I still see fires blazing on the road to Yangzhou.  

How unbearable to look back—  
At the temple of Buddha Li,  
Where crows cry and drums beat for the gods,  
A scene of chaos and noise.  

Who will ask—  
Is General Lianpo old?  
Can he still eat his meal?"}

{"source": {"title": "登高", "author": "杜甫", "text": "风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。"}, "translation": "Wind swift, sky high, gibbons wail with pain,  
Islets clear, sands white, birds wheel back again.  
Endless leaves rustle down with autumn's sigh,  
The Yangtze's tide rolls on, ceaseless and high.  
Ten thousand miles of sorrow, wanderer's plight,  
A hundred years of illness, climb this height.  
Hardship and bitter hate, hoarfrost on the hair,  
In decline, I've set the rough wine cup aside."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。

At Xunyang's riverhead, night I bade my guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reeds, autumn rustling low.
The host dismounted, guest aboard the boat,
Raising cups, no strings or pipes to flow.
Drunken, joy could not be found, sorrowful we part,
Mingling sea, the moon sinks deep in river's heart.

Suddenly, from river's face, pipa sounds arise,
Host forgets return, guest holds fast to boat.
Following the sound, I whisper who it is,
Pipa falls silent, words hesitating slow.
Draw near the boat, invite her to the light,
Add wine, adjust lamps, a feast anew ignite.

Thousands of calls, she finally appears,
Still holding pipa half-concealed by face.
Three or two plucks, the strings begin to stir,
Before the tune, emotion's in its grace.
Each muffled string, each sound, a thought profound,
As if to tell a lifetime of unmet ground.

Bowed head, fingers move, slowly, without pause,
Saying all heart's depths, a silent, endless stream.
Gently pluck, softly twist, stroke, and pluck again,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao" she would play.
Larger strings clash like sudden raindrops pour,
Smaller strings whisper soft as lovers' words.

Clash and whisper, interwoven, loud and clear,
Pearls and jade, a shower falling fast.
Oriole's song glides through blossoms, smooth and light,
Beneath ice, spring's flow struggles, scarce and slow.
Cold spring, strings stiffen, silence breaks the line,
Another hidden sorrow, bitter, deep, and twined.

At this stillness, louder than all sound,
Silver jar shatters, water gushes forth.
Steel cavalry charges, swords and spears now ring,
Four strings strike as one, like silk ripped apart.
East and west boats fall silent, no sound heard,
Only the river's heart, autumn moon, white, clear.

Musing, I place the plectrum in the strings,
Adjust my robe, face now solemn, calm, and straight.
"My home," she said, "beneath Toad's Hill I dwell,
At thirteen, pipa mastered, first in the Academy's grace.
After my song, even Shanzang bowed in awe,
My painted face, each time, the envy of Qiu Niang.
Five-Ling youths vied to lavish me with gold,
One song, countless red silks, a river uncontrolled.
Silver hairpins shattered with each rhythmic beat,
Crimson silk, stained with wine, my robes did wear.
Year after year, laughter, joy, and spring and autumn spent,
Until my brother joined the army, aunt passed on.

Days and nights pass, beauty fades, no more the gate,
Older, I wed a merchant, lost in his trade.
Merchants prize profit, parting they disdain,
Last month he went to Fuliang, bought tea, left me here.
He left, I guard the empty boat at river's mouth,
Moonlight circles, cold river water flows.

Deep in night, dreams of youth again return,
Awake, tears streak my painted face, red and wet.
Hearing your pipa, I sighed; hearing your tale, I sighed again.
We too are lost souls adrift on this earth, why need we knew before?
Since last year, I left the capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang.
Xunyang, remote, no music heard all year long.
Near Pien River, low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow,
What sounds do I hear day and night? Cuckoos bleeding, apes wailing.

In spring's river, flower dawn, autumn's moonlit night,
I often pour wine, alone, unshared, unpleased.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their rough tunes, harsh, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, like celestial music, my ears wake.
Do not refuse, sit again and play a tune;
I'll compose a Pipa Song for you.

Moved by your words, I stood long, then sat,
Strings now swift, sorrowful, not like before.
All seated wept anew, tears falling fast.
Who cried the most? The Governor of Jiangzhou,
His blue robe soaked with tears, wet to the bone."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At Xunyang’s riverbank, where I bade farewell at night,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn’s chill.  
I dismounted while guests remained aboard the boat,  
Raised the cup to drink, but no strings or flutes to cheer.  

Drunken joy could not mask the sorrow of parting,  
As the river, moonlight-blurred, swallowed the night.  
Sudden sound of the lute on the water stirred the air—  
Host forgot home, guest forgot to leave.  

Following the music, I softly asked who played,  
The lute fell silent, hesitant to speak.  
We drew the boat near, invited her to join us,  
Added wine, relit lamps, restored the feast.  

After many calls, she finally appeared,  
Still holding her lute, half-face concealed from view.  
She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times,  
Before the tune began, emotion filled the air.  

Each string, a suppressed note; each sound, a sorrowful thought—  
Like a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams, she spoke without words.  
Low brow, steady fingers, slowly moving,  
Conveying all her heart’s deep secrets in the music.  

Gentle touch, slow pluck, then sweep and pick,  
First *Feather Dress*, then *Sixth of the Moon* she played.  
The deep strings thundered like a sudden rain,  
The high strings whispered like a lover’s soft refrain.  

Thunder and whispers mingled, bright pearls on jade plate,  
A nightingale’s song through blossoms, smooth and clear.  
A stream choked beneath ice, struggling to flow,  
Cold springs, the strings grew stiff—then silence fell.  

Another sorrow, another hidden hate—  
In silence, more than sound, the heart’s lament.  
Like a silver vase shattering, water spurts forth,  
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears in the air.  

The song ended, final stroke across the strings—  
Four chords struck, as if silk tore apart.  
East and west boats silent, no word spoken,  
Only the autumn moon, white in the river’s heart.  

She paused, placed the lute back in its case,  
Adjusted her robe, composure regained.  
She said, “I was born in the capital city,  
Lived beneath Cricket Hill, my home.”  

“Thirteen years, I mastered the lute’s art,  
First in the Imperial Music Academy’s line.  
After my song, even Shan Cai bowed in awe,  
After my makeup, Qiu Niang grew jealous.”  

“Rich young men of the Five Hills vied to spend,  
One song brought red silk in heaps untold.  
Silver hairpins struck the beat, shattered in time,  
Crimson silk skirts stained with wine, turned red.”  

“This year’s laughter, next year’s joy, autumn moons and spring breezes pass by.  
Brother joined the army, auntie passed away—  
Days fade, her beauty gone, the door now empty,  
In old age, she married a merchant, left behind.”  

“Merchants love profit, parting easily,  
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
He left, she stays at the river’s mouth, empty boat,  
Moonlight bright, the river cold around her.”  

“Deep in the night, she dreams of youth’s time,  
Wakes to tears, makeup streaked red.  
Hearing her lute, I sighed; hearing her words, I sighed again.  
We’re both castaways on life’s vast sea—why need we have met before to know?”  

“Last year, I left the capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang,  
Xunyang’s remote, no music to be heard all year.  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, around my house they grow,  
In every dawn and dusk, what sounds do I hear?  
Cuckoos weep blood, apes cry out in the mountains.  
On spring’s river, flower mornings, autumn’s moonlit nights,  
I often pour wine alone, in silent rites.  
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes to hear?  
But their harsh sounds are music, barely bearable.”  

“Tonight, hearing your lute, my ears are filled with heaven’s tune.  
Do not refuse, sit again and play one more song—  
I’ll compose this ballad for you, as you have sung.”  

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,  
Then, sitting down, the strings grew tight, more fast.  
The sound was sadder now, not like before,  
All the audience wept, their faces hid in sorrow.  

Who wept the most? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou’s blue robe  
Was soaked with tears."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。

Maple and reed in autumn's silent sway.  
Host dismounts, guest remains aboard the boat,  
Raising wine cups, yet no music plays.  

Drunken, we cannot feast—sorrowful farewell—  
The river merges with the moon's pale gleam.  
Suddenly, pipa music from the water,  
Host forgets return, guest stays in dream.  

Seeking the sound, I ask in hushed tone,  
Pipa halts, silence lingers, words delay.  
Move our boats near, invite her forth to see,  
Add wine, relight lamps, feast anew display.  

Thousands of calls, she finally appears,  
Holding pipa, half her face concealed.  
Tuning the axis, plucking strings three times,  
Emotion speaks before the tune is sealed.  

Each string a muffled sigh, each note a thought,  
As if her life’s unfulfilled ambitions speak.  
Bowing head, fingers glide on strings,  
Pouring out all her heart’s unspoken grief.  

Gently stroke, slowly pluck, sweep and pick,  
First the Nai Chang, then the Liuyao’s strain.  
Thick strings rattle like sudden rain,  
Thin strings whisper soft as lovers’ pain.

Pearls and beads fall like jade plate ringing.  
Like nightingales through blossoms glide,  
Like stream beneath ice, choked and straining.

Pause—then silence reigns, deeper than sound.  
Another sorrow, hidden hate,  
In this stillness, louder than the ground.  

Silver bottle shatters, water gushes forth,  
Iron cavalry charges, blades clash loud.  
Finishing stroke, heart of the pipa,  
Four strings snap like tearing silk’s shroud.  

East and west boats, silent, all around,  
Only the autumn moon on river’s heart.  
Musing, she sets the pick aside,  
Adjusts her gown, composes her face.  

She says she’s from the capital city,  
Lives beneath the Toad’s Hill’s shade.  
Thirteen learned pipa, fame in first rank,  
In the Imperial Music Bureau’s parade.  

After each tune, Shancai would bow,  
Her makeup admired, yet Qiumiang envied.  
Five-Lin youth vied for her,  
Each song, a red silk robe, countless.  

Silver hairpins beat the rhythm, break,  
Crimson silk skirts stained with wine.  
Year’s laughter, next year’s joy,  
Autumn moons, spring breezes, all unheeded.  

Brother joined the army, aunt died,  
Morning to evening, face grows old.  
Front gate deserted, few horses pass,  
Old age, she married a merchant, cold.  

Merchant cares for profit, not farewells,

River cold, moon’s glow forevermore.

I’ve sighed at pipa’s sound,
